title: The Big Picture: How Software Reaches Users
text: The Big Picture: How Software Reaches Users You wrote code on your laptop and it works. Between that and a stranger using it at 3 a.m. there is a long chain: build, package, ship, run, expose, monitor. DevOps is the discipline of making that chain fast, repeatable and safe. The journey of a code change Developer laptop Git host CI server Registry/Storage ┌────────────┐ push ┌─────────┐ trigger ┌────────────┐ publish ┌───────────────┐ │ write code │───────▶│ GitHub │────────▶│ test+build │────────▶│ image/artifact│ └────────────┘ └─────────┘ └────────────┘ └───────┬───────┘ │ deploy (CD) Users ──▶ DNS ──▶ Load balancer ──▶ Reverse proxy ──▶ App servers ◀──────┘ │ Database / cache Logs + metrics ──▶ Monitoring ──▶ Alerts to humans Every box is a topic in this handbook. You'll learn them bottom-up: servers first, then automation on top. What "deployment" actually means Deploying is taking a version of your software and making it the thing that real users hit. Concretely that means: Get the code/artifact onto a machine (physical, virtual, or a container host) that is reachable from the internet. Install its runtime and dependencies (Node, JVM, Python, libraries). Supply configuration and secrets (DB URL, API keys) without baking them into code. Start the process and keep it running (restart on crash, on reboot). Route traffic to it (DNS, TLS certificate, reverse proxy). Verify it works, and be able to undo it if it doesn't. The core insight "It works on my machine" is the root problem DevOps solves. Your laptop and the server differ in OS, versions, config and data. Everything in this handbook — CI/CD, containers, IaC — exists to make environments identical, automated and reproducible . The eras of deploying Era How Pain Manual SSH in, git pull , restart Human error, no history, "snowflake" servers Scripted Bash / Capistrano scripts Scripts drift; works on one server only CI/CD Pipeline builds, tests, deploys on every push Pipelines must be maintained Containers Ship the app plus its environment Need orchestration at scale Orchestration + IaC + GitOps Declare desired state; the system converges to it Complexity; steep learning curve Roles and vocabulary Dev writes features; Ops keeps systems running. Historically they were separate teams with opposing incentives (change vs. stability). DevOps merges the responsibilities. SRE (Site Reliability Engineering): Google's take — treat operations as a software problem with measurable reliability targets. Platform engineering : build internal tooling so product developers can deploy themselves. How to read this handbook Follow the sidebar in order if you are new. Each lesson ends with things to try. Spin up a cheap VPS or use Docker locally — you learn deployment by deploying.

title: Environments: Dev, Staging, Production
text: Environments: Dev, Staging, Production An environment is a complete, isolated copy of "your system running somewhere": its own servers, database, config and secrets. Having more than one is how teams change software without gambling with real users. Why multiple environments exist Imagine you only have production. Every experiment, every half-finished feature, every database migration runs against real customer data. A typo in a migration drops a table and customers see errors. So you add a second place to try things first. Then you notice that place needs to resemble production or its results are meaningless. That tension, isolated enough to be safe, similar enough to be trustworthy , drives everything in this lesson. The classic trio Environment Purpose Who uses it Data Typical size Local / dev Write and debug code fast One developer Fake or seeded Laptop, Docker Compose CI / test Automated tests on every push The pipeline Created and destroyed per run Ephemeral containers Staging (pre-prod, UAT) Final rehearsal; QA, demos, load tests QA, product, the team Anonymised copy or synthetic Smaller than prod, same shape Production Serve real users Customers Real Full scale laptop ──push──▶ CI (tests) ──merge──▶ staging ──approve──▶ production fast feedback automated gate human/QA gate real users (seconds) (minutes) (minutes-hours) (careful) Environment parity The more staging differs from production, the less a green staging result tells you. The Twelve-Factor App calls this dev/prod parity . Differences that commonly bite: Different database engines. SQLite locally, PostgreSQL in production. SQL dialects, locking and JSON behaviour differ. Run the same engine and major version everywhere. Different OS or runtime versions. macOS laptop, Debian server, Node 18 vs 22. Containers fix most of this. Different topology. One staging server vs. three behind a load balancer in prod hides session, caching and race-condition bugs. Different data volume. A query that is instant on 100 rows takes minutes on 50 million. Different network. Prod sits behind HTTPS and a CDN; dev talks plain HTTP on localhost, so cookie flags and CORS issues only appear in prod. Parity is a spectrum, not a switch You rarely afford a full-size staging. Keep kind identical (same engines, versions, OS image, deploy method) and let scale differ (smaller instances, fewer replicas). Deploying to staging with the exact same pipeline and artifact as production is the single most valuable parity rule. Configuration per environment Code is the same everywhere; configuration is what differs: database URL, API keys, log level, feature flags, the public hostname. The rule: build once, configure at deploy time . If you rebuild per environment, what you tested is not what you shipped. Environment variables The simplest, most portable mechanism. Every language reads them and every platform (systemd, Docker, Kubernetes, PaaS) can set them. # Node const dbUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL; if (!dbUrl) throw new Error("DATABASE_URL is required"); # Python import os db_url = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"] # KeyError if missing = fail fast .env files # .env.development (committed is OK only if it holds NO secrets) DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:app@localhost:5432/app_dev LOG_LEVEL=debug # .env.production (NEVER commit; generated or injected by the platform) DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:S3cr3t@db.internal:5432/app LOG_LEVEL=info Add real .env files to .gitignore and commit a .env.example with dummy values so newcomers know which variables exist. What belongs where Kind Examples Where to keep it Non-secret config log level, feature toggles, timeouts Env vars, config files in the repo per environment Secrets DB passwords, API tokens, signing keys Secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), CI secret store; never in git or images Build-time constants public API base URL for a frontend Build variables (note: baked into the bundle, so not secret and not changeable without rebuild) Never branch on environment name in code if (env === "production") { ... } scattered through the code means production-only paths that are never tested in staging. Drive behaviour from named settings ( EMAIL_PROVIDER=smtp ) rather than "which environment am I". Data in non-production environments Synthetic/seed data : safe, reproducible, but may not exercise odd real-world shapes. Anonymised production snapshot : realistic. Must scrub emails, names, payment data; GDPR and similar laws still apply to copies. Automate the scrub, never copy raw prod data to a laptop. Isolation of side effects : staging must not send real emails, charge real cards or call production webhooks. Use sandbox keys (Stripe test mode), a mail catcher (Mailpit), and separate accounts. Promotion: one artifact, many environments commit abc123 ──▶ build ──▶ artifact app:abc123 ─┬─▶ deploy to staging (config: staging) └─▶ deploy to prod (config: production) same bytes, different config Tag artifacts with the commit SHA or a version, never "latest". Promoting means "deploy that exact tag to the next environment". Rollback is deploying the previous tag. Preview (ephemeral) environments A long-lived shared staging becomes a queue: "who is testing on staging?" Preview environments solve it by creating a throwaway environment per pull request with its own URL (e.g. pr-482.preview.example.com ), torn down on merge. Reviewers and designers click a link instead of checking out a branch. Platforms: Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages (frontends); Render, Fly.io, Railway; self-built with Kubernetes namespaces or Docker Compose plus a wildcard DNS/reverse proxy. Pitfalls: cost (auto-expire them), shared databases (give each preview its own schema or a seeded copy), and secrets exposure (never give previews production credentials, especially for PRs from forks). How many environments do you need? Team / product Reasonable setup Solo project Local + production (with CI tests). Preview deploys if available. Small team SaaS Local, CI, PR previews, production. Staging optional. Regulated / large Local, CI, dev, QA, staging, production, plus a DR region. More environments mean more cost and more drift. Add one only when it removes a real risk. Pitfalls Config drift : someone hand-edits a staging server. Fix: manage config as code (later: IaC). Staging used as a dumping ground : multiple half-merged features make results meaningless. Secrets copy-pasted between environments : a staging leak becomes a production breach. Use distinct credentials per environment. "Test in prod" fear : some testing in production is healthy (feature flags, canaries, synthetic checks) when done deliberately. Later lessons cover it. Try it Take any small app and read all its config from environment variables. Make it crash at startup with a clear message when one is missing. Create .env.example , add .env to .gitignore , and run the app with set -a; source .env; set +a; node app.js (or your language equivalent). List every difference between your laptop and what you imagine production to be (OS, versions, DB, network). Which would you eliminate first?

title: The Request Lifecycle
text: The Request Lifecycle What really happens between typing a URL and seeing a page? Knowing every hop tells you where to look when something breaks, and which DevOps tool lives at which hop. Why this matters "The site is down" can mean DNS is wrong, a certificate expired, the load balancer has no healthy backends, the app crashed, or the database is out of connections. Each has a different symptom and a different owner. A mental model of the path lets you bisect: where does the request stop? The full path Browser │ 1. DNS lookup: app.example.com ─▶ 203.0.113.10 │ 2. TCP connect to port 443 │ 3. TLS handshake (certificate check) ▼ CDN / edge ──(cache hit? return)──────────────────────────┐ │ miss │ ▼ │ Load balancer ─ health checks ─▶ picks a healthy backend │ ▼ │ Reverse proxy (nginx/Caddy): TLS termination, routing │ ▼ │ App server (Node/Java/Python): business logic │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ Cache (Redis) Database (PostgreSQL) │ └──────────── response travels back up ◀────────────────┘ Step by step 1. DNS: name to address Computers route by IP, humans type names. The browser asks a resolver (usually your ISP's or 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8), which walks root, .com , then the domain's authoritative nameserver. Answers are cached for the record's TTL. Pitfall: lowering a record's TTL after you need a change is too late, so lower it before migrations. dig +short app.example.com # the A record dig app.example.com +trace # watch the delegation chain curl -v https://app.example.com 2>&1 | head -30 # connect, TLS, headers 2. TCP and TLS The client opens a TCP connection to port 443 (HTTP is 80), then performs the TLS handshake: the server presents a certificate, the client verifies it was issued by a trusted authority for that hostname and not expired, and both derive session keys. Expired certificates are one of the most common production outages. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP but the idea is the same. 3. CDN and edge Static assets and cacheable responses can be served from a node near the user (Cloudflare, CloudFront, Fastly), never reaching your servers. It lowers latency and absorbs traffic spikes and attacks. 4. Load balancer Spreads requests across several identical backends and removes unhealthy ones (via health checks like GET /healthz ). This is how you scale horizontally and deploy with no downtime. 5. Reverse proxy nginx, Caddy, Traefik or HAProxy sits in front of apps: terminates TLS, routes by host/path ( /api to service A, / to service B), compresses, rate-limits, adds headers. Your app listens on a private port (3000) and never faces the internet directly. 6. The application Your code parses the request, authenticates, runs logic, and talks to backing services. Most time is usually spent waiting on I/O, not computing. 7. Data layer Typically a relational database, often fronted by a cache. Databases are the hardest tier to scale and to change safely, because they hold state. 8. The response A status code (200, 301, 404, 500, 503) and body flow back. Each layer can modify or replace it: a proxy returns 502 Bad Gateway when the app is down, a load balancer 503 when no backend is healthy, a gateway 504 on timeout. Symptom Likely layer "Server not found" DNS Connection timed out/refused Firewall, nothing listening, load balancer Certificate warning TLS (expired, wrong host) 502 Bad Gateway Proxy reached nothing/invalid reply from app 503 Service Unavailable No healthy backends or app overloaded 504 Gateway Timeout App or DB too slow 500 Internal Server Error Application bug (check logs) Architectures: how the app tier is organised Tiers A 3-tier design separates presentation (frontend), logic (API) and data (database). Each tier can be scaled and secured independently; the database sits in a private network unreachable from the internet. Monolith vs microservices Monolith Microservices Shape One deployable containing everything Many small services, each owning its data Deploy Simple: one artifact Many pipelines, versioning between services Scaling Scale the whole thing Scale only hot services Failure One bug can take down all Isolation, but cascading failures over the network Debugging One stack trace Need distributed tracing Team fit Small teams Many teams needing autonomy Start with a well-structured monolith Microservices trade code complexity for operational complexity. Most products should split only when team size or scaling pain demands it. A "modular monolith" keeps the option open. Stateless vs stateful A stateless process keeps nothing between requests that another instance couldn't reconstruct. Any request can go to any instance, so you can add, kill and replace instances freely. That property is what makes load balancing, autoscaling, rolling deploys and containers easy. State still exists, so push it to dedicated places: State Where it lives User sessions Signed cookie/JWT, or Redis Uploaded files Object storage (S3), not local disk Business data Database Background work Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ, Redis) The local-disk trap An app that saves uploads to ./uploads works on one server and silently breaks behind a load balancer: the next request lands on a server without the file. Treat the app's filesystem as disposable. Synchronous vs asynchronous Slow work (sending email, resizing images) should not block the response. Put a message on a queue, return 202 Accepted , and let a worker process it. Workers are separate processes you must also deploy and monitor. Where DevOps tools plug in Hop Topic in this handbook DNS, TLS, proxy, LB, CDN Networking section App process, systemd Linux, Deploy Packaging the app Containers Running many copies Kubernetes, Cloud Seeing what happened Observability Try it Run curl -v https://example.com and identify: the resolved IP, TLS version, certificate subject, status line, and headers. Run dig +trace example.com and name each server in the chain. Use browser DevTools (Network tab) on a site you like. Which requests came from a CDN? (Look for cf-cache-status , x-cache , age headers.) Draw your own app's path from browser to database. Mark which parts are stateful.

title: DevOps Culture, History and Metrics
text: DevOps Culture, History and Metrics DevOps is first a way of working and only second a toolset. Understanding the problem it grew out of explains why every tool in this handbook looks the way it does. The problem: the wall of confusion In traditional organisations, developers were rewarded for shipping features and operations for keeping systems stable. Those goals conflict: every change risks stability. So developers "threw code over the wall", operations resisted change with approval boards and quarterly release windows, and releases became rare, huge and terrifying. Large releases contain many changes, so failures are hard to diagnose, which reinforces the fear. A vicious cycle. Dev: "ship features" ──code──▶ ║WALL║ ──▶ Ops: "never break prod" ◀── "it works on my machine" / "your code is broken" ── A short history Year Milestone 2001 Agile Manifesto: iterate quickly with customers (but ops stayed slow) 2006 AWS launches EC2: servers become an API call 2009 Flickr's "10+ deploys per day" talk; Patrick Debois organises the first DevOpsDays 2010 "Continuous Delivery" book by Humble and Farley 2013 Docker released; "The Phoenix Project" popularises the ideas 2014-15 Kubernetes open-sourced; Terraform; Google's SRE concepts reach the public 2016 "Site Reliability Engineering" book; DORA research begins annual reports 2018+ GitOps, DevSecOps, platform engineering 2020s Internal developer platforms, supply-chain security (SBOMs, signing), AI-assisted operations CALMS: the framework Letter Meaning In practice C ulture Shared ownership, blameless learning "You build it, you run it"; on-call for developers; blameless postmortems A utomation Automate repetitive, error-prone work CI/CD, IaC, automated tests and rollbacks L ean Small batches, limit work in progress Small PRs, frequent releases, remove waiting time M easurement Decide with data DORA metrics, SLOs, dashboards S haring Knowledge flows across teams Runbooks, documentation, shared tooling, demos The Three Ways (from The Phoenix Project) Flow : speed work from left (idea) to right (production). Smaller batches, automation, fewer hand-offs. Feedback : fast, amplified feedback from right to left. Monitoring, tests, alerts, user data. Continual learning : experiment, tolerate failure, practise recovery. Measuring it: DORA metrics The DevOps Research and Assessment programme (now part of Google Cloud) has surveyed tens of thousands of teams for a decade. It found four measures that correlate with both delivery speed and organisational performance, and, crucially, speed and stability are not a trade-off: high performers have both. Metric Question Kind Deployment frequency How often do we ship to production? Throughput Lead time for changes Commit to running in production: how long? Throughput Change failure rate What percent of deploys cause a failure needing remediation? Stability Failed deployment recovery time (formerly MTTR) How fast do we restore service after a bad change? Stability Recent reports also emphasise reliability and team well-being. Elite teams typically deploy on demand (many times per day), with lead times under a day, low failure rates and recovery within an hour. Metrics are a mirror, not a target Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure. Do not rank developers by deploy count. Use DORA to find bottlenecks in the system . Why CI/CD adoption matters Small batches reduce risk. A deploy of 3 commits is easy to reason about and revert; a deploy of 3 months of work is not. Feedback in minutes. A failing test found 5 minutes after the commit costs far less than a bug found by customers weeks later. Repeatability. The pipeline does the same steps every time; no forgotten step at 6 p.m. on Friday. Deploys become boring. The goal is that releasing is a non-event, so teams release more, learn faster, and recover faster. Auditability. Every production change maps to a commit, a review and a pipeline run. SRE: reliability as engineering Site Reliability Engineering, born at Google, applies software engineering to operations. If DevOps is the philosophy, SRE is one concrete implementation ("class SRE implements DevOps"). Key ideas: SLI (indicator): a measurement, e.g. fraction of requests under 300 ms and non-5xx. SLO (objective): the target, e.g. 99.9% over 30 days. Error budget : 100% minus SLO. At 99.9% you may "spend" ~43 minutes of badness a month. Budget left? Ship faster. Budget exhausted? Freeze features and fix reliability. This turns the dev vs ops argument into data. Toil : manual, repetitive, automatable work. Cap it (Google suggests under 50%) and automate the rest. Blameless postmortems : ask "how did the system allow this?" not "who did this?". People who fear blame hide information. DevSecOps: security shifted left Security reviews at the end of a project find problems when they are most expensive to fix. DevSecOps moves checks into the pipeline so every commit is scanned: Stage Check Commit Secret scanning (gitleaks), pre-commit hooks Build Dependency scanning (Dependabot, npm audit ), SAST (static analysis) Package Container image scanning (Trivy), SBOM, signing Deploy Policy-as-code, least-privilege credentials Run Runtime monitoring, patching, DAST Platform engineering: the current trend As toolchains grew (Kubernetes, Terraform, observability), asking every product developer to master all of it caused cognitive overload. Platform teams build an internal developer platform with "golden paths": opinionated, self-service templates ("create a service", "get a database") so developers get safe defaults without becoming infrastructure experts. The product is the platform; the customers are your developers. Common anti-patterns The DevOps team. Renaming the ops team "DevOps" and keeping the wall. DevOps is shared responsibility, not a job silo (platform/SRE teams are fine when they enable, not gatekeep). Tool-first adoption. Buying Kubernetes before having automated tests. Ticket-driven infrastructure. If developers wait days for a server, automate self-service. Hero culture. One person who "just knows" how prod works. Write runbooks and automate. Try it Estimate your team's four DORA metrics from git history and deploy logs. Which is worst? Compute the monthly downtime allowed by 99%, 99.9% and 99.99% (hint: 30 days is 43,200 minutes). Write a five-line blameless summary of the last outage you remember: timeline, contributing factors (not people), one fix.

title: Glossary A to Z
text: Glossary A to Z Terms you will meet across this handbook, in plain language. Skim it now, return when a word trips you up. Term Meaning A record DNS record mapping a hostname to an IPv4 address (AAAA for IPv6). Ansible Agentless configuration-management tool that applies YAML "playbooks" over SSH. API gateway Single entry point that routes, authenticates and rate-limits calls to backend services. Artifact The build output you deploy: a binary, JAR, zip, or container image. Autoscaling Automatically adding or removing instances based on load. Availability zone (AZ) An isolated data centre (or group) within a cloud region; spread across AZs for resilience. Backup A copy of data that lets you restore after loss. Untested backups are hopes, not backups. Bastion host Hardened server used as the single SSH entry point into a private network. Blue-green deployment Run old (blue) and new (green) versions side by side, then switch traffic at once. Branch Independent line of development in Git. Build Compiling/bundling source into a deployable artifact. Cache Fast storage of previously computed results (Redis, CDN, browser). Canary release Send a small share of traffic to the new version first, watch, then expand. CDN Content Delivery Network: edge servers caching content near users. CI (continuous integration) Merging often and automatically building and testing every change. CD (delivery / deployment) Delivery: every change is releasable. Deployment: every passing change is released automatically. CIDR Notation for IP ranges, e.g. 10.0.0.0/16 . Cluster A group of machines managed together (e.g. a Kubernetes cluster). CNAME DNS alias pointing one name to another name. Config management Keeping servers in a declared state (Ansible, Puppet, Chef). Container Isolated process with its own filesystem view, sharing the host kernel. Cron Unix scheduler that runs commands at set times. Daemon Background process, usually a service. Deployment Releasing a version to an environment; also a Kubernetes object managing replicas. DevSecOps Integrating security checks throughout the pipeline. Disaster recovery (DR) Plan and capability to restore service after a major failure. DNS Domain Name System: translates names to IP addresses. Docker Tooling for building and running containers. Dockerfile Recipe describing how to build a container image. DORA metrics Four delivery metrics: deploy frequency, lead time, change failure rate, recovery time. Egress / ingress Traffic leaving / entering a network. In Kubernetes, Ingress routes external HTTP to services. Environment An isolated deployment of the system (dev, staging, production). Environment variable Named value passed to a process, used for configuration. Error budget Allowed unreliability implied by an SLO (100% minus SLO). Firewall Rules that allow or block network traffic (ufw, security groups). Feature flag Runtime switch that enables code paths without redeploying. GitOps Git is the source of truth for desired state; an agent applies it (Argo CD, Flux). Health check Endpoint or probe that tells a load balancer or orchestrator whether an instance is OK. Helm Package manager for Kubernetes manifests (charts). Horizontal scaling Adding more instances (vs vertical: a bigger instance). HTTP / HTTPS Web protocol; HTTPS adds TLS encryption. IaaS / PaaS / SaaS Rent infrastructure / a platform to run apps / finished software. IaC Infrastructure as Code: defining infrastructure in version-controlled files. IAM Identity and Access Management: who can do what in a cloud account. Idempotent Running an operation many times yields the same result as once. Essential for automation. Image Immutable template from which containers (or VMs) are started. Immutable infrastructure Replace servers with new versions instead of modifying them in place. Incident An event degrading service that needs response. Ingress controller Component implementing Kubernetes Ingress rules (nginx, Traefik). JWT JSON Web Token: signed token carrying identity claims. Kubernetes (K8s) Orchestrator that schedules and heals containers across machines. Latency Time for a request to complete. Load balancer Distributes traffic across backends. Log Timestamped record of events emitted by software. Metric Numeric measurement over time (CPU, requests/sec). Microservices Architecture of small, independently deployable services. Migration (database) Versioned change to a database schema. Monitoring / observability Collecting signals (logs, metrics, traces) to understand system behaviour. Namespace Logical partition (Kubernetes namespaces; Linux kernel namespaces for containers). nginx Popular web server and reverse proxy. On-call Rotation of people who respond to alerts. Orchestration Automated placement, scaling and healing of workloads. Pipeline Automated sequence of stages (build, test, deploy). Pod Smallest Kubernetes unit: one or more containers sharing network and storage. Port Number identifying a service on a host (22 SSH, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS). Postmortem Blameless write-up of an incident and follow-up actions. Provisioning Creating infrastructure (servers, networks, databases). Pull request (PR/MR) Proposal to merge a branch, reviewed and checked by CI. Registry Storage for container images or packages (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR). Replica One of several identical copies of a workload. Reverse proxy Server in front of apps that forwards client requests to them. Rollback Returning to a previous known-good version. Rolling update Replace instances gradually so service stays up. Runbook Step-by-step guide for an operational task or alert. Secret Sensitive value (password, key, token) that must be stored and rotated carefully. Security group Cloud-level virtual firewall attached to instances. Service mesh Infrastructure layer handling service-to-service traffic, mTLS and telemetry (Istio, Linkerd). SLA / SLO / SLI Contractual promise / internal target / the measurement. SRE Site Reliability Engineering: operations approached with software engineering. SSH Secure Shell: encrypted remote login and tunnelling. Stateless Keeps no per-client data between requests; easy to scale. Systemd Linux init system and service manager. Terraform Declarative IaC tool for provisioning cloud resources (OpenTofu is the open fork). Throughput Work completed per unit time. TLS Transport Layer Security: encryption and identity for connections. Toil Manual, repetitive operational work that could be automated. Trace Record of one request's path through multiple services. TTL Time to live: how long a DNS answer or cache entry stays valid. VPC Virtual Private Cloud: your private network in a cloud provider. VPS Virtual Private Server: a rented virtual machine. Volume Persistent storage attached to a container or VM. Webhook HTTP callback one system sends to another when an event happens. YAML Indentation-based data format used by CI, Kubernetes and Ansible. Zero downtime Deploying without users seeing errors or outages. Acronym habit When you meet a new acronym, expand it once in your notes. Most DevOps jargon is a simple idea with an intimidating name. Try it Pick ten terms you could not define before and explain each aloud in one sentence. Group the terms into the 12 handbook sections. Which section has the most unfamiliar vocabulary for you? Start there.

title: What Is a Server?
text: What Is a Server? A server is just a computer that runs a program waiting for requests, usually with no screen or keyboard, always on, reachable over a network. There is no magic: everything you do on a server is something you can do on a Linux laptop. Why servers, and why Linux Your laptop sleeps, changes networks and sits behind your home router. A server has a stable public IP address, runs 24/7 in a data centre with redundant power and networking, and is administered remotely. Roughly 90%+ of public cloud workloads and nearly all containers run Linux: it is free, scriptable, stable, secure and the target every tool in this handbook assumes. Learning it is the foundation of everything else. Kinds of servers Type What it is Pros Cons Bare metal A whole physical machine (yours or rented) Max performance, no neighbours Slow to provision, you manage hardware Virtual machine A slice of a physical host with its own kernel Strong isolation, any OS Some overhead VPS A rented VM with fixed monthly price (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Linode/Akamai, Vultr) Cheap ($4-10/mo), simple Manual scaling, you secure it Cloud instance VM from a hyperscaler (AWS EC2, GCP Compute Engine, Azure VM), billed per second API-driven, huge ecosystem Pricing and IAM complexity Container host / serverless You supply code or an image; the provider runs it No server to patch Less control, platform lock-in Bare metal Virtual machines Containers ┌──────────┐ ┌─────┐┌─────┐┌─────┐ ┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐ │ OS │ │ App ││ App ││ App │ │App ││App ││App │ │ │ │ OS ││ OS ││ OS │ └────┘└────┘└────┘ │ hardware │ └─────┘└─────┘└─────┘ ┌──────────────────┐ └──────────┘ ┌────────────────────┐ │ one host OS kernel│ │ hypervisor + hardware│ └──────────────────┘ └────────────────────┘ Choosing a distribution A distro bundles the Linux kernel with a package manager and defaults. For servers, pick something boring and widely documented. Distro Family Package tool Notes Ubuntu Server LTS (24.04, 26.04) Debian apt Best default for learners; biggest tutorial base; 5 years support per LTS Debian Debian apt Very stable, minimal Rocky / AlmaLinux RHEL dnf Free RHEL-compatible; common in enterprises Fedora Server RHEL upstream dnf Newer packages, short lifecycle Alpine Independent apk Tiny; popular for container images (uses musl libc) Recommendation Use the latest Ubuntu LTS for this handbook. Always choose an LTS (long-term support) release for servers so you get security patches for years without forced upgrades. Commands for Rocky/Alma are noted where they differ. Sizing a first server 1 vCPU and 1-2 GB RAM runs a small Node/Python app plus nginx fine. A database plus app wants 2-4 GB. Pick a region near your users. Pick SSD/NVMe disk. 25 GB is plenty to learn. Check bandwidth/traffic allowance and whether snapshots/backups cost extra. Getting your first VPS Create an account with a provider (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Vultr, Linode, or an AWS Lightsail/EC2 free tier). Generate an SSH key on your laptop before creating the server (next lesson covers SSH deeply): ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@laptop" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub # paste this PUBLIC key into the provider's form Create the server: choose Ubuntu LTS, a small plan, your region, and select your SSH key. Prefer key auth over a root password. Note the public IPv4 address the provider displays. Connecting ssh root@203.0.113.10 # first login (some providers use "ubuntu" or "debian") # The authenticity prompt appears once: # "The authenticity of host ... can't be established. ED25519 key fingerprint is SHA256:..." # Type "yes" to trust it; it's stored in ~/.ssh/known_hosts. You are now typing commands on a computer in a data centre. Verify: hostnamectl # hostname, OS, kernel, virtualization type cat /etc/os-release # distro and version uname -r # kernel version nproc; free -h; df -h # CPUs, memory, disk ip -br addr # network interfaces and IPs uptime # how long running, load averages First 10 minutes on a new server A fresh public server is scanned by bots within minutes. Do this immediately: # 1. Update everything apt update && apt upgrade -y # 2. Create a normal user with sudo rights adduser deploy usermod -aG sudo deploy # 3. Install your key for that user rsync --archive --chown=deploy:deploy ~/.ssh /home/deploy # 4. Test login in a SECOND terminal before closing the first ssh deploy@203.0.113.10 sudo whoami # should print "root" # 5. Enable a firewall allowing SSH (and web later) sudo ufw allow OpenSSH sudo ufw allow 80,443/tcp sudo ufw enable sudo ufw status Do not lock yourself out Enable the firewall only after allowing SSH, and keep your existing session open while testing a new login. If you do get locked out, providers offer a web console and rescue mode. The SSH lesson covers disabling root and password logins. Pets vs cattle A hand-configured server you nurse and fear to reboot is a pet . Servers that are created from a script, interchangeable, and replaced rather than repaired are cattle . This handbook starts with a pet to learn the mechanics, then moves toward cattle with scripts, containers and infrastructure as code. Keep notes of every command you run; those notes are your future automation. Cost hygiene Servers bill while they exist, even if idle. Delete what you no longer use. Set a billing alert on cloud accounts, especially AWS/GCP. Snapshots and unattached volumes and IPs also cost money. Try it Create the cheapest Ubuntu LTS VPS you can, with your SSH key. SSH in and run the verification commands above; write down the kernel version, RAM and disk size. Do the "first 10 minutes" steps: new user, key, firewall. No spare money? Install Multipass ( multipass launch --name lab ) or Vagrant/UTM to get a local Ubuntu VM and follow along identically.

title: Shell Essentials
text: Shell Essentials On a server there is usually no GUI. The shell is how you inspect, change and automate everything. A small set of commands and the idea of pipes cover 90% of daily work. Why the command line GUIs are great for one-off tasks but cannot be scripted, version-controlled, repeated on 50 servers, or used over a slow SSH link. Every command you type is also something you can paste into a script, a Dockerfile or a CI job. The shell is the common language of DevOps. Shell, terminal, bash Terminal : the window. Shell : the program interpreting your commands (bash on most servers, zsh on macOS, sh/dash for minimal scripts). The prompt deploy@web1:~$ means user deploy on host web1 in the home directory ( ~ ); $ means normal user, # means root. Command anatomy: command [options] [arguments] , e.g. ls -l /var/log . Navigating and looking around pwd # where am I? ls # list files ls -lah # long format, hidden files, human sizes cd /var/log # absolute path cd .. # up one level cd ~ # home (or just: cd) cd - # back to previous directory tree -L 2 /etc/nginx # directory tree (apt install tree) file /bin/ls # what kind of file is this? stat app.log # size, owner, permissions, timestamps Working with files mkdir -p app/releases/v1 # -p creates parents, no error if exists touch notes.txt # create empty file / update timestamp cp config.yml config.yml.bak # copy cp -r src/ backup/ # copy directory recursively mv old.txt new.txt # rename OR move rm file.txt # delete (no trash can!) rm -r olddir/ # delete directory recursively ln -s /opt/app/releases/v2 /opt/app/current # symbolic link rm has no undo Never run rm -rf with a variable you have not checked: rm -rf "$DIR/" with DIR empty becomes rm -rf / . Modern GNU rm refuses / , but not /* or a wrongly-set path. Use ls with the same argument first, and quote variables. Reading and searching cat file.txt # print whole file less /var/log/syslog # page through (q quit, / search, G end, F follow) head -n 20 file # first 20 lines tail -n 50 file # last 50 lines tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log # follow new lines live (Ctrl+C to stop) wc -l file # count lines grep "error" app.log # lines containing "error" grep -i -n "timeout" app.log # case-insensitive, with line numbers grep -r "DATABASE_URL" /etc/myapp # recursive search grep -v "healthz" access.log # invert: lines NOT matching find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime -1 # modified in last day find . -type f -size +100M # big files rg "pattern" # ripgrep: faster grep (apt install ripgrep) Pipes and redirection: the superpower Every program has three streams: stdin (0), stdout (1), stderr (2). The shell lets you wire them together. Small tools doing one thing, composed with pipes, is the Unix philosophy. command > out.txt # stdout to file (overwrite) command >> out.txt # append command 2> err.txt # stderr to file command > all.txt 2>&1 # both to the same file command &> all.txt # bash shorthand for the same command > /dev/null 2>&1 # discard everything command1 | command2 # stdout of 1 becomes stdin of 2 command < input.txt # file as stdin A realistic pipeline: top 5 client IPs hitting nginx. awk '{print $1}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -5 # 1. take field 1 (IP) 2. group 3. count 4. numeric desc 5. top 5 Tool Use sort , uniq Order and deduplicate/count lines cut -d, -f2 Extract a column by delimiter awk Field-based processing and arithmetic sed 's/old/new/g' Stream find/replace xargs Turn stdin lines into command arguments tee file Write stdin to file and still pass it on jq Query and reshape JSON (essential for APIs) curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/torvalds/linux | jq '.stargazers_count' echo "deploy ok" | sudo tee -a /var/log/deploys.log # append with sudo (redirection ignores sudo!) Variables, quoting and exit codes NAME="web server" # no spaces around = echo "$NAME" # double quotes: variable expands echo '$NAME' # single quotes: literal export APP_ENV=production # visible to child processes echo "$HOME $USER $PATH" today=$(date +%F) # command substitution echo "Backup-$today.tar.gz" ls /nonexistent; echo $? # $? = exit code of last command: 0 = success, nonzero = failure mkdir build && cd build # run second only if first succeeded cmd || echo "failed" # run second only if first failed cmd1; cmd2 # run both regardless Exit codes are the glue of automation: CI jobs, cron and deploy scripts all decide success by them. Productivity shortcuts Keys Effect Tab Autocomplete paths and commands (press twice for options) Ctrl+R Reverse search history Ctrl+C / Ctrl+D Interrupt / end of input (logout) Ctrl+A / Ctrl+E Start / end of line Ctrl+L Clear screen !! Repeat last command ( sudo !! is a classic) Alt+. Insert last argument of previous command Also useful: man ls or ls --help for docs; tldr tar for friendly examples; which node and type cmd to see what will run; history | grep ssh ; alias ll='ls -lah' in ~/.bashrc . Running things in the background long_task & # run in background of this shell jobs # list fg %1 # bring to foreground nohup ./task.sh & # survive logout (output to nohup.out) tmux new -s work # better: a persistent session; detach with Ctrl+B then D tmux attach -t work # come back after SSH dropped Use tmux on servers If your SSH connection drops mid-upgrade, a plain shell kills the job. Inside tmux it keeps running and you reattach later. Pitfalls Unquoted variables with spaces split into several arguments. Quote: "$file" . sudo cmd > /root/file : the redirect is done by your shell, not sudo. Use tee . Copy-pasting commands from the web without reading them, especially curl ... | sudo bash . Download, inspect, then run. Smart quotes from documents break commands. Plain " and ' only. Try it In a scratch directory create 5 files with touch f{1..5}.log , then list, rename one, and delete the rest with a single rm . Generate some data: seq 1 1000 | shuf | head -20 | sort -n . Explain each stage. Find the five largest directories under /var : sudo du -h --max-depth=2 /var 2>/dev/null | sort -hr | head -5 . Start tmux , run ping 1.1.1.1 , detach, close the terminal, reconnect and reattach.

title: Filesystem and Permissions
text: Filesystem and Permissions Linux treats almost everything as a file and controls access with a simple owner/group/other permission model. Most "permission denied" errors, and a large share of security incidents, trace back to this lesson. The filesystem hierarchy Linux has one tree rooted at / (no drive letters). The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) says what lives where, so you always know where to look. / ├── bin, sbin, lib ─ essential programs/libs (often symlinks into /usr) ├── etc/ ─ system-wide configuration (text files) ├── home/alice ─ users' personal files ├── root/ ─ root's home ├── var/ │ ├── log/ ─ logs │ ├── lib/ ─ persistent app state (databases, docker) │ └── www/ ─ conventional web content ├── opt/ ─ self-contained third-party software ├── srv/ ─ data served by this host ├── usr/ ─ installed programs (usr/bin, usr/local) ├── tmp/ ─ temporary files (cleared on reboot) ├── dev/ ─ device files (/dev/null, /dev/sda) ├── proc, sys/ ─ virtual: kernel and process info └── run/ ─ runtime data (PID files, sockets) Path What you do there /etc Edit configs: /etc/nginx/ , /etc/ssh/sshd_config , /etc/systemd/system/ /var/log Read logs /var/lib Data that must survive (back it up) /opt or /srv Put your deployed app, e.g. /opt/myapp /tmp Scratch; never store anything important /proc cat /proc/cpuinfo , /proc/meminfo : live kernel info Disks and mounts df -h # free space per mounted filesystem lsblk # block devices and mount points mount | column -t # what is mounted where du -sh /var/* # size of each directory cat /etc/fstab # filesystems mounted at boot Adding a disk means formatting ( mkfs.ext4 ), mounting it at a directory ( mount /dev/sdb1 /data ) and adding it to /etc/fstab (use the UUID from blkid ) to persist across reboots. Running out of space, or of inodes ( df -i ), is a classic outage. Users and groups Every process and file belongs to a user (a number, the UID) and a group (GID). root (UID 0) bypasses all permission checks. Service accounts ( www-data , postgres ) exist so each daemon runs with minimal privileges: if nginx is compromised, the attacker is not root. whoami; id # uid=1000(deploy) gid=1000(deploy) groups=1000(deploy),27(sudo) cat /etc/passwd # user list (name:x:uid:gid:comment:home:shell) cat /etc/group # groups getent passwd deploy sudo adduser alice # interactive, creates home (Debian/Ubuntu) sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash bob # low-level, portable sudo usermod -aG docker alice # ADD to group (-a is crucial; without it groups are replaced) sudo passwd -l bob # lock the password sudo userdel -r bob # delete user and home sudo useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin myapp # service account Group membership needs a new login After usermod -aG docker alice , alice must log out and in (or newgrp docker ). Also note: membership in docker is effectively root access. Reading permissions $ ls -l -rwxr-xr-- 1 deploy www-data 4096 Oct 5 10:12 deploy.sh drwxr-x--- 2 deploy deploy 4096 Oct 5 10:10 secrets lrwxrwxrwx 1 deploy deploy 18 Oct 5 10:11 current -> releases/v2 - rwx r-x r-- deploy www-data │ │ │ │ │ └─ group owner │ │ │ │ └─ user owner │ │ │ └─ other (everyone else): r-- │ │ └─ group: r-x │ └─ user (owner): rwx └─ type: - file, d directory, l symlink Bit On a file On a directory Octal r read contents list names 4 w modify create/delete/rename entries 2 x execute enter ( cd ) and access items 1 Add digits per class: rwx = 7, r-x = 5, r-- = 4. So rwxr-xr-- is 754 . Changing permissions and ownership chmod 755 deploy.sh # rwxr-xr-x scripts, directories chmod 644 index.html # rw-r--r-- normal files chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 # rw------- private keys (ssh insists) chmod 700 ~/.ssh # rwx------ chmod +x script.sh # symbolic: add execute chmod u+w,g-w,o-rwx file # user add write, group remove write, other remove all chmod -R 750 /opt/myapp # recursive (careful!) sudo chown deploy:www-data /opt/myapp -R # owner and group sudo chgrp www-data /var/www/site Mode Typical use 600 Private keys, secret env files 640 Config readable by a service group 644 Public files, most configs 700 / 750 Private / group-shared directories 755 Executables, public dirs 777 Almost never. Anyone can modify. A symptom of not understanding the real problem. Never chmod 777 to "fix" it When you hit "permission denied", find out who is running the process ( ps -o user,cmd -p PID ) and give that user or its group the minimal access needed. Check every directory on the path: you need x on each parent. namei -l /path/to/file shows the permissions along the entire path. Special bits and umask setuid ( 4755 ): executable runs as its owner (how sudo and passwd work). Audit with find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null . setgid on a directory ( 2775 ): new files inherit the directory's group; great for shared project folders. sticky bit ( 1777 , as on /tmp ): users can delete only their own files. umask : default mask subtracted from new files; 022 gives 644 files / 755 dirs, 077 gives private. ACLs ( setfacl -m u:alice:rx dir ) provide per-user rules beyond owner/group/other. sudo: controlled root Logging in as root is dangerous: no audit trail of who did what, and a typo has no guardrail. sudo runs one command with root rights, after your own password, and logs it ( /var/log/auth.log or the journal). sudo apt update # one command as root sudo -i # root shell (use sparingly) sudo -u postgres psql # run as another user sudo -l # what may I run? sudo visudo # safely edit /etc/sudoers (syntax-checked) sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/deploy # /etc/sudoers.d/deploy : let the deploy user restart only one service, no password deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart myapp, /bin/systemctl status myapp Principle of least privilege: give people and services only what they need. Automation users get narrow sudo rules, not blanket NOPASSWD: ALL . Putting it together: a deploy directory sudo useradd --system --home /opt/myapp --shell /usr/sbin/nologin myapp sudo mkdir -p /opt/myapp/releases /etc/myapp sudo chown -R deploy:myapp /opt/myapp # deployer owns, app group reads sudo chmod -R 750 /opt/myapp sudo chmod 2770 /opt/myapp/releases # setgid: new releases keep group myapp echo 'DATABASE_URL=...' | sudo tee /etc/myapp/env >/dev/null sudo chown root:myapp /etc/myapp/env sudo chmod 640 /etc/myapp/env # app can read secrets, others cannot Try it Create a user alice . As alice, try to read a file you made with mode 600 owned by you. Observe the error, then fix with a group and mode 640. Run namei -l /etc/ssh/sshd_config and explain each permission on the path. Make a shared directory /srv/team with setgid so files created by any member are group-writable by the group. Find the biggest consumer of disk in /var and check df -i for inode usage.

title: Processes and systemd
text: Processes and systemd Your app on a server is a process. Production means that process starts at boot, restarts on crash, runs as the right user, has its logs captured and can be stopped cleanly. On modern Linux, systemd does all of that. Why you need a process manager If you start your app with node server.js over SSH it dies when you log out, does not restart when it crashes, does not start after a reboot, and its output vanishes. You could run it with nohup or tmux , but that is a hack. A service manager supervises it properly. On virtually every mainstream distro that is systemd (PID 1, the first process; it starts everything else). Processes 101 A process is a running program with a PID, an owner, memory, open files and a parent (PPID). Programs start other programs, forming a tree rooted at PID 1. ps aux # every process (BSD style) ps -ef --forest # tree view with parent relationships ps -o pid,ppid,user,%cpu,%mem,etime,cmd -p 1234 pgrep -a nginx # find PIDs by name pstree -p # tree top # live view (q quits); htop is friendlier lsof -p 1234 # files and sockets a process has open lsof -i :3000 # who is using port 3000? ss -tlnp # listening TCP ports with owning process (needs sudo for others) Process states in ps : R running, S sleeping, D uninterruptible I/O wait (often a stuck disk/NFS), Z zombie (finished, parent has not collected it), T stopped. Signals: talking to processes Signal Number Meaning Catchable? SIGTERM 15 "Please shut down gracefully" (default of kill ) Yes SIGINT 2 Ctrl+C Yes SIGHUP 1 Terminal closed; by convention "reload config" Yes SIGKILL 9 Kill immediately, no cleanup No SIGUSR1/2 10/12 App-defined Yes kill 1234 # SIGTERM: let it finish requests, flush, close DB kill -HUP 1234 # reload (nginx, many daemons) kill -9 1234 # last resort pkill -f "node server.js" killall nginx Handle SIGTERM in your app Deploys, systemd and Kubernetes all stop apps by sending SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a timeout. If your app ignores SIGTERM, in-flight requests are cut off on every deploy. Listen for it, stop accepting new connections, finish current work, then exit. Containers have a twist: if your app is PID 1 it must handle signals itself (or use tini / --init ). // Node.js graceful shutdown process.on("SIGTERM", () => { server.close(() => { db.end().then(() => process.exit(0)); }); setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 10000).unref(); // hard stop after 10s }); systemd basics systemd manages units ; the most common is a .service . Others: .timer (scheduling), .socket , .mount , .target (groups of units, like "multi-user"). systemctl status nginx # state, recent logs, PID, memory sudo systemctl start nginx sudo systemctl stop nginx sudo systemctl restart nginx # stop then start (brief downtime) sudo systemctl reload nginx # re-read config without dropping connections, if supported sudo systemctl enable nginx # start at boot sudo systemctl enable --now nginx # enable and start together sudo systemctl disable nginx systemctl is-active nginx; systemctl is-enabled nginx systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running systemctl --failed # what is broken? enable and start are independent: enabled means "at boot", started means "now". Writing a unit file for your app Suppose a Node app lives in /opt/myapp , runs node server.js on port 3000, and reads config from /etc/myapp/env . Create /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service (your own units go in /etc/systemd/system ; packages use /usr/lib/systemd/system ). [Unit] Description=My App (Node.js) Documentation=https://example.com/docs After=network-online.target postgresql.service Wants=network-online.target [Service] Type=simple User=myapp Group=myapp WorkingDirectory=/opt/myapp/current EnvironmentFile=/etc/myapp/env ExecStart=/usr/bin/node server.js Restart=on-failure RestartSec=3 # Stop behaviour KillSignal=SIGTERM TimeoutStopSec=30 # Hardening (cheap, big security win) NoNewPrivileges=true ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=true PrivateTmp=true ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/myapp # Resource limits LimitNOFILE=65535 MemoryMax=512M [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Directive Why After= / Wants= Ordering and soft dependency (start after the network and DB) User= Never run apps as root EnvironmentFile= Config and secrets outside the unit (mode 640, root:myapp) ExecStart= Absolute path to the binary; systemd does not use your shell or PATH like you do Restart=on-failure Auto-restart on crash; always also restarts after clean exit Type= simple (foreground process), forking (old-style daemons), oneshot (run and exit) WantedBy=multi-user.target What enable hooks into Activate it: sudo systemctl daemon-reload # REQUIRED after creating/editing unit files sudo systemctl enable --now myapp systemctl status myapp systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service # lint sudo systemctl edit myapp # drop-in override without editing the original systemd-analyze security myapp # hardening score Common unit mistakes Forgetting daemon-reload after edits. Relative paths in ExecStart , or shell syntax ( && , $VAR expansion, pipes). Wrap in /bin/sh -c '...' if you truly need it. Quotes in EnvironmentFile are handled differently than in a shell; use plain KEY=value . ProtectSystem=strict makes the filesystem read-only, so list writable paths in ReadWritePaths . Reading logs with journalctl systemd captures stdout and stderr of services into the journal . Your app need only log to stdout (a 12-factor best practice). journalctl -u myapp # all logs for the unit journalctl -u myapp -f # follow live journalctl -u myapp -n 100 --no-pager # last 100 lines journalctl -u myapp --since "1 hour ago" journalctl -u myapp --since "2026-10-05 09:00" --until "09:30" journalctl -u myapp -p err # only errors and worse journalctl -b # this boot; -b -1 = previous boot journalctl -u myapp -o json-pretty | head journalctl --disk-usage; sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=14d Alternatives and context Tool When systemd Default for long-running processes on a VM. Zero extra install. PM2 / supervisord Older/Node-centric supervisors; if you use PM2, still run it under systemd ( pm2 startup ) Docker --restart unless-stopped / Compose Containerised apps Kubernetes Many containers across many nodes; replaces what systemd does for apps The concepts carry over: a declared command, a user, env vars, restart policy, health, graceful stop, captured logs. Zero-downtime-ish restarts A plain restart drops requests for a moment. Options: reload where supported (nginx), run two instances behind a proxy and restart one at a time, or socket activation. The Deploy section builds proper strategies on this. Try it Create a trivial server: python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory /srv/demo . Write a unit for it (user nobody is fine for the exercise), enable and start it. Find its PID with systemctl status , then kill -9 it. Watch systemd restart it ( Restart=always ). Look at the restart in journalctl -u . Reboot the VM and confirm it came back by itself. Run systemd-analyze security on your unit, add two hardening options, and re-score.

title: SSH: Secure Remote Access
text: SSH: Secure Remote Access SSH is the front door to every server you will ever manage, and also what CI systems use to deploy. Understanding keys, the client config file, tunnels and hardening will save you hours and protect you from the most common attacks. Why SSH, and why keys Older tools (telnet, rsh, FTP) sent everything, including passwords, in clear text. SSH encrypts the session and authenticates both sides. Passwords work, but any server on the internet gets thousands of password-guessing attempts per day (check sudo journalctl -u ssh | grep "Failed password" | wc -l ). Public-key authentication replaces guessable secrets with cryptography that cannot be brute-forced. How key authentication works Your laptop Server ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (private: NEVER share) ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (public: copy anywhere) ──▶ ~/.ssh/authorized_keys 1. client: "I'd like to log in as deploy, here is my public key" 2. server: finds that key in authorized_keys, sends a random challenge 3. client: signs the challenge with the private key (key never leaves laptop) 4. server: verifies signature with public key ──▶ access granted Also, on first connection the client records the server's host key in ~/.ssh/known_hosts . If it later changes you get a loud REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED warning: either the server was rebuilt or someone is intercepting. Verify before removing the old entry ( ssh-keygen -R host ). Generating and installing keys ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "jane@work-laptop" # Enter a passphrase! It encrypts the private key on disk. ssh-copy-id deploy@203.0.113.10 # appends your public key to authorized_keys # manual equivalent: cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | ssh deploy@203.0.113.10 \ 'mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh && cat >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys' Key type Verdict ed25519 Modern default: short, fast, strong rsa (4096 bit) Fine for legacy compatibility ecdsa Works; ed25519 preferred dsa Obsolete, disabled ssh-agent: type the passphrase once eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 # macOS: ssh-add --apple-use-keychain ssh-add -l # loaded keys ssh -A bastion # agent forwarding: convenient but risky; prefer ProxyJump The client config file Stop typing long commands. ~/.ssh/config (mode 600) defines aliases and defaults. Host web1 HostName 203.0.113.10 User deploy Port 22 IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 IdentitiesOnly yes Host db1 HostName 10.0.1.5 # private IP, reachable only via bastion User admin ProxyJump bastion # hop through bastion automatically Host bastion HostName bastion.example.com User jump Host * ServerAliveInterval 30 # keep idle connections from dropping ServerAliveCountMax 3 AddKeysToAgent yes ControlMaster auto # reuse one connection for many sessions (fast) ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p ControlPersist 10m ssh web1 # that's it ssh db1 # transparently via bastion ssh -v web1 # verbose debugging (-vvv for more) Running commands and copying files ssh web1 'uptime; df -h /' # run and return ssh web1 'sudo systemctl restart myapp' ssh -t web1 'sudo -i' # -t allocates a TTY for interactive programs scp app.tar.gz web1:/tmp/ # simple copy scp -r ./dist web1:/var/www/site/ rsync -avz --delete --progress ./dist/ web1:/var/www/site/ # -a archive (perms, times, recursion) -v verbose -z compress # --delete remove remote files not present locally (mirror) --dry-run to preview rsync -avz -e "ssh -p 2222" ./ web1:/opt/myapp/ # custom SSH options rsync -avz --exclude node_modules --exclude .git ./ web1:/opt/myapp/ Prefer rsync over scp rsync copies only the differences, resumes interrupted transfers and has --dry-run . Mind the trailing slash: ./dist/ copies the contents , ./dist copies the directory itself. Tunnels (port forwarding) SSH can carry other traffic through its encrypted connection, so you can reach services that are not exposed to the internet. # Local forward: make remote DB reachable at localhost:5433 on my laptop ssh -L 5433:localhost:5432 web1 -N psql -h localhost -p 5433 -U app mydb # Reach a private DB that web1 can see but you cannot ssh -L 5433:db.internal:5432 web1 -N # Remote forward: expose my laptop's :3000 as :8080 on the server (demo/webhook testing) ssh -R 8080:localhost:3000 web1 -N # Dynamic forward: SOCKS proxy for browsing via the server ssh -D 1080 web1 -N laptop:5433 ═══ encrypted SSH tunnel ═══▶ web1 ───▶ db.internal:5432 (psql connects here) (db port never public) -N means no remote command; add -f to background. This beats opening the database port to the internet, always. Hardening the server After you confirmed key login works for a non-root user (in a second terminal!), edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config or better a drop-in at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf : PermitRootLogin no PasswordAuthentication no KbdInteractiveAuthentication no PubkeyAuthentication yes AllowUsers deploy alice MaxAuthTries 3 LoginGraceTime 20 X11Forwarding no ClientAliveInterval 300 ClientAliveCountMax 2 sudo sshd -t # validate config: prints nothing if OK sudo systemctl reload ssh # service is "sshd" on RHEL-family # Keep your current session open; test a NEW login before closing it. Measure Benefit Disable password auth Eliminates brute-force of passwords Disable root login Attackers must also guess a username; sudo gives audit trail Firewall / security group on port 22 Allow only your office/VPN IPs where possible fail2ban or sshguard Bans IPs after repeated failures Changing the port Reduces log noise only; not real security Bastion host or VPN (Tailscale/WireGuard) Private servers have no public SSH at all Short-lived certificates (SSH CA), SSM, Teleport Better than long-lived static keys at scale sudo apt install fail2ban sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban sudo fail2ban-client status sshd SSH keys in CI/CD Create a dedicated deploy key per project/environment, with no passphrase (CI cannot type one), stored in the CI secret store. Limit its power on the server with a restricted sudo rule, or a forced command in authorized_keys : command="/opt/myapp/bin/deploy.sh",no-port-forwarding,no-agent-forwarding,no-pty ssh-ed25519 AAAA... ci-deploy Pin the host key instead of disabling checking: ssh-keyscan -H host >> known_hosts . Never use StrictHostKeyChecking=no in production pipelines. Troubleshooting Symptom Check Permission denied (publickey) ssh -v : is the key offered? Server's authorized_keys perms (700 ~/.ssh , 600 file, home not group-writable)? Right user? journalctl -u ssh on the server. Connection timed out Firewall/security group, wrong IP, server down Connection refused sshd not running or other port: ss -tlnp | grep ssh Too many authentication failures Agent offers many keys; use IdentitiesOnly yes Session freezes Add ServerAliveInterval ; use tmux UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE chmod 600 the key Protect the private key Anyone with it (and no passphrase) is you. Never commit it, paste it in chat or copy it to servers. If leaked, remove its public half from every authorized_keys immediately and generate a new pair. Try it Create an alias in ~/.ssh/config for your VPS and log in with ssh myserver . Run a local web server on the VPS bound to 127.0.0.1:8000 and view it in your laptop browser with ssh -L 8080:localhost:8000 myserver -N . Harden sshd as above, validate with sshd -t , test a new session, then try logging in with -o PubkeyAuthentication=no and confirm it is refused. Use rsync -avzn (dry run) to preview syncing a folder, then run it for real.

title: Package Management and Runtimes
text: Package Management and Runtimes Installing software on a server should be repeatable, verifiable and updatable. Package managers give you that; downloading random tarballs and running "make install" gives you a snowflake. Why package managers A package manager knows what files belong to which package, what other packages are required (dependencies), which versions are available, and how to verify authenticity (cryptographic signatures). It lets you install, upgrade, list and cleanly remove software, and apply security patches with a single command. Without it you track versions in your head and leave orphaned files everywhere. apt (Debian, Ubuntu) sudo apt update # refresh the package INDEX (does not install anything) sudo apt upgrade -y # install available updates sudo apt full-upgrade # also allow removals/new deps (kernel upgrades) sudo apt install -y nginx curl git # install apt search redis # search apt show nginx # details, version, dependencies apt policy nginx # installed vs candidate versions and sources sudo apt remove nginx # remove program, keep config sudo apt purge nginx # remove program AND config sudo apt autoremove # remove no-longer-needed dependencies dpkg -l | grep nginx # installed packages dpkg -L nginx # files a package installed dpkg -S /usr/sbin/nginx # which package owns this file? sudo apt install ./package.deb # local .deb with dependency resolution dnf (RHEL, Rocky, Alma, Fedora) sudo dnf check-update sudo dnf upgrade -y sudo dnf install -y nginx dnf search redis; dnf info nginx sudo dnf remove nginx rpm -qa | grep nginx # installed rpm -ql nginx # files in package rpm -qf /usr/sbin/nginx # owner of a file dnf provides '*/bin/dig' # which package supplies this command? sudo dnf install epel-release # extra packages repo for RHEL family Task apt dnf apk (Alpine) Refresh index apt update (automatic) apk update Install apt install x dnf install x apk add x Remove apt remove x dnf remove x apk del x Upgrade all apt upgrade dnf upgrade apk upgrade Search apt search x dnf search x apk search x In scripts and Dockerfiles Use apt-get (stable CLI for scripting) and non-interactive mode: DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl . In Docker, combine update , install and rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* in one layer. Repositories and trust Packages come from repositories listed in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ or /etc/yum.repos.d/ . Distro repos are conservative: stable but often older versions (e.g. an old Node or Postgres). Vendors publish their own repos for newer versions. Adding one means trusting that vendor with root on your machine, so do it deliberately and use signed keyrings: # Example: PostgreSQL's official apt repository (current, documented method) sudo apt install -y postgresql-common sudo /usr/share/postgresql-common/pgdg/apt.postgresql.org.sh # Generic modern pattern (keyring per repo, not the deprecated apt-key): curl -fsSL https://example.com/repo.gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/example.gpg echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/example.gpg] https://example.com/apt stable main" \ | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/example.list sudo apt update Automatic security updates Unpatched servers are the easiest targets. On Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt install -y unattended-upgrades sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades cat /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades # APT::Periodic::Update-Package-Lists "1"; # APT::Periodic::Unattended-Upgrade "1"; [ -f /var/run/reboot-required ] && echo "reboot needed (kernel update)" On RHEL family use dnf-automatic . Kernel updates need a reboot (or live patching) to take effect. In a fleet, patch via rebuilding images rather than patching in place. Language runtimes: the version problem Your app needs Node 22, another needs Node 20; the distro ships Node 18. Installing a language runtime globally with the system package manager couples every app to one version. Use a version manager or isolate per app. Language Tools Isolation of dependencies Node.js nvm , fnm , volta , NodeSource apt repo, mise node_modules per project, lockfile ( package-lock.json ) Python pyenv , uv , distro python3 Virtualenv ( python3 -m venv .venv ), requirements.txt / uv.lock Java SDKMAN! , apt install openjdk-21-jre-headless Maven/Gradle Go Download tarball from go.dev; produces single static binaries Go modules Ruby rbenv , rvm Bundler Any mise / asdf (multi-language) .tool-versions file Node with nvm curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.3/install.sh | bash # check latest version first source ~/.bashrc nvm install --lts nvm use --lts node -v; npm -v echo "22" > .nvmrc # pin per project; then "nvm use" nvm and systemd do not mix automatically nvm modifies your interactive shell's PATH, which a systemd service never sees. In the unit file use the absolute path: ExecStart=/home/deploy/.nvm/versions/node/v22.11.0/bin/node server.js , or install Node system-wide (NodeSource repo, or unpack the official tarball in /opt/node ). Better yet, build a container image with the runtime baked in. Python sudo apt install -y python3-venv python3-pip cd /opt/myapp python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt # systemd: ExecStart=/opt/myapp/.venv/bin/gunicorn app:app -b 127.0.0.1:8000 # Do not "sudo pip install" system-wide: modern distros block it (PEP 668) Installing binaries directly Many tools ship as a single static binary on GitHub releases. Safe pattern: download, verify checksum, install into /usr/local/bin . curl -fsSLO https://example.com/tool_1.2.3_linux_amd64.tar.gz curl -fsSLO https://example.com/checksums.txt sha256sum -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing tar xzf tool_1.2.3_linux_amd64.tar.gz sudo install -m 0755 tool /usr/local/bin/tool Others: snap (Ubuntu's sandboxed packages, auto-updating), Flatpak (desktop), Homebrew on Linux , and of course containers , which bundle runtime and dependencies and avoid most problems here. Best practices Pin versions of important software; upgrade deliberately and test in staging first ( apt-mark hold pkg to freeze). Keep a list of what you installed (script or Ansible later). A server built from a script can be rebuilt in minutes. Minimise installed software: every package is attack surface and something to patch. Never pipe unknown scripts to a root shell. Read it, pin a version, verify checksums. Commit lockfiles so every environment installs the same dependency tree. Troubleshooting Error Fix Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock Another apt is running (often unattended-upgrades). Wait; do not delete lock files. Unable to locate package Run apt update ; wrong release/repo. Broken dependencies sudo apt --fix-broken install NO_PUBKEY / signature errors Repo key missing or expired; re-add via signed-by keyring. command not found after install New shell/ hash -r ; check which and $PATH . Try it Install nginx with apt. Use dpkg -L nginx to see where its files went, and apt policy nginx for the version. Enable unattended-upgrades and run sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run -d . Install Node via nvm, create a tiny app, and note why the systemd unit needs the absolute node path. Create a Python venv, install flask in it, and confirm pip list differs from the system pip.

title: Logs and Troubleshooting
text: Logs and Troubleshooting Something is broken at 2 a.m. The difference between a 5-minute fix and a 3-hour guessing game is knowing where logs live, which four resources can run out, and following a method rather than a hunch. Where logs live Source Location / command systemd journal (services, kernel, boot) journalctl System messages (Debian/Ubuntu) /var/log/syslog , /var/log/auth.log (logins, sudo) System messages (RHEL family) /var/log/messages , /var/log/secure nginx /var/log/nginx/access.log , error.log Kernel ring buffer dmesg -T or journalctl -k Package manager /var/log/apt/history.log , /var/log/dnf.log Last logins last , lastb (failed) Your app stdout into the journal (best), or a file you configured journalctl recipes journalctl -u myapp -f # follow a service journalctl -u myapp --since "30 min ago" -p warning journalctl -b -p err # errors since boot journalctl -k | grep -i "out of memory" # OOM killer events journalctl _PID=1234 journalctl -u ssh -u nginx --since today # multiple units interleaved Working with plain log files sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log sudo grep -E " 5[0-9]{2} " /var/log/nginx/access.log | tail # recent 5xx # status code breakdown awk '{print $9}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr # slowest requests, if $request_time is the last field in your log_format awk '{print $NF, $7}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort -nr | head zgrep "ERROR" /var/log/myapp/app.log.*.gz # rotated, compressed logs Log rotation Logs grow forever and fill disks. logrotate rotates, compresses and prunes them. Config in /etc/logrotate.d/ : /var/log/myapp/*.log { daily rotate 14 compress delaycompress missingok notifempty copytruncate # for apps that keep the file open and cannot reopen on signal } Test with sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/myapp . The journal has its own limits ( SystemMaxUse=500M in /etc/systemd/journald.conf ). Log levels and structure Use levels (debug, info, warn, error), include timestamps, request IDs and enough context to reproduce. Prefer structured JSON logs; they can be queried by tools later (Observability section). Never log passwords, tokens or full card numbers. The four resources Most performance problems are one of CPU, memory, disk or network being exhausted. Check each quickly. uptime # load averages (1, 5, 15 min). Compare against nproc. top -o %CPU # or htop; press M to sort by memory free -h # memory: look at "available", not "free" vmstat 1 5 # r=runnable, si/so = swap in/out (nonzero = memory pressure), wa = I/O wait df -h # disk space df -i # inodes (millions of tiny files can exhaust them) du -xh / --max-depth=2 2>/dev/null | sort -hr | head -15 # what is eating disk sudo lsof +L1 # deleted files still held open (space not freed!) iostat -x 1 3 # disk utilisation/latency (apt install sysstat) ss -s # socket summary Resource Symptoms Typical causes / fixes CPU Load above core count, slow responses Runaway process, inefficient code, too few cores. top , profile, scale. Memory Swapping, processes killed, Killed messages Leak or undersized box. Check OOM killer in journalctl -k ; set limits; add RAM. Disk No space left on device , DB/app write errors Logs, old releases, Docker images ( docker system df ), core dumps. Rotate and clean. Network Timeouts, connection resets Firewall, DNS, port exhaustion, remote down. See below. "free" memory is a trap Linux uses spare RAM as disk cache, so "free" looks tiny on a healthy box. The available column estimates what applications can actually get. Worry when available is low and swap is busy. Network diagnostics ip -br addr; ip route # my addresses and gateway ss -tlnp # what is LISTENING (and which process) ss -tn state established | wc -l # connection count curl -v http://localhost:3000/healthz # does the app answer locally? curl -sI https://example.com # headers only dig +short example.com # DNS ping -c 3 1.1.1.1 # reachability (ICMP may be blocked) traceroute example.com # path (or mtr: continuous) nc -vz db.internal 5432 # can I open a TCP connection to this port? sudo tcpdump -i any port 3000 -nn -c 20 # look at actual packets sudo ufw status verbose # host firewall Key distinction in ss -tlnp : an app listening on 127.0.0.1:3000 is reachable only from the machine itself; 0.0.0.0:3000 or [::]:3000 means all interfaces. "Works locally, not remotely" is very often this, or a firewall. A debugging checklist 1. What exactly is the symptom? Who is affected? Since when? 2. What changed? Deploy, config, cert, dependency, traffic, time? 3. Reproduce / observe curl it, read the error verbatim 4. Work along the request path DNS ▶ firewall ▶ proxy ▶ app ▶ DB 5. Check the four resources CPU, memory, disk, network 6. Read logs around the failure time-bounded, errors first 7. Form ONE hypothesis, test it change one thing at a time 8. Fix, verify, write it down runbook + postmortem Worked example: "the site returns 502" Symptom : curl -I https://example.com gives 502 Bad Gateway . 502 comes from the proxy: it could not get a valid reply from the app. On the server: systemctl status myapp shows failed (Result: exit-code) . journalctl -u myapp -n 50 --no-pager shows Error: listen EADDRINUSE :::3000 or ECONNREFUSED db:5432 or Killed . Port in use: ss -tlnp | grep 3000 reveals a leftover process; stop it, restart the service. DB refused: systemctl status postgresql , then df -h (a full disk crashes databases). Killed : journalctl -k | grep -i oom confirms memory exhaustion; add swap or RAM, or fix the leak. After fixing, curl -I again, then add a monitoring alert so you hear about it before users do. Common error messages decoded Message Meaning Permission denied Wrong user/mode, or a parent directory lacks x ; SELinux/AppArmor can also deny No space left on device Disk full or inodes exhausted Address already in use Another process holds the port Connection refused Host reachable, nothing listening on that port Connection timed out Packets dropped: firewall, wrong IP, host down Too many open files File-descriptor limit; raise LimitNOFILE in the unit Name or service not known DNS failure Exec format error Wrong CPU architecture (arm64 vs amd64) or bad shebang Principles Change one thing at a time and note it; otherwise you will not know what fixed it. Read the actual error completely. The answer is often in the line above the one you copied. Restarting is not a fix , it destroys evidence. Capture logs and state first ( journalctl , ps , ss output) then restart to restore service. Binary search the path : test from the middle (e.g. curl localhost:3000 ) to learn which half is broken. Use strace -p PID or lsof as last resorts to see what a stuck process is doing. Try it Create a 1 GB file with fallocate -l 1G /tmp/big , find it with du , delete it, and watch df -h . Break your own service: set a wrong ExecStart path, reload, start it, and diagnose with only systemctl status and journalctl . Start two servers on port 8000 and read the EADDRINUSE error. Find the culprit with ss -tlnp . Write a one-page runbook for "disk full" using the commands above.

title: Shell Scripting for Automation
text:
Shell Scripting for Automation A script is a saved list of commands that runs the same way every time. It is the first step from "I deployed it by hand" to "anyone (or any pipeline) can deploy it". The risk is that bash fails silently by default, so safe habits matter. Why script Manual steps get forgotten, mistyped and undocumented. A script is documentation that executes. Every CI job, Dockerfile RUN line, cron entry and cloud-init file is ultimately shell. Use bash for glue (30-200 lines); when logic gets complex (data structures, many branches, APIs) switch to Python or Go. Your first script #!/usr/bin/env bash # hello.sh name="${1:-world}" # first argument, default "world" echo "Hello, $name" chmod +x hello.sh ./hello.sh Alice # Hello, Alice bash hello.sh # also works without chmod The first line, the shebang , selects the interpreter. #!/usr/bin/env bash finds bash on the PATH. The safety header By default, bash keeps going after errors, treats unset variables as empty and ignores failures in pipelines. That turns rm -rf "$BUILD_DIR/"* with a typo into a disaster. Start every script with: #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail IFS=$'
	' Option Effect -e Exit immediately if a command fails (nonzero status) -u Error on use of an unset variable -o pipefail A pipeline fails if any stage fails, not just the last IFS=$'
	' Split words on newline/tab only, safer with filenames containing spaces set -x Trace: print each command as it runs (debugging; leaks secrets in logs) set -e is not magic It does not trigger inside if conditions, && / || lists or a ! -negated command. Handle expected failures explicitly: grep -q foo file || true , or test with if .
