Variables, quoting, defaults APP_DIR=/opt/myapp # no spaces around = readonly KEEP=5 # constant echo "Deploying to ${APP_DIR}/releases" # braces delimit names : "${DEPLOY_ENV:?DEPLOY_ENV must be set}" # abort with message if unset/empty PORT="${PORT:-3000}" # default value files=(a.txt "b c.txt") # array for f in "${files[@]}"; do echo "$f"; done # quote "${arr[@]}" to preserve elements now=$(date -u +%Y%m%d%H%M%S) # command substitution echo "${file%.txt}" # strip suffix; ${file##*/} = basename Always quote expansions: "$var" . Unquoted, a value with spaces or * gets split or globbed. Conditionals, loops, functions if [[ -f "$file" ]]; then echo "exists"; elif [[ -d "$file" ]]; then echo "dir"; else echo "no"; fi [[ -z "$x" ]] # empty [[ -n "$x" ]] # non-empty [[ "$a" == "$b" ]] # string equal [[ $n -gt 5 ]] # numeric greater [[ -e path ]] [[ -r path ]] [[ -x path ]] # exists / readable / executable command -v docker >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "docker missing" >&2; exit 1; } for i in 1 2 3; do echo "$i"; done for f in /var/log/*.log; do wc -l "$f"; done while read -r line; do echo "got: $line"; done < hosts.txt until curl -fsS localhost:3000/healthz >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done # wait for service case "$1" in start) echo "starting" ;; stop) echo "stopping" ;; *) echo "usage: $0 {start|stop}" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac log() { printf '%s [%s] %s
' "$(date -Is)" "$1" "${*:2}"; } die() { log ERROR "$*" >&2; exit 1; } log INFO "started" Use [[ ]] (bash) over [ ] . Scripts using #!/bin/sh must stick to POSIX features (no arrays, no [[ ). Cleanup with trap tmp=$(mktemp -d) cleanup() { rm -rf "$tmp"; } trap cleanup EXIT # runs on any exit, including errors trap 'echo "failed at line $LINENO" >&2' ERR Real example: a deploy script Deploys a prebuilt tarball using the release-directory pattern: each version in its own folder, current is a symlink, switching is atomic and rollback is just re-pointing the link. /opt/myapp ├── releases/ │ ├── 20261005101500/ (previous) │ └── 20261005113000/ (new) ├── shared/ (uploads, .env: survive deploys) └── current ─▶ releases/20261005113000 #!/usr/bin/env bash # deploy.sh <artifact.tar.gz> set -euo pipefail APP_DIR=/opt/myapp SERVICE=myapp KEEP=5 HEALTH_URL="http://127.0.0.1:3000/healthz" log() { printf '%s %s
' "$(date -Is)" "$*"; } die() { log "ERROR: $*" >&2; exit 1; } [[ $# -eq 1 ]] || die "usage: $0 <artifact.tar.gz>" artifact=$1 [[ -f "$artifact" ]] || die "artifact not found: $artifact" # Prevent two deploys at once exec 9>/tmp/myapp-deploy.lock flock -n 9 || die "another deploy is running" release="$APP_DIR/releases/$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)" previous=$(readlink -f "$APP_DIR/current" || true) log "Unpacking to $release" mkdir -p "$release" tar -xzf "$artifact" -C "$release" ln -sfn "$APP_DIR/shared/.env" "$release/.env" log "Installing production dependencies" (cd "$release" && npm ci --omit=dev) rollback() { if [[ -n "$previous" && -d "$previous" ]]; then log "Rolling back to $previous" ln -sfn "$previous" "$APP_DIR/current" sudo systemctl restart "$SERVICE" fi } log "Switching current symlink" ln -sfn "$release" "$APP_DIR/current" sudo systemctl restart "$SERVICE" log "Waiting for health check" for i in $(seq 1 30); do if curl -fsS "$HEALTH_URL" >/dev/null; then log "Healthy after ${i}s" # prune old releases, keep newest $KEEP ls -1dt "$APP_DIR"/releases/*/ | tail -n +$((KEEP + 1)) | xargs -r rm -rf log "Deploy OK: $release" exit 0 fi sleep 1 done log "Health check failed" rollback die "deploy failed, rolled back" Run it from your laptop or CI: scp build.tar.gz web1:/tmp/ && ssh web1 '/opt/myapp/bin/deploy.sh /tmp/build.tar.gz' Notice the DevOps principles at work: idempotent-ish steps, locking, health verification, automatic rollback, retained history, and logging with timestamps. Best practices checklist set -euo pipefail and quote everything. Check prerequisites first ( command -v ), fail fast with clear messages to stderr. Make scripts idempotent : safe to run twice ( mkdir -p , ln -sfn , check-before-create). Never hard-code secrets; read from environment or a root-only file. Use mktemp and trap for temp files; never fixed names in /tmp . Lint with ShellCheck ( apt install shellcheck ): it catches quoting bugs and more. Format with shfmt . Run both in CI. Add --dry-run modes for destructive scripts, and print usage on bad input. Avoid parsing ls ; use globs or find -print0 | xargs -0 . Bash vs alternatives Tool Choose when Bash Glue commands, small tasks, CI steps, available everywhere Python Parsing JSON/YAML, APIs, complex logic, tests Make / Just / Taskfile Named project tasks ( make deploy ) Ansible/Terraform Declarative server configuration and provisioning at scale (later sections) Try it Write backup.sh that tars a directory into /var/backups/NAME-DATE.tar.gz , keeps only the 7 newest, and exits nonzero with a message on any failure. Run shellcheck on it and fix every warning. Adapt the deploy script to your app and test a failing health check to see the rollback work (hint: make /healthz return 500). Add a --dry-run flag that only prints the steps.

title: Cron and Scheduled Automation
text: Cron and Scheduled Automation Backups, certificate renewals, log cleanup, report generation: servers constantly need things done on a schedule. Linux offers two tools, the classic cron and the modern systemd timers. Both fail quietly unless you design for it. Why scheduling needs care Scheduled jobs run unattended, with no terminal, a minimal environment and nobody watching. The typical failure: a nightly backup has silently failed for three months and you discover it when you need to restore. A good scheduled job is logged, idempotent, locked against overlap and monitored . cron basics The cron daemon reads tables ("crontabs") and runs commands when the time matches. crontab -e # edit YOUR crontab crontab -l # list sudo crontab -u deploy -l # another user's # system-wide: /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d/* (these have an extra USER column) # also drop scripts into /etc/cron.daily, .hourly, .weekly, .monthly The five fields ┌───────────── minute (0-59) │ ┌─────────── hour (0-23) │ │ ┌───────── day of month (1-31) │ │ │ ┌─────── month (1-12) │ │ │ │ ┌───── day of week (0-7, 0 and 7 = Sunday) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * command to run Expression Meaning */5 * * * * Every 5 minutes 0 * * * * Top of every hour 30 2 * * * Daily at 02:30 0 9 * * 1-5 09:00 Monday to Friday 0 0 1 * * Midnight on the 1st of each month @reboot Once at startup (also @daily , @hourly , @weekly ) Use a tool like crontab.guru to check expressions. Note: if both day-of-month and day-of-week are set, cron runs when either matches. A sensible crontab SHELL=/bin/bash PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin MAILTO=ops@example.com # m h dom mon dow command 30 2 * * * /opt/myapp/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/myapp/backup.log 2>&1 */10 * * * * flock -n /tmp/sync.lock /opt/myapp/bin/sync.sh >> /var/log/myapp/sync.log 2>&1 0 4 * * 0 /usr/bin/certbot renew --quiet Cron pitfalls (they all bite once) Minimal environment. Cron has a tiny PATH and none of your shell profile (no nvm, no env vars). Use absolute paths, set PATH at the top, source env files inside the script. Silent output. stdout/stderr go to mail (usually unconfigured) and vanish. Redirect to a log file as above, or pipe to logger -t backup to land in the journal. Overlapping runs. If a job takes longer than its interval, copies pile up. Wrap in flock -n . The % character means newline in crontab lines; escape as \% (e.g. in date +\%F ). Time zones. Cron uses the server's local time; DST can skip or repeat jobs. Run servers in UTC. Missed jobs. If the machine is off at the scheduled time, plain cron skips it (anacron or systemd timers with Persistent=true catch up). No failure alerting. Nothing tells you it stopped working. Add a dead-man's-switch ping (below). Many servers, one schedule. If three replicas each run the nightly job, it runs three times. Use a leader, a lock in the DB, or a central scheduler. # See what cron ran journalctl -u cron --since today # Debian/Ubuntu: service "cron" journalctl -u crond --since today # RHEL family grep CRON /var/log/syslog | tail Dead man's switch monitoring Alerting on "job failed" misses the case where the job never ran. Invert it: the job pings a monitoring URL on success, and the service alerts if the ping does not arrive on schedule (Healthchecks.io, Cronitor, Uptime Kuma push monitors). 30 2 * * * /opt/myapp/bin/backup.sh && curl -fsS -m 10 --retry 3 https://hc-ping.com/YOUR-UUID >/dev/null systemd timers A timer is a unit that activates a matching service unit. Compared with cron you get journal logging, dependency ordering, resource limits, hardening, catch-up of missed runs, random delay, and a clear list of next/last run times. 1. The job: /etc/systemd/system/backup.service [Unit] Description=Nightly database backup After=network-online.target postgresql.service [Service] Type=oneshot User=backup ExecStart=/opt/myapp/bin/backup.sh # Failure notification hook (optional) # OnFailure=notify-failure@%n.service Nice=10 IOSchedulingClass=idle 2. The schedule: /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer [Unit] Description=Run backup nightly [Timer] OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00 RandomizedDelaySec=300 Persistent=true [Install] WantedBy=timers.target 3. Enable and inspect sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now backup.timer # enable the TIMER, not the service systemctl list-timers --all # NEXT / LEFT / LAST / PASSED sudo systemctl start backup.service # run it right now to test journalctl -u backup.service -n 50 # output of runs systemd-analyze calendar "Mon..Fri *-*-* 09:00" # validate and preview schedules Timer setting Meaning OnCalendar= Wall-clock schedule: hourly , daily , Mon *-*-* 03:00 , *:0/15 OnBootSec= , OnUnitActiveSec= Relative: 5 minutes after boot, every 1 hour after last run Persistent=true Run missed executions after downtime RandomizedDelaySec= Spread load across many servers AccuracySec= Allow coalescing wakeups (default 1 min) cron vs systemd timers cron systemd timer Setup effort One line Two files Logging Manual redirects Automatic in journal Missed runs Skipped Persistent=true Overlap protection Add flock Built in (a service is not started twice) Environment and sandboxing Minimal, DIY Full unit directives Portability Everywhere, including macOS/BSD systemd distros only Rule of thumb: quick personal chores, cron; anything operationally important on a modern Linux server, a timer. Beyond one machine Kubernetes CronJob : schedule container jobs in a cluster (Kubernetes section). CI schedules : on: schedule: - cron: "0 3 * * *" in GitHub Actions for nightly builds and dependency checks. Cloud schedulers : EventBridge Scheduler, Cloud Scheduler; use workflow engines (Airflow, Temporal) for complex dependent jobs. Best practices Make each job a script you can run by hand ( set -euo pipefail ), then schedule the script. Idempotent, with locking and a timeout ( timeout 30m cmd ). Log with timestamps; alert on failure and on silence. Test restores, not just backups. A backup you never restored is unproven. Stagger heavy jobs; avoid the top of the hour when everyone else runs theirs. Try it Add a cron entry that runs every minute: * * * * * date >> /tmp/cron-test.log 2>&1 . Confirm it works, then remove it. Write a script that fails, schedule it, and notice how you find out (logs, mail). Wrap it with flock and a log redirect. Convert the same job to a systemd service plus timer with OnCalendar=*:0/2 , watch systemctl list-timers and journalctl -u . Sign up for a free Healthchecks.io account and add the ping so a missed run alerts you.

title: IP Addresses, Ports and Sockets
text: IP Addresses, Ports and Sockets Every deployment problem eventually becomes "can machine A reach machine B on port N?" This lesson gives you the mental model and the commands to answer that question in seconds instead of hours. Why this matters You deploy an app, open the browser and get "connection refused" or a spinning timeout. Without a networking model you can only guess. With one, you can ask precise questions: Is the process listening? On which address? Is a firewall dropping packets? Does DNS point at the right machine? Each question maps to a layer and a tool. The layers you actually need Application HTTP, SSH, Postgres protocol (your code, nginx) Transport TCP / UDP + port numbers (the OS kernel) Network IP addresses + routing (routers) Link Ethernet / Wi-Fi frames (switches, NICs) The full OSI model has seven layers, but in practice you reason about four: link, IP, TCP/UDP, application. "L4 load balancer" and "L7 load balancer" (later lessons) refer to the transport and application layers. IP addresses An IP address identifies a network interface. It is how packets find their destination across routers. IPv4 : 32 bits, written 203.0.113.10 . About 4.3 billion addresses, which ran out, hence NAT and IPv6. IPv6 : 128 bits, written 2001:db8::1 . Effectively unlimited. Most clouds and CDNs support it; many home networks do too. Public vs private addresses Range (CIDR) Use 10.0.0.0/8 Private (large networks, cloud VPCs) 172.16.0.0/12 Private (Docker uses 172.17.0.0/16 by default) 192.168.0.0/16 Private (home routers) 127.0.0.0/8 Loopback: this machine only ( 127.0.0.1 , localhost ) 169.254.0.0/16 Link-local (cloud metadata service at 169.254.169.254 ) Everything else Public, routable on the internet Private addresses are not routable on the internet. A NAT gateway (your home router, or a cloud NAT gateway) rewrites outgoing packets to a public address. That is why your laptop at 192.168.1.20 can browse the web but nobody can connect to it directly. CIDR notation 10.0.1.0/24 means "the first 24 bits are the network, the last 8 bits are hosts", so 256 addresses ( 10.0.1.0 to 10.0.1.255 ). A /16 has 65,536 addresses, a /32 is exactly one host. You will see CIDR in firewall rules, security groups and VPC design. CIDR Addresses Typical use /32 1 A single host ("allow only my IP") /24 256 A subnet /16 65,536 A whole VPC /0 All "Anywhere" ( 0.0.0.0/0 ) Ports An IP gets a packet to a machine. A port (0 to 65535) gets it to the right program on that machine. One process "listens" on a port; clients connect to it. Port Protocol Notes 22 SSH Remote shell 25 / 587 SMTP Mail 53 DNS UDP and TCP 80 HTTP 443 HTTPS TCP, and UDP for HTTP/3 3306 MySQL Never expose publicly 5432 PostgreSQL Never expose publicly 6379 Redis Never expose publicly 3000, 8000, 8080 Dev servers Convention only Ports 0 to 1023 are "privileged": on Linux only root (or a process with CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE ) may bind them. This is why you run your Node app on 3000 and let nginx (which binds 80/443) forward to it. Sockets, TCP and UDP A socket is the OS object that represents one end of a connection. A TCP connection is uniquely identified by a 4-tuple: (client IP, client port, server IP, server port) (198.51.100.7, 51514, 203.0.113.10, 443) The client's port is an ephemeral port (roughly 32768 to 60999 on Linux) picked by the OS. One server port can serve thousands of clients because each connection has a different 4-tuple. TCP UDP Connection Yes (3-way handshake) No Reliable, ordered Yes (retransmits) No Overhead Higher Lower Used by HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, SSH, databases DNS queries, HTTP/3 (QUIC), video, VPNs The TCP handshake and common errors Client Server │── SYN ────────────────────▶│ "can we talk?" │◀────────────── SYN-ACK ────│ "yes" │── ACK ────────────────────▶│ connection established The way a connection fails tells you where to look: Symptom Meaning Check Connection refused Host reachable, but nothing listening on that port (the OS replied with RST) Is the process running? Right port? Bound to the right address? Connection timed out Packets silently dropped. Usually a firewall or security group, or wrong IP Firewall rules, security group, routing No route to host Network layer cannot find a path Routing, VPC, wrong subnet Could not resolve host DNS failure See the DNS lesson Refused vs timeout "Refused" is good news: the network works and the machine answered, so the problem is the process. "Timeout" means something in the path is dropping your packets, almost always a firewall. Memorise this distinction; it halves your debugging time. Listening addresses: the 0.0.0.0 trap A server chooses which local address to bind: 127.0.0.1 : only reachable from the same machine. Perfect for an app behind nginx or a database that only the app uses. 0.0.0.0 : all IPv4 interfaces, reachable from anywhere the network allows. :: is the IPv6 equivalent. A specific private IP such as 10.0.1.5 : only that interface. // Node/Express app.listen(3000, '127.0.0.1'); // only nginx on the same box can reach it app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0'); // reachable from the network (needed inside Docker) Two classic bugs: (1) the app binds 127.0.0.1 inside a Docker container, so published ports never work; (2) the database binds 0.0.0.0 on a public IP with a weak password, and gets found by scanners within hours. Diagnostic toolbox # What is listening on this machine? (-t tcp, -l listening, -n numeric, -p process) sudo ss -tlnp # LISTEN 0 511 127.0.0.1:3000 0.0.0.0:* users:(("node",pid=1234,fd=19)) # LISTEN 0 511 0.0.0.0:80 0.0.0.0:* users:(("nginx",pid=800,fd=6)) # Who is using port 3000? sudo lsof -i :3000 # My addresses and routes ip addr ip route # Can I open a TCP connection to host:port? (-z scan only, -v verbose) nc -zv example.com 443 # Full HTTP exchange with timing curl -v https://example.com/ curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'dns=%{time_namelookup} connect=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} total=%{time_total}\n' https://example.com/ # Path to a destination (where do packets stop?) traceroute example.com # or mtr example.com # What is my public IP? curl -s https://ifconfig.me netstat is the older equivalent of ss ; on macOS use lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -n -P . A debugging ladder Is the process up? systemctl status myapp , ss -tlnp | grep 3000 . Does it answer locally? curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/ on the server. Does it answer from the server's public/private IP? Tests the bind address. Is the host firewall open? sudo ufw status . Is the cloud firewall open? Security group / network ACL. Does DNS point here? dig +short example.com . Work outward from the process. The first failing step is your culprit. Pitfalls Hard-coding IPs. Cloud IPs change when instances are replaced. Use DNS names or service discovery. Forgetting UDP. Opening 443/tcp but not 443/udp silently disables HTTP/3 (it falls back to HTTP/2, so it still works). Port conflicts. EADDRINUSE means another process already has that port. Find it with ss or lsof . Ephemeral port exhaustion. A client making huge numbers of short connections to one server can run out of source ports ( TIME_WAIT pile-up). Fix with connection reuse (keep-alive, pooling). Try it Run ip addr (Linux) or ifconfig (macOS). Identify your loopback and LAN addresses. Is your LAN address in a private range? Start a throwaway server: python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 . In another terminal run ss -tlnp | grep 8000 (or lsof -i :8000 ) and note the bind address. From another machine on your network (or by using your LAN IP), try to reach it. It should be refused or time out. Restart with --bind 0.0.0.0 and retry. Run nc -zv localhost 9999 (nothing is listening) and observe "refused". Compare with nc -zv -w 3 10.255.255.1 80 , which should time out. Use the curl -w timing command against any site and identify which phase is slowest.

title: DNS: The Internet's Phone Book
text: DNS: The Internet's Phone Book Humans use names like app.example.com ; networks use IP addresses. DNS translates between them. It is also the root cause of a startling share of outages, and the lever you pull for most deployment cutovers. Why DNS exists Without DNS you would give users 203.0.113.10 . When you moved servers, every user and every config file would need updating. DNS adds a level of indirection: users hold a stable name , and you change what it points to. Almost every migration, failover and traffic-shifting trick relies on this indirection. How resolution works When your laptop looks up www.example.com , several parties cooperate: Browser ──▶ OS stub resolver ──▶ Recursive resolver (ISP, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8) │ (cache miss) 1. ask a ROOT server ─────┤ "who handles .com?" → TLD servers 2. ask a .com TLD server ─┤ "who handles example.com?" → authoritative NS 3. ask example.com's │ AUTHORITATIVE server ──┘ "www.example.com?" → 203.0.113.10 │ answer cached for TTL seconds, returned to you Stub resolver : the tiny client in your OS. It forwards the question and caches briefly. Recursive resolver : does the legwork and caches answers for many users. Root servers : know only who runs each top-level domain. TLD servers : know which name servers are authoritative for each domain under them. Authoritative servers : hold the real records. Your DNS provider (Cloudflare, Route 53, your registrar) runs these. Caching at every level is why DNS is fast, and also why changes are not instant. Record types Type Maps Example A Name to IPv4 app.example.com. 300 IN A 203.0.113.10 AAAA Name to IPv6 app 300 IN AAAA 2001:db8::10 CNAME Name to another name (alias) www 300 IN CNAME app.example.com. MX Mail servers, with priority @ IN MX 10 mail.example.com. TXT Free text: SPF, DKIM, domain verification @ IN TXT "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all" NS Which servers are authoritative for the zone @ IN NS ns1.dnsprovider.com. SOA Zone metadata (serial, refresh, negative TTL) Managed by your provider CAA Which CAs may issue certificates @ IN CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org" SRV Host + port for a service Used by some internal service discovery PTR IP to name (reverse DNS) Important for mail servers The apex CNAME problem A CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name, and the zone apex ( example.com itself) must have SOA and NS records. So you cannot put a standard CNAME at the apex. Solutions: use an A record at the apex; or use your provider's proprietary "ALIAS"/"ANAME"/"CNAME flattening" (Route 53 Alias, Cloudflare flattening) which resolves the target server-side and returns A records. TTL and "propagation" Every record has a TTL (time to live, in seconds): how long resolvers may cache it. TTL 300 means "reuse this answer for up to 5 minutes." "DNS propagation" is a misleading term. Nothing is pushed anywhere. Your authoritative server changes instantly; the delay is the world's recursive resolvers still holding the old answer until their cached copy expires. A change from IP X to IP Y takes up to the old TTL to be seen everywhere. Some resolvers and ISPs ignore low TTLs, and browsers and JVMs add their own caches. The migration playbook 24 to 48 hours before a planned cutover, lower the TTL to 60 to 300 seconds. Wait out the old TTL. Switch the record. Verify. Later raise the TTL again (3600 or more) to reduce query load and improve resilience. Lowering the TTL at the moment of cutover does nothing: caches already hold the old value with the old TTL. TTL Pros Cons 60 to 300 s Fast failover and cutover More queries; slightly slower first lookups 3600 s (1 h) Good default for stable records Hour-long wait to change 86400 s (1 day) Cheapest; resilient to DNS provider hiccups Painful to change Negative caching: a lookup for a name that does not exist ( NXDOMAIN ) is also cached, for the SOA's minimum TTL. If you query a hostname before creating its record, you may keep seeing "not found" for a while. dig: your main tool # Full answer with all sections dig example.com # Just the answer dig +short example.com dig +short AAAA example.com dig +short MX example.com dig +short TXT example.com dig +short CNAME www.example.com # Ask a specific resolver (bypass your local cache/ISP) dig @1.1.1.1 example.com dig @8.8.8.8 example.com # Ask the authoritative server directly: the source of truth, no caching dig NS example.com +short dig @ns1.dnsprovider.com example.com # Follow the whole delegation chain from the root dig +trace example.com # Reverse lookup dig -x 203.0.113.10 +short Reading the full output: ;; ->>HEADER Key statuses: NOERROR (ok, possibly with an empty answer), NXDOMAIN (name does not exist), SERVFAIL (resolver could not get a valid answer; often a broken DNSSEC setup or dead name servers), REFUSED . Alternatives: nslookup , host , and resolvectl query on systemd systems. Setting up a domain for your app Register the domain with a registrar (Namecheap, Cloudflare Registrar, Porkbun, Route 53 Domains). Choose where DNS is hosted. The registrar's default or a dedicated provider. At the registrar, set the domain's NS records (delegation) to the provider's name servers. Create records in that provider's zone: @ 300 A 203.0.113.10 ; example.com www 300 CNAME example.com. ; www.example.com api 300 A 203.0.113.20 ; api.example.com @ 300 CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org" Note: NS records at the registrar (delegation) and the records in the zone are two different things. Beginners edit the wrong place and see no effect. Check with dig NS example.com +short to see who really is authoritative. DNS as a deployment tool Cutover : point the name at the new server. Weighted routing (Route 53, Cloudflare): 5 percent of answers to the new stack. A crude canary. Health-checked failover : the provider stops returning an unhealthy IP. Geo/latency routing : answer with the nearest region. Wildcards : *.example.com catches all subdomains (useful for preview environments per pull request). Split-horizon : internal resolvers return private IPs for the same name that resolves publicly elsewhere. Cloud private zones (Route 53 private hosted zones) do this. Limit: DNS-based traffic shifting is coarse, because clients cache answers and you cannot drain instantly. Load balancers (see that lesson) are the precise tool. Pitfalls Trailing dots : in zone files example.com. is absolute; example.com without a dot gets the zone name appended ( example.com.example.com. ). Web UIs usually hide this, but file-based zones bite. CNAME at apex or alongside MX/TXT breaks mail and verification. Dangling records : a CNAME to a deleted cloud resource can be claimed by an attacker (subdomain takeover). Clean up DNS when you delete infrastructure. Expired domains take everything down. Enable auto-renew and keep a valid payment method. Forgetting the local cache : your machine may still hold the old answer. Flush with sudo resolvectl flush-caches (Linux) or sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder (macOS). Test with dig @1.1.1.1 instead. Single DNS provider is a single point of failure for the entire company. Large organisations use two. Testing before DNS is ready : use curl --resolve app.example.com:443:203.0.113.10 https://app.example.com/ or temporarily edit /etc/hosts . DNSSEC and DoH DNSSEC signs records so resolvers can detect tampering (a misconfiguration can make your domain fail to resolve entirely, so enable it deliberately and keep DS records in sync). DNS over HTTPS/TLS encrypts the client-to-resolver hop for privacy. Neither changes how records work. Try it Run dig +trace github.com and identify the root, TLD and authoritative steps. Run dig github.com twice a few seconds apart and watch the TTL count down. Find a domain's mail servers ( dig +short MX gmail.com ), name servers and SPF record ( dig +short TXT gmail.com ). Compare dig @1.1.1.1 +short example.com with dig @8.8.8.8 +short example.com for a CDN-fronted site; you may see different IPs (geo routing). Test a site without DNS: curl -I --resolve example.com:443:93.184.215.14 https://example.com/ . If you own a domain, create a test record test.yourdomain.com with TTL 60, change its value, and time how long dig takes to show the new value.

title: HTTP and HTTPS
text: HTTP and HTTPS HTTP is the language your app, browser, reverse proxy, load balancer and CDN all speak. Knowing it well turns mysterious 502s, stale caches and CORS errors into five-minute fixes. Why learn the protocol and not just the framework Frameworks hide HTTP. But in production the request passes through a CDN, a load balancer and nginx before reaching your code. Each hop reads and rewrites headers, enforces timeouts and returns its own errors. To debug, you must see the raw conversation. Anatomy of a request and response GET /api/users/42?include=orders HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com User-Agent: curl/8.7.1 Accept: application/json Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi... HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 Content-Length: 87 Cache-Control: private, max-age=0 ETag: "a1b2c3" {"id":42,"name":"Ada","orders":[]} A request has a method , a path+query , headers and an optional body . A response has a status code , headers and a body. The Host header is how one IP address serves many sites (virtual hosting): nginx picks the config by it. Methods Method Purpose Safe Idempotent GET Read a resource Yes Yes HEAD Like GET, headers only (health checks) Yes Yes POST Create / run an action No No PUT Replace a resource No Yes PATCH Partially modify No Not guaranteed DELETE Remove No Yes OPTIONS Capabilities; CORS preflight Yes Yes Idempotency matters operationally: a load balancer or client may retry idempotent requests automatically after a failure. A retried POST can double-charge a customer unless you use an idempotency key. Status codes Class Code Meaning and operational note 2xx 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content Success 3xx 301 / 308 permanent redirect, 302 / 307 temporary, 304 Not Modified 301/302 may change POST to GET; 307/308 preserve the method. 304 means "your cached copy is still valid". 4xx 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthenticated, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 413 Payload Too Large, 429 Too Many Requests The client is at fault. A spike in 4xx after a deploy often means you broke an API contract. 5xx 500 Internal Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout The server is at fault. Decoding the gateway errors 502 : the proxy reached the upstream but got garbage or the connection was refused/reset (your app crashed or is not listening). 503 : no healthy upstream, or the service is deliberately overloaded or in maintenance. 504 : the upstream accepted the request but did not answer in time (slow query, timeout too short). 502 and 504 are the proxy telling you the problem is behind it. Look at the app logs. Important headers Header Direction Why it matters Host Req Selects the virtual host Authorization , Cookie Req Credentials. Never log them. Content-Type Both Body format ( application/json ) Accept-Encoding / Content-Encoding Req / Res Compression: gzip, br (Brotli), zstd X-Forwarded-For , X-Forwarded-Proto , Forwarded Req Real client IP and original scheme behind proxies. Only trust them from your own proxy. Location Res Redirect target Set-Cookie Res Use Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax Strict-Transport-Security Res HSTS: force HTTPS for a period Content-Security-Policy Res Restrict what scripts/resources run Access-Control-Allow-Origin Res CORS permission for browsers Retry-After Res With 429/503: when to try again Caching headers Caching is the cheapest performance and scalability feature you have. HTTP defines it precisely. # Immutable, fingerprinted assets (app.3f9c1a.js): cache a year, never revalidate Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable # HTML pages: always check with the server, but allow cheap 304s Cache-Control: no-cache ETag: "v123" # Per-user API data: never store in shared caches (CDN) Cache-Control: private, no-store # Let CDN cache 60s, browser not at all Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60 # Serve stale while refreshing in the background Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300 Directive Meaning max-age=N Fresh for N seconds in any cache s-maxage=N Like max-age but only for shared caches (CDN, proxy) no-cache May store, but must revalidate before each use (confusing name) no-store Do not store at all public / private Shared caches allowed / browser only immutable Will never change; skip revalidation Revalidation : the server sends ETag: "abc" (or Last-Modified ). The client later sends If-None-Match: "abc" ; if unchanged the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body. Vary: Accept-Encoding tells caches the response differs per that request header; a wrong Vary causes serving the wrong variant. Best practice: fingerprint static file names with a content hash so they can be cached forever, and keep the HTML short-lived so a deploy takes effect immediately. Connections: keep-alive, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 A new TCP+TLS connection costs several round trips. Keep-alive (default in HTTP/1.1) reuses a connection for many requests. Between nginx and your app, enable upstream keep-alive too, or you pay connection setup on every proxied request. Version Transport Key ideas Weakness HTTP/1.1 TCP Text protocol, keep-alive, one request at a time per connection (browsers open ~6 connections) Head-of-line blocking at HTTP level HTTP/2 TCP + TLS Binary, multiplexed streams on one connection, header compression (HPACK) One lost TCP packet stalls all streams HTTP/3 QUIC over UDP Independent streams, faster handshake (1-RTT, 0-RTT resumption), connection migration (Wi-Fi to cellular) UDP sometimes blocked; needs UDP 443 open Typically TLS terminates at the CDN/load balancer/nginx which speaks HTTP/2 or 3 to browsers and plain HTTP/1.1 to your app. Your app rarely needs to care. Browsers discover HTTP/3 via the Alt-Svc response header and fall back gracefully. HTTPS in one paragraph HTTPS is HTTP carried inside a TLS-encrypted connection. It provides confidentiality (no eavesdropping), integrity (no tampering) and authentication (you are talking to the real example.com ). It is mandatory today: browsers mark HTTP as insecure, HTTP/2 in browsers requires it, and many browser APIs only work on secure origins. The next lesson covers how TLS works. Operationally: Redirect all HTTP to HTTPS (301/308). Send Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains once you are confident (a mistake is sticky for the max-age). Mark cookies Secure . Avoid mixed content (an HTTPS page loading HTTP assets gets blocked). Behind a proxy: the scheme and client IP problem If TLS ends at nginx and your app sees plain HTTP from 127.0.0.1 , then req.protocol is http and req.ip is 127.0.0.1 . Redirect loops and wrong rate limiting follow. Fix: the proxy sets X-Forwarded-* and the app trusts exactly that proxy: // Express app.set('trust proxy', 1); // trust one hop (nginx). Don't use `true` blindly. // now req.ip is the real client IP and req.secure reflects X-Forwarded-Proto Timeouts Every hop has them, and the smallest wins. Typical defaults: nginx proxy_read_timeout 60 s, AWS ALB idle timeout 60 s, Cloudflare 100 s. Long-running work (report generation, uploads) should return 202 Accepted and complete in a background job rather than hold a connection open. Make your app's keep-alive timeout longer than the load balancer's idle timeout, or you will see sporadic 502s when the app closes a connection the LB believes is still open (Node's server.keepAliveTimeout defaults to 5 s, a classic ALB 502 cause). curl for HTTP debugging curl -i https://example.com/ # include response headers curl -I https://example.com/ # HEAD request only curl -v https://example.com/ # verbose: TLS, request, response curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' https://example.com/ curl -X POST https://api.example.com/items \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"widget"}' curl -L https://example.com/ # follow redirects curl --http2 -I https://example.com/ # force a protocol (also --http3 if built in) curl -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' -I https://example.com/ # check compression curl -I -H 'Origin: https://other.com' https://api.example.com/ # check CORS headers Pitfalls Returning 200 with an error body, which breaks monitoring and retries. Use correct status codes. Using 301 for something you may change: browsers cache permanent redirects aggressively. Caching authenticated responses on a CDN. Always set Cache-Control: private or no-store for personalised data. Trusting X-Forwarded-For from the open internet: clients can forge it. Only accept it from your proxy. CORS is enforced by browsers, not servers; curl working does not mean the browser will. Try it Run curl -v https://example.com/ 2>&1 | less . Find the TLS version, the negotiated protocol (ALPN: h2), the status and the headers. Run curl -I https://github.com/ and list the security and caching headers. Which have max-age ? Fetch a static asset from a big site twice with curl -I and look for Age , X-Cache or CF-Cache-Status headers that reveal CDN caching. Test revalidation: take an ETag from a response and send curl -I -H 'If-None-Match: "THE-ETAG"' URL . Expect 304. Write a 10-line Express app that returns different Cache-Control headers on two routes and observe browser behaviour in DevTools (Network tab, "Disable cache" off).

title: TLS and Certificates
text: TLS and Certificates TLS is what makes the padlock appear. Operationally it is about one thing: getting a valid certificate onto your server and renewing it before it expires. Expired certificates are among the most common, most embarrassing and most preventable outages. The problem TLS solves Plain HTTP crosses many machines you do not control: Wi-Fi routers, ISPs, corporate proxies. Anyone along the path can read passwords and cookies, or alter the page. TLS (Transport Layer Security, the successor to SSL) gives you three guarantees: Confidentiality : traffic is encrypted. Integrity : tampering is detected. Authentication : the server proves it is really example.com . Without this, an attacker could encrypt traffic to themselves and relay it (man-in-the-middle). Authentication is the job of certificates . Key ideas: asymmetric and symmetric crypto Asymmetric (public/private key pairs): what the public key encrypts or verifies, only the private key can decrypt or sign. Slow, but solves "how do two strangers agree on a secret". Symmetric (AES, ChaCha20): one shared key, very fast. Used for the bulk of the data. TLS uses asymmetric techniques during the handshake to authenticate the server and agree on a shared secret, then switches to symmetric encryption. The TLS 1.3 handshake Client Server │── ClientHello ───────────────────────────────▶│ supported versions/ciphers, │ (SNI: example.com, key share, ALPN h2) │ SNI = which hostname I want │ │ │◀─ ServerHello (chosen cipher, key share) ─────│ both sides can now derive keys │◀─ {Certificate chain} (encrypted) ───────────│ "here is my proof of identity" │◀─ {CertificateVerify} (signature) ───────────│ proves I own the private key │◀─ {Finished} ─────────────────────────────────│ │ │ │── {Finished} ────────────────────────────────▶│ │══ encrypted HTTP request/response ═══════════│ TLS 1.3 needs one round trip (TLS 1.2 needs two). The key agreement uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, which gives forward secrecy : even if the server's private key leaks later, recorded past traffic cannot be decrypted. SNI (Server Name Indication) is the hostname sent in the clear in ClientHello, which lets one IP host many certificates. Disable TLS 1.0/1.1 (and SSLv3). Allow TLS 1.2 and 1.3. Certificates and the chain of trust A certificate is a signed statement: "this public key belongs to example.com ", signed by a Certificate Authority (CA) . Your browser/OS ships with a trust store of root CA certificates. Roots do not sign server certificates directly; they sign intermediate CAs, which sign yours: Root CA (in browser trust store, offline, long-lived) └── Intermediate CA (signs leaf certs) └── Leaf certificate: example.com, www.example.com (yours, 90 days) The server must send the leaf plus intermediates (the "full chain"). Missing intermediates is a common bug: it works in Chrome (which can fetch them) but fails in curl , Java or mobile apps. A leaf certificate contains: the subject names (Subject Alternative Names, SANs, are what browsers check), the public key, validity dates, and the issuer's signature. Validation checks: signature chain to a trusted root, the name matches the host, the date is valid, not revoked. Certificate types Type Validates Notes DV (domain validated) You control the domain Automated; what Let's Encrypt issues. Enough for nearly everything. OV / EV Organisation identity Paid; browsers no longer show special UI, little practical benefit Wildcard *.example.com Covers one label level only (not a.b.example.com ); needs DNS-01 validation Self-signed Nothing Fine for local dev or internal mTLS with your own CA; browsers warn Let's Encrypt and ACME Let's Encrypt is a free, automated, non-profit CA. It uses the ACME protocol: your server proves it controls a domain by completing a challenge, and the CA issues a certificate with a short lifetime (90 days; the industry is moving toward even shorter lifetimes, so automation is not optional). Challenge How Use when HTTP-01 CA fetches http://example.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/TOKEN on port 80 Single public web server. Port 80 must be reachable. No wildcards. DNS-01 You publish a TXT record _acme-challenge.example.com Wildcards; servers not publicly reachable. Needs DNS provider API access. TLS-ALPN-01 Special handshake on 443 Port 80 unavailable Rate limits exist (for example, a limited number of certificates per registered domain per week). Use the staging environment ( --staging ) while experimenting so you do not get locked out. certbot on Ubuntu with nginx # Prerequisites: DNS A record points to this server; ports 80 and 443 are open. sudo apt update sudo apt install -y certbot python3-certbot-nginx # Obtain a cert AND let certbot edit your nginx server block sudo certbot --nginx -d example.com -d www.example.com \ --redirect --agree-tos -m you@example.com # Or obtain only (you edit nginx yourself) sudo certbot certonly --nginx -d example.com -d www.example.com # Without a web server on the box (standalone mode: certbot binds port 80 briefly) sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d example.com # Wildcard via DNS-01 (example with the Cloudflare plugin) sudo apt install -y python3-certbot-dns-cloudflare sudo certbot certonly --dns-cloudflare \ --dns-cloudflare-credentials /root/.secrets/cloudflare.ini \ -d example.com -d '*.example.com' Files land in /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/ : File Contains fullchain.pem Your leaf cert plus intermediates. Use as ssl_certificate . privkey.pem Private key. Use as ssl_certificate_key . Guard it; mode 600/root only. cert.pem , chain.pem Separate pieces (rarely needed) These are symlinks into /etc/letsencrypt/archive/ ; always reference the live/ paths so renewals are picked up. The nginx side server { listen 443 ssl; listen 443 quic reuseport; # HTTP/3 (nginx 1.25+), also open UDP 443 http2 on; # nginx 1.25.1+ syntax server_name example.com www.example.com; ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem; ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:10m; ssl_session_timeout 1d; add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000" always; add_header Alt-Svc 'h3=":443"; ma=86400' always; # ... location blocks ... } server { listen 80; server_name example.com www.example.com; return 301 https://$host$request_uri; } Renewal The Ubuntu package installs a systemd timer (or cron job) that runs certbot renew twice a day. It renews only certificates within 30 days of expiry. systemctl list-timers | grep certbot # confirm the timer exists sudo certbot renew --dry-run # simulate renewal against staging: DO THIS sudo certbot certificates # list certs and expiry dates # Reload nginx after a successful renewal so it loads the new file sudo tee /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/reload-nginx.sh <<'EOF' #!/bin/sh systemctl reload nginx EOF sudo chmod +x /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/reload-nginx.sh The nginx plugin normally reloads nginx automatically, but a deploy hook makes it explicit and works for any setup. A server that renews the file but never reloads keeps serving the old, soon-expired certificate. Why renewals fail in practice Port 80 got firewalled or redirected oddly; DNS no longer points to this server; the DNS API token expired (DNS-01); nginx config changed so the challenge location is shadowed; disk full; the timer was never enabled. Always alert on days until expiry (monitoring a probe such as openssl s_client , Prometheus blackbox exporter, or your uptime tool) rather than trusting that renewal works. Inspecting certificates # What does the server present? (expiry, issuer, SANs) echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null \ | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName # Only the expiry echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null \ | openssl x509 -noout -enddate # Is the chain complete? openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -showcerts </dev/null # Verbose TLS info via curl curl -vI https://example.com/ 2>&1 | grep -iE 'TLS|subject|issuer|expire' # Generate a self-signed cert for local testing openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 365 \ -keyout dev.key -out dev.crt -subj "/CN=localhost" Where to terminate TLS Option Pros Cons On the app server / nginx Simple, full control Certs on every server; you manage renewal On the load balancer (ALB, ACM) One place; cloud-managed auto-renewing certs Traffic to backends is plain unless you re-encrypt On the CDN (Cloudflare) Zero ops; edge performance Needs a secure CDN-to-origin link (see "Full (strict)" mode) End-to-end / mTLS Encrypted everywhere; mutual authentication (service meshes) Operational complexity Managed options (AWS ACM, Cloudflare, Caddy's automatic HTTPS, Kubernetes cert-manager) automate everything in this lesson. The concepts remain the same when they break. Pitfalls and best practices Serve fullchain.pem , not cert.pem . Protect and never commit private keys. If one leaks, revoke and reissue. Do not rely on email expiry warnings; monitor expiry yourself. Add a CAA DNS record to restrict who can issue for your domain. Clients with wrong clocks see "certificate not yet valid / expired" errors. Run NTP (chrony) on servers. Pinning certificates in mobile apps without a rotation plan creates outages when certs change. Internal hostnames ( db.internal ) cannot get public certs; use a private CA (step-ca, Vault PKI, cloud private CA). Try it Run the openssl s_client command against three sites. Compare issuers and expiry dates. How many days remain on each? Count the certificates in the chain with -showcerts . Which one is the leaf? On a VPS with a real domain: install certbot, run sudo certbot --nginx --staging -d yourdomain.com first, then repeat without --staging . Run sudo certbot renew --dry-run and read the output. Then run systemctl list-timers and find the renewal timer. Locally: generate a self-signed cert, point an nginx server block at it, and observe the browser warning and what curl -k does differently. Run curl https://expired.badssl.com/ and curl https://self-signed.badssl.com/ to see the exact error messages you would see in production.

title: Reverse Proxies and nginx
text: Reverse Proxies and nginx A reverse proxy sits in front of your application and handles the messy edge of the internet: TLS, compression, static files, slow clients, rate limits. It is the first piece of infrastructure almost every production app gets, and nginx is the most common choice. Forward vs reverse proxy A forward proxy acts for clients (a corporate proxy hiding employees). A reverse proxy acts for servers: clients talk to it believing it is the site, and it forwards requests to one or more backends. Internet ┌──────────── your server ─────────────────────────┐ │ │ Browser ──443──▶ nginx ──▶ 127.0.0.1:3000 Node app (API) (HTTPS) │ ├──▶ 127.0.0.1:3001 Another service │ └──▶ /var/www/site static files (served directly) └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Why not just expose Node/Python/Java directly? Privileged ports : nginx binds 80/443 while your app runs as an unprivileged user on 3000. TLS termination : certificates, ciphers, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 handled by battle-tested code. Slow clients : nginx buffers a slow mobile client's upload/download so your app worker is not tied up ("slowloris" resistance). Static files : nginx serves them via the kernel's sendfile orders of magnitude cheaper than your framework. Compression, caching, rate limiting, access logs in one place. Multiple apps on one IP : route by hostname or path. Zero-downtime reloads and upstream failover . Security boundary : malformed requests are rejected before reaching your code; the app is not directly reachable. nginx basics On Ubuntu: sudo apt install nginx . Layout: Path Purpose /etc/nginx/nginx.conf Main config; includes the files below /etc/nginx/sites-available/ One file per site (Debian/Ubuntu convention) /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/ Symlinks to the enabled sites /etc/nginx/conf.d/*.conf Extra config snippets, also included /var/log/nginx/access.log, error.log Logs. error.log is where 502s are explained. Config is hierarchical: http { server { location { } } } . A request picks a server by port and server_name (matching the Host header), then a location by the best path match (exact = , longest prefix, then regex). sudo nginx -t # ALWAYS test config before reloading sudo systemctl reload nginx # graceful: new workers start, old ones finish requests sudo systemctl restart nginx # drops connections; rarely needed sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log Example 1: the minimal reverse proxy # /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp server { listen 80; server_name example.com www.example.com; location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; } } sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/ sudo rm -f /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx Without the proxy_set_header lines your app sees Host: 127.0.0.1:3000 and every client as 127.0.0.1 . Remember app.set('trust proxy', 1) in Express. The trailing slash in proxy_pass proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000; forwards the original path unchanged. proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000/; (with a URI part) replaces the matched location prefix. With location /api/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000/; } a request for /api/users arrives at the app as /users . This is the most common source of unexpected 404s behind nginx. Example 2: a production-grade config Full server with HTTPS, static files, compression, upstream keep-alive, caching of assets, security headers and timeouts: # /etc/nginx/conf.d/rate-limit.conf (http context; shared zones live here) limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=10r/s; limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=login:10m rate=5r/m; limit_conn_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=perip:10m; # WebSocket support: choose Connection header based on the Upgrade header map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade { default upgrade; '' close; } # /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp upstream app_backend { server 127.0.0.1:3000; # server 127.0.0.1:3001; # add more for load balancing keepalive 32; # reuse connections to the app } server { listen 80; server_name example.com www.example.com; # Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 and everything else redirects location /.well-known/acme-challenge/ { root /var/www/certbot; } location / { return 301 https://example.com$request_uri; } } server { listen 443 ssl; http2 on; server_name example.com; ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem; ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:10m; add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000" always; add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always; add_header X-Frame-Options "DENY" always; add_header Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin" always; client_max_body_size 10m; # default 1m: uploads above get 413 limit_conn perip 50; # --- Compression -------------------------------------------------- gzip on; gzip_comp_level 5; gzip_min_length 1024; gzip_vary on; gzip_proxied any; gzip_types text/plain text/css text/javascript application/javascript application/json application/xml image/svg+xml; # Images/video are already compressed: do not list them. # --- Static files served directly by nginx ------------------------ root /var/www/myapp/current/public; location /assets/ { expires 1y; add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable"; try_files $uri =404; access_log off; } # --- API with rate limiting -------------------------------------- location /api/ { limit_req zone=api burst=20 nodelay; limit_req_status 429; proxy_pass http://app_backend; include /etc/nginx/snippets/proxy.conf; } location = /api/login { limit_req zone=login burst=3 nodelay; limit_req_status 429; proxy_pass http://app_backend; include /etc/nginx/snippets/proxy.conf; } # --- WebSockets --------------------------------------------------- location /socket.io/ { proxy_pass http://app_backend; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_read_timeout 3600s; # keep idle sockets open for an hour proxy_send_timeout 3600s; } # --- Everything else goes to the app ------------------------------- location / { proxy_pass http://app_backend; include /etc/nginx/snippets/proxy.conf; } # Health endpoint not exposed publicly beyond the LB location = /nginx-health { access_log off; return 200 "ok\n"; } } # /etc/nginx/snippets/proxy.conf proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Connection ""; # required for upstream keepalive proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_connect_timeout 5s; proxy_read_timeout 60s; proxy_send_timeout 60s; What each part does Directive Why upstream ... keepalive 32 Avoids a TCP handshake per request to the app. Needs proxy_http_version 1.1 and an empty Connection header. gzip_types Text compresses 70 to 90 percent; text/html is always on. Brotli needs a module; often done at the CDN. expires 1y + immutable For fingerprinted build assets. Never for HTML. limit_req zone=api burst=20 nodelay Average 10 req/s per IP, tolerate bursts of 20 immediately, reject the rest with 429. Upgrade / Connection headers Required for the HTTP Upgrade handshake that creates a WebSocket. Without it you get 400 or silent fallback to polling. proxy_read_timeout 3600s for sockets Default 60 s would kill idle WebSockets. (Or send app-level pings.) always on add_header Otherwise headers are omitted on error responses. Example 3: serving a single-page app and an API server { listen 443 ssl; http2 on; server_name app.example.com; # ssl_* omitted root /var/www/spa/dist; index index.html; location /api/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000; include snippets/proxy.conf; } location /assets/ { expires 1y; add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable"; } # index.html must not be cached long, so deploys take effect location = /index.html { add_header Cache-Control "no-cache"; } # Client-side routing: unknown paths return index.html location / { try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html; } } Example 4: several apps behind one nginx server { listen 443 ssl; server_name api.example.com; location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000; } } server { listen 443 ssl; server_name admin.example.com; location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:4000; } } server { listen 443 ssl default_server; server_name _; ssl_reject_handshake on; } # unknown hosts Debugging nginx Symptom Likely cause (check error.log ) 502 Bad Gateway, "connect() failed (111: Connection refused)" App is down or on a different port/address 502, "upstream prematurely closed connection" App crashed mid-request or keep-alive mismatch 504, "upstream timed out" App too slow; raise proxy_read_timeout only if truly needed 413 Request Entity Too Large client_max_body_size Wrong site served No matching server_name ; falls to the default server 403 on static files nginx user ( www-data ) cannot read the path (directory execute bits!) Change not visible Forgot reload, or the browser/CDN cached the old response Real IPs not logged Behind a CDN/LB: use the realip module ( set_real_ip_from , real_ip_header ) Useful: sudo nginx -T dumps the entire effective config; curl -I -H 'Host: example.com' http://127.0.0.1/ tests a vhost locally; custom log_format with $request_time and $upstream_response_time shows where latency is. Alternatives and trade-offs Tool Strength Consider when nginx Fast, ubiquitous, great docs Default choice Caddy Automatic HTTPS, tiny config You want the simplest possible setup Traefik Dynamic config from Docker/K8s labels Containerised environments HAProxy / Envoy Advanced load balancing, observability Heavy traffic, service meshes Apache httpd .htaccess, legacy PHP Legacy stacks Caddy equivalent of Examples 1 plus HTTPS in full: example.com { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000 } . That is the whole file, and certificates are obtained and renewed automatically. Try it Run a tiny backend: python3 -m http.server 3000 --bind 127.0.0.1 . Install nginx and write Example 1 so http://your-server/ reaches it. Stop the backend and request the site. Find the matching line in error.log and the 502 in access.log . Add the /assets/ block and verify headers with curl -I . Add rate limiting rate=1r/s burst=2 and fire for i in $(seq 1 10); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' localhost/api/; done . See the 429s. Test the trailing-slash behaviour by logging the incoming path in a tiny app, with and without the slash on proxy_pass . Break the config on purpose and see nginx -t catch it before reload.

title: Load Balancers
text: Load Balancers One server is a single point of failure and a scaling ceiling. A load balancer spreads traffic over many servers, removes unhealthy ones automatically, and lets you deploy without downtime. The problem With one app server: when it crashes, you are down; when you deploy, you are down; when traffic doubles, you are slow. Adding a second server does not help by itself, because clients need a single address to talk to. A load balancer (LB) is that address. It accepts connections and forwards each to one of several backends. ┌──▶ app-1 10.0.1.11:3000 healthy Clients ──▶ LB ────────┼──▶ app-2 10.0.1.12:3000 healthy (one address) │ └──▶ app-3 10.0.1.13:3000 FAILED health check: removed from rotation │ └─ periodically probes GET /health on each backend Benefits: availability (failed nodes bypassed), scalability (add nodes), zero-downtime deploys (drain one node at a time), TLS offload , a single place for logging and WAF rules. Layer 4 vs Layer 7 L4 (transport) L7 (application) Sees IPs, ports, TCP/UDP HTTP: host, path, headers, cookies Decision based on Connection 4-tuple Request content Speed Very fast, millions of connections More CPU (parses and often terminates TLS) Features Pass-through, any protocol (Postgres, MQTT, SMTP, gRPC raw) Path/host routing, redirects, header rewrite, WAF, sticky cookies, HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1 TLS Usually passes through encrypted traffic Usually terminates TLS Examples AWS NLB, HAProxy mode tcp , nginx stream , IPVS AWS ALB, HAProxy mode http , nginx http , Envoy, Traefik Rule of thumb: use L7 for web apps and APIs (routing by path is invaluable: /api to one pool, / to another). Use L4 for non-HTTP protocols, extreme throughput, static IPs, or when you must preserve end-to-end TLS. Balancing algorithms Algorithm How Best for / caveat Round robin Rotate through servers in order Equal servers, similar request costs. Ignores load. Weighted round robin Servers get a share proportional to weight Mixed instance sizes; also canary (weight 5 to the new node) Least connections Send to the server with fewest active connections Long or uneven requests, WebSockets Least response time Fewest connections plus fastest responses Heterogeneous backends IP hash / consistent hash Same client (or key) maps to same server Cheap stickiness; per-key caches. Skews behind NAT. Random (power of two choices) Pick two at random, take the less loaded Large pools; avoids herd effects Health checks The LB is only as good as its health checks. Two kinds: Passive : observe real traffic; mark a backend down after N failures (nginx max_fails ). Active : the LB probes an endpoint on an interval (HAProxy check , ALB target group health checks). Typical settings: probe every 5 to 10 s, mark unhealthy after 2 to 3 failures, healthy after 2 to 5 successes, timeout 2 to 5 s. // A useful /health endpoint (Express) app.get('/health', async (req, res) => { try { await db.query('SELECT 1'); // can I do my job? res.status(200).json({ status: 'ok', version: process.env.GIT_SHA }); } catch (e) { res.status(503).json({ status: 'degraded' }); } }); Shallow vs deep health checks A check that only returns 200 hides a broken database connection. But a check that fails whenever any dependency (a third-party API) is down can make the LB eject every node at once, turning a partial outage into a total one. Prefer: liveness (process responds) for restart decisions, readiness (can serve traffic: DB reachable, caches warm) for LB membership, and never check non-essential dependencies. Connection draining When removing a node (deploy, scale-in) the LB should stop sending new requests but let in-flight ones finish: "connection draining" (ALB: deregistration delay , default 300 s; lower it to match your longest request). Combined with graceful shutdown in your app (see the zero-downtime lesson), deploys drop no requests. Session stickiness If the app keeps user session state in server memory, the user must keep hitting the same server, or they appear logged out. Options: Sticky sessions : LB sets a cookie (ALB duration-based or app cookie; HAProxy cookie SERVERID insert ) or hashes the client IP. Externalise state (preferred) : sessions in Redis or a database, or stateless signed tokens (JWT). Any server can then handle any request. Stickiness hurts: uneven load, lost sessions when a node dies, awkward scaling and draining. Treat it as a stopgap and design services stateless (a core 12-factor principle). nginx as a simple load balancer upstream app_pool { least_conn; server 10.0.1.11:3000 weight=3 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=15s; server 10.0.1.12:3000 weight=1; server 10.0.1.13:3000 backup; # used only if the others are down keepalive 64; } server { listen 80; location / { proxy_pass http://app_pool; proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502 http_503; # retry another node proxy_next_upstream_tries 2; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Connection ""; proxy_set_header Host $host; } } Open-source nginx has only passive health checks (active probes need nginx Plus). Be careful with proxy_next_upstream and non-idempotent requests: nginx does not retry POST by default after the request was sent unless you add non_idempotent . HAProxy example HAProxy is a dedicated, extremely efficient LB with rich active health checks and stats. # /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg global log /dev/log local0 maxconn 20000 defaults mode http log global option httplog timeout connect 5s timeout client 30s timeout server 30s frontend https_in bind :80 bind :443 ssl crt /etc/haproxy/certs/example.pem alpn h2,http/1.1 http-request redirect scheme https unless { ssl_fc } http-request set-header X-Forwarded-Proto https if { ssl_fc } acl is_api path_beg /api use_backend api_pool if is_api default_backend web_pool backend web_pool balance roundrobin option httpchk GET /health http-check expect status 200 server web1 10.0.1.11:3000 check inter 5s fall 3 rise 2 server web2 10.0.1.12:3000 check inter 5s fall 3 rise 2 backend api_pool balance leastconn cookie SERVERID insert indirect nocache # sticky sessions option httpchk GET /health server api1 10.0.1.21:4000 check cookie a1 server api2 10.0.1.22:4000 check cookie a2 listen stats bind 127.0.0.1:8404 stats enable stats uri /stats haproxy -c -f /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg # validate sudo systemctl reload haproxy Managed load balancers (AWS example) Service Layer Notes ALB (Application LB) L7 Host/path routing, TLS via ACM certs, WebSockets, gRPC, auth via OIDC, WAF integration, target groups (instances, IPs, Lambda, containers) NLB (Network LB) L4 Static IPs, ultra-low latency, TCP/UDP/TLS GWLB L3 Insert firewall appliances Key ALB concepts: listeners (port 443 with a certificate) have rules (if host is api.example.com or path is /img/* ) that forward to target groups , each with a health check config. Put the ALB in at least two Availability Zones, targets in private subnets, and a security group allowing 80/443 from the internet while the targets allow traffic only from the ALB's security group . GCP (Cloud Load Balancing) and Azure (Application Gateway / Front Door) offer equivalents; Kubernetes Ingress and Service type LoadBalancer provision them for you. Is the load balancer itself a single point of failure? Yes, if you run one. Solutions: managed LBs are redundant across zones by design; self-hosted ones use two nodes with a floating IP (keepalived/VRRP), or DNS with multiple A records, or anycast. This is why teams usually pay for the managed one. Pitfalls Real client IP lost : backends see the LB's IP. Use X-Forwarded-For (L7) or the PROXY protocol (L4). Idle timeout mismatches : app keep-alive shorter than LB idle timeout causes sporadic 502/504. Uneven deploys : new version unhealthy but health check too shallow: LB sends traffic to broken nodes. Thundering herd after restart : all nodes start cold and are marked healthy before caches/JIT are warm. Use slow-start (ALB slow start mode, HAProxy slowstart ). Retry storms : aggressive retries on a struggling backend amplify the overload. Stateful in-memory data (uploads on local disk, in-memory sessions or caches) breaks the moment there are two servers. Try it Start three tiny backends that print their port: for p in 3001 3002 3003; do (python3 -m http.server $p --bind 127.0.0.1 &); done (or three Node processes returning their PID). Configure the nginx upstream above with those ports. Request repeatedly: for i in $(seq 6); do curl -s localhost/ | head -1; done and watch the distribution; try weight and least_conn . Kill one backend. Observe failed requests (and then none, once nginx has marked it down or retried with proxy_next_upstream ). Install HAProxy, use the config above with check , open the stats page and watch a backend flip to DOWN when stopped. Write down: which of your app's state lives in memory or on local disk and would break behind a load balancer?

title: Firewalls and Security Groups
text: Firewalls and Security Groups The moment a server gets a public IP, automated scanners find it, usually within minutes. A firewall decides which network traffic is allowed in and out. The guiding principle is simple: expose only what must be exposed. The problem A default server may run SSH, a database, a metrics endpoint, and a debug port, all listening on every interface. Each open port is attack surface. Real incidents: Redis or MongoDB listening publicly with no password (instantly ransomed), Elasticsearch dumps leaking millions of records, SSH brute force. Many are not software bugs, only things that should never have been reachable. Firewalls enforce least exposure : deny everything by default, then allow specific ports from specific sources. How packet filtering works A firewall matches each packet (or connection) against an ordered rule list using source/destination IP, port and protocol, then ACCEPTs, DROPs (silently discard; scanner sees a timeout) or REJECTs (reply with an error; sees "refused"). Stateful firewalls track connections. If you allowed an outbound request, the reply is automatically allowed back in. Almost everything today (iptables conntrack, nftables, security groups) is stateful. Stateless filters (AWS Network ACLs) evaluate each packet in isolation, so you must allow both directions including ephemeral return ports. Default policy matters most: default deny inbound, allow outbound . Layers of defence Internet │ ▼ [ CDN / WAF ] filters HTTP attacks, absorbs DDoS │ [ Cloud firewall ] security groups / NACLs: outside the VM, cannot be disabled by an intruder on the box │ [ Host firewall ] ufw / nftables on the server itself │ [ Service binding ] app listens on 127.0.0.1 or private IP only │ [ App authn/authz ] Defence in depth: any single layer may be misconfigured; several rarely fail together. ufw: the simple host firewall (Ubuntu) ufw ("uncomplicated firewall") is a friendly front-end for the kernel's netfilter. Critical: allow SSH before enabling , or you lock yourself out of a remote machine. sudo ufw status verbose sudo ufw default deny incoming sudo ufw default allow outgoing sudo ufw allow OpenSSH # or: sudo ufw allow 22/tcp sudo ufw allow 80/tcp sudo ufw allow 443/tcp sudo ufw allow 443/udp # HTTP/3 # Restrict SSH to your office/home IP (better) and rate-limit brute force sudo ufw allow from 203.0.113.7 to any port 22 proto tcp sudo ufw limit 22/tcp # alternative: throttle repeated connection attempts # Allow DB only from the app server's private IP sudo ufw allow from 10.0.1.11 to any port 5432 proto tcp sudo ufw enable sudo ufw status numbered sudo ufw delete 3 # delete rule number 3 Docker bypasses ufw Docker inserts its own iptables rules for published ports ( -p 8080:80 ), and they are evaluated before ufw's. A container published like that is reachable from the internet even though ufw status shows it denied. Bind to loopback instead ( -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 ), put a cloud security group in front, or manage rules in the DOCKER-USER chain. iptables and nftables: the concept Underneath ufw is the kernel's netfilter. iptables (older) and nftables (current default on modern distros; iptables is often a compatibility shim) organise rules into tables and chains . The main chains for a host: INPUT (to this machine), OUTPUT (from it), FORWARD (routed through it, e.g. container traffic). Rules are checked top to bottom; first match wins; then the chain's default policy applies. # Show rules sudo iptables -L -n -v --line-numbers # A minimal stateful ruleset (conceptual) sudo iptables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT sudo iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT sudo iptables -P INPUT DROP # default policy: drop everything else # nftables equivalent table inet filter { chain input { type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop; iif lo accept ct state established,related accept tcp dport { 22, 80, 443 } accept } } Rules set with these commands vanish on reboot unless persisted ( netfilter-persistent , or /etc/nftables.conf ). Most people should use ufw/firewalld or cloud security groups and learn raw iptables only for debugging. Cloud security groups A security group (AWS; GCP calls them firewall rules, Azure NSGs) is a stateful firewall enforced by the hypervisor around each instance's network interface. You only write allow rules; anything not allowed is denied. Rules specify protocol, port range and a source: a CIDR or another security group . The security-group-as-source feature is the key to clean architecture: 0.0.0.0/0 ──443──▶ [ sg-alb ] │ 3000 (source: sg-alb) ▼ [ sg-app ] │ 5432 (source: sg-app) ▼ [ sg-db ] no public IP at all, private subnet Your IP/32 ──22──▶ bastion/SSM (or use SSM Session Manager and open no SSH at all) Group Inbound rules sg-alb TCP 80, 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 sg-app TCP 3000 from sg-alb ; TCP 22 from your admin IP only sg-db TCP 5432 from sg-app . Nothing else. Even if someone learns the database IP, the network will not let them connect. AWS CLI example: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0app \ --protocol tcp --port 3000 --source-group sg-0alb aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0app \ --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 203.0.113.7/32 Compare with Network ACLs : stateless, subnet-level, allow and deny rules, evaluated in numeric order. Use as a coarse second layer (for example to block a hostile CIDR); do most work in security groups. Least exposure checklist Inventory : sudo ss -tlnp on every server. For each listener ask "does it need to exist, and for whom?" Bind to localhost or a private IP when the only client is local or internal. Databases: listen_addresses = 'localhost' in Postgres unless remote access is required; Redis bind 127.0.0.1 and requirepass . Public ports: 80 and 443 only. Not 3000, not 5432, not 6379, not 9090 (Prometheus), not 2375 (Docker API, equivalent to root). SSH : keys only, PasswordAuthentication no , PermitRootLogin no , restrict by source IP or use a VPN/bastion/SSM; optionally fail2ban. Egress : allow outbound by default, but sensitive environments restrict it to limit data exfiltration and malware calling home. Use private subnets for databases and internal services; use a NAT gateway for their outbound needs. Audit regularly : security groups with 0.0.0.0/0 on anything but 80/443 deserve a ticket. Tools: AWS Config rules, Security Hub, Trivy/Prowler, nmap . Verifying from the outside # From a machine OUTSIDE your network: what does the world see? nmap -Pn -p 1-1000 your.server.ip # scan only systems you own or are authorised to test nmap -Pn -p 22,80,443,3000,5432,6379 your.server.ip nc -zv -w 3 your.server.ip 5432 # expect timeout (dropped), not open # On the server: what is actually listening, and which rules are active? sudo ss -tlnp sudo ufw status verbose Interpreting nmap states: open (something answered), closed (reachable host, nothing listening: RST), filtered (packets dropped by a firewall). A DROP policy yields filtered , which also slows scanners down. Pitfalls Locking yourself out by enabling a firewall without an SSH rule. Cloud consoles can fix it; bare VPSs often need a recovery console. Keep a second session open while testing. "Temporary" 0.0.0.0/0 rules that become permanent. Add a description and an owner to every rule. Dynamic home IPs in SSH allow-lists: you get locked out when it changes. Use a VPN with a fixed address or SSM. Forgetting IPv6 : a rule for 0.0.0.0/0 but none for ::/0 (or vice versa), or ufw IPv6 disabled while the service listens on :: . Firewall as the only protection : services should still authenticate. Internal networks get breached too. Debugging blind : dropped packets produce timeouts and no log. Enable VPC Flow Logs or ufw logging on to see rejects. Try it On a throwaway Ubuntu VM or VPS, keep one SSH session open, then apply: ufw default deny incoming , ufw allow OpenSSH , ufw allow 80,443/tcp , ufw enable . Open a second SSH session to confirm you can still get in. Run python3 -m http.server 8000 on the box. From your laptop, curl it: it should time out. Then sudo ufw allow 8000/tcp and retry. Remove the rule afterwards. From your laptop, run nmap -Pn -p 22,80,443,8000,5432 SERVER_IP before and after. Note the open/filtered states. In a cloud account, sketch the three security groups from this lesson and write the exact inbound rules. Which instances need a public IP? (Answer: only the load balancer, and possibly none other.) Run sudo ss -tlnp on a server you own and justify each listening port or close it.

title: CDNs and Caching
text: CDNs and Caching Physics sets a floor on latency: a round trip from Sydney to a server in Virginia costs roughly 200 ms, however fast your code is. A CDN puts copies of your content near users and absorbs traffic before it ever reaches your servers. The problem a CDN solves Latency : distance. Several round trips for TCP, TLS and HTTP add up. Origin load : every image, script and font request hits your server. A traffic spike (front page of Hacker News) can topple it. Bandwidth cost : egress from a cloud provider is expensive; CDN egress is usually cheaper, sometimes free. Availability and attacks : DDoS traffic must be absorbed somewhere; a CDN's distributed network has far more capacity than one origin. How a CDN works A CDN is a globally distributed fleet of caching reverse proxies called edge servers (points of presence, PoPs). Your origin is your real server. Users are steered to a nearby edge, via anycast routing or DNS that answers with the closest PoP. User (Sydney) ──▶ Edge PoP (Sydney) │ ├─ HIT: has fresh copy → returns it in ~10 ms. Origin never sees the request. │ └─ MISS: fetch from origin ───────────────▶ Origin (Virginia) store copy (obey Cache-Control) ◀── response return to user Next Sydney user: HIT. Many CDNs add an intermediate shield / tiered cache layer so that dozens of edges missing at once result in one request to the origin, not dozens. Setup in the common "proxy" model: you change your domain's DNS (or name servers) so www.example.com points at the CDN, which is configured with your origin address. Users hit the CDN; the CDN talks to you. Your origin firewall can then accept traffic only from the CDN's IP ranges. What gets cached? Static assets : JS, CSS, images, fonts, video segments, downloads. Cached by default by file extension in most CDNs. HTML and API responses : only if you opt in or your headers allow it ( Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60 ). Hugely effective for public, read-heavy content (news, product pages, public APIs). Never cache personalised or authenticated responses with shared caches. Mark them Cache-Control: private or no-store . The cache key The CDN decides "is this the same request?" using a cache key : normally scheme + host + path + query string. Rules matter: Tracking parameters ( ?utm_source=... ) make each URL unique and tank your hit ratio; configure the CDN to ignore them. Vary: Accept-Encoding and Vary: Accept-Language multiply cache entries. Vary: Cookie effectively disables caching. By default, requests with cookies or an Authorization header are often not cached; verify for your CDN. Measure cache hit ratio (hits divided by total). For static sites aim for above 95 percent. Check responses for headers such as CF-Cache-Status: HIT (Cloudflare), X-Cache: Hit from cloudfront (CloudFront), or Age: 253 (seconds in cache). Cache control: telling the CDN what to do # Origin response headers # Fingerprinted build artefacts: cache everywhere for a year Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable # Public HTML or API: edge caches 5 min; browsers always revalidate Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=300 # Serve stale content while refreshing, and keep serving it if origin errors Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300, stale-if-error=86400 # Personalised Cache-Control: private, no-store s-maxage targets shared caches (CDN) separately from the browser's max-age , allowing "CDN caches 5 minutes; users' browsers always ask the CDN". stale-if-error is a free resilience feature: if your origin falls over, users still see the last good copy. Cache invalidation "There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things." When content changes, stale copies sit at hundreds of edges and in users' browsers. Strategies, best first: Cache busting by fingerprinting (best). Put a content hash in the file name: app.3f9c1a7b.js . A new build produces a new URL; old URLs stay cached harmlessly. Nothing to invalidate. Webpack, Vite, Next.js and most bundlers do this by default. Only the HTML that references the files needs a short TTL.
