Short TTLs for content that changes unpredictably: 30 to 300 s caps staleness and still shields the origin from spikes ("micro-caching"). Purge by URL / tag / prefix / everything. Explicit API calls on content change. Tag-based purging (Cloudflare Cache-Tags, Fastly surrogate keys) lets you purge "all pages that mention product 42". Purge propagates in seconds to a minute, depending on the CDN. Versioned paths ( /v2/api/... ), with query strings ( ?v=123 ) as a weaker form. # Cloudflare: purge specific URLs (API token with Cache Purge permission) curl -X POST "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/$ZONE_ID/purge_cache" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CF_API_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data '{"files":["https://example.com/index.html","https://example.com/pricing"]}' # Purge everything (use sparingly: the next minute hits your origin hard) curl -X POST "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/$ZONE_ID/purge_cache" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CF_API_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data '{"purge_everything":true}' # AWS CloudFront invalidation aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id E123ABC --paths "/index.html" "/blog/*" The deploy pattern for frontends Upload hashed assets first (immutable, one-year cache), then upload the small index.html last ( no-cache or a short s-maxage), and purge only index.html . Users then never see HTML pointing at assets that do not exist yet, and never see old assets that were cleaned up too early. Keep the previous build's assets around for a while: users with an old page open still request them. Cloudflare in practice Cloudflare is the most common starting point because the free tier is generous and setup is only a DNS change. Add your domain; Cloudflare scans existing DNS records. Change your registrar's NS to the two Cloudflare name servers. For each record, the cloud icon is Proxied (orange: traffic goes via Cloudflare, you get CDN/WAF and your origin IP is hidden) or DNS only (grey: plain DNS). Proxy web traffic; do not proxy SSH, mail or database hostnames (non-HTTP ports are not proxied on the free plan). SSL/TLS mode: use Full (strict) : Cloudflare connects to your origin over HTTPS and validates the certificate (install a Let's Encrypt or Cloudflare Origin Certificate on the origin). Flexible mode sends plain HTTP to the origin and invites redirect loops and interception; avoid it. Turn on "Always Use HTTPS", HTTP/3, Brotli, and Auto Minify/Rocket features as appropriate. Add Cache Rules (what to cache, edge TTL, bypass for /admin and /api ). Lock the origin: allow 80/443 only from Cloudflare's published IP ranges (cloudflare.com/ips), or use Authenticated Origin Pulls / Cloudflare Tunnel ( cloudflared ) so the origin needs no inbound ports at all. Note: by default Cloudflare caches by file extension (static assets), not HTML. To cache HTML, add a Cache Rule ("Eligible for cache") and set edge TTL or respect origin headers. Other CDNs: Amazon CloudFront (tight AWS integration, S3 origins with Origin Access Control), Fastly (instant purge, VCL/Compute programmability), Akamai (enterprise), Bunny.net (cheap, simple), Vercel/Netlify (built in). More than caching TLS termination near the user : the expensive handshake is short-haul; the CDN reuses long-lived connections to the origin. DDoS mitigation and WAF : block bad traffic at the edge; rate limiting; bot management. Image optimisation : resizing and converting to WebP/AVIF per device. Edge compute (Cloudflare Workers, CloudFront Functions/Lambda@Edge, Fastly Compute): run small code at the edge for redirects, A/B tests, auth checks, header rewriting. Origin failover and load balancing across origins. Caching layers overall Layer Where Controlled by Browser cache User's device Cache-Control: max-age , ETag CDN edge Near the user s-maxage , CDN rules, purge Reverse proxy cache nginx proxy_cache , Varnish Config Application cache Redis, memcached, in-process Your code, TTLs, explicit deletes Database Buffer pool, query cache Engine Every layer is a place where stale data can hide. When "my change does not show up", walk the layers from the browser inwards: hard-refresh, curl -I to see the CDN status header, curl the origin directly, then check app caches. Pitfalls Caching a response that contains user data and serving it to others. This is a serious security incident. Default to private for anything personalised and test with two accounts. Caching error pages : a transient 500 cached for an hour. Make sure errors are not cacheable, or use short negative TTLs. Long TTL on non-fingerprinted files ( style.css cached for a year, unfixable except by purge). Origin IP leaks (old DNS records, mail headers) let attackers bypass the CDN. Firewall the origin to CDN ranges. Purging everything during peak : cold cache plus full traffic equals an origin outage ("cache stampede"). Use request coalescing/tiered caching and purge selectively. Treating CDN as a fix for a slow app : dynamic, uncacheable requests still go to your origin. Cookies on static domains can make assets uncacheable. Serve static content from cookieless paths/hosts. Try it Run curl -sI https://www.cloudflare.com/ | grep -iE 'cf-cache-status|age|cache-control|server' . Run it twice and watch Age . Compare headers for an HTML page versus a hashed asset ( .js ) on a large site. How do their Cache-Control values differ and why? Put a free Cloudflare account in front of a domain pointing at a small VPS. Request a static file twice and confirm cf-cache-status: HIT on the second. Change the file on the origin. Request it again: you get the old content. Purge that URL through the dashboard or API and fetch again. Add a hashed filename to a test asset instead of purging, and notice no purge is required. Restrict your origin's firewall ( ufw allow from <CF range> to any port 443 ) and confirm direct access to the origin IP fails while the proxied domain works.

title: Static vs Dynamic Hosting: What Goes Where
text: Static vs Dynamic Hosting: What Goes Where Before choosing tools, decide what kind of thing you are deploying. A pile of HTML and JavaScript files and a long-running server process have very different needs, costs and failure modes. Picking the simplest hosting that fits is the cheapest optimisation in DevOps. Why this decision comes first Many teams run a full server (OS patches, process manager, nginx, monitoring) to serve files that could be uploaded to a CDN for pennies with no servers to maintain. Others try to run a stateful, long-lived backend on a platform built only for static files and hit a wall. Match the hosting model to the workload. Static content Static means the bytes served are the same for every user and exist before the request arrives: HTML, CSS, JS, images, PDFs. A server (if any) only reads files and returns them. Examples: a marketing site, documentation (like this one), a blog built with a static site generator (Hugo, Astro, Jekyll, Eleventy), and a single-page app (React, Vue, Angular) compiled to a dist/ folder. An SPA is static hosting plus a separate API: the browser downloads files, then JavaScript calls the backend. npm run build ──▶ dist/ (index.html, assets/app.3f9c.js, ...) │ upload ▼ Object storage + CDN (S3+CloudFront, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages) ▲ Users ───────────────┘ served from the nearest edge. No server of yours is involved. Why it is great: no servers to patch, nothing to crash, virtually infinite scale, global speed, very low cost (often free), and a tiny attack surface (no code executing on the server means nothing to exploit there). Dynamic content Dynamic means code runs per request: reads a database, checks a session, calls other services, builds a response. REST/GraphQL APIs, server-rendered pages (Rails, Django, Laravel, Express with templates), WebSockets, background workers, cron jobs. Why it needs more: it needs a runtime, a process that stays up, secrets, a database, scaling for CPU/memory, deployments that do not drop requests, logging and monitoring. It is where most DevOps work lives. The spectrum Many sites live in between: Model What it means Example Pure static Built once, files served as-is Docs site, blog Static + API (JAMstack) Static front-end calls APIs / third-party services React SPA + Stripe + a backend Static generation with revalidation (ISR) Pages pre-built, regenerated in the background Next.js product catalogue Server-side rendering (SSR) HTML produced on demand per request Next.js/Nuxt/Remix app with personalised pages Classic dynamic app Server + database process Django, Rails, Express + Postgres Real-time / stateful Persistent connections Chat, multiplayer, collaboration Batch / event-driven No HTTP; jobs on a schedule or queue Image processing, emails, ETL A useful trick: make as much static as possible . A product page that changes hourly can be a cached or pre-rendered file, not a database query per visitor. Where to host: the options Option Best for You manage Typical cost Static hosts : GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel, S3+CloudFront, Firebase Hosting Static sites and SPAs Just your build output Free to a few dollars PaaS : Heroku, Render, Railway, Fly.io, DigitalOcean App Platform, Google Cloud Run, Azure App Service, AWS Elastic Beanstalk Dynamic apps when you want to push code, not run servers App + config; platform handles OS, TLS, scaling, rollouts $5 to hundreds / month Serverless functions : AWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers, Vercel/Netlify Functions Spiky, event-driven, small APIs Function code; limits on runtime, cold starts Pay per invocation; often tiny VPS (virtual private server): DigitalOcean Droplet, Hetzner, Linode, Lightsail, EC2 Full control; predictable cost; learning Everything: OS, patches, nginx, backups, monitoring $4 to $40 / month for typical small apps Containers on managed orchestration : ECS/Fargate, GKE, EKS, AKS Many services, teams, scale Images, cluster config Higher; needs expertise Bare metal / on-prem Special hardware, compliance, huge steady load Everything, including hardware Capex / colocation Decision flow Does any code need to run on a server per request? │ ├─ No ──▶ Static host + CDN. Done. │ └─ Yes ─▶ Need persistent connections, long jobs, or local state? │ ├─ No, small/spiky ──▶ Serverless functions (+ managed DB) │ └─ Yes / typical web app │ ├─ Small team, want speed of shipping ──▶ PaaS (Render, Fly, Cloud Run, Heroku) ├─ Want control / cheap / to learn ──▶ VPS + nginx + systemd (next lesson) └─ Many services, scale, platform team ──▶ Containers + Kubernetes/ECS Trade-offs in depth PaaS versus VPS PaaS VPS Time to first deploy Minutes ( git push ) An hour or more first time Ops burden Low: patching, TLS, restarts handled High: all yours Cost at small scale Higher per unit of compute Cheapest Cost at large scale Can become very expensive Cheaper, but engineer time counts Flexibility Constrained by platform Anything Lock-in Some (platform-specific features); less if you use containers Low Learning value Hides the fundamentals Teaches everything in this handbook Neither is "better". A common path: start on a PaaS, move to containers when you outgrow it. Learning on a VPS first makes every later abstraction understandable, which is why the next lesson is a full manual deployment. Serverless Pros: no idle cost, automatic scaling to zero and to thousands, no servers. Cons: cold-start latency, execution time limits, awkward with persistent database connections (use a pooler/proxy), harder local debugging, vendor-specific APIs, costs that can spike unpredictably under sustained high load. Don't forget the supporting pieces Whatever hosts the app, you also need decisions for: Database : managed (RDS, Cloud SQL, Neon, Supabase, PlanetScale) versus self-run on the VPS. Managed gives backups and failover for a fee. Self-run is cheap but you own backups and recovery. File uploads : object storage (S3), never the app server's local disk if you may ever run two servers. Background jobs and cron : where does the worker run? DNS, TLS, email sending, monitoring : each a separate service or setup. Rule of thumb Use the highest-level thing that meets your needs. Static host before PaaS, PaaS before VPS, VPS before Kubernetes, unless you have a concrete reason (cost, control, compliance, learning). Complexity is a cost you pay every day, not once. Worked example: one product, three hosting choices A SaaS has a marketing site, a React dashboard, a REST API with Postgres, and nightly report generation. Part Hosting Why Marketing site (Astro) Cloudflare Pages Static; free; global Dashboard (React SPA) S3 + CloudFront or Netlify Static files; calls the API API (Node/Express) VPS or Cloud Run/Fly.io Dynamic; needs process, secrets, DB access Postgres Managed Postgres Backups and failover handled Nightly reports Scheduled job (cron on the VPS, or a Cloud Run job) No HTTP needed Three kinds of hosting in one product is normal. The DNS records tie them together: www to the CDN, app to the SPA host, api to the server. Pitfalls Running an SSR framework in "static export" mode and wondering why dynamic routes 404, or the reverse. SPA deep links returning 404 on refresh: static hosts need a rewrite of unknown paths to index.html (nginx try_files , Netlify _redirects , CloudFront custom error response). CORS: API and SPA on different origins need explicit CORS headers on the API. Putting secrets in front-end bundles. Anything shipped to the browser is public. API keys that must stay secret belong on a server or function. Running state (uploads, sessions, SQLite files) on ephemeral PaaS or serverless filesystems; it vanishes on restart. Choosing Kubernetes for a single app with ten users. Try it Take an existing project (or npm create vite@latest ) and run the build. Look at the output folder: could any web server serve it as-is? That is a static deploy. Deploy that folder for free to GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages or Netlify. Note the URL, the TLS certificate and the response headers ( curl -I ). Test the SPA refresh problem: open a deep link, refresh, and add the rewrite rule your host needs. List the components of an app you work on. For each, classify static / dynamic / job / data and name the simplest hosting that could work. Compare the monthly cost of a $6 VPS, a PaaS tier running one small container, and a serverless function at 1 million requests. Which is cheapest at your real traffic?

title: Manual Deploy to a VPS: Node.js, Postgres, nginx, HTTPS
text: Manual Deploy to a VPS: Node.js, Postgres, nginx, HTTPS This is the capstone of the first half of the handbook: take an Express app with a Postgres database from your laptop to a real domain over HTTPS on an Ubuntu server, by hand. Everything later (CI/CD, Docker, Terraform) automates exactly these steps, so doing them manually once is how you understand what the automation is doing. What we will build Browser ──HTTPS 443──▶ nginx ──▶ Express (127.0.0.1:3000, systemd service, user "deploy") │ │ certbot cert Postgres (127.0.0.1:5432) DNS: app.example.com ──▶ VPS public IP ufw: only 22, 80, 443 open Assumptions: a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 LTS VPS (DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Linode, EC2...) with a public IP and root or sudo SSH access; a domain you control; an Express app in a Git repo with package.json , a start script, and a /health route. Replace 203.0.113.10 , app.example.com , you and the repo URL with yours. Step 0: The sample app Your app should read its configuration from the environment (see the config lesson), listen on 127.0.0.1 behind the proxy, and expose a health check: // server.js const express = require('express'); const { Pool } = require('pg'); const app = express(); app.set('trust proxy', 1); // we sit behind nginx const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL }); app.get('/health', async (req, res) => { try { await pool.query('SELECT 1'); res.json({ status: 'ok' }); } catch (e) { res.status(503).json({ status: 'db_unreachable' }); } }); app.get('/', (req, res) => res.send('Hello from ' + (process.env.NODE_ENV || 'dev'))); const port = process.env.PORT || 3000; const host = process.env.HOST || '127.0.0.1'; const server = app.listen(port, host, () => console.log(`listening on ${host}:${port}`)); process.on('SIGTERM', () => { // graceful shutdown (systemd sends SIGTERM) server.close(() => pool.end().then(() => process.exit(0))); }); // package.json (relevant part) { "scripts": { "start": "node server.js" }, "engines": { "node": ">=22" } } Step 1: Point DNS at the server Do this first, because DNS takes time to be visible and certificates need it. At your DNS provider, create A app 203.0.113.10 with TTL 300 (and an AAAA record if the VPS has IPv6). Verify from your laptop: dig +short app.example.com should print the IP. Step 2: First login and a non-root user Running everything as root means any bug is a total compromise. Create two accounts: an admin (sudo) for you, and a service account that runs the app with minimal privileges. ssh root@203.0.113.10 apt update && apt -y upgrade timedatectl set-timezone UTC # Admin user with sudo adduser --gecos "" you usermod -aG sudo you # Copy your SSH public key to the new user rsync --archive --chown=you:you ~/.ssh /home/you In a new terminal, confirm ssh you@203.0.113.10 works and sudo whoami prints root . Only then harden SSH: sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf # PermitRootLogin no # PasswordAuthentication no # KbdInteractiveAuthentication no sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh # (service is "ssh" on Ubuntu) Keep your existing session open while testing a new login, so a typo cannot lock you out. Now the service user: no password, no login shell, home directory for the app: sudo adduser --system --group --home /srv/myapp --shell /usr/sbin/nologin myapp sudo mkdir -p /srv/myapp sudo chown myapp:myapp /srv/myapp Step 3: Firewall sudo ufw default deny incoming sudo ufw default allow outgoing sudo ufw allow OpenSSH sudo ufw allow 80/tcp sudo ufw allow 443/tcp sudo ufw enable sudo ufw status verbose Postgres and Node are deliberately not opened. Only nginx is public. Optionally install fail2ban to ban IPs that brute-force SSH, and enable unattended security upgrades: sudo apt install -y unattended-upgrades fail2ban . Step 4: Install Node.js Ubuntu's packaged Node is often old. Use NodeSource (system-wide, good for servers) or a version manager. Install the current LTS (check nodejs.org for the active LTS line; 22.x or newer in 2026): curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | sudo -E bash - sudo apt install -y nodejs build-essential git node -v && npm -v Piping a script from the internet into a root shell is trust-on-first-use. Read it first ( curl -fsSL URL | less ) or use the signed apt repository instructions from NodeSource's docs. Step 5: Install and configure Postgres sudo apt install -y postgresql postgresql-contrib sudo systemctl status postgresql # active (exited/running) sudo ss -tlnp | grep 5432 # should show 127.0.0.1:5432 only Create an application role with a strong generated password, and its database: DBPASS=$(openssl rand -base64 24 | tr -d '/+=') echo "Save this password in your password manager: $DBPASS" sudo -u postgres psql <<SQL CREATE ROLE myapp LOGIN PASSWORD '$DBPASS'; CREATE DATABASE myapp OWNER myapp; SQL # Test the TCP login the app will use PGPASSWORD="$DBPASS" psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U myapp -d myapp -c 'SELECT version();' Default Ubuntu Postgres listens on localhost only: good, leave it. Do not change listen_addresses unless you have a specific reason. Backups come later in the production section, but at minimum plan pg_dump to somewhere off this machine. Step 6: Get the code onto the server Use a read-only deploy key so the server can clone a private repo without your personal credentials. # On the server, as the service user (use sudo -u, since it has no login shell) sudo -u myapp ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f /srv/myapp/.ssh_deploy_key -N "" -C "myapp-deploy" sudo cat /srv/myapp/.ssh_deploy_key.pub # paste into GitHub: Repo ▸ Settings ▸ Deploy keys (read-only) # Clone sudo -u myapp GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -i /srv/myapp/.ssh_deploy_key -o IdentitiesOnly=yes' \ git clone git@github.com:you/myapp.git /srv/myapp/app cd /srv/myapp/app sudo -u myapp npm ci --omit=dev # reproducible install from package-lock.json # If your app needs a build step (TypeScript, bundler): install dev deps, build, then prune # sudo -u myapp npm ci && sudo -u myapp npm run build && sudo -u myapp npm prune --omit=dev npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says and fails if it disagrees with package.json ; npm install can drift. Use ci in deployments. Step 7: Environment variables and secrets Create an env file outside the repo, readable only by the service user. systemd will load it. sudo mkdir -p /etc/myapp sudo tee /etc/myapp/myapp.env >/dev/null <<EOF NODE_ENV=production HOST=127.0.0.1 PORT=3000 DATABASE_URL=postgres://myapp:${DBPASS}@127.0.0.1:5432/myapp SESSION_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32) EOF sudo chown root:myapp /etc/myapp/myapp.env sudo chmod 640 /etc/myapp/myapp.env ls -l /etc/myapp/myapp.env # -rw-r----- root myapp Special characters in the password would need URL-encoding in a connection string; our tr removed the troublesome ones. If you have migrations, run them now (see the migrations lesson), for example sudo -u myapp env $(cat /etc/myapp/myapp.env | xargs) npm run migrate . A quick manual run to sanity check the app before involving systemd: sudo -u myapp bash -c 'set -a; . /etc/myapp/myapp.env; set +a; cd /srv/myapp/app; timeout 5 node server.js' # expect: listening on 127.0.0.1:3000 Step 8: systemd service systemd starts the app at boot, restarts it on crash and collects logs. sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service >/dev/null <<'EOF' [Unit] Description=My Express App After=network-online.target postgresql.service Wants=network-online.target [Service] Type=simple User=myapp Group=myapp WorkingDirectory=/srv/myapp/app EnvironmentFile=/etc/myapp/myapp.env ExecStart=/usr/bin/node server.js Restart=on-failure RestartSec=3 KillSignal=SIGTERM TimeoutStopSec=30 # Sandboxing: cheap, effective hardening NoNewPrivileges=true PrivateTmp=true ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=true ReadWritePaths=/srv/myapp LimitNOFILE=65536 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target EOF sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now myapp systemctl status myapp --no-pager journalctl -u myapp -f # live logs (Ctrl-C to stop) curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/health # {"status":"ok"} If it fails: journalctl -u myapp -n 50 --no-pager shows the error. Common causes: wrong ExecStart path ( which node ), file permissions, bad DATABASE_URL . Step 9: nginx reverse proxy sudo apt install -y nginx sudo tee /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp >/dev/null <<'EOF' server { listen 80; listen [::]:80; server_name app.example.com; client_max_body_size 10m; location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade"; proxy_read_timeout 60s; } } EOF sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/myapp sudo rm -f /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx curl -i http://app.example.com/health # from your laptop If DNS has not propagated, test with curl -i -H 'Host: app.example.com' http://203.0.113.10/health . Step 10: HTTPS with certbot sudo apt install -y certbot python3-certbot-nginx sudo certbot --nginx -d app.example.com --redirect --agree-tos -m you@example.com --no-eff-email sudo certbot renew --dry-run # confirm automatic renewal works systemctl list-timers | grep certbot Certbot edits the nginx file to add the listen 443 ssl server block and certificate paths, plus the HTTP to HTTPS redirect. View the result with sudo nginx -T | less and add HSTS if you like: add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000" always; Verify from outside: curl -I https://app.example.com/ , and run an SSL test in your browser. Check http:// redirects to https:// . Step 11: Verify end to end curl -sS https://app.example.com/health # {"status":"ok"} sudo systemctl restart myapp && sleep 2 && curl -s https://app.example.com/health sudo reboot # after boot, the site must come back by itself # then: curl -s https://app.example.com/health The reboot test is the one that separates "it works" from "it will keep working". Everything should start on its own: Postgres, the app, nginx. Step 12: How you deploy updates This is the manual routine every later lesson improves on: cd /srv/myapp/app sudo -u myapp GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -i /srv/myapp/.ssh_deploy_key -o IdentitiesOnly=yes' git pull --ff-only sudo -u myapp npm ci --omit=dev # sudo -u myapp ...run migrations... sudo systemctl restart myapp sleep 2 && curl -fsS https://app.example.com/health || echo "DEPLOY FAILED, ROLL BACK" Rolling back: git log --oneline , git checkout <previous-sha> (or git reset --hard ), npm ci , restart. Notice the weaknesses: restart drops in-flight requests; the code changes in place while running; a failed npm ci leaves a half-updated app; no history. The zero-downtime lesson fixes these with release directories and symlinks. Troubleshooting map Symptom Where to look Site unreachable (timeout) DNS ( dig ), ufw status , cloud firewall, nginx running? 502 Bad Gateway systemctl status myapp , journalctl -u myapp , /var/log/nginx/error.log App crashes at start Env file path/permissions, DATABASE_URL , Node version "password authentication failed" Role password differs from env file; recreate with ALTER ROLE Certbot fails DNS not pointing here yet, port 80 blocked, wrong server_name Works until reboot Forgot systemctl enable Permission denied reading files Owner is root from a previous sudo command; chown -R myapp:myapp /srv/myapp What is still missing (and where it is covered) Backups of Postgres, tested restores (production readiness). Logs shipped off the box and monitoring/alerts (observability). Reproducibility: if this server dies, can you rebuild it in minutes? Today it took an hour of typing. Infrastructure as Code and containers fix that. Zero-downtime releases and fast rollbacks (this section, later lessons). CI: tests running before anything reaches the server. Try it Rent the cheapest Ubuntu VPS you can find (a few dollars a month; destroy it afterwards) and a domain or a free subdomain, and perform every step above with your own small Express + Postgres app. Kill the process with sudo kill -9 $(systemctl show -p MainPID --value myapp) and watch systemd restart it ( journalctl -u myapp ). Stop Postgres ( sudo systemctl stop postgresql ) and look at what /health returns and what nginx and the app log. Start it again. Run nmap -Pn SERVER_IP from your laptop. Confirm only 22, 80 and 443 are visible. Write the whole procedure as a single Bash script. Where does it get hard to make safe to re-run? (This is the motivation for idempotent tools such as Ansible.)

title: Process Managers: systemd, PM2, supervisor
text: Process Managers: systemd, PM2, supervisor Running node server.js in an SSH session works until you close the terminal, the process crashes, or the server reboots. A process manager keeps your app alive, restarts it when it fails, captures its logs and starts it at boot. The problem Run node server.js & and log out: depending on the shell, the process gets SIGHUP and dies. Use nohup or screen and it survives logout, but when it crashes at 3 a.m. nobody restarts it, logs go to a random file, and after a reboot it is gone. A process manager (also called a supervisor or init system) is a small, trusted program whose job is to run your programs and keep them running: Start on boot, in the right order (after network, after database). Restart on crash, with back-off so a crash loop does not melt the CPU. Run as a specific unprivileged user with resource limits. Collect stdout/stderr and manage logs. Offer start/stop/restart/status commands and send signals correctly for graceful shutdown. Option 1: systemd (the default on modern Linux) systemd is PID 1 on Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL, Fedora. It is already installed, supervises everything on the machine, and needs no extra runtime. For a single server, it is usually the right answer. A unit file: # /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service [Unit] Description=My Node API After=network-online.target postgresql.service Wants=network-online.target [Service] Type=simple User=myapp Group=myapp WorkingDirectory=/srv/myapp/current EnvironmentFile=/etc/myapp/myapp.env ExecStart=/usr/bin/node server.js Restart=on-failure # restart if exit code != 0, killed by signal, or timeout RestartSec=3 StartLimitIntervalSec=60 # give up (mark failed) if it restarts too often... StartLimitBurst=5 # ...more than 5 times in 60 s TimeoutStopSec=30 # how long to wait after SIGTERM before SIGKILL LimitNOFILE=65536 MemoryMax=1G # cgroup limit: OOM-kill this service, not the whole box NoNewPrivileges=true PrivateTmp=true [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target sudo systemctl daemon-reload # after editing any unit file sudo systemctl enable --now myapp # start now AND at boot sudo systemctl restart myapp sudo systemctl status myapp sudo systemctl reload myapp # if you defined ExecReload (e.g. send SIGHUP) journalctl -u myapp -f # follow logs journalctl -u myapp --since "1 hour ago" -p err systemctl list-units --failed systemd-analyze security myapp # hardening score card Logs: stdout and stderr go to the journal automatically. Just console.log ; no log files to rotate. Make sure the journal is persistent ( /var/log/journal exists) and size-limited ( SystemMaxUse= in /etc/systemd/journald.conf ). Restart policies Restart= Restarts when Use for no Never One-shot jobs on-failure Non-zero exit, signal, timeout Most services (a clean systemctl stop stays stopped) always Any exit Daemons that should never exit Running several instances: template units # /etc/systemd/system/myapp@.service (the "@" makes it a template; %i is the instance name) [Service] Environment=PORT=%i ExecStart=/usr/bin/node server.js # ...rest as above sudo systemctl enable --now myapp@3000 myapp@3001 myapp@3002 # then load-balance across 3000-3002 with nginx upstream Other useful systemd features: .timer units (a better cron), socket activation, ExecStartPre (run migrations or checks), DynamicUser=yes , WatchdogSec with sd_notify for liveness. Option 2: PM2 (Node-specific) PM2 is a Node process manager with batteries: clustering, zero-downtime reload, built-in log management and a monitor UI. It is popular because it is easy for Node developers and does not require systemd knowledge. sudo npm install -g pm2 pm2 start server.js --name myapp -i max # cluster mode: one worker per CPU core pm2 list pm2 logs myapp pm2 monit pm2 reload myapp # graceful zero-downtime reload (cluster mode) pm2 restart myapp pm2 stop myapp # Survive reboots: PM2 registers itself with systemd pm2 startup systemd -u myapp --hp /srv/myapp # prints a command to run with sudo pm2 save # remember the current process list Better to declare it in a file: // ecosystem.config.js module.exports = { apps: [{ name: 'myapp', script: 'server.js', instances: 'max', // or a number exec_mode: 'cluster', max_memory_restart: '500M', // restart a leaking worker kill_timeout: 10000, // ms before SIGKILL after SIGINT/SIGTERM wait_ready: true, // wait for process.send('ready') before routing traffic listen_timeout: 10000, env_production: { NODE_ENV: 'production', PORT: 3000 } }] }; // pm2 start ecosystem.config.js --env production Pros: cluster mode with rolling reload; simple for Node; cross-platform (works on a laptop and macOS). Cons: another daemon (which itself needs supervising, hence pm2 startup using systemd); logs live in ~/.pm2/logs unless configured (add pm2-logrotate ); a Node-centric tool, so mixed-language servers need a second manager; the free tier pushes toward the paid PM2 Plus. Option 3: supervisor Supervisor ( supervisord ) is a Python-based, language-agnostic process control system, historically popular for Python/PHP/Ruby apps before systemd was universal, and still common inside containers that must run several processes. # /etc/supervisor/conf.d/myapp.conf [program:myapp] command=/usr/bin/node /srv/myapp/current/server.js directory=/srv/myapp/current user=myapp autostart=true autorestart=true startretries=5 stopsignal=TERM stopwaitsecs=30 numprocs=1 environment=NODE_ENV="production",PORT="3000" stdout_logfile=/var/log/myapp/out.log stderr_logfile=/var/log/myapp/err.log stdout_logfile_maxbytes=50MB stdout_logfile_backups=5 sudo apt install -y supervisor sudo supervisorctl reread && sudo supervisorctl update sudo supervisorctl status sudo supervisorctl restart myapp On a modern server it duplicates what systemd already does; choose it when you are inside a container or on a system without systemd. Comparison systemd PM2 supervisor Installed by default Yes No (npm) No (apt/pip) Language Any Node (others possible) Any Starts at boot Native Via systemd hook Via init/systemd Clustering over cores Template units + LB Built in ( -i max ) numprocs + LB Zero-downtime reload Not built in (use proxy/LB drain) pm2 reload No Logs journald Files in ~/.pm2 Files you configure Resource limits and sandboxing Excellent (cgroups, namespaces) Memory restart only Minimal Dependencies between services Yes ( After= , Requires= ) No Priority ordering only Clustering: using every core A Node process runs JavaScript on one thread, so a 4-core VPS wastes 3 cores with a single process. Options: PM2 cluster mode or Node's cluster module: the master process listens on the port and distributes connections to workers. Easiest. Multiple processes behind nginx : systemd template units on ports 3000, 3001, ... listed in an nginx upstream . More explicit, plays well with drain-and-restart one at a time. Containers : one container per core or many replicas behind a load balancer (the Kubernetes way). Constraints: workers share nothing. In-memory sessions, caches, rate-limit counters and WebSocket rooms are per process. Move shared state to Redis/Postgres. This is the same stateless-app requirement as for load balancers. For other stacks the equivalents are gunicorn/uvicorn workers ( -w 4 ), Puma workers, PHP-FPM pools. JVM apps typically use threads in one process instead. Signals and graceful stop All managers stop a process the same way: send SIGTERM, wait a timeout, then SIGKILL. Your app should handle SIGTERM by finishing in-flight work (details in the zero-downtime lesson). Two traps: running via npm start or a shell wrapper puts an intermediate process between the manager and Node that may not forward signals. Execute node directly in ExecStart . And in Docker, the same applies to PID 1. Which should you choose? A Linux server, any language : systemd. Fewer moving parts, best isolation, native logging. Node, want clustering and graceful reloads with minimal fuss : PM2 (ideally started by systemd), or systemd with several instances behind nginx. Inside a container : usually none. One process per container; the orchestrator (Docker restart policy, Kubernetes) is the manager. Multiple processes in one container or no systemd : supervisor (or s6-overlay). Don't forget what supervises the supervisor Whatever you choose, check it survives a reboot and that its own crash is handled. A process manager that is not enabled at boot is just a more elaborate way to forget to start your app. Pitfalls Crash loops hiding a real bug: a restart policy with no limit and no alert. Alert on restart count. Memory leaks "fixed" by max_memory_restart forever. It is a safety net, not a cure. Relative paths and missing environment: services run with a minimal environment, not your shell's. Specify WorkingDirectory , absolute paths and EnvironmentFile . Forgetting daemon-reload after editing a unit; changes silently do not apply. Running as root. Always set User= . PM2 started as your login user, so it does not run after reboot unless pm2 startup and pm2 save were done. Try it Write a tiny Node HTTP server, create a systemd unit for it with Restart=on-failure , start it and curl it. Kill it with kill -9 and confirm it comes back ( journalctl -u ). Add process.exit(1) on a route to make it crash on demand; check StartLimitBurst behaviour by triggering it repeatedly. Set MemoryMax=100M and write a route that leaks memory. Watch systemd kill and restart the service. Install PM2, run the same app with -i 2 , and hit the endpoint repeatedly while it returns process.pid to see requests spread across workers. Run pm2 reload under load with curl in a loop and count failures. Reboot the machine and verify which of the two setups came back on its own.

title: Config and Secrets Basics
text: Config and Secrets Basics The same code must run on your laptop, in CI, in staging and in production, talking to different databases with different credentials. The way to achieve this is to keep configuration out of the code. Secrets deserve extra care, because a leaked key is an incident, not a bug. Why separate config from code Hard-coded values cause two kinds of pain: Inflexibility : changing a URL or feature switch requires a rebuild and redeploy; the same build cannot be promoted from staging to production because the database address is baked in. Leaks : a password committed to Git lives in history forever, in every clone and fork. Bots scan public GitHub in real time for cloud keys and use them within minutes (crypto mining on your account; five-figure bills are common stories). The principle (from the Twelve-Factor App, factor III): strict separation of config from code; store config in the environment . Build once, deploy the same artifact everywhere, and inject differences at runtime. What is "config"? Anything that varies between deploys of the same code: Kind Examples Sensitive? Environment settings NODE_ENV , LOG_LEVEL , PORT , feature flags, timeouts No Endpoints API_BASE_URL , REDIS_HOST , S3 bucket names Usually no Secrets DB passwords, API keys, JWT signing keys, OAuth client secrets, TLS private keys, webhook secrets Yes Not config: internal application constants that do not change per environment (route definitions, business rules). Those belong in code. A good test: could you open-source the repo right now without leaking anything? If not, something sensitive is in it. Environment variables Environment variables are key/value strings the OS passes to every process. They are language-agnostic, supported everywhere (shells, systemd, Docker, Kubernetes, every cloud), and cannot be accidentally committed. # Shell export DATABASE_URL="postgres://app:s3cret@db.internal:5432/app" node server.js # One-shot for a single command LOG_LEVEL=debug node server.js // Node const dbUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL; if (!dbUrl) throw new Error('DATABASE_URL is required'); // fail fast! # Python import os; db_url = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"] # KeyError if missing: good Best practices: read config once at startup into a typed object; validate and fail fast if a required variable is missing (use zod, envalid, pydantic-settings, Spring @ConfigurationProperties ); remember all values are strings ( "false" is truthy in JavaScript, parse explicitly); provide safe defaults only for non-sensitive values. // config.js const { z } = require('zod'); const schema = z.object({ NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'test', 'production']).default('development'), PORT: z.coerce.number().int().default(3000), DATABASE_URL: z.string().url(), SESSION_SECRET: z.string().min(32), ENABLE_BETA: z.enum(['true', 'false']).default('false').transform(v => v === 'true'), }); module.exports = schema.parse(process.env); // throws a clear error at boot if invalid .env files Typing exports every time is tedious, so a .env file holds KEY=value lines that a library (dotenv, node --env-file=.env in modern Node, python-dotenv, Docker Compose env_file ) loads into the environment for local development . # .env (local only: NEVER committed) NODE_ENV=development DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/app_dev SESSION_SECRET=dev-only-not-a-real-secret STRIPE_API_KEY=sk_test_xxx # .env.example (committed: documents which variables exist, with fake values) NODE_ENV=development DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/dbname SESSION_SECRET=change-me-32-chars-minimum STRIPE_API_KEY=sk_test_replace_me # .gitignore .env .env.* !.env.example node --env-file=.env server.js # Node 20.6+, no dotenv package needed Conventions: commit .env.example so newcomers know what to set; keep the real .env out of version control; do not rely on .env files in production. There, the platform injects variables (systemd EnvironmentFile , Docker/Kubernetes, PaaS dashboards, a secrets manager). Per-environment configuration Typical environments: development (laptop), test/CI, staging (production-like), production. Two approaches: Same code, different variables (preferred) : every environment sets DATABASE_URL , API_BASE_URL . No if (env === 'production') branches scattered through the code. Config files per environment ( config/production.yml , Spring profiles, Rails credentials ): fine for non-secret structured settings. Resist the explosion of environment-named files; the "staging" and "production" variants drift apart. Keep the set of differing keys small. Avoid the antipattern of a single NODE_ENV switching dozens of behaviours. Use explicit variables ( LOG_LEVEL , CACHE_TTL ) so staging can be genuinely similar to production. The more production differs from staging, the less staging proves. Secrets: handling them properly Never commit secrets Not in code, .env , Dockerfiles, CI YAML, Terraform state or Slack. Deleting the file in a later commit does not remove it from history. Treat any committed secret as compromised : rotate it first (generate a new one, revoke the old), then clean up history ( git filter-repo , BFG) as a secondary step. Where secrets can live (weakest to strongest) Method Notes In the repo Never. Env file on the server ( /etc/myapp/myapp.env , mode 640, owned root:app) Fine for a single VPS. Manual rotation. Back up securely. CI/CD secret store (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab CI variables) Masked in logs; injected at deploy time PaaS config vars (Heroku, Render, Fly secrets) Managed in the dashboard or CLI Encrypted-in-repo (SOPS with age/KMS, git-crypt, sealed-secrets) Secrets versioned but unreadable without keys; great for GitOps Secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store, GCP Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Doppler, 1Password) Central, audited, access-controlled, rotation support, dynamic short-lived credentials Workload identity (IAM roles, no static secret at all) Best: the instance/pod itself is the credential. Prefer it over long-lived keys wherever possible. Leak surfaces to watch Logs : printing the whole config or request headers. Redact Authorization , cookies, passwords. Process listings and crash dumps : command-line arguments are visible to all users in ps ; environment is readable via /proc/PID/environ by the same user and root. Do not pass secrets as CLI arguments. Docker images : ENV and COPY .env bake secrets into layers anyone with the image can read. Inject at run time; use BuildKit --mount=type=secret for build-time secrets. Front-end bundles : anything in client-side code is public. VITE_* / NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables are embedded in the JavaScript sent to browsers. Error trackers and analytics capturing request bodies. Shell history : export SECRET=... lands in ~/.bash_history . Use read -s or prefix the command with a space (with HISTCONTROL=ignorespace ). Chat, tickets and screenshots . Practices Least privilege : a DB user limited to the app's database and needed operations, not the superuser; scoped API tokens, read-only deploy keys. Separate secrets per environment : a leaked staging key must not open production. Developers rarely need production secrets. Rotate : on a schedule and immediately on suspicion or when someone leaves. Design for rotation (accept two valid keys during a changeover; load secrets without a rebuild). Generate strong secrets : openssl rand -base64 32 or openssl rand -hex 32 . Never reuse a password across environments. Scan : pre-commit hooks and CI with gitleaks, trufflehog, GitHub secret scanning and push protection. Audit access : managed secret stores log who read what. Back up and document where each secret lives, so a rebuilt server is not blocked by a missing value. # Install a pre-commit secret scan (gitleaks) brew install gitleaks # or download from GitHub releases gitleaks detect --source . -v # scan the repo history gitleaks protect --staged -v # scan staged changes (use in a pre-commit hook) # Example: fetch a secret at deploy time from AWS SSM instead of storing it on disk long-term aws ssm get-parameter --name /myapp/prod/DATABASE_URL --with-decryption \ --query Parameter.Value --output text Injecting config on a server (systemd) # /etc/myapp/myapp.env → chmod 640, chown root:myapp DATABASE_URL=postgres://myapp:REDACTED@127.0.0.1:5432/myapp # unit file [Service] EnvironmentFile=/etc/myapp/myapp.env # For systemd 250+, secrets can also be passed as files with LoadCredential= # (not exposed in the process environment). Remember: environment variables need a restart to change. For values that must change live, read from a file or secret store with caching and a refresh. Trade-offs Choice Pro Con Env vars Universal, simple Flat strings; visible to child processes; no audit; need restart Config files Structured, versioned (non-secret) Drift per environment; risk of secrets creeping in Secret manager Audit, rotation, access control Another dependency, cost, startup latency, bootstrapping (how does the app authenticate to it? IAM role) Encrypted in Git (SOPS) Reviewable changes, GitOps-friendly Key management; easy to mis-encrypt Pitfalls Committing .env "just once". Add it to .gitignore before the first commit. Different variable names across environments, discovered at deploy time. Validate config at startup everywhere, including CI. Production fallback defaults ( DATABASE_URL || 'localhost' ) hiding misconfiguration. Fail instead. Using production data and secrets in development. Printing process.env in a debug route or startup log. Try it Take a project with hard-coded values. Move each to an environment variable, create .env.example , and add the validation snippet so the app refuses to start when a variable is missing. Run gitleaks detect on one of your own repos. Anything found? Decide how you would rotate it. Create /tmp/test.env with a fake secret, then run a program with it via env $(cat /tmp/test.env | xargs) node -e "console.log(process.env.FOO)" and compare with node --env-file . On a Linux box, start a process with a secret in its environment and read it back via sudo cat /proc/PID/environ | tr '\0' '\n' to see who can read it. Then check file mode and ownership on a systemd EnvironmentFile . Write the secret-rotation procedure for your database password step by step. How would you do it without downtime?

title: Database Migrations in Deployments
text: Database Migrations in Deployments Code is easy to roll back; data is not. The database schema is the one part of a deployment that carries state, and most "bad deploy" horror stories (locked tables, dropped columns, hours of downtime) are migration mistakes. Learn to change schemas safely while the app keeps running. What a migration is, and why you need them Your code expects a certain schema: tables, columns, indexes. When a feature needs a new column, the schema must change in lockstep with the code. If you apply changes by hand ( psql on production, "I'll run this SQL after the deploy"), you get environments that disagree, forgotten steps, and no history. A migration is a small, ordered, versioned script that moves the schema from version N to N+1. The tool records which migrations have run (in a table such as schema_migrations ) so each runs exactly once, in the same order, in every environment: your laptop, CI, staging, production. Schema becomes code, reviewed in pull requests and reproducible from scratch. Ecosystem Tools Node Prisma Migrate, Knex, Drizzle Kit, TypeORM, node-pg-migrate, Sequelize Python Alembic (SQLAlchemy), Django migrations Ruby / PHP ActiveRecord migrations, Laravel migrations JVM Flyway, Liquibase Language-agnostic Flyway, Liquibase, golang-migrate, Atlas, sqitch, dbmate Anatomy of a migration -- migrations/20260314_001_add_users_phone.up.sql ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone text; -- migrations/20260314_001_add_users_phone.down.sql ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN phone; // Knex style exports.up = (knex) => knex.schema.alterTable('users', t => t.string('phone')); exports.down = (knex) => knex.schema.alterTable('users', t => t.dropColumn('phone')); # Typical commands npx knex migrate:latest # apply all pending npx prisma migrate deploy # apply committed migrations (use in production; not "migrate dev") alembic upgrade head flyway migrate Rules: never edit a migration that has already been applied anywhere shared (add a new one instead); commit migrations with the code that needs them; keep each small and focused; test them against a copy of production-sized data. Where migrations fit in the deploy Old code (v1) running ──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ ▼ 1. Run migration ──▶ schema S1 → S2 v1 code must STILL work on S2 ◀── the key constraint 2. Deploy v2 code (rolling / blue-green) v1 and v2 BOTH run during the rollout 3. v2 verified; v1 gone The critical insight: during a deploy, old and new code run simultaneously (rolling update, canary, or just the seconds between processes), and a rollback means old code runs against the new schema. So every migration must be compatible with both the previous and the next version of the application. The golden rule Schema changes must be backwards-compatible with the code that is currently running. If a change breaks the old code, you cannot deploy without downtime, and you cannot roll back. Split the change into several safe steps across several deployments. Safe versus dangerous changes Change Safe? Why / how to do it safely Add a nullable column Safe Old code ignores it. (PostgreSQL 11+ also makes ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT const instant.) Add a table Safe Nothing uses it yet. Add an index Careful Plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in Postgres (outside a transaction). Add NOT NULL Dangerous Old code inserting without it fails. Add nullable, backfill, then add constraint ( NOT VALID then VALIDATE ). Add a foreign key / check constraint Careful Full-table scan under lock. In Postgres: ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (lighter lock). Rename a column or table Dangerous Old code references the old name. Use expand/contract (below). Drop a column or table Dangerous Old code (or a rollback) will break. Only after no running code references it. Change a column type Dangerous May rewrite the whole table under an exclusive lock. Add a new column and migrate. Backfill millions of rows in one UPDATE Dangerous Long transaction, bloat, replication lag, lock contention. Batch it. The expand / contract pattern Also called "parallel change". To make a breaking change, do it in phases where each phase is individually safe and deployable: Expand : add the new structure alongside the old (migration only; app unchanged). Migrate code (dual write) : deploy code that writes to both old and new, still reading from old. Backfill : copy existing data into the new structure, in batches. Switch reads : deploy code that reads from new (still writes both, so rollback is safe). Stop writing old : deploy code that only uses new. Contract : later, drop the old column in a separate migration, after you are sure you will not roll back past step 5. Worked example: rename users.fullname to users.display_name -- Release 1 (expand): add new column ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name text; -- Optional: keep both in sync even for old code, using a trigger CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION sync_display_name() RETURNS trigger AS $$ BEGIN IF NEW.display_name IS NULL THEN NEW.display_name := NEW.fullname; END IF; IF NEW.fullname IS NULL THEN NEW.fullname := NEW.display_name; END IF; RETURN NEW; END $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; CREATE TRIGGER users_sync BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE ON users FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION sync_display_name(); -- Backfill in batches (repeat until 0 rows updated; sleep between batches) UPDATE users SET display_name = fullname WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM users WHERE display_name IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000); // Release 2: code reads display_name, writes both await db.query('UPDATE users SET display_name=$1, fullname=$1 WHERE id=$2', [name, id]); const { display_name } = row; // Release 3: code only uses display_name (fullname untouched) -- Release 4 (contract), days or weeks later: DROP TRIGGER users_sync ON users; ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN fullname; It takes four deploys instead of one. That is the price of doing it without downtime or rollback risk. For small apps with a maintenance window and a few users, a single "rename" migration at 2 a.m. may be perfectly acceptable. Choose deliberately. Locks: how migrations cause outages In PostgreSQL, ALTER TABLE commonly takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, blocking even reads. Worse: if a long-running query holds a conflicting lock, your ALTER waits in the queue, and every query that arrives after it queues behind your ALTER . The whole table freezes. Defend with timeouts so the migration fails quickly instead of stalling the app: SET lock_timeout = '3s'; -- give up if we cannot get the lock quickly SET statement_timeout = '60s'; -- cap runtime of the statement ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text; -- If it fails with "canceling statement due to lock timeout", retry later; nothing broke. -- Index without blocking writes (cannot run inside a transaction block) CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_id ON orders (user_id); -- Constraint with minimal locking ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_user_fk FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) NOT VALID; ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_user_fk; -- NOT NULL safely (Postgres 12+ uses a validated CHECK to avoid a full scan under lock) ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_note_nn CHECK (note IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID; ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_note_nn; ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN note SET NOT NULL; -- fast, uses the validated check ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT orders_note_nn; MySQL has its own online DDL rules ( ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE , tools like gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change for huge tables). Linters such as squawk (Postgres), strong_migrations (Rails) and Atlas lint can flag unsafe migrations in CI. Running migrations during deployment Strategy How Trade-off Separate deploy step (recommended) Pipeline runs migrate once, before rolling out new code Single runner, no races; schema is ahead of code (hence backward compatibility) App runs migrations at startup Every instance runs migrate when booting Simple, but N instances race (use advisory locks - most tools do); slow migrations delay readiness; the app DB user needs DDL rights Init container / pre-deploy hook Kubernetes Job or Helm pre-upgrade hook; Heroku release phase Good: runs once per release Manual DBA runs it For risky migrations, with a human watching # Example pipeline order 1. CI: run tests including a migration test on a fresh DB AND on a copy of the previous schema 2. Backup / snapshot (or confirm point-in-time recovery is on) 3. Run migrations (with lock_timeout) using a dedicated migration DB role 4. Deploy new code (rolling) 5. Smoke test; keep the old version ready for rollback Use a separate database role for migrations (can ALTER) and for the app (only SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) when feasible, limiting what an SQL injection can do. Rollbacks and down migrations "Down" migrations look reassuring but are often a trap: a down that drops a column destroys the data written since. In practice, many mature teams do not rely on down migrations in production: they roll back the code (which still works against the expanded schema) and roll forward with a fix migration. Hence: make every release compatible with the previous schema, keep destructive contract steps separate, and treat dropped data as unrecoverable except from a backup. Test your restore. Other practices Seed/reference data as migrations (idempotent), separate from test fixtures. Test migrations on production-like data volume : a migration instant on 100 rows can lock for minutes on 100 million. Idempotency and transactions : Postgres supports transactional DDL (a failed migration rolls back cleanly), MySQL does not (DDL auto-commits, leaving half-applied migrations). Use IF NOT EXISTS where helpful. Branching : two branches adding migrations produce ordering conflicts; use timestamp prefixes and resolve in review. Schema drift : nobody should hand-edit production. Tools like Atlas and Prisma migrate diff can detect drift. Document the plan in the pull request for anything risky: expected duration, lock levels, rollback. Pitfalls Deploying code that needs the new column before the migration has run, or running a destructive migration before all old instances are gone. ORM auto-sync ( synchronize: true in TypeORM, db push , Django --run-syncdb ) in production, which can drop data silently. Long migrations inside the request path or app startup, blowing health-check timeouts and causing crash loops. Backfilling in one giant transaction. No backup before a risky migration. Try it Start Postgres locally ( docker run -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw -p 5432:5432 postgres:17 ). Create users(id, fullname) and insert 1 million rows with generate_series . In one psql session, open a transaction that reads from users and does not commit. In another run ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN x int; and watch it hang; in a third session try a plain SELECT and see it queue behind the ALTER. Then retry with SET lock_timeout='2s' . Time CREATE INDEX versus CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY while a loop inserts rows from another session. Walk through the rename example using a migration tool of your choice: write the four releases as separate migrations and a tiny app version for each. Confirm that app v1 still works after release 1 and release 2's schema. Add a migration linter (squawk or Atlas lint) to a CI job and see what it flags on a DROP COLUMN .

title: Deployment Strategies
text: Deployment Strategies "Stop the old version, start the new one" works until the first time it fails with real users watching. Deployment strategies are different answers to one question: how do you move users from version A to version B while limiting the damage if B is broken? What you are trading Every strategy balances four things: Downtime : is there a gap where nobody can be served? Blast radius : if the new version is bad, how many users see it before you notice? Rollback speed : how fast can you get back to the good version? Cost and complexity : extra capacity, extra tooling, harder database changes. Underneath all of them, remember the rule from the migrations lesson: two versions of the app will coexist, so the database and any shared state must support both. 1. Recreate (big bang) Time ──▶ v1 ████████████████│ │ (downtime) v2 │░░░░░████████████████ stop v1 start v2 Stop everything, deploy, start again. It is what git pull && systemctl restart does. Pros : simplest; no version coexistence (migrations can be breaking); cheapest. Cons : downtime on every release; the whole user base meets any bug; slow recovery. Use for : internal tools, dev/staging, apps with maintenance windows, major migrations that cannot coexist. 2. Rolling update Servers: [v1] [v1] [v1] [v1] step 1: [v2] [v1] [v1] [v1] take one out of the LB, update, health check, put back step 2: [v2] [v2] [v1] [v1] step 3: [v2] [v2] [v2] [v1] step 4: [v2] [v2] [v2] [v2] Replace instances gradually, a few at a time (batch size, "max surge", "max unavailable"). Traffic flows throughout. This is the default in Kubernetes Deployments, ECS and Auto Scaling group instance refresh. Pros : no downtime; no duplicate full environment; native in most platforms. Cons : v1 and v2 serve simultaneously (need compatibility); rollback is another rolling update (minutes); a bug is already on part of the fleet when detected; capacity dips if you remove instances before adding new ones. Use for : the default for stateless services with backward-compatible changes. # Kubernetes rolling update parameters strategy: type: RollingUpdate rollingUpdate: maxSurge: 25% # extra pods allowed above desired during the rollout maxUnavailable: 0 # never drop below desired capacity # Needs a readinessProbe, otherwise "ready" is declared before the app can serve 3. Blue-green ┌─────────────┐ Users ─────▶ │ Router / LB │───────────────┐ (switch) └─────────────┘ │ │ today ▼ after verification ▼ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ │ GREEN (v2) │ full copy, already running and tested │ BLUE (v1) │ └────────────┘ └────────────┘ keep BLUE idle for instant rollback Run two complete, identical environments. Blue serves production. Deploy v2 to green, test it with real infrastructure (smoke tests, internal traffic), then flip the router/DNS/LB target group so all traffic goes to green at once. To roll back, flip back. Pros : near-zero downtime; instant, simple rollback; the new version is tested in a production-like environment before users see it. Cons : double the infrastructure during the release; the switch is all-or-nothing (100 percent of users hit v2 immediately); database must serve both (shared DB means expand/contract; separate DBs means data sync pain); in-flight requests and sessions at switch time; warm-up (cold caches). Use for : when fast rollback matters and extra capacity is affordable (cheap with cloud or containers). On a single VPS you can emulate it with two app instances on different ports and an nginx proxy_pass pointing at one; switching means editing the upstream and nginx -s reload . On AWS, swap target groups on an ALB listener, or use CodeDeploy blue/green; on Kubernetes, switch a Service selector. 4. Canary 100% ─ v1 ████████████████████████████████████████ stage 1: v1 95% ███████████████████░ v2 5% █ watch error rate, latency, business KPIs stage 2: v1 75% ███████████████░░░░░ v2 25% █████ stage 3: v1 50% ██████████░░░░░░░░░░ v2 50% ██████████ done: v2 100% any stage fails ──▶ route 100% back to v1 (smallest possible blast radius) Named after the canary in the coal mine. Send a small share of real traffic (1 to 5 percent, or only employees or one region) to v2, compare its metrics against v1, and increase gradually only while healthy. Pros : minimal blast radius; real production validation; data-driven promotion; automatic rollback possible (Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Spinnaker/Kayenta, AWS CodeDeploy, Istio/Envoy weighted routing). Cons : needs good observability (without metrics a canary is blind); needs fine-grained traffic splitting; more complex; slow; both versions must be compatible; low traffic means too few samples to detect problems; sticky users (decide whether a user stays on one version). Use for : high-traffic services where a bad release is costly. # nginx: crude canary with weighted upstream (about 10% to canary) upstream app { server 10.0.1.11:3000 weight=9; server 10.0.1.12:3000 weight=1; # canary running v2 } # Better: pin specific users via a cookie or header map $http_x_canary $backend { default stable; "1" canary; } 5. Shadow (mirroring / dark launch) Users ──▶ LB ──▶ v1 (production) ──▶ response to the user │ └────▶ copy of each request ──▶ v2 (shadow) ──▶ response DISCARDED, compared/logged Duplicate live traffic to the new version, but ignore its responses. Users are never affected; you compare behaviour, performance and diffs against production load. Pros : zero user impact; tests with real traffic shape and volume; great for rewrites and migrations (new database, new language, new algorithm). Cons : the shadow must not cause side effects (duplicate emails, payments, writes to the shared database): requires stubbing or a separate datastore; doubles load; nondeterministic comparison; engineering effort. Tools : nginx mirror directive, Envoy/Istio traffic mirroring, GitHub Scientist-style libraries. 6. A/B testing Not a safety mechanism, but an experiment : route different user segments (by cookie, user id hash, geography, plan) to different versions of a feature to measure which performs better on a business metric (conversion, retention). It needs a stable assignment per user and statistical analysis. Canary asks "is v2 healthy?" A/B asks "is v2 better for the business?" They can use the same routing machinery but have different goals and durations (A/B runs for days or weeks). 7. Feature flags (decouple deploy from release) // The code ships dark; the flag decides who sees it if (flags.isEnabled('new-checkout', { userId: user.id, plan: user.plan })) { return newCheckout(req); } return oldCheckout(req); A feature flag is a runtime conditional controlled outside the code (config service, LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, OpenFeature standard, or a database table). You deploy the code with the feature off , then turn it on for staff, then 1 percent, then everyone, and can turn it off in seconds without a deploy or a rollback . Pros : separates deployment (technical act) from release (business decision); instant kill switch; enables trunk-based development, canary by user, A/B tests, gradual rollouts, per-customer features. Cons : code complexity (two paths); tests multiply; flags rot into permanent clutter ("flag debt"); a flag service becomes a dependency (needs safe defaults and caching); flags interacting in unforeseen ways; schema must support both paths. Discipline : give each flag an owner and an expiry date; delete it once fully rolled out; default to the safe state if the flag service is unreachable. Comparison Strategy Downtime Blast radius Rollback Extra cost Complexity Recreate Yes 100% Slow (redeploy) None Lowest Rolling No Grows during rollout Minutes (re-roll) Small (surge) Low Blue-green No 100% at switch Instant (flip) 2x during release Medium Canary No Small, controlled Fast (shift weight) Small High (needs metrics) Shadow No None (users unaffected) n/a High (duplicate load) High A/B test No Segment only Flag off Low High (experiment design) Feature flags No Per flag, per user Instant (toggle) Low Medium (flag hygiene) Combining strategies Real systems combine them. A typical modern setup: rolling or blue-green for the deploy mechanism, canary analysis to gate promotion, feature flags to release functionality independently, and expand/contract migrations to keep it all compatible. Shadowing is reserved for big rewrites. Choosing Internal tool, few users, downtime fine: recreate . Normal web service, backward-compatible changes: rolling , with health checks. Need one-click rollback, can afford duplicate capacity: blue-green . High traffic, strong monitoring, risky changes: canary , automated. Rewriting a critical component: shadow first, then canary. Product experiments or gradual feature rollout: feature flags (and A/B). No strategy rescues a missing health check or metric All of the above depend on knowing whether the new version is healthy. Without readiness probes, error-rate dashboards and alerting, a rolling update will happily roll out a broken version to 100 percent, just slowly. Build observability first or alongside. Pitfalls Forgetting that v1 and v2 share the database, caches, queues and message formats. A new message schema consumed by old workers breaks them. Blue-green with sessions stored in app memory: users are logged out at the switch. Canary on too little traffic: 1 percent of 100 requests per hour tells you nothing. Choosing the strategy before the problem. A single-server hobby app does not need canaries. Permanently-on "temporary" flags. Rolling back code but not config or flags that were changed at the same time. Try it Build two tiny apps that return "v1" and "v2" on ports 3001 and 3002. With nginx, simulate a blue-green flip: proxy_pass to 3001, curl in a loop, change to 3002, nginx -s reload , and observe no failed requests. Do a canary: upstream with weights 9 and 1. Run 100 requests and count versions. Make v2 fail 50 percent of the time and compute the overall error rate; at what weight would your alert fire? Try nginx mirroring: mirror /shadow; location = /shadow { internal; proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3002$request_uri; } and watch v2's logs receive copies. Implement a feature flag as an environment variable or JSON file read per request, flip it live and observe the behaviour without a restart. For a service you know, fill in the comparison table: which strategy fits, what would break if v1 and v2 ran concurrently?

title: Zero-Downtime Deploys and Rollbacks
text: Zero-Downtime Deploys and Rollbacks Users should never notice you deployed, and when a release is bad, you should be able to undo it in seconds, not hours. Both goals come from the same few techniques: graceful shutdown, health checks, atomic switching of releases, and a rehearsed rollback plan. Where downtime comes from With git pull && npm ci && systemctl restart myapp on a live server: The restart gap : the old process dies, the new one needs seconds to boot. Requests in that window get 502 from nginx. Dropped in-flight requests : a request halfway through is cut off when the process is killed. Half-updated code : while git pull and npm ci run, files on disk change under a running app; a lazy require() may load a new file against old ones. Broken release, no way back : npm ci fails midway and node_modules is gone; the previous version no longer exists on disk. Not ready, but receiving traffic : the new process is listening but still warming up its DB pool and caches. The fixes, in the order we will cover them: (1) shut down gracefully, (2) report readiness honestly, (3) build the new release next to the old one and switch atomically, (4) verify and roll back automatically. 1. Graceful shutdown When a process manager or orchestrator stops your app it sends SIGTERM , waits a grace period, then SIGKILL . A well-behaved app on SIGTERM: stops accepting new connections, finishes in-flight requests, closes DB pools and queues, then exits 0. const server = app.listen(port, '127.0.0.1'); let shuttingDown = false; function shutdown(signal) { if (shuttingDown) return; shuttingDown = true; console.log(`${signal} received: draining`); // Fail readiness immediately so the LB stops sending new requests // (health endpoint checks the `shuttingDown` flag) server.close(async (err) => { // stops accepting; waits for open connections to end try { await pool.end(); // DB pool await redis.quit(); } finally { process.exit(err ? 1 : 0); } }); server.closeIdleConnections?.(); // Node 18.2+: drop idle keep-alive sockets now // Hard deadline: never hang forever. Must be shorter than the manager's kill timeout. setTimeout(() => { console.error('forced exit'); process.exit(1); }, 25_000).unref(); } process.on('SIGTERM', () => shutdown('SIGTERM')); process.on('SIGINT', () => shutdown('SIGINT')); app.get('/health/ready', (req, res) => res.status(shuttingDown ? 503 : 200).end()); Checklist: the manager's stop timeout ( TimeoutStopSec , Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds , Docker --stop-timeout ) must exceed your drain deadline, which must exceed your longest legitimate request. Run node directly, not via npm start or a shell wrapper that swallows signals. Long-lived WebSockets need an explicit "reconnect to another server" message, and background workers should finish or re-queue the current job. Kubernetes extra Pods are removed from Service endpoints asynchronously, so for a few seconds after SIGTERM they may still receive new requests. A preStop hook of sleep 5 before the app starts draining prevents a burst of errors during rolling updates. 2. Health checks: liveness and readiness Check Question Failure action What to test Liveness Is the process stuck beyond repair? Restart it Cheap: the event loop answers. Do not check dependencies, or a DB blip restarts every instance. Readiness Can it serve traffic right now? Remove from load balancer (do not restart) DB reachable, migrations applied, caches warm, not shutting down Startup Has it finished booting? Wait; restart if too slow Slow-starting apps (JVM) A deploy tool that waits for readiness before shifting traffic, and aborts if readiness is never reached, converts "deployed a broken build" from an outage into a failed deployment that users never saw. 3. Atomic releases with symlinks (the Capistrano pattern) Instead of updating one directory in place, each deploy creates a new timestamped release directory , prepares it completely (install, build, migrate), and only then atomically repoints a current symlink to it. Switching a symlink is one atomic filesystem operation; there is never a half-updated state. Capistrano (Ruby) popularised this layout; Deployer (PHP), Mina, and many hand-rolled scripts use it. /srv/myapp/ ├── releases/ │ ├── 20260610-101500-a1b2c3d/ ← old release (still on disk: instant rollback) │ ├── 20260611-143000-e4f5a6b/ ← previous │ └── 20260612-091200-c7d8e9f/ ← new, fully prepared BEFORE the switch ├── shared/ ← persists across releases │ ├── .env (or /etc/myapp/myapp.env) │ ├── uploads/ │ └── logs/ └── current ─────────▶ releases/20260612-091200-c7d8e9f (symlink: the "switch") Rules: code is immutable once released; anything that must persist (uploads, local files) lives in shared/ and is symlinked in (better: object storage); keep the last N releases (3 to 5) and delete older ones. A deploy script #!/usr/bin/env bash # /srv/myapp/deploy.sh - usage: ./deploy.sh [git-ref] (run as the service user) set -euo pipefail APP=/srv/myapp REPO=git@github.com:you/myapp.git REF=${1:-main} KEEP=5 HEALTH_URL=http://127.0.0.1:3000/health SERVICE=myapp TS=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S) RELEASE="$APP/releases/$TS" PREV=$(readlink -f "$APP/current" || true) log() { echo "[deploy $(date +%T)] $*"; } rollback_to_prev() { if [ -n "$PREV" ] && [ -d "$PREV" ]; then log "ROLLING BACK to $PREV" ln -sfn "$PREV" "$APP/current.tmp" && mv -Tf "$APP/current.tmp" "$APP/current" sudo systemctl restart "$SERVICE" fi } mkdir -p "$APP/releases" "$APP/shared" log "cloning $REF into $RELEASE" git clone --depth 1 --branch "$REF" "$REPO" "$RELEASE" SHA=$(git -C "$RELEASE" rev-parse --short HEAD) rm -rf "$RELEASE/.git" echo "$SHA" > "$RELEASE/REVISION" log "installing dependencies" ( cd "$RELEASE" && npm ci --omit=dev ) # ( cd "$RELEASE" && npm ci && npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev ) # if you build log "linking shared files" ln -sfn "$APP/shared/uploads" "$RELEASE/uploads" log "running migrations (must be backward compatible!)" ( cd "$RELEASE" && set -a && . /etc/myapp/myapp.env && set +a && npm run migrate ) log "switching current -> $RELEASE" ln -sfn "$RELEASE" "$APP/current.tmp" mv -Tf "$APP/current.tmp" "$APP/current" # atomic rename: no moment without a valid current log "restarting service" sudo systemctl restart "$SERVICE" # or: pm2 reload / HUP / start new then drain log "health check" ok=0 for i in $(seq 1 30); do if curl -fsS --max-time 2 "$HEALTH_URL" >/dev/null; then ok=1; break; fi sleep 1 done if [ "$ok" -ne 1 ]; then log "health check FAILED" rollback_to_prev exit 1 fi log "cleaning old releases (keep $KEEP)" ls -1dt "$APP"/releases/* | tail -n +$((KEEP+1)) | xargs -r rm -rf log "deployed $SHA" The unit file uses WorkingDirectory=/srv/myapp/current . The sudoers file allows only systemctl restart myapp without a password for the deploy user ( %deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart myapp ). Two details: ln -sfn alone is not atomic (it unlinks then creates), so create the symlink under a temp name and mv -T (rename) over current , as above. And a plain systemctl restart still has a short gap; the next section removes it. Closing the restart gap Technique How PM2 cluster reload Starts new workers, waits for ready, then stops old ones, one at a time Two instances behind nginx Restart A (nginx sends traffic to B, via proxy_next_upstream or health marks), then restart B Blue-green ports New release on 3001 while old runs on 3000. Health check 3001, switch nginx upstream, nginx -s reload , drain and stop old Socket activation / Unix socket handoff systemd holds the listening socket during the restart so connections queue instead of failing (advanced) Orchestrator rolling update Docker Swarm, Kubernetes, ECS: handled for you with readiness probes # Blue-green on one box (sketch): the nginx include file selects the live port # /etc/nginx/conf.d/active_upstream.conf contains: server 127.0.0.1:3000; new_port=3001 start_new_release_on_port $new_port wait_until_healthy "http://127.0.0.1:$new_port/health" echo "server 127.0.0.1:$new_port;" | sudo tee /etc/nginx/conf.d/active_upstream.conf sudo nginx -t && sudo nginx -s reload # graceful: old workers finish their requests stop_old_release_gracefully # SIGTERM; it drains and exits 4. Rollback plans A rollback is not a failure; it is a feature you must have designed before you need it at 2 a.m. under stress. Rollback script #!/usr/bin/env bash # /srv/myapp/rollback.sh - switch to the previous release set -euo pipefail APP=/srv/myapp CUR=$(readlink -f "$APP/current") PREV=$(ls -1dt "$APP"/releases/* | grep -vxF "$CUR" | head -n1) [ -n "$PREV" ] || { echo "no previous release"; exit 1; } echo "rolling back: $(basename "$CUR") -> $(basename "$PREV")" ln -sfn "$PREV" "$APP/current.tmp" mv -Tf "$APP/current.tmp" "$APP/current" sudo systemctl restart myapp for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:3000/health >/dev/null && { echo "healthy"; exit 0; }; sleep 1; done echo "rollback unhealthy!"; exit 1 It takes seconds because the previous release is still on disk with its dependencies installed. Compare with "git revert, rebuild, reinstall, restart" taking 5 to 15 minutes while customers are failing. What can and cannot be rolled back Thing Rollback Application code Easy: switch symlink / previous image tag / previous Kubernetes ReplicaSet ( kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp ) Configuration and flags Easy if versioned; hard if edited by hand on servers with no record Database schema Only if backward compatible (expand/contract). Rolling the code back must work against the new schema. Data written by the new version Cannot be un-written. Plan data fixes; take a backup/snapshot before risky releases. External side effects (emails sent, payments made) Impossible. Feature-flag risky behaviour so it can be switched off. Because of the last rows, "roll forward" (ship a quick fix) is sometimes the right answer when the change is a data migration or the bad release has been live for hours with new data. Decide the policy beforehand: default to rollback when the problem started with the deploy; roll forward only when rollback is unsafe or the fix is trivial and certain. A rollback runbook Detect : error rate, latency, failing smoke test, alerts, user reports. Compare timing with the deploy time. Decide fast : if in doubt, roll back first, investigate afterwards. Set a rule such as "error rate above X for 5 minutes after deploy triggers rollback". Execute : ./rollback.sh or the platform's equivalent. Announce in the incident channel.
