Verify : health, error rate, key user journey. Confirm the version running ( /health returns the git SHA). Freeze further deploys until the cause is understood. Then write up a short post-mortem. Automate steps 1 to 3 where you can: pipelines that run smoke tests after the switch and roll back on failure, Kubernetes progressDeadlineSeconds plus automated undo, Argo Rollouts or Flagger analysis, AWS CodeDeploy alarms. Putting it together build immutable artifact ──▶ run migrations (backward compatible) ──▶ start new release beside old │ │ │ readiness check passes? │ │ yes │ no │ ▼ ▼ │ shift traffic / flip symlink abort, old keeps serving │ │ │ old instances SIGTERM → drain → exit │ │ └────────────────────── smoke tests + metrics watch ◀────────┘ │ regression? ──▶ rollback (previous release still ready) Pitfalls Health endpoint returns 200 before the app is actually ready (no DB connection yet), so the deploy "passes" and users get errors. Shutdown deadline longer than the manager's kill timeout: SIGKILL arrives mid-drain. Keeping uploads or SQLite files inside the release directory; they vanish on the next deploy. Put them in shared/ or object storage. Deleting old releases too eagerly (rollback target gone) or not at all (disk full). Rollback never rehearsed: the script rots, or depends on a tool missing on the server. Practise in staging. Releases that cannot run against the previous schema, making rollback impossible. Build on the server taking minutes and consuming CPU; prefer building once in CI and shipping the artifact, so what you tested is what runs. Try it Add the SIGTERM handler to a small Express app with a route that sleeps 10 seconds. Start a request with curl , then kill -TERM the process: the request should still complete. Remove the handler and see it fail. Measure downtime of the naive approach: while true; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' localhost:3000/health; sleep 0.1; done | sort | uniq -c in one terminal while running systemctl restart in another. Count the non-200s. Set up the releases/ + current layout and the deploy and rollback scripts (clone from a local bare repo if you have no remote). Deploy three versions, then roll back. Deliberately ship a version whose /health returns 500 and confirm the script rolls back by itself. Repeat the downtime measurement using the two-port blue-green nginx switch and compare. Write the rollback runbook for your own app: who decides, what command, how you verify, and what cannot be undone.

title: The Deploy Checklist
text: The Deploy Checklist Experienced engineers are not people who never break production; they are people who run the same boring checks every time. A checklist moves deployment from heroics to routine. Use this one as a starting point and edit it after every incident. Why checklists work Pilots and surgeons use checklists not because they are novices, but because under time pressure and routine, humans skip steps. Most failed deployments come from a short list of repeated mistakes: a missing environment variable, a migration that was not run, a port not opened, a certificate that expired, no one watching after release. Writing them down converts tribal knowledge into something a new teammate (or you at 5 p.m. on Friday) can follow. Better still: automate every checkbox you can (CI gates, pipeline steps) and keep humans for judgement. Before you deploy Code and build [ ] Changes are merged via a reviewed pull request; the main branch is green in CI (lint, unit tests, integration tests). [ ] You know exactly what is being deployed: version/tag/commit SHA, and you have read the diff or changelog since the last release. [ ] The artifact (image, tarball) was built once in CI and is the same one that passed on staging. No "build on the server". [ ] Dependencies are locked ( package-lock.json , poetry.lock ); security scan passed or accepted. Configuration and secrets [ ] Any new environment variables or secrets are already set in the target environment (diff your .env.example against production). [ ] Config is validated at startup (app refuses to boot on missing values), so a mistake fails the deploy rather than a user. [ ] Feature flags for risky features are defined and set to the safe state. Database [ ] Migrations are backward-compatible with the version currently running (expand before contract), and tested on production-like data volume. [ ] A recent backup or snapshot exists, and you know how to restore it. Point-in-time recovery is on if available. [ ] Long-running or locking migrations have lock_timeout , batching, and a scheduled quiet period. Infrastructure and timing [ ] Disk space, memory and CPU headroom are fine ( df -h , free -m ): a full disk kills deploys. [ ] Dependencies are healthy (DB, cache, third-party APIs, certificate expiry more than 14 days away). [ ] It is a sensible time: avoid Friday afternoon, peak traffic, and when the one person who knows the system is unreachable. Ideal: small, frequent deploys on weekdays with people around. [ ] Stakeholders/support know if user-visible changes or brief degradation are expected. Incident channel open. Rollback readiness [ ] The previous version is still available (previous release dir, previous image tag) and you know the exact rollback command. [ ] You have decided in advance the signal that triggers a rollback (for example "error rate above 2 percent for 5 minutes"). During the deploy [ ] Announce the start (team chat) with version and expected duration. Change freeze for others touching the same system. [ ] Run migrations first (if any) and confirm success before shipping code. [ ] Roll out using the agreed strategy (rolling/blue-green/canary). Watch logs live: journalctl -u myapp -f or kubectl logs -f . [ ] Do not make unrelated changes in the same window. One change at a time makes failures attributable. After the deploy: smoke tests A smoke test is a tiny, fast, automatic check that the most critical paths work, named after turning on new electronics to see if smoke comes out. It does not prove correctness; it proves "not obviously broken". #!/usr/bin/env bash # smoke.sh - usage: ./smoke.sh https://app.example.com EXPECTED_SHA set -euo pipefail BASE=${1:?base url}; WANT=${2:-} fail() { echo "SMOKE FAIL: $*" >&2; exit 1; } # 1. Process healthy, dependencies reachable curl -fsS --max-time 5 "$BASE/health" >/dev/null || fail "/health" # 2. Correct version is live if [ -n "$WANT" ]; then GOT=$(curl -fsS "$BASE/health" | jq -r .version) [ "$GOT" = "$WANT" ] || fail "version $GOT != $WANT" fi # 3. Home page renders code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 10 "$BASE/") [ "$code" = 200 ] || fail "home returned $code" # 4. HTTPS and redirect behave curl -sI "http://${BASE#https://}/" | grep -qi '^location: https://' || fail "no http->https redirect" # 5. A critical read path works with test credentials curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $SMOKE_TOKEN" "$BASE/api/me" >/dev/null || fail "/api/me" # 6. Static assets and TLS expiry curl -fsSI "$BASE/assets/app.js" >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "warn: assets not found at the guessed path" exp=$(echo | openssl s_client -connect "${BASE#https://}:443" -servername "${BASE#https://}" 2>/dev/null \ | openssl x509 -noout -enddate | cut -d= -f2) echo "TLS expires: $exp" echo "SMOKE OK" Run it from outside the server (CI runner or your laptop) so it exercises DNS, TLS, the proxy and the firewall, not just localhost. Run it in the pipeline automatically, and fail the deploy (and trigger rollback) if it fails. Test credentials should belong to a dedicated test account with minimal rights. Post-deploy observation (the "bake" period) [ ] Error rate (5xx, exceptions) is at or below baseline. Compare with the same time yesterday. [ ] Latency (p50, p95, p99) has not regressed. [ ] Saturation : CPU, memory (leaks show up as a slow climb), DB connections, queue depth, disk. [ ] Business metrics : signups, checkouts, jobs processed. A deploy can be technically healthy and functionally broken. [ ] Logs : no new error patterns, no flood of warnings. Check the error tracker for new issue types. [ ] Background workers and cron jobs are running the new version and consuming from queues. [ ] Watch for at least 15 to 30 minutes (longer for risky changes, covering at least one peak or cron cycle). [ ] Announce completion. Tag the release in Git; update the changelog. Remove temporary flags you are done with. Common failure modes and how to spot them Failure Typical symptom Prevention Missing or wrong env var / secret Crash at boot or "undefined" behaviour; auth to third parties fails Startup validation; config diff in checklist; per-environment secret store Migration not run, or run in wrong order column does not exist errors straight after deploy Migration step in pipeline before code; expand/contract Migration locks a table Whole app hangs, connection pool exhausted, timeouts lock_timeout , concurrent index builds, test on large data Port, firewall or security group not updated Timeouts from the load balancer; health checks fail Infrastructure as code; verify with nc -zv Wrong Node/Python/JVM version on the server Syntax errors, native module failures Pin versions ( engines , .nvmrc , container images) Dependency drift ( npm install picks newer versions) "Worked in staging" differences npm ci with lockfile; build once and promote the artifact Disk full Install fails, DB crashes, logs stop Monitor disk; rotate logs; prune old releases/images File permissions / wrong user EACCES , nginx 403 Consistent owner/group; deploy as the service owner; no stray sudo Process not restarted (or old code still running) New code deployed but old behaviour persists Version in /health ; smoke test verifies version Cache serves stale content Users see old UI or API; broken mix of HTML and assets Fingerprinted assets; purge HTML; short HTML TTL Certificate expired or wrong chain Browser warnings, API clients failing Expiry monitoring; certbot renew --dry-run DNS not propagated / TTL too high Some users hit the old server Lower TTL days ahead; verify with multiple resolvers Health check too shallow or too strict Broken build accepted, or healthy nodes ejected Separate liveness and readiness; test the checks Old and new versions incompatible (queues, caches, API clients) Errors only during rollout Versioned message formats; backward-compatible APIs; mobile clients stay old for months Resource limits too low OOM kills, CPU throttling, connection exhaustion under real load Load test; alert on restarts and memory Timezone / locale / clock differences Cron at wrong time, token expiry issues UTC everywhere; NTP Third-party dependency changed or rate-limited Sudden failures independent of your deploy Timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, status page watch Nobody was watching Bug found by customers hours later Dashboards open during deploys; alerting; the bake period When it goes wrong Stay calm and communicate : post in the incident channel what you see and what you are doing. Roll back first, debug later when the deploy is the likely cause. Restoring service beats diagnosing in production. Preserve evidence : logs, metrics screenshots, the failing request, before restarting things. Verify recovery with the same smoke tests. Blameless post-mortem : what happened, why the system allowed it, what automatic check would have caught it. Add that check to this list (or better, to the pipeline). Maturing the checklist into automation Manual checklist item Becomes Tests pass Required CI status check on the main branch Env vars present Config schema validation; pipeline step diffing required keys Migration safe Migration linter in CI Deploy and wait for health Orchestrator readiness gates; deploy tool health check with auto-rollback Smoke tests Post-deploy pipeline job; synthetic monitoring running continuously Watch dashboards SLO-based alerts; automated canary analysis Announce Pipeline posts the deploy and version to chat; deploy markers on graphs The goal is not a longer checklist but a shorter one, because the system itself refuses to do the unsafe things. Pitfalls Checklist fatigue: ticking boxes without looking. Keep it short, specific, and tied to real past incidents. Treating smoke tests as full regression tests: they should run in seconds and cover only critical paths. Smoke tests that call localhost and miss DNS, TLS and proxy problems. Deploying and immediately leaving. The first 30 minutes are when most issues surface. A checklist that exists only in one person's head or an out-of-date wiki page. Version it in the repo next to the deploy scripts. Try it Copy this checklist into your repo as DEPLOY.md . Delete the items that do not apply and add two that come from your own past incidents. Adapt smoke.sh to your app, run it against staging, then deliberately break something (stop the service, break the nginx config in a staging copy) and confirm the script fails with a clear message. Hook the smoke test into your deploy script so a failure triggers rollback (see the previous lesson). Take the failure-mode table and, for three rows, write the exact command you would run to detect that failure on your server. Run a "game day": have a teammate (or a future-you) break one thing in staging after a deploy, and practise detecting and rolling back within five minutes. Time it.

title: Why CI/CD Matters
text: Why CI/CD Matters Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery are not "nice automation". They are the difference between a team that ships a change in an hour with confidence and a team that ships once a quarter with a prayer. This lesson explains the pain CI/CD removes, what it is worth in money and sleep, and how the industry measures it. A story: the release that took a weekend Imagine a team of 12 engineers building a web shop. There is no pipeline. Here is how a typical month goes. Each developer works on a long-lived feature branch for 2-4 weeks. Nobody merges until the feature is "done". Release day is the last Friday of the month. A release manager creates a release branch and asks everyone to merge. Twelve branches that have never seen each other collide. Merge conflicts take 6 hours. Two people's changes compile separately but break each other (one renamed a function, one added a new call to the old name). Someone builds the app on their own laptop, because the build server is "Dave's old desktop". The build uses Node 16 on that laptop; production runs Node 20. A transitive dependency resolved to a different version than anyone tested. QA runs a 200-line manual checklist for a day and a half. They find 31 bugs. 9 are blockers. Half were introduced three weeks ago, and the author no longer remembers the code. Saturday night: deployment. Someone follows a 40-step wiki page, SSHs into 4 servers, and runs steps by hand. Step 27 was changed last month and the wiki wasn't updated. Server 3 ends up different from servers 1, 2 and 4. Sunday 2 a.m.: checkout is broken for 20% of users (those routed to server 3). Rollback means "redo the wiki in reverse, from memory". It takes 3 hours. This is not a story about bad engineers. It is the predictable result of a system that batches up risk and delays feedback. The same team, with CI/CD Everyone integrates into main at least daily, through small pull requests. On every push, a pipeline compiles the code in a clean container, runs lint, unit tests and integration tests in about 8 minutes, and reports pass/fail on the pull request. When a PR merges, the pipeline builds one immutable Docker image, tags it with the commit SHA, and deploys it to staging automatically. Smoke tests run against staging. A human clicks "Approve" (continuous delivery) or nothing is needed (continuous deployment), and the exact same image is rolled out to production using a rolling update. If error rates rise, the pipeline (or an engineer) redeploys the previous image tag. Rollback takes 2 minutes and is the same code path as a deploy. Metric Before After Deploy frequency 1 per month 15-30 per day Lead time (commit to production) ~3 weeks ~45 minutes Change failure rate ~35% of releases need a hotfix ~5% Time to restore service 3-6 hours 5-15 minutes Release effort 12 people x 1 weekend 0 people-hours of ceremony Size of a typical change ~4,000 lines ~80 lines About these numbers They are illustrative, composites of what teams commonly report, not one specific company. The ratios, however, line up with industry research (see DORA below). The core problem: integration hell "Integration hell" is the pain that arrives when separately developed changes are combined late. The cost of integration grows non-linearly with the time and size of what is being integrated, for three reasons: Conflicts multiply. Two branches that diverge for a day conflict rarely. Two that diverge for a month touch hundreds of the same files. With N branches there are N*(N-1)/2 pairs that can collide. Semantic conflicts are invisible to Git. Git merges text. It cannot tell you that branch A deleted an API that branch B just started calling. Only compiling and testing the combined result reveals that. Debugging is a search problem. When a single day's change breaks the build, the culprit is among a handful of commits. When a month's worth of change breaks, it is among hundreds. Bisecting a huge batch is slow and demoralizing. Cost of finding the bug ^ | * production | * | * release testing | * | * QA | * code review | * on the developer's machine / in CI +--------------------------------------------------> time since the bug was written This is the economic heart of CI: make the feedback loop shorter than the developer's memory. A test that fails 6 minutes after you push is fixed in minutes, because the code is still in your head. The same bug found three weeks later costs a context switch, a bisect, a meeting, and often a hotfix. The cost of bugs found late The classic claim, popularised by Barry Boehm's work from the 1980s and widely repeated, is that fixing a defect gets roughly an order of magnitude more expensive for each phase it survives. Exact multipliers vary by study and are contested, but the direction is not controversial. Walk through one bug: Found where What it takes Rough cost In your editor / pre-commit Fix the line Minutes In CI on your PR Read the failing test, push a fix ~15-30 minutes In QA / staging Bug report, reproduce, find the owner, fix, re-test Hours, 2-3 people In production Incident, rollback, customer comms, hotfix, postmortem Days, 10+ people, lost revenue, lost trust A back-of-the-envelope business case: if your site makes $50,000 per hour and a bad release causes a 2-hour partial outage that costs 30% of revenue, that single incident costs $30,000 in lost sales, before engineer time, refunds and reputation. A pipeline that catches even one such release a year pays for a lot of CI minutes. What CI/CD gives the business Speed to market. A feature that is finished on Tuesday is in users' hands on Tuesday, not at the next release train. Competitors that ship daily learn from users daily. Lower risk per change. Small changes are easy to review, easy to test, easy to reason about, and easy to roll back. Counter-intuitively, deploying more often is safer because each deploy is smaller. A deploy is a risk-reduction technique, not a risk. Predictability. A pipeline that does the same thing every time removes "works on my machine", "only Dave knows how to release", and "we think it's the same as last time". Developer happiness and retention. Nobody enjoys weekend deployments or merge hell. Engineers repeatedly rank slow builds and painful releases among their top frustrations. Retention is a real cost. Auditability and compliance. Every production change maps to a commit, a reviewed PR, a passing test run and an approver, recorded automatically. Auditors (SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI) love this; manual releases make it painful. Security. Dependency scanning, secret scanning and SAST run on every change, not once a year. Patching a critical CVE becomes "merge a PR" instead of a project. Experimentation. Feature flags, canaries and A/B tests need cheap, frequent, safe deploys. Without CD, you cannot run experiments at the pace the product team wants. DORA: measuring delivery performance Since 2014 the DORA research programme (DevOps Research and Assessment, now part of Google Cloud), published in the annual State of DevOps reports and the book Accelerate (Forsgren, Humble, Kim), has surveyed tens of thousands of professionals. It found that a small set of metrics predicts both software delivery performance and organizational outcomes (profitability, market share, customer satisfaction). Metric Measures Question it answers Deployment frequency Throughput How often do we ship to production? Lead time for changes Throughput How long from commit to running in production? Change failure rate Stability What % of deployments cause a failure needing remediation? Failed deployment recovery time (formerly MTTR) Stability How fast do we recover when a deployment fails? More recent reports add reliability (meeting SLOs) and, since 2024, distinguish "rework rate". Reports typically cluster teams into performance tiers; elite or high performers deploy on demand (multiple times a day), have lead times under a day, change failure rates in the low teens or below, and recover in under an hour. Low performers deploy between once a month and once every six months with lead times measured in weeks to months. The headline finding Speed and stability are not a trade-off. Teams that deploy more often also have lower change failure rates and faster recovery. The practices that give you speed (small batches, automation, fast tests, trunk-based development) are the same ones that give you stability. CI/CD is the engine behind both. The principles underneath Small batches. Reduce the size of what you integrate and release. Everything gets easier. Fast feedback. Tell the developer as soon as possible, in the place they are already looking (the PR). Automate the repeatable. Humans are for judgment; machines are for checklists. Build once, promote the same artifact. What you tested is what you ship. Everything as code. Pipelines, infrastructure and config live in Git, reviewed like code. Make the main branch always releasable. A red build is the team's top priority. What happens without it: the failure modes Symptom Root cause CI/CD addresses "Works on my machine" Build and test in a clean, defined environment every time Fear of deploying; deploy freezes Small, tested, reversible changes Hero engineer who does releases Release knowledge encoded in the pipeline (bus factor) Staging and prod behave differently Same artifact promoted through environments Bugs found by customers Automated tests on every change Long, stressful rollbacks Versioned, immutable artifacts; redeploy previous Nobody knows what's running in prod Every deploy is traceable to a commit SHA Honest trade-offs Upfront investment. A good pipeline and test suite take weeks to build. The payoff is compounding, but it is not free. Maintenance. Pipelines are software. They need owners, upgrades and care (see the best-practices lesson). Tests are the real prerequisite. Automating deployment of an untested app only ships bugs faster. CI/CD amplifies your engineering quality, good or bad. Cultural change. Trunk-based development, small PRs and "red build stops the line" require team agreement, not just tools. CI minutes cost money and slow pipelines cost far more in developer time. Budget for both. Common misconception "We have Jenkins, so we do CI/CD." A server that runs a nightly build is automation, not continuous integration. If developers only merge every two weeks, or the build is red for days and nobody reacts, you do not have CI regardless of tooling. A maturity ladder Manual. Builds on laptops, deploys by SSH. Scripted. A build server compiles and runs tests, maybe nightly. Continuous Integration. Every push builds and tests; main stays green. Continuous Delivery. Every green main build is automatically deployable; production deploy is one click. Continuous Deployment. Every green change goes to production automatically, with progressive rollout and automatic rollback. You do not need to jump to the top. Each rung pays for itself. The rest of this section walks up the ladder. Try it Pick a project you work on. Write down its four DORA numbers as honestly as you can: deploys per week, days from merge to production, % of deploys that needed a fix, hours to recover. You now have a baseline. Find the most recent production bug. Trace it back: which commit introduced it, how long until it was found, which stage could have caught it earlier? Estimate your own "cost of a bad release" in engineer-hours and revenue. Compare it with the monthly cost of a CI service (often under $100 for a small team).

title: Git Workflows: Branching, Reviews and Releases
text: Git Workflows: Branching, Reviews and Releases CI/CD is only as good as the workflow that feeds it. How your team branches, reviews, merges and tags code determines how often you integrate, how risky releases are, and how easily you can trace what is running in production. Why a workflow at all? Git gives you cheap branches and no rules. Without an agreed workflow, teams drift into the worst of all worlds: long-lived personal branches, unreviewed pushes to main, "which branch is production?" confusion, and releases nobody can reproduce. A workflow is a small set of conventions that answers: where does new work happen, how does it get reviewed, how does it reach production, and how do we fix production quickly? The three models you will meet 1. Trunk-based development Everybody integrates into a single branch ( main , the "trunk") at least once a day. Branches, if used at all, live hours to a couple of days. Incomplete work is hidden behind feature flags so unfinished code can be merged and even deployed safely. main ──●──●──●──●──●──●──●──●──●──▶ (always releasable) \/ \/ \/ short-lived branches (< 1-2 days) / small PRs releases: tag a commit on main (v1.8.0), or cut a release branch only when needed Pros: minimal integration pain, fastest feedback, simplest model, best DORA outcomes. Cons: needs strong automated tests, feature flags, and team discipline. It is the model CI was designed around, and the one the DORA research most strongly associates with high performance. 2. GitHub Flow A lightweight variant: main is always deployable; every change is a short feature branch plus a pull request; merge after review and green checks; deploy from main (often immediately). main ──●────────────●────────────●──▶ \ /\ / feature ●──●──●───● ●──●──●───● (PR, review, CI, merge) This is trunk-based development with a pull request gate. For most web teams it is the right default. 3. GitFlow Introduced by Vincent Driessen in 2010. It uses several long-lived branches: main (production), develop (integration), plus feature/* , release/* and hotfix/* . main ──●───────────────────●────────●──▶ (tags v1.0, v1.1) \ / \ / release \ ●──●──●/ \ / \ / \ / develop ──●───●──●──●──●──●──●───●──●──▶ \ / \ / feature ●● ●● hotfix ●──● (from main, merged to main AND develop) Pros: explicit release stabilization; fits software that ships in numbered versions and supports several versions at once (desktop apps, firmware, libraries with LTS lines). Cons: long-lived branches recreate integration hell; double merges (to main and develop); slow flow; poor fit for continuous deployment. Even its author later added a note recommending simpler flows for web apps that deploy continuously. Trunk-based GitHub Flow GitFlow Long-lived branches main only main only main + develop (+ release) Branch lifetime Hours Days Weeks Release cadence On demand, many/day On demand Scheduled versions Needs feature flags Yes Helpful Rarely Best for SaaS, high-performing teams Most web teams Versioned/multi-release products CI/CD fit Excellent Excellent Awkward Recommendation If you deploy a service you control, use GitHub Flow or trunk-based development. Reach for GitFlow-style release branches only when you truly must maintain several released versions in parallel. Pull requests and code review A pull request (GitHub, Bitbucket) or merge request (GitLab) is where CI and humans meet. It bundles the diff, the discussion and the automated checks in one place. What a good PR looks like Small. Aim for under ~400 lines changed. Review quality collapses on big diffs ("10 lines = 10 comments; 500 lines = LGTM"). One purpose. A bug fix and a refactor are two PRs. Described. Why the change, how it was tested, screenshots, links to the issue, rollout/rollback notes. Green before review. Reviewers should not spend time on something a linter or test already rejects. What reviewers should do Check design, correctness, edge cases, security, and tests. Leave style to the formatter and linter. Review within hours, not days; slow review is a hidden lead-time killer. Many teams set a norm like "first response within one working day". Distinguish blocking comments from suggestions ("nit:"). Merge strategies Strategy Result Use when Merge commit Preserves branch history, adds a merge commit You want full history Squash and merge One commit per PR on main Most teams: linear, readable, each commit = one reviewed change, easy revert Rebase and merge Replays commits linearly Clean, meaningful individual commits Branch protection: enforcing the rules A convention nobody enforces will be broken at 6 p.m. on a Friday. Branch protection (GitHub "rulesets" / protected branches, GitLab protected branches) makes the rules mechanical. For main , a sensible baseline: Require a pull request; no direct pushes, including for admins. Require at least 1 approving review (2 for sensitive repos); dismiss stale approvals when new commits land. Require status checks to pass (your CI jobs by name) and require the branch to be up to date before merging. Require signed commits or linear history if your policy demands it. Use a CODEOWNERS file so changes to certain paths auto-request the owning team. Block force-pushes and branch deletion. # .github/CODEOWNERS * @acme/backend /infra/ @acme/platform /.github/workflows/ @acme/platform # pipeline changes need platform review /docs/ @acme/docs Pipeline changes are code changes Anyone who can change the workflow file can change what runs with your secrets. Put workflow files under CODEOWNERS and require review for them. Commits: conventional commits The Conventional Commits specification gives commit messages a machine-readable shape: <type>(<optional scope>): <description> [optional body] [optional footer(s)] Type Meaning Version bump feat New feature MINOR fix Bug fix PATCH feat! or footer BREAKING CHANGE: Incompatible API change MAJOR docs , chore , refactor , test , ci , perf , build Non-user-facing none (usually) feat(cart): allow applying multiple discount codes fix(auth): refresh token before expiry to avoid 401 loop feat(api)!: remove deprecated /v1/orders endpoint BREAKING CHANGE: clients must migrate to /v2/orders. Why bother? Tools such as semantic-release , release-please and git-cliff read these messages to compute the next version and generate a changelog automatically, so releasing becomes a merge instead of a ceremony. A commit-lint check in CI ( commitlint ) enforces the format. With squash merging, you only need to enforce the PR title . Semantic versioning SemVer ( MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH , e.g. 2.14.3 ) is a contract with consumers: MAJOR : incompatible API changes. MINOR : backward-compatible new functionality. PATCH : backward-compatible bug fixes. Pre-release and build metadata: 2.0.0-rc.1 , 1.4.2+build.567 . SemVer is essential for libraries. For continuously deployed services, users do not care about version numbers, so many teams identify releases by commit SHA or date-based tags ( 2026.10.05-3 , CalVer). Pick one scheme and apply it consistently to artifacts. Tags and releases A tag is a permanent name for a commit. Use annotated tags for releases; they store author, date and message. # create and push an annotated tag git tag -a v1.8.0 -m "Release 1.8.0" git push origin v1.8.0 # list, inspect, check out a release git tag --list 'v1.*' git show v1.8.0 git switch --detach v1.8.0 # what changed between releases? git log --oneline v1.7.0..v1.8.0 A release on GitHub/GitLab is a tag plus release notes and attached assets (binaries, checksums). The common automation pattern: pushing a tag v* triggers a pipeline that builds, tests, publishes the artifacts (npm package, Docker image tagged 1.8.0 ) and creates the release page. Release from a tag, deploy from a SHA Tag the image with both the commit SHA (immutable, always unique) and the semantic version. Never deploy latest ; you cannot tell what it contains or roll back to it. Hotfixes and rollbacks Trunk/GitHub Flow: a hotfix is just a normal small PR through the fast pipeline. Often, git revert <sha> of the bad PR is the fastest fix and goes through the same pipeline. Release branches: branch from the release tag, fix, tag v1.8.1 , then merge or cherry-pick the fix back to main so it is not lost. Prefer git revert over rewriting history on shared branches. Never force-push main. Pitfalls Long-lived feature branches. The number one cause of integration hell. Use feature flags and merge daily. Giant PRs. Split them; stack PRs if needed. Rubber-stamp reviews. Approvals without reading give a false sense of safety. Admins bypassing protection. Rules apply to everyone, or to no one. Secrets committed to Git. Rotating is mandatory; rewriting history is not enough. Enable secret scanning/push protection. Merging when CI is red "just this once". That is how red builds become normal. Try it Create a throwaway GitHub repo. In Settings, add a ruleset for main requiring a PR and one approval. Try to push directly and observe the rejection. Make a branch, commit with feat: add greeting , open a PR, and squash merge it. Tag v0.1.0 with git tag -a , push it, and create a GitHub release from it. Install commitlint or try npx release-please to see how commit types drive versions.

title: Continuous Integration
text: Continuous Integration Continuous Integration (CI) is the practice of merging every developer's work into a shared mainline frequently, and verifying each merge with an automated build and test run. It is a behavior first and a tool second. The problem CI solves Software is built by many people changing the same codebase. Two changes that each work alone can fail together. The longer they stay apart, the more expensive and mysterious the failure. Before CI, teams scheduled a painful "integration phase" near the end of a project. CI (coined by Grady Booch, made a core practice of Extreme Programming, and popularised by Martin Fowler's 2000 article) inverts this: integrate so often that integration is boring. Without CI, you learn that the build is broken from a teammate, from QA, or from a customer. With CI, you learn within minutes, from a bot, on your own pull request. What CI actually is: the practices Fowler's list, still the best definition, with modern commentary: Maintain a single source repository. Everything needed to build lives in version control: code, tests, build scripts, DB migrations, pipeline definitions. Automate the build. One command ( make build , npm ci && npm run build ) produces the artifact from a clean checkout. If it takes tribal knowledge, CI cannot run it. Make the build self-testing. Tests run as part of the build, and a failing test fails the build. Everyone commits to the mainline every day. This is the "continuous" in CI. Branches that live for weeks mean you are not doing CI, even if a server builds them. Every commit builds on an integration machine. A clean environment, not a developer laptop. Keep the build fast. The classic target is under 10 minutes. Beyond that, developers stop waiting, batch their changes, and the feedback loop breaks. Fix broken builds immediately. A red main is a stop-the-line event. Revert first, investigate second. Test in a clone of production. Same OS, same runtime version, ideally the same container image. Make it easy to get the latest artifact. Anyone, including QA and product, can fetch what the latest build produced. Everyone can see what is happening. Status on the PR, in chat, on a dashboard. The CI loop developer Git host CI runner (clean, ephemeral) ┌───────┐ push/PR ┌──────────┐ webhook ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ commit│──────────▶│ branch/PR│──────────▶│ 1 checkout 2 install deps │ └───▲───┘ └────┬─────┘ │ 3 lint 4 unit tests │ │ │ status check │ 5 build 6 integration test│ │ fix, push again ▼ └───────────────┬───────────────┘ └──────── red ◀── PR shows pass/fail ◀─────────────────┘ │ green + review ▼ merge to main ──▶ pipeline again ──▶ artifact (CD takes over) The pipeline runs in two modes: on the PR (verifying the proposed change, often merged with the target branch) and on main after merge (producing the release artifact). Some teams use a merge queue (GitHub merge queue, GitLab merge trains) that tests each PR on top of the other queued changes, preventing "green PR, red main" races. Fast feedback is the whole point Think of CI as a latency problem. What matters is the time from git push to a trustworthy answer. Feedback time Developer behavior < 5 min Waits, stays in flow, fixes immediately 5-15 min Starts something small, returns 15-45 min Context switches; PRs batch up; fixes cost more Hours "Run CI" becomes a chore; people merge without waiting; trust erodes Techniques to stay fast: run cheap checks first (fail fast), parallelise independent jobs, cache dependencies, run only affected tests in large repos, split slow suites into shards, and move slow end-to-end tests to after-merge or nightly runs. The test pyramid in a pipeline /\ /e2e\ few, slow, brittle (minutes) - critical user journeys /──────\ /integr. \ some, medium (seconds-min) - DB, queues, HTTP APIs /──────────\ / unit \ many, fast, isolated (ms) - pure logic /────────────────\ Mike Cohn's pyramid says: write many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few end-to-end tests. In pipeline terms this maps onto ordering and cost: Layer Runs Speed Catches Flakiness risk Static analysis (lint, type check) Every push, first Seconds Style, type errors, obvious bugs Very low Unit Every push Seconds-1 min Logic errors Low Integration Every PR 1-5 min Wiring, SQL, serialization, contracts Medium End-to-end / UI After merge, on staging; a small smoke subset on PR 5-30 min Whole-system regressions High The anti-pattern is the ice cream cone : few unit tests, a mountain of slow UI tests, and a manual QA layer on top. It is slow, flaky and expensive. Invert it. Build once, run everywhere A pillar of both CI and CD: build the artifact once , then test and deploy that exact artifact in every environment. Do not rebuild for staging and again for production. A rebuild can pick up different dependency versions or a different base image, so "what we tested" is no longer "what we shipped". Make the artifact immutable and uniquely identified (Docker image tagged with the commit SHA, or a package with a version and checksum). Keep environment differences in configuration injected at deploy time (env vars, config maps, secrets), never in the build. Pin dependencies with lockfiles ( package-lock.json , poetry.lock , go.sum ) and use the strict install command ( npm ci , not npm install ). A minimal CI job, explained name: ci on: pull_request: push: branches: [main] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest # fresh VM for each run timeout-minutes: 15 # never let a stuck job burn money steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 # get the code - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version-file: .nvmrc # same Node as everyone else cache: npm # restore ~/.npm keyed on the lockfile - run: npm ci # exact, reproducible install - run: npm run lint - run: npm test -- --coverage Notice what this guarantees: a clean machine, pinned runtime, locked dependencies, and a result attached to the PR. The next lessons build this up properly. Practices around the pipeline Run the same commands locally. Put steps in npm scripts or a Makefile / justfile ; the pipeline calls them. Debugging a pipeline you can only run by pushing is miserable. Pre-commit hooks (husky, lefthook, pre-commit ) catch trivial failures before pushing. They complement CI; they never replace it because they can be skipped. Treat the build as a team alarm. Whoever broke it fixes or reverts it; notify via chat. Keep branches short and rebase/merge main frequently. Test the database migrations in CI against a real database (service containers) so schema changes are validated every time. Use ephemeral environments. Spin up a disposable preview deployment per PR for reviewers. Pitfalls Nightly builds mistaken for CI. Feedback must be per-change. Ignoring red builds or retrying until green. That hides flakiness and teaches the team that failures mean nothing. Tests that depend on order, shared state, wall-clock time or the network. They pass locally and fail randomly in CI. CI that differs from local and prod (different Node/Java version, missing system library). Everything in one giant job. You cannot parallelise or tell what failed. Too little coverage of what matters. A green build is only as meaningful as the tests behind it. Definition of done A good rule: a change is not "done" when it works on your machine, or even when it is merged, but when it has passed CI on main and is available as a deployable artifact. CI turns "done" from an opinion into a fact. Trade-offs Choice Benefit Cost Hosted runners Zero maintenance, clean VM each run Per-minute cost, limited hardware, data leaves your network Self-hosted runners Cheap at scale, custom hardware, private network access You patch and secure them; risk of state leaking between jobs Test everything on every PR Maximum safety Slower, costlier Test only affected parts Fast in monorepos Needs dependency-graph tooling (Nx, Bazel, Turborepo) Try it Take any small project and write down the exact commands to go from a clean clone to "tests pass". If you need more than three, script them. Add the minimal workflow above (adjusted to your language) and open a PR that deliberately breaks a test. Watch the check fail on the PR. Time your pipeline. List the three slowest steps and one way to speed up each.

title: Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment
text: Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment "CD" means two different things, and mixing them up causes real confusion. Both extend CI by automating the path to production. They differ in one decision: does a human press the final button? Why CD exists CI leaves you with a tested artifact on main. Without CD, getting that artifact to users is a separate, manual, error-prone project: a ticket to ops, a deployment window, a wiki checklist. That final step is where a lot of lead time and risk hide. CD closes the gap so the path from "merged" to "running in production" is automated, repeatable and boring. Definitions Term Definition Production deploy trigger Continuous Integration Merge often; automatically build and test every change n/a Continuous Delivery Every change that passes the pipeline is releasable ; deploying to production is a manual, one-click business decision Human approval Continuous Deployment Every change that passes the pipeline is deployed to production automatically None, fully automated commit ─▶ build ─▶ unit/int tests ─▶ package ─▶ deploy staging ─▶ acceptance tests ─┐ │ Continuous DELIVERY: ┌────────── [ human approves ] ◀─────────────────────────┤ ▼ │ deploy production │ Continuous DEPLOYMENT: │ deploy production ◀─────────────────────────────────────────────┘ (automatic, with canary + auto-rollback) The only difference In delivery, the pipeline is capable of deploying at any time and a person decides when. In deployment, the pipeline always deploys. Delivery is a capability; deployment is a policy. Most organisations should first achieve delivery, then decide whether deployment fits their risk profile. Deploy is not release A powerful mental split: deployment is putting code on production servers. Release is exposing a feature to users. With feature flags , you deploy dark code continuously, then release by flipping a flag, for 1% of users, then 10%, then everyone. Deploys become technical, frequent and low-drama; releases become a business decision, reversible in seconds without a redeploy. // the code ships to production but is invisible until the flag is on if (flags.isEnabled('new-checkout', { userId })) { return renderNewCheckout(); } return renderOldCheckout(); Remember to delete flags after rollout; stale flags are tech debt and a source of untested combinations. Environment promotion Changes move through a series of environments, each more production-like and more costly to break. Environment Purpose Typical trigger Data Preview / ephemeral Review a PR in a live URL Each PR; destroyed on close Seed/fake Dev / integration Shared playground, integration with other services Every merge to main Fake Staging / pre-prod Production clone for acceptance, performance, rehearsal Every merge, or release candidate Anonymised or synthetic Production Real users Approval or automatic Real Rules of promotion Promote the artifact, not the code. The image shop:3f9a1c2 that passed staging is the one deployed to prod. No rebuild. Configuration differs, binaries don't. Environment-specific values come from environment config and a secrets manager. Keep staging as close to prod as is affordable (same Kubernetes version, same DB engine and version, same topology in miniature). Drift is how "it passed staging" lies. Gate each hop with automated checks (tests, health checks, security scans) and, where needed, approvals. artifact: shop:3f9a1c2 (built once) ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌──────────┐ approve ┌────────────┐ │ dev │──▶│ staging │──▶│ smoke + │────────▶│ production │ │ auto │ │ auto │ │ e2e pass │ │ (canary → │ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └──────────┘ │ 100%) │ └────────────┘ Approvals and gates Approvals are controls, and they have a cost. Use them intentionally. Manual approval (GitHub environment "required reviewers", GitLab when: manual , Jenkins input ): good for regulated industries, high-blast-radius changes, or until trust in tests is earned. Automated gates: tests, vulnerability scan thresholds, SLO checks ("error budget remaining?"), time windows (no deploys Friday afternoon), change-freeze calendars. Separation of duties: the author of a change cannot be the sole approver of its deployment; the platform enforces this, not a policy document. Approval theater A manager clicking "Approve" without looking at anything adds delay but no safety. Real safety comes from tests, progressive rollout and fast rollback. If you must keep approvals for compliance, make the information they need visible (diff, test results, risk) and keep the approval fast, ideally minutes. Progressive delivery: making deployment safe Continuous deployment is only responsible if blast radius is small and rollback is automatic. Combine CD with: Rolling update: replace instances gradually, health-checking each batch. Blue-green: run the new version beside the old, switch traffic at once, switch back instantly if bad. Canary: send 1-5% of traffic to the new version, compare error rate and latency against the baseline, then expand (tools: Argo Rollouts, Flagger, service mesh, load balancer weights). Automated rollback triggered by SLO/metric regression. Database migrations that are backward compatible (expand then contract), so old and new code can both run during rollout and rollback is possible. These strategies are covered in depth in the Deploying section; the key point here is that they are what lets "every merge goes to prod" be a safe sentence. Release trains A release train ships on a fixed schedule (say, every two weeks or every Tuesday) with whatever is ready; if your feature misses the train, it takes the next one. It is common for mobile apps (app store review), on-prem software and big organisations. Pros: predictable cadence for marketing, support and customers; amortises release overhead; works when the deploy channel is slow (app stores). Cons: batching increases risk and lead time; features wait for the train; pressure to rush onto it. Tip: even on a train, keep main always releasable and use feature flags; the train just selects a commit to cut, it should not require stabilisation heroics. Which should you choose? Situation Choice Web SaaS, strong tests, flags, good observability Continuous deployment Web app, still building trust in tests Continuous delivery with one-click prod Regulated (finance, health), change approval boards Delivery with automated evidence collection and an approval gate Mobile apps Delivery to store/TestFlight on every merge; scheduled release trains; staged rollout in store Libraries / packages Automated release on tag or commit-type (semantic-release) Embedded / on-prem Delivery to a release candidate channel; customers upgrade on their schedule Pitfalls "We do CD" but production deploys still need three tickets. That is automation of one stage, not delivery. Rebuilding per environment. Breaks traceability. Shared mutable staging that ten teams fight over. Prefer ephemeral environments. Skipping observability. You cannot deploy continuously if you cannot tell within minutes whether the deploy hurt. Irreversible changes (destructive migrations) bundled into a routine deploy. Deploy windows by fear. If "never on Fridays" is a rule, your rollback or monitoring is not trusted. Fix that, don't schedule around it. Try it Draw your project's path from merge to production. Mark every manual step and every wait. These are your CD backlog. Decide: delivery or deployment? List what would need to be true (tests, flags, monitoring, rollback) to move one step toward deployment. In GitHub, create an environment named production with a required reviewer and reference it from a job; observe the pause for approval (you will build this in the GitHub Actions lesson).

title: Anatomy of a Pipeline
text: Anatomy of a Pipeline Every CI/CD tool has its own syntax, but they all model the same thing: a graph of stages made of jobs made of steps, passing artifacts along, running on machines called runners. Learn the shape once and you can read any pipeline. Why think in stages? A pipeline is an assembly line for software. Each station does one job and either passes the work on or stops the line. Ordering matters for two reasons: fail fast (cheap checks first so you do not waste 20 minutes building something that fails lint in 10 seconds) and confidence gradient (each stage raises confidence before you risk the next, more expensive, more dangerous stage). The canonical pipeline ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌───────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌───────┐ │ source │▶│ lint │▶│ test │▶│ build │▶│ scan │▶│ package │▶│publish │▶│deploy │▶ smoke test │checkout│ │ format │ │unit + │ │compile │ │SAST,deps│ │ docker │ │registry │ │staging│ │ │ │ │ types │ │integr.│ │bundle │ │secrets │ │ image │ │ push │ │ prod │ ▼ └────────┘ └────────┘ └───────┘ └────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └───────┘ rollback? seconds seconds 1-5 min 1-3 min 1-3 min 1-2 min seconds minutes <──────── CI: runs on every PR ────────▶ <──────────── CD: runs on main / tags ─────────▶ Stage What happens Why it exists Typical tools Checkout Clone the repo at the exact commit Reproducibility git, actions/checkout Lint / format / type-check Static analysis without running code Cheapest, fastest feedback ESLint, Prettier, tsc , ruff, golangci-lint Test Unit, then integration tests Prove behavior Jest, pytest, JUnit, Go test Build Compile / bundle / transpile Prove it builds in a clean env npm, Maven, Gradle, go build Scan SAST, dependency CVEs, secrets, IaC, container scan Shift security left CodeQL, Semgrep, Trivy, Snyk, gitleaks Package Create the deployable unit One immutable artifact Docker/BuildKit, jar, wheel, tarball Publish Push to a registry/artifact store with a unique tag Make the artifact available to deployers GHCR, ECR, Docker Hub, Artifactory, npm Deploy Roll the artifact to an environment Get it running kubectl/Helm, Argo CD, SSH, Terraform, cloud CLIs Smoke / verify Hit a health endpoint, run a few critical checks Know the deploy worked curl, k6, Playwright, synthetic checks Rollback / notify Revert on failure; tell humans Contain damage Slack, PagerDuty, previous tag redeploy Vocabulary Pipeline / workflow: the whole automated process, triggered by an event. Trigger / event: push, pull request, tag, schedule (cron), manual, webhook, another pipeline finishing. Stage: a phase grouping jobs (GitLab, Jenkins). Stages run in order. Job: a unit of work that runs on one runner. Jobs may run in parallel; each starts with a clean environment. Step: one command or action inside a job. Steps in a job share a filesystem and run sequentially. Runner / agent: the machine or container that executes jobs. Artifact: files a job produces for later jobs or for download (build output, test reports). Cache: files reused between runs to save time (dependencies). Not a source of truth. Environment: a deployment target (staging, production) with its own secrets, protection rules and history. Jobs are isolated: artifacts vs cache Each job typically starts on a fresh runner. Anything you want to survive must be passed explicitly. Two mechanisms, constantly confused: Artifacts Cache Purpose Pass outputs between jobs; keep results (reports, binaries) Speed up by reusing inputs (downloaded dependencies) Guaranteed? Yes, if the producing job succeeded No, best effort; a miss must still work Keyed by Run + name A key you choose (e.g. hash of package-lock.json ) Example dist/ , coverage XML, test reports, SBOM ~/.npm , ~/.m2 , pip wheels, Docker layers Cache key design Key on the lockfile hash so the cache invalidates exactly when dependencies change, with a fallback prefix key so a near-match still helps. Never cache build outputs you then ship; that breaks reproducibility. Speed: parallelism, fan-out, matrix, sharding ┌─────▶ lint ────────┐ checkout ───▶├─────▶ unit tests ──┤ ├─────▶ type-check ──┼──▶ build ──▶ scan ─┬─▶ deploy staging ─▶ e2e ─▶ deploy prod └─────▶ integration ─┘ └─▶ (parallel) SBOM/sign (fan-out: independent jobs in parallel) (fan-in: wait for all via needs) Fan-out / fan-in: independent jobs run concurrently; a downstream job declares dependencies ( needs: in GitHub/GitLab) and waits. Matrix: run the same job across combinations (Node 20/22 x ubuntu/windows). One definition, N jobs. Sharding: split a long test suite into N slices run in parallel ( jest --shard=1/4 , Playwright --shard ), then merge reports. A 20-minute suite on 4 shards finishes in about 5. Caching and incremental builds: dependency cache, Docker layer cache, build caches (Turborepo, Gradle, Bazel remote cache). Path filters: skip jobs when only docs changed. Cancel superseded runs: a new push to a PR cancels the older run (concurrency groups). Parallelism trades money (more concurrent runners) for time. Developer time is almost always more expensive than runner time. Pipeline types by trigger Trigger Runs Does NOT do Pull request Lint, tests, build, scan, preview deploy Publish release artifacts or touch prod; PRs from forks get no secrets Push to main All the above + publish artifact + deploy staging (+ prod) Tag v* Release build, publish versioned artifacts, create release Schedule Nightly full e2e, dependency audit, base image rebuild Manual ( workflow_dispatch ) Ad-hoc deploy / rollback to a chosen version Pipeline as code Pipelines are defined in a file in the repo ( .github/workflows/*.yml , .gitlab-ci.yml , Jenkinsfile ). Benefits: versioned, reviewed, branch-specific (a PR can change the pipeline and test the change), reproducible, and visible. The old way, clicking jobs together in a web UI, produced undocumented, unreproducible "snowflake" CI servers. What a stage must provide Determinism: same inputs, same outputs. Pin tool versions, lock dependencies. Idempotence: re-running a deploy for the same version is safe. Clear failure signal: non-zero exit code means stop; logs say why. Timeouts so hung jobs do not run forever. Isolation: no dependence on state left by earlier runs. A pipeline in pseudo-YAML # tool-agnostic sketch on: [pull_request, push to main] jobs: lint: {runs: "npm run lint"} test: {runs: "npm test", needs: []} build: {runs: "npm run build", needs: [lint, test], outputs: [dist/]} scan: {runs: "trivy fs .", needs: [build]} package: {runs: "docker build -t app:$SHA .", needs: [scan]} publish: {runs: "docker push app:$SHA", needs: [package], only: main} deploy-stg: {runs: "deploy app:$SHA staging", needs: [publish], env: staging} smoke: {runs: "curl -f https://stg/health", needs: [deploy-stg]} deploy-prod: {runs: "deploy app:$SHA production", needs: [smoke], env: production, approval: true} Pitfalls One enormous job. No parallelism, hard to read failures. Order that wastes time : running a 10-minute build before a 5-second lint. Relying on cache for correctness. It can be evicted; builds must work cold. Rebuilding per stage. Pass the artifact (or image digest) instead. Mutable tags ( latest ) between publish and deploy. Deploy by immutable SHA or digest. No verification after deploy. A deploy job that exits 0 only means the command ran, not that the app is healthy. Environment logic hard-coded in scripts with if branch == main sprinkled everywhere; use the platform's rules/conditions. Trade-offs Decision Upside Downside Many small jobs Parallel, clear failures Per-job setup overhead (checkout, install), more YAML Few big jobs Less overhead Serial, opaque Strict gates everywhere Safer Slower, more friction Full scan on every PR Early detection Costly; consider diff-aware scans plus nightly full scans Try it Draw your project's pipeline using the stage table. Which stages are missing? Which run in the wrong order? For each stage, note its duration from a recent run. Find the critical path (the longest chain of dependent jobs); that, not the sum, is your pipeline time. Decide for each of these whether it belongs in a cache or an artifact: node_modules , dist/ , JUnit XML, a Docker image layer, a downloaded Go module.

title: GitHub Actions
text: GitHub Actions GitHub Actions is the CI/CD system built into GitHub. Workflows are YAML files in your repo, triggered by repository events, executed on hosted or self-hosted runners. It is the most widely used CI system today; this lesson goes from concepts to a complete Node app pipeline that tests, builds and pushes a Docker image, and deploys over SSH. Core concepts Event (push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch, release ...) │ triggers ▼ Workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml) ├─ Job A ── runs-on: ubuntu-latest ──▶ Runner VM #1 │ ├─ Step 1: uses: actions/checkout@v4 (reusable Action) │ ├─ Step 2: run: npm ci (shell command) │ └─ Step 3: run: npm test └─ Job B (needs: A) ── Runner VM #2 ... Concept Meaning Workflow A YAML file under .github/workflows/ . A repo can have many. Event What triggers it: push , pull_request , schedule , workflow_dispatch (manual), release , workflow_call (reusable), etc. Job A set of steps on one runner. Jobs run in parallel unless needs orders them. Step Either run: (a shell command) or uses: (an action). Steps share the runner's filesystem. Action A reusable unit (JavaScript, Docker or composite) from the Marketplace or your own repo. Runner The machine executing a job: GitHub-hosted ( ubuntu-latest , windows-latest , macos-latest , ARM variants) or self-hosted. Context / expressions ${{ github.sha }} , ${{ secrets.X }} , ${{ matrix.node }} , ${{ needs.build.outputs.tag }} Part 1: Continuous integration for a Node app Save as .github/workflows/ci.yml . name: CI on: pull_request: push: branches: [main] # least privilege: the default token can only read the repo permissions: contents: read # cancel older runs of the same PR/branch when a new commit arrives concurrency: group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }} cancel-in-progress: true jobs: lint: runs-on: ubuntu-latest timeout-minutes: 10 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version-file: .nvmrc cache: npm # caches ~/.npm keyed by package-lock.json - run: npm ci - run: npm run lint - run: npm run typecheck test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest timeout-minutes: 15 strategy: fail-fast: false # let all matrix legs finish matrix: node: [20, 22] # run on two Node versions services: postgres: # real DB for integration tests image: postgres:16 env: POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test POSTGRES_DB: app_test ports: ["5432:5432"] options: >- --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres" --health-interval 5s --health-timeout 5s --health-retries 10 env: DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:test@localhost:5432/app_test steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: ${{ matrix.node }} cache: npm - run: npm ci - run: npm test -- --coverage - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 # keep the report for download/inspection if: always() # even when tests fail with: name: coverage-node${{ matrix.node }} path: coverage/ retention-days: 7 Key points: permissions narrows the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN ; concurrency saves minutes; services starts sidecar containers on the runner; if: always() runs the step regardless of earlier failures; the matrix creates two independent jobs. Part 2: Build and push a Docker image Save as .github/workflows/release.yml . It runs only on main after CI passes (via a shared trigger) and publishes to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR). name: Build and Deploy on: push: branches: [main] workflow_dispatch: # manual re-run / redeploy permissions: contents: read concurrency: group: deploy-production cancel-in-progress: false # never cancel a deploy mid-flight; queue instead env: IMAGE: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }} # e.g. ghcr.io/acme/shop jobs: test: uses: ./.github/workflows/ci.yml # reuse CI (needs "on: workflow_call" in ci.yml) build: needs: test runs-on: ubuntu-latest timeout-minutes: 20 permissions: contents: read packages: write # needed to push to GHCR outputs: tag: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }} digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3 - uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - id: meta # computes tags and labels uses: docker/metadata-action@v5 with: images: ${{ env.IMAGE }} tags: | type=sha,format=long type=raw,value=latest,enable={{is_default_branch}} - id: push uses: docker/build-push-action@v6 with: context: . push: true tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }} labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }} cache-from: type=gha # reuse layers between runs cache-to: type=gha,mode=max provenance: true # attach build provenance attestation To use uses: ./.github/workflows/ci.yml as a reusable workflow, add workflow_call: under on: in ci.yml . The image gets an immutable sha-<40-char> tag; latest is a convenience pointer only, never what you deploy. Part 3: Deploy over SSH with an approval gate Append this job to release.yml . It targets a GitHub environment named production . deploy: needs: build runs-on: ubuntu-latest timeout-minutes: 10 environment: name: production # applies protection rules + environment secrets url: https://shop.example.com steps: - name: Set up SSH env: SSH_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY }} KNOWN_HOSTS: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS }} # output of: ssh-keyscan host run: | install -m 700 -d ~/.ssh printf '%s\n' "$SSH_KEY" > ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 printf '%s\n' "$KNOWN_HOSTS" > ~/.ssh/known_hosts - name: Deploy image by digest env: HOST: ${{ vars.DEPLOY_HOST }} IMAGE_REF: ${{ env.IMAGE }}@${{ needs.build.outputs.digest }} run: | ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 deploy@"$HOST" bash -s -- "$IMAGE_REF" <<'EOF' set -euo pipefail IMAGE_REF="$1" cd /opt/shop echo "IMAGE=$IMAGE_REF" > .env.deploy docker pull "$IMAGE_REF" docker compose --env-file .env.deploy up -d --remove-orphans EOF - name: Smoke test run: | for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do if curl -fsS https://shop.example.com/healthz; then exit 0; fi sleep 10 done echo "Health check failed" >&2 exit 1 Notes: the server's docker-compose.yml would reference image: ${IMAGE} ; the private key lives in an environment secret , not repository-wide; the server user deploy should have only the rights it needs; deploying by digest guarantees you run exactly what was built. Using known_hosts instead of disabling host key checking prevents man-in-the-middle attacks. Environments and approvals In Settings > Environments create staging and production . For production configure: Required reviewers: the job pauses until one of them approves in the UI. Wait timer: optional delay before deploy. Deployment branches: only main (and tags) may deploy here. Environment secrets and variables: scoped to jobs that reference the environment; only released after approval. The Deployments tab then gives a history of what version went where and who approved. Concurrency, caching and artifacts concurrency.group ensures only one run per group; cancel-in-progress: true for CI, false for deploys. actions/cache (or the cache: input of setup actions) restores directories by key. Entries unused for 7 days are evicted and each repo has a size cap (10 GB by default); never rely on it for correctness. upload-artifact / download-artifact pass files between jobs and attach them to the run. Set retention-days . Job outputs pass small strings ( needs.build.outputs.digest ); use artifacts for files. Reusable workflows and composite actions Stop copy-pasting pipelines across repos. A reusable workflow is a full workflow with on: workflow_call , called by other workflows: # in acme/platform-workflows/.github/workflows/node-ci.yml on: workflow_call: inputs: node-version: {type: string, default: "22"} secrets: NPM_TOKEN: {required: false} jobs: ci: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: {node-version: "${{ inputs.node-version }}", cache: npm} - run: npm ci && npm test # in a service repo jobs: ci: uses: acme/platform-workflows/.github/workflows/node-ci.yml@v2 with: {node-version: "20"} secrets: inherit A composite action ( action.yml with runs: using: composite ) bundles several steps into one reusable step. Use reusable workflows for whole jobs, composite actions for step sequences. OIDC to the cloud: no long-lived keys Instead of storing AWS keys as secrets, let the workflow prove its identity with a short-lived OpenID Connect token that the cloud exchanges for temporary credentials. permissions: id-token: write # allow requesting the OIDC token contents: read steps: - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with: role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gha-deploy aws-region: eu-west-1 - run: aws sts get-caller-identity On the AWS side the role's trust policy restricts the token's sub claim, for example to repo:acme/shop:environment:production , so only that repo and environment can assume it. The same pattern works with GCP Workload Identity Federation and Azure federated credentials. See the secrets lesson for details. Other useful features Path filters: on.push.paths: ['src/**', 'package*.json'] skips irrelevant runs. Conditionals: if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' , if: failure() . Schedules: on.schedule: [{cron: '0 3 * * *'}] (UTC). Dependabot keeps actions and dependencies updated via PRs. Job summaries: write Markdown to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY . Self-hosted runners / ARC: run on your own machines or Kubernetes (Actions Runner Controller) for private networking and cost control. Debugging: re-run with debug logging; use act to run workflows locally (approximate). Pitfalls Using pull_request_target with untrusted code checkout : it runs with secrets and write token on code from forks. A classic supply-chain hole. Use pull_request for untrusted code. Script injection: never interpolate untrusted values ( ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} ) directly into run: . Pass them via env: and quote. Unpinned third-party actions: @main or even @v3 tags can be moved. Pin to a full commit SHA for anything non-trivial. Over-broad GITHUB_TOKEN permissions. Declare permissions explicitly. Cache poisoning / stale caches and cache used as artifact store. Secrets in logs: secrets are masked, but transformed values (base64, substrings) may not be. YAML gotchas: on and numeric versions: write node-version: "22" quoted so 20.10 is not parsed as 20.1 . Hosted-runner minutes are billed (free tier for public repos); long matrices on macOS cost multiples of Linux. Validate before you push Use actionlint (a linter for workflow files) locally or in CI. It catches expression typos, bad needs references and shell issues in run: blocks. Trade-offs Pros Cons Zero setup for GitHub repos; huge action ecosystem; tight PR integration; free for public repos Lock-in to GitHub; Marketplace actions are third-party code you must vet Environments + OIDC give good deploy governance YAML expression language is quirky; complex flows get verbose Reusable workflows for platform teams Local reproduction of runs is imperfect Try it Create a tiny Node app ( npm init -y , one test with node --test ), add ci.yml , push on a branch and open a PR. Watch the checks. Add the Docker build job to push to GHCR. Find your image under the repo's Packages. Create a production environment with yourself as required reviewer; add a deploy job that just echo s and see the approval pause. Replace one third-party action version tag with its commit SHA ( uses: actions/checkout@<sha> # v4.x.y ).

title: GitLab CI/CD
text: GitLab CI/CD GitLab bundles source hosting, CI/CD, a container registry, security scanning and environments into one product. Its pipeline model, stages containing jobs, defined in a single .gitlab-ci.yml , is concise and has influenced many other tools. The model .gitlab-ci.yml in repo root │ push / merge request / schedule / API / tag ▼ Pipeline stage: build ──▶ stage: test ──────────▶ stage: package ──▶ stage: deploy build_app unit_tests ┐ docker_image staging lint ├ parallel production (manual) sast ┘ (jobs in a stage run in parallel; next stage starts when all succeed) │ each job ▼ GitLab Runner (shell / docker / kubernetes executor) pulls the job and runs it Concept Meaning Pipeline The whole run for a commit or MR. Stage Ordered phase; default order: .pre , build , test , deploy , .post . You can define your own with stages: . Job A named block with a script: ; assigned to a stage. Runner The agent that executes jobs. Shared (GitLab.com), group, or project runners; executor types: docker, kubernetes, shell, etc. Artifacts / cache Same distinction as everywhere: artifacts pass outputs; cache speeds dependencies. Environment A named deploy target with history, URL, rollback button and protected access. Variables Predefined ( CI_COMMIT_SHA , CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE ) and custom, set in UI/API, can be masked, protected, or file-type. A complete example Node app: lint and test in parallel, build, package a Docker image to the built-in GitLab registry, deploy to staging automatically, to production after a manual click. stages: [lint, test, build, package, deploy] default: image: node:22-alpine interruptible: true # newer pipelines on same branch may cancel this job timeout: 15 minutes variables: npm_config_cache: "$CI_PROJECT_DIR/.npm" # keep npm cache inside the project for caching IMAGE: "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA" # --- reusable hidden template: names starting with "." are not run --- .node_setup: cache: key: files: [package-lock.json] # invalidate when lockfile changes paths: [.npm/] before_script: - npm ci --prefer-offline lint: extends: .node_setup stage: lint script: - npm run lint - npm run typecheck unit_tests: extends: .node_setup stage: test script: - npm test -- --coverage coverage: '/All files[^|]*\|[^|]*\s+([\d\.]+)/' # parse % from output artifacts: when: always reports: junit: junit.xml # shows test results in the MR paths: [coverage/] expire_in: 1 week integration_tests: extends: .node_setup stage: test services: - name: postgres:16 alias: db variables: POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test DATABASE_URL: "postgres://postgres:test@db:5432/postgres" script: - npm run test:integration build_app: extends: .node_setup stage: build script: - npm run build artifacts: paths: [dist/] expire_in: 1 day docker_image: stage: package image: docker:27 services: [docker:27-dind] # Docker-in-Docker for building images variables: DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: "/certs" before_script: - echo "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin "$CI_REGISTRY" script: - docker build --pull -t "$IMAGE" . - docker push "$IMAGE" rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH # only on main deploy_staging: stage: deploy image: alpine:3.20 environment: name: staging url: https://staging.shop.example.com before_script: - apk add --no-cache openssh-client - install -m 700 -d ~/.ssh - echo "$SSH_PRIVATE_KEY" > ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 - echo "$SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS" > ~/.ssh/known_hosts script: - ssh deploy@"$STAGING_HOST" "IMAGE=$IMAGE /opt/shop/deploy.sh" rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH deploy_production: extends: deploy_staging environment: name: production url: https://shop.example.com script: - ssh deploy@"$PROD_HOST" "IMAGE=$IMAGE /opt/shop/deploy.sh" rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH when: manual # human clicks "play" resource_group: production # serialise prod deploys Highlights: extends and hidden .templates remove duplication; cache:key:files keys on the lockfile; artifacts:reports:junit surfaces failures in the merge request; resource_group prevents two deploys to the same environment at once; environment gives a deployments page and one-click rollback to a previous deployment. Rules: controlling when jobs run rules: replaces the older only/except . Rules are evaluated top to bottom; the first match decides. job: script: ./run.sh rules: - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event" # MR pipelines - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/ # release tags variables: {DEPLOY_TARGET: "prod"} - changes: ["docs/**/*"] # only when docs changed when: never - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH when: manual allow_failure: false - when: never # default: don't run A common trap: a pipeline can be triggered both by a branch push and by an MR event, producing duplicate pipelines . Use workflow:rules at the top level to choose one: workflow: rules: - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event" - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS when: never # avoid duplicate branch pipeline - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH || $CI_COMMIT_TAG DAG pipelines and parallelism needs: [job] lets a job start as soon as its dependencies finish rather than waiting for the whole previous stage, forming a DAG and shortening pipelines. parallel: 4 runs N copies (with CI_NODE_INDEX / CI_NODE_TOTAL ) for test sharding; parallel: matrix: runs combinations of variables. interruptible: true + auto-cancel redundant pipelines saves runner time. Includes, templates and components Share pipeline logic across projects with include: : include: - local: ci/node.yml # file in this repo - project: acme/ci-templates # another project ref: v3.2.0 # pin a version file: /templates/docker-build.yml - template: Security/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml # GitLab-provided template - component: gitlab.com/acme/components/deploy@1.4.0 # CI/CD component (catalog) inputs: environment: production CI/CD components (the catalog) are versioned, parameterised building blocks, the modern way to share pipelines. Pin versions to avoid surprise breakage. Runners Shared runners on GitLab.com need no setup and run jobs in a fresh VM/container (consumption of compute minutes applies). Self-managed runners: install gitlab-runner , register with a token, pick an executor. The Docker executor runs each job in the image named by image: ; the Kubernetes executor spawns a pod per job (good for autoscaling). Tags: label runners ( gpu , arm64 , prod-deploy ) and select with tags: in the job. Docker-in-Docker needs privileged mode, which is a security risk on shared runners. Alternatives: Kaniko, BuildKit rootless, Buildah, or a dedicated build runner. # register a runner (interactive flags shown non-interactively) gitlab-runner register \ --url https://gitlab.example.com \ --token "$RUNNER_AUTH_TOKEN" \ --executor docker \ --docker-image alpine:3.20 Variables, secrets and security Set variables in Settings > CI/CD > Variables . Tick Masked (hidden in logs), Protected (only available on protected branches/tags) and scope by environment. Prefer ID tokens (OIDC) ( id_tokens: keyword) to authenticate to cloud and Vault without stored keys. Built-in security templates : SAST, secret detection, dependency scanning, container scanning, DAST, with findings shown in merge requests (some features in paid tiers). Merge request pipelines from forks do not receive protected variables. Auto DevOps and Review Apps Review apps deploy every merge request to a temporary URL ( environment: name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG with an on_stop job to tear it down) so reviewers and product people can click the real change. Auto DevOps provides an opinionated, zero-config pipeline (build, test, scan, deploy to Kubernetes); good for learning, usually replaced by a custom pipeline later. Pitfalls Duplicate pipelines from mixing branch and MR triggers (fix with workflow:rules ). Forgetting that each job starts clean: pass dist/ with artifacts , use dependencies / needs to control which artifacts are downloaded. Cache not shared across runners (local cache); configure a distributed cache (S3/GCS) for fleets. Privileged DinD on shared runners. Unmasked secrets: masking requires the value to meet format rules (e.g. min length, no spaces). Unpinned include refs ( ref: main ) mean someone else's change can break your pipeline. YAML anchors vs extends vs !reference : prefer extends ; use !reference [.job, script] to reuse fragments. GitLab CI vs GitHub Actions at a glance Topic GitLab CI GitHub Actions Config One .gitlab-ci.yml (+ includes) Many files in .github/workflows/ Ordering Stages + needs needs only Reuse extends, include, components Reusable workflows, composite actions, Marketplace Runner model Executors (docker, k8s, shell) VM per job; ARC for k8s Built-in extras Registry, environments, security scans, review apps in one platform Packages, Environments, Dependabot, code scanning Self-hosting the platform First-class (GitLab self-managed) GitHub Enterprise Server Try it Create a free GitLab project, add a .gitlab-ci.yml with two stages ( test , deploy ) and echo jobs; open the pipeline graph. Add rules so the deploy job is manual on main and never runs on MRs. Add the Security/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml template and review the report in the pipeline's Security tab. Run CI Lint (Pipeline editor) to validate your file before committing.

title: Jenkins and Other CI/CD Tools
text: Jenkins and Other CI/CD Tools GitHub Actions and GitLab CI are not the only options. Jenkins is the veteran you will meet in many companies; CircleCI, Argo and Tekton cover other niches. This lesson shows what each is, how its pipeline looks, and how to choose.
