An image built for one will not run natively on the other. Build one tag that serves both: docker buildx create --name multi --use docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \ -t ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.4.2 --push . docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.4.2 # shows both platforms Pushing creates a manifest list; clients automatically pull the matching platform. Non-native platforms build under QEMU emulation (slow for compiled languages). Faster: cross-compile in the build stage using FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM and the TARGETARCH arg: FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.24 AS build ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH RUN GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/server . Measuring the result docker build -t myapp:fat -f Dockerfile.single . docker build -t myapp:slim . docker images myapp dive myapp:slim # visualize wasted space per layer docker buildx build --progress=plain . # full, unfolded build log Example Single-stage Optimized Go API ~850 MB (golang image) ~12 MB (distroless/static) Node + TS API ~1.2 GB ~180 MB (slim, prod deps only) Python API ~1.0 GB ~150 MB (slim, no cache) Pitfalls and trade-offs Forgetting runtime-only needs when going distroless/scratch: CA certificates, /etc/passwd , timezone data, shared libraries (a dynamically linked Go binary fails on scratch; set CGO_ENABLED=0 ). Cache mounts are not shared by default across CI runners ; they speed local builds more than ephemeral CI. Over-optimizing : debugging a shell-less image is harder. Keep a debug target. Alpine + Python : often slower and bigger once compilers are added. Prefer python:3.13-slim . Cache never refreshes : a cached apt-get update layer hides security fixes. Rebuild with --pull --no-cache on a schedule. Try it Write a tiny Go "hello server". Build it single-stage ( FROM golang ) and multi-stage with distroless. Compare docker images sizes. Add a cache mount to a Python Dockerfile, change requirements.txt by one line and compare the second build time with and without the mount. Try docker run --rm -it your-distroless-image sh and read the error. Then build the :debug variant and retry. Run docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 . (without --push use --output type=image,push=false or a local registry) and inspect the result.

title: Volumes and Data Persistence
text: Volumes and Data Persistence A container's writable layer is born with the container and dies with it. Delete the container and every file it wrote is gone. That is perfect for stateless web apps and disastrous for databases. Volumes and mounts are how you attach durable storage to disposable containers. The problem docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw postgres:16 # ... create tables, insert data ... docker rm -f db docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw postgres:16 # all your data is gone Container filesystems are also slower (copy-on-write overlay) and cannot be shared easily between containers. Docker offers three ways to mount something from outside the writable layer into a container. Docker host ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Container │ │ /var/lib/postgresql/data ◀── volume │──▶ /var/lib/docker/volumes/pgdata/_data │ /app (source code) ◀── bind mount │──▶ /home/you/project (any host path) │ /run/secrets, /tmp ◀── tmpfs │──▶ host RAM only (never on disk) └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ The three mount types Named volume Bind mount tmpfs Where data lives Docker-managed dir ( /var/lib/docker/volumes ) Any host path you choose Host memory Managed by Docker Yes (create, list, remove, drivers) No Yes Survives container removal Yes Yes (it is your files) No Best for Databases, production state Local development (live code reload), config files Scratch data, secrets, performance Pre-populated from image Yes, copies image content on first use No, host content hides the image's No Portable / backup-friendly Yes Depends on host layout n/a Named volumes docker volume create pgdata docker run -d --name db \ -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw \ -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data \ postgres:16 docker rm -f db # container gone... docker run -d --name db2 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw \ -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16 # ...data is back docker volume ls docker volume inspect pgdata # shows Mountpoint docker volume rm pgdata # permanent delete docker volume prune # remove volumes not used by any container The -v name:/path form creates the volume automatically if it does not exist. The modern, explicit syntax is --mount , which errors on typos rather than silently creating things: docker run --mount type=volume,source=pgdata,target=/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16 docker run --mount type=bind,source="$PWD",target=/app,readonly node:22-slim ls /app -v pitfall If you write -v ./data:/data with a path, you get a bind mount. If you write -v data:/data with a bare name, you get a named volume. A missing ./ changes the semantics entirely, and with -v a mistyped host path is silently created as an empty directory owned by root. Prefer --mount in scripts. Bind mounts for development Mount your source directory into the container so edits on the host appear instantly, enabling hot reload without rebuilding: docker run --rm -it -p 3000:3000 \ -v "$PWD":/app \ -v /app/node_modules \ node:22-slim sh -c "cd /app && npm run dev" The second -v creates an anonymous volume that masks the host node_modules . The trick of masking /app/node_modules stops your macOS-built native modules from overriding the Linux ones installed in the image. Bind mount gotchas Permissions/ownership : files are owned by your host UID. A container running as a different UID may be unable to write. Match with --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" or fix with chown . Performance on Mac/Windows : file sharing across the VM boundary is slow for large trees (many small files such as node_modules ). Use named volumes for dependency dirs; Docker Desktop's VirtioFS and Compose watch help. Host content hides image content : mounting an empty dir over /app makes the code baked into the image invisible. SELinux (Fedora/RHEL): add :z or :Z to the mount, e.g. -v "$PWD":/app:z . Use :ro for anything the container should not modify. tmpfs docker run --rm --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=64m,mode=1777 alpine df -h /tmp docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run myapp # read-only root + writable scratch tmpfs data lives in RAM and vanishes when the container stops. Use it for temp files that must never touch disk, and in tandem with --read-only for hardening. Persisting a real database docker run -d --name pg \ --restart unless-stopped \ -e POSTGRES_USER=app \ -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/pgpass \ -e POSTGRES_DB=appdb \ -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data \ -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 \ postgres:16 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U app appdb # connect from the host Notes: bind published DB ports to 127.0.0.1 unless remote access is truly required (a plain -p 5432:5432 exposes it on every interface, and Docker bypasses most host firewall rules). Pin the major version: pointing a newer Postgres at an older data directory fails, and upgrades require pg_upgrade or dump/restore. Backup and restore Volumes are just directories, so you can archive them with a throwaway container that mounts the volume plus a host directory: # Backup volume "pgdata" to ./backup/pgdata-2026-10-05.tgz docker run --rm \ -v pgdata:/source:ro \ -v "$PWD/backup":/backup \ alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata-$(date +%F).tgz -C /source . # Restore into a (new) volume docker volume create pgdata-restored docker run --rm \ -v pgdata-restored:/target \ -v "$PWD/backup":/backup:ro \ alpine tar xzf /backup/pgdata-2026-10-05.tgz -C /target File-level copies of live databases can be corrupt Tarring a running Postgres data directory may capture a half-written state. For databases prefer logical backups, which are consistent and portable across versions: docker exec pg pg_dump -U app -Fc appdb > appdb.dump # backup docker exec -i pg pg_restore -U app -d appdb --clean < appdb.dump # restore # MySQL: docker exec db mysqldump -u root -p"$PW" --all-databases > all.sql Also test restores regularly. An untested backup is a hope, not a backup. Sharing and copying data docker run -v shared:/data writer ... # several containers can mount one volume docker run -v shared:/data:ro reader ... # read-only for the consumer docker cp web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./nginx.conf # one-off copy out of a container docker cp ./index.html web:/usr/share/nginx/html/ docker run --rm -v pgdata:/d alpine ls -la /d # peek into a volume Concurrent writers to the same volume need application-level coordination. Two Postgres instances on one data directory will destroy it. Volumes in production Single host: named volumes on a fast local disk, with scheduled backups shipped off-host (S3, etc.). Orchestrators: Kubernetes uses PersistentVolumes backed by cloud disks (EBS, GCE PD). The volume lives independently of any node. Managed databases (RDS, Cloud SQL) are often the better answer: "databases in containers" in production means you own backups, upgrades, failover and tuning. Containerized databases shine in dev, CI and test. Volume drivers (NFS, cloud storage) exist but network filesystems often have poor locking and latency characteristics for databases. Design principle: keep containers stateless Treat state as an external dependency: databases, object storage (S3), caches. A stateless container can be killed, rescheduled and scaled freely. Write logs to stdout, uploads to object storage, sessions to Redis. Where state must be local, make the volume explicit and documented. Pitfalls docker compose down -v deletes your named volumes. Know before you type the -v . docker system prune --volumes removes unused volumes, including a stopped DB's data. Anonymous volumes (from VOLUME in a Dockerfile or -v /path ) pile up as random-hash names. Name your volumes. Changing POSTGRES_PASSWORD on an existing volume has no effect; init variables apply only when the data directory is empty. Try it Run Postgres with a named volume, create a table, remove the container, start a new one on the same volume and confirm the table survived. Repeat without a volume and watch the data vanish. Bind-mount a folder with an index.html into nginx ( -v "$PWD/site":/usr/share/nginx/html:ro ), edit the file and refresh the browser. Back up the volume with the tar command and a pg_dump . Restore the dump into a fresh container.

title: Docker Networking
text: Docker Networking Every container gets its own network namespace: its own IP address, interfaces and ports. Docker's job is to wire those namespaces together and to the outside world. Most "my containers cannot talk to each other" problems come down to five ideas: network drivers, user-defined networks with built-in DNS, port publishing, localhost meaning something different inside a container, and bind addresses. How it works under the hood On Linux, Docker creates a virtual bridge ( docker0 ), then for each container a veth pair: one end inside the container's namespace ( eth0 ), the other attached to the bridge. Outbound traffic is NAT'd (masqueraded) through the host with iptables/nftables rules, and published ports are implemented as DNAT rules. Container A (172.18.0.2) Container B (172.18.0.3) eth0 ─┐ eth0 ─┐ │ veth │ veth ┌─────┴────────────────────┬─────┴──────┐ │ bridge (172.18.0.1) │ ← Docker network "appnet" └───────────────┬───────────────────────┘ │ NAT / iptables Host eth0 (192.168.1.50) ──▶ Internet host:8080 ──DNAT──▶ container A:80 (port publishing) Network drivers Driver Behavior Use for bridge (default) Private virtual network on one host; NAT to outside Almost everything on a single host host Container shares the host's network stack; no isolation, no port mapping Max network performance, tools that need host network visibility. Linux only (limited support in Docker Desktop) none Only loopback; no networking Offline batch jobs, maximum isolation overlay Multi-host network (Swarm) Docker Swarm; Kubernetes uses CNI plugins instead macvlan / ipvlan Container gets its own MAC/IP on the physical LAN Legacy apps needing to look like a physical host docker network ls docker network inspect bridge docker run --rm --network host nginx # shares host stack: nginx on host :80 directly docker run --rm --network none alpine ip a # only "lo" The default bridge vs. user-defined bridges Containers started without --network join the legacy default bridge . It works, but containers there can reach each other only by IP address (which changes on every restart) and all share one flat network. User-defined bridge networks fix both: Automatic DNS : containers resolve each other by name (or service alias) via Docker's embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 . Better isolation : only containers on the same network can talk. Live attach/detach without restarting. docker network create appnet docker run -d --name db --network appnet -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw postgres:16 docker run -d --name api --network appnet -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:pw@db:5432/postgres myapp:1.0 # ^^ resolved by name docker exec api getent hosts db # 172.18.0.2 db docker exec api ping -c1 db docker network connect appnet other # attach a running container docker network rm appnet Always use a user-defined network Docker Compose does this for you automatically: each project gets its own network and each service name becomes a DNS name. That is why your app connects to host db or redis instead of an IP. Port publishing A container's ports are private to its network by default. -p publishes them on the host so outside clients can reach them. -p 8080:80 # host 8080 -> container 80, on ALL host interfaces (0.0.0.0) -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 # only reachable from the host itself -p 8080:80/udp # UDP -p 3000-3005:3000-3005 # ranges -p 80 # random host port; find it with: docker port web -P # publish all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports EXPOSE in a Dockerfile is just documentation; only -p / -P actually publishes. Published ports bypass your firewall Docker inserts its own iptables rules ahead of ufw/firewalld rules. -p 5432:5432 on a cloud VM exposes Postgres to the internet even if ufw says "deny". Bind to 127.0.0.1 for anything not meant to be public, put only your reverse proxy on public ports, and use cloud security groups as the real perimeter. Container-to-container vs. container-to-host From To Address to use Container Another container, same user-defined network Service/container name and the container's port: http://api:3000 Container The host machine (Docker Desktop) host.docker.internal Container The host machine (Linux) --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway then the same name, or the bridge gateway IP Host A container localhost:<published host port> Container Internet Works via NAT; DNS comes from the host's resolver "localhost" inside a container is the container itself The single most common networking bug: your API container uses localhost:5432 to reach Postgres. That points at the API container's own loopback, where nothing listens. Use the service name ( db:5432 ). Also note that between containers you use the container's internal port ( 5432 ), not the host-published one. Bind to 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1 If your app listens only on 127.0.0.1 inside the container, traffic arriving via the bridge (or a published port) is refused. Configure the server to listen on 0.0.0.0 (e.g. uvicorn --host 0.0.0.0 , app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0') ). Putting it together: three-tier example docker network create front docker network create back docker run -d --name db --network back postgres:16 docker run -d --name api --network back myapi:1.0 docker network connect front api # api is on BOTH networks docker run -d --name proxy --network front -p 80:80 nginx:1.27 # proxy can reach api (front) but NOT db; db is invisible from the proxy. Internet ──:80──▶ [proxy] ── front ──▶ [api] ── back ──▶ [db] proxy cannot see db ────────────╳ Segmenting networks like this is cheap defense in depth. For a stronger variant, docker network create --internal back blocks all outbound internet access from that network. DNS details On user-defined networks, name resolution uses the embedded DNS server; unresolved names are forwarded to the host's DNS. Add aliases: docker run --network appnet --network-alias cache redis . Multiple containers sharing an alias get round-robin DNS. Override DNS: --dns 1.1.1.1 ; add static entries with --add-host name:ip . Corporate VPN or split-horizon DNS often breaks name resolution inside containers. Check docker exec c cat /etc/resolv.conf . Host networking and its trade-offs --network host removes the NAT hop and the namespace boundary: no -p needed, slightly better throughput and latency, ability to bind many ports. In exchange you lose port isolation (two containers cannot both listen on 80), and the container can see and bind host interfaces. It is useful for network monitoring agents or high-throughput proxies; avoid for ordinary apps. IPv6 and custom subnets docker network create --subnet 10.50.0.0/24 --gateway 10.50.0.1 appnet docker network create --ipv6 --subnet 2001:db8:1::/64 v6net docker network inspect appnet --format '{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}} {{.IPv4Address}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}' If your corporate network or VPN uses the same private ranges Docker picks by default (172.17-31.x), routing silently breaks. Define default-address-pools in /etc/docker/daemon.json to avoid overlaps. Pitfalls Default bridge: no name resolution. Use a user-defined network. Using the host-published port between containers. Starting the app before the DB is ready (see Compose healthchecks). Port already allocated: another process or container holds the host port; lsof -i :8080 or docker ps . Docker Desktop's host mode behaves differently from Linux since the engine runs in a VM. Try it Start two alpine containers on the default bridge and try ping by name (fails) and by IP (works). Repeat on a user-defined network. Run nginx with -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 , then try reaching it from another machine or via your LAN IP and see it refused. Compare with -p 8080:80 . Run docker run --rm --network host alpine ip addr and compare with the default. What changed? Build the front/back network example and prove with docker exec proxy ping db that isolation works.

title: Docker Compose
text: Docker Compose Real applications are several containers: an API, a database, a cache, a reverse proxy. Starting each with a long docker run line, creating networks and volumes by hand and remembering the order is error-prone. Compose lets you describe the whole stack in one YAML file and manage it with a single command. Why Compose Declarative: the file is the documentation and the source of truth. Check it into Git. One command: docker compose up creates the network, volumes and containers in dependency order. Service discovery: each service name becomes a DNS name on the project network. Reproducible dev environments: a new teammate clones the repo and runs one command. Compose is the V2 plugin invoked as docker compose (with a space). The old Python docker-compose binary is end-of-life. The file is named compose.yaml (preferred) or docker-compose.yml , and the old top-level version: key is obsolete: omit it. A complete example: app + Postgres + Redis + nginx name: shop # project name (prefixes networks/volumes) services: nginx: image: nginx:1.27-alpine ports: - "80:80" volumes: - ./nginx/default.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro depends_on: api: condition: service_healthy networks: [front] restart: unless-stopped api: build: context: ./api target: runtime image: shop/api:dev environment: NODE_ENV: production PORT: 3000 REDIS_URL: redis://cache:6379 DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:${DB_PASSWORD}@db:5432/shop env_file: - .env # extra vars, lower priority than "environment" depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy cache: condition: service_started healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "node", "-e", "fetch('http://localhost:3000/health').then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1)).catch(()=>process.exit(1))"] interval: 10s timeout: 3s retries: 5 start_period: 15s networks: [front, back] restart: unless-stopped db: image: postgres:16 environment: POSTGRES_USER: app POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:?DB_PASSWORD must be set} POSTGRES_DB: shop volumes: - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data - ./db/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d shop"] interval: 5s timeout: 3s retries: 10 networks: [back] restart: unless-stopped cache: image: redis:7-alpine command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes"] volumes: - redisdata:/data networks: [back] restart: unless-stopped volumes: pgdata: redisdata: networks: front: back: And the nginx config the proxy mounts, forwarding to the API by service name: # nginx/default.conf server { listen 80; location / { proxy_pass http://api:3000; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; } } Internet ─:80─▶ [nginx] ── front ── [api] ── back ──┬─▶ [db] (pgdata volume) └─▶ [cache] (redisdata volume) Only nginx publishes a port. db and cache are unreachable from outside. Key concepts in that file Healthchecks and depends_on Plain depends_on: [db] only waits until the db container has started , not until Postgres accepts connections. The app then crashes with "connection refused". Using condition: service_healthy waits for the healthcheck to pass. Conditions are service_started (default), service_healthy and service_completed_successfully (for one-shot init jobs such as migrations). Your app should still retry connections on startup, since databases restart at any time. Environment variables and env files environment: sets variables directly; values can interpolate from your shell or .env : ${VAR} , ${VAR:-default} , ${VAR:?error message} . A file named .env next to compose.yaml is read automatically for interpolation in the compose file . env_file: injects variables into the container . They are different mechanisms. Never commit real secrets. Commit a .env.example and gitignore .env . Precedence (high to low): docker compose run -e , shell environment, environment: , env_file: , image ENV . Secrets services: db: environment: POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password secrets: [db_password] secrets: db_password: file: ./secrets/db_password.txt # mounted at /run/secrets/db_password Profiles Profiles make services optional so they do not start by default: services: adminer: image: adminer profiles: ["debug"] ports: ["8081:8080"] migrate: build: ./api command: ["node", "migrate.js"] profiles: ["tools"] depends_on: db: { condition: service_healthy } # docker compose up -d # core services only # docker compose --profile debug up -d # + adminer # docker compose run --rm migrate # explicit run of a profiled service Dev vs. prod: override files Compose merges compose.yaml with compose.override.yaml automatically. Put production-safe defaults in the base and developer conveniences in the override; or use explicit files per environment. # compose.override.yaml (auto-loaded in dev) services: api: build: target: dev command: ["npm", "run", "dev"] volumes: - ./api:/app # live code via bind mount - /app/node_modules ports: - "3000:3000" - "9229:9229" # node debugger environment: NODE_ENV: development db: ports: - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432" # let your local psql connect # compose.prod.yaml services: api: image: ghcr.io/acme/shop-api:${TAG:?set TAG} # pull a built image, never build in prod restart: always deploy: resources: limits: { cpus: "1.0", memory: 512M } logging: driver: json-file options: { max-size: "10m", max-file: "3" } # Production invocation (skips the override file): # docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d Merge rules: scalars are replaced, maps are merged, lists such as ports and volumes are appended. Run docker compose config to see the final merged result, which is the best debugging tool for override confusion. For hot reload without bind mounts, Compose has develop: watch: with docker compose watch , which syncs or rebuilds on file changes (and avoids many bind mount performance issues on Mac). Common commands Command Does docker compose up -d Create and start everything in the background docker compose up -d --build Rebuild images first docker compose up -d --wait Block until services are healthy (great in CI) docker compose ps Status and health of services docker compose logs -f api Follow one service's logs docker compose exec api sh Shell in a running service docker compose run --rm api npm test One-off container from a service definition docker compose build [--no-cache] Build images docker compose pull Pull newer images docker compose restart api Restart one service docker compose stop / start Stop/start without removing docker compose down Stop and remove containers and networks (volumes kept) docker compose down -v Also delete named volumes (data loss!) docker compose config Validate and print resolved config docker compose up -d --scale worker=3 Run multiple replicas (service must not publish a fixed host port) Pitfalls and best practices Do not use Compose as a production orchestrator for critical multi-host systems. It is excellent for dev, CI and small single-host deployments; for rolling updates, self-healing across machines and autoscaling, move to Kubernetes or a managed container service. Pin image tags , same rule as everywhere. Do not publish every port. Only the entry point needs to be public; internal services reach each other via the network. YAML indentation errors : use docker compose config to catch them. .env quoting : values are taken literally; quotes and trailing spaces can end up in the value. Changed Dockerfile but no effect : you need --build or docker compose build . Stale data after changing init scripts : files in docker-entrypoint-initdb.d only run on an empty data volume. Remove the volume to re-run. Set name: or use -p so two checkouts of the same repo do not collide on project names. Try it Write the compose file above for a small app of your own (any API that reads DATABASE_URL ). Add a .env with DB_PASSWORD . Run docker compose up -d --wait , then docker compose ps . Stop the db with docker compose stop db and watch the api's health respond. Remove the condition: service_healthy and see whether the API fails on a cold start. Put it back. Add a compose.override.yaml with a bind mount and inspect the merge with docker compose config . Run docker compose down , then up again: is the data still there? Now try down -v .

title: Container Registries
text: Container Registries An image on your laptop helps nobody else. A registry is the server that stores and distributes images, the "package repository" of the container world. Your CI pushes to it; your servers, Kubernetes clusters and teammates pull from it. How you tag, secure and scan what lives there decides how safe and repeatable your deployments are. How registries work CI pipeline Registry Production host ┌───────────┐ docker push ┌──────────────────┐ docker pull ┌───────────────┐ │ build img │───────────────▶│ repo: acme/api │──────────────▶│ run container │ └───────────┘ │ tags: 1.4.2,... │ └───────────────┘ │ blobs (layers) │ └──────────────────┘ Registries speak the OCI Distribution API over HTTPS. An image reference is registry-host/namespace/repo:tag . When the host is omitted, Docker assumes Docker Hub: nginx means docker.io/library/nginx:latest . Pushes upload only layers the registry does not already have (by digest), so repeated pushes are fast. Choosing a registry Registry Host Notes Docker Hub docker.io Largest public catalog and official images. Anonymous and free-tier pulls are rate-limited, which can break CI at scale. Private repos on paid plans. GitHub Container Registry ghcr.io Tied to GitHub orgs/repos; authenticates with GITHUB_TOKEN in Actions; free for public images. GitLab Container Registry registry.gitlab.com Built into each GitLab project. Amazon ECR <acct>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com IAM-based auth, same-region pull is fast and cheap, built-in scanning, lifecycle policies, replication. Google Artifact Registry <region>-docker.pkg.dev GCP's registry (successor to GCR). IAM auth. Azure Container Registry <name>.azurecr.io Entra ID auth, geo-replication. Self-hosted your own Harbor (full-featured: RBAC, scanning, replication), the minimal registry:2 /Distribution, Nexus, Artifactory. Rule of thumb: put images in the registry closest to where they run (ECR for AWS, Artifact Registry for GCP) for speed, IAM integration and lower egress cost. Use GHCR when your code and CI are on GitHub and you deploy anywhere. Authentication and push/pull # Docker Hub docker login -u myuser # prompts for a personal access token (not your password) # GHCR (use a PAT with write:packages, or GITHUB_TOKEN in Actions) echo "$GHCR_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u myuser --password-stdin # AWS ECR (token valid 12 hours) aws ecr get-login-password --region eu-west-1 \ | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com aws ecr create-repository --repository-name acme/api # Tag and push docker tag myapp:1.4.2 ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 docker pull ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 Credentials are stored in ~/.docker/config.json Without a credential helper that file holds a base64 (not encrypted) token. Use --password-stdin so secrets stay out of shell history, prefer short-lived tokens or OIDC in CI, and configure a credential store ( osxkeychain , pass , ecr-login ). Running your own registry docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --restart always --name registry \ -v registry-data:/var/lib/registry registry:2 docker tag myapp:1.0 localhost:5000/myapp:1.0 docker push localhost:5000/myapp:1.0 curl http://localhost:5000/v2/_catalog This is fine for local testing. For anything shared, you need TLS (Docker refuses plain HTTP except for localhost unless configured as insecure-registries ), authentication and garbage collection. At that point use Harbor or a managed registry. Tagging strategy Tags are mutable pointers (see the layers lesson), so a deliberate scheme prevents confusion and enables rollbacks. Tag Example Purpose Git SHA api:3f2a9c1 Traceable to an exact commit; unique per build. Best for deploys. Semantic version api:1.4.2 , 1.4 , 1 Release tags for humans; moving 1.4 follows patches. Branch/env api:main , api:staging Moving pointers; convenient but never the sole source of truth. PR/preview api:pr-123 Ephemeral test environments. latest api:latest Avoid deploying it. It tells you nothing about what is running. Build once, promote the same image Build an image once in CI, tag it with the commit SHA, test it, then promote by adding tags ( staging , 1.4.2 , prod ) to that same digest. Never rebuild for production: a rebuild is a different artifact that was never tested. Deploy by digest or immutable tag. Enable tag immutability on ECR/Artifact Registry for release tags so they cannot be overwritten. # Promote without rebuilding (copies manifest, no layer re-upload) docker buildx imagetools create \ --tag ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 \ --tag ghcr.io/acme/api:prod \ ghcr.io/acme/api:3f2a9c1 Pushing from CI (GitHub Actions) name: build-and-push on: push: branches: [main] tags: ["v*"] permissions: contents: read packages: write # lets GITHUB_TOKEN push to ghcr.io jobs: image: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3 - uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - id: meta uses: docker/metadata-action@v5 with: images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }} tags: | type=sha type=semver,pattern={{version}} type=ref,event=branch - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6 with: context: . push: true platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64 tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }} labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }} cache-from: type=gha cache-to: type=gha,mode=max provenance: true sbom: true Pin third-party actions to a commit SHA in sensitive pipelines. For AWS, use GitHub's OIDC and an IAM role ( aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials ) instead of long-lived access keys. Image scanning Images contain OS packages and language libraries that accumulate known vulnerabilities (CVEs). Scanners compare the image's package inventory against vulnerability databases. trivy image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 docker scout cves ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 # Docker Scout grype ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 # Anchore Grype Scan in CI to fail the build on new critical findings, and continuously in the registry (ECR enhanced scanning, Harbor, GHCR with Dependabot/Trivy), because new CVEs are published against images you built months ago. Use --ignore-unfixed to focus on actionable issues; track accepted risks in an ignore file with expiry dates. Most fixes come from rebuilding on a newer base image. Automate with Renovate or Dependabot bumps. Signing and provenance Scanning tells you what is in an image; signing tells you who built it. Tools like Sigstore cosign sign images (keyless, using your CI's OIDC identity), and Kubernetes admission policies can then refuse unsigned images. Attach an SBOM (software bill of materials) and build provenance attestations with BuildKit's --sbom and --provenance . Housekeeping Registries grow forever. Set lifecycle/retention policies : e.g. ECR rule "expire untagged images after 7 days; keep last 30 tagged pr-* ". Use per-repo, least-privilege tokens: CI can push, production hosts can only pull. Docker Hub rate limits: authenticate pulls, or mirror base images into your own registry (pull-through cache) so an outage or limit upstream does not stop your deploys. Do not put secrets in images. Public images are world-readable; "private" images are one misconfiguration away. Try it Run a local registry:2 , push an image tagged localhost:5000/hello:1 and list it via the /v2/_catalog endpoint. Create a free GHCR or Docker Hub repo, log in with a token and push an image tagged both with a version and a short git SHA. Confirm both tags point to the same digest. Run trivy image node:22 and trivy image node:22-slim . Compare vulnerability counts. Write the GitHub Actions workflow above for a sample repo and watch the image appear in the Packages tab.

title: Container Security and Best Practices
text: Container Security and Best Practices Containers share the host kernel, so their isolation is thinner than a VM's, and default settings are permissive. Security here is mostly about shrinking what a compromised process can do: run as an unprivileged user, drop capabilities, make the filesystem read-only, cap resources, keep secrets out of images and keep the contents patched. The threat model Assume your application will eventually be exploited (a vulnerable library, an injection bug). The question is what the attacker gets next: Root inside the container, then escape to the host via a kernel bug or misconfiguration. Network access to other containers, the cloud metadata service ( 169.254.169.254 , which holds IAM credentials) or the Docker socket. Secrets baked into image layers or environment variables. A vulnerable or malicious base image or dependency (supply chain). Defense in depth: each control below removes one rung from the attacker's ladder. 1. Run as a non-root user By default the process in a container is root (UID 0). Container root is not host root, but it is dangerously close: with a kernel bug, a writable host mount or an extra capability, it can become host root. And inside the container root can modify everything the app can see. # Debian/Ubuntu-based RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 app && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app --no-create-home app USER 10001:10001 # Alpine RUN addgroup -S -g 10001 app && adduser -S -u 10001 -G app app USER app # Many images ship one: node has "node", distroless has ":nonroot" (UID 65532), nginx-unprivileged FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot Use a numeric UID so Kubernetes' runAsNonRoot check can verify it. Non-root processes cannot bind ports below 1024; listen on 8080 and map it with -p 80:8080 . Enforce at run time with --user 10001 . 2. Read-only root filesystem docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run -v appdata:/data myapp:1.4.2 If an attacker cannot write to the filesystem, they cannot drop tools or modify your code. Give the app only the writable spots it really needs (tmpfs for temp files, one volume for data). 3. Drop capabilities and block privilege escalation Linux splits root's power into ~40 capabilities. Docker grants a default subset (including NET_RAW , CHOWN , SETUID ). A typical web app needs none. docker run \ --cap-drop ALL \ --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \ --security-opt no-new-privileges:true \ myapp:1.4.2 NET_BIND_SERVICE is only needed to bind ports below 1024. no-new-privileges stops setuid binaries from gaining privileges. Docker's default seccomp profile (blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls) and AppArmor/SELinux profiles are enabled by default; do not disable them ( --security-opt seccomp=unconfined ). Never do these --privileged : gives nearly all capabilities and device access; equals root on the host. Mounting /var/run/docker.sock : lets the container control Docker, hence the host. Mounting / , /etc or /proc from the host. --network host / --pid host without a specific reason. Rootless Docker/Podman and user namespace remapping ( userns-remap ) go further: container "root" maps to an unprivileged host UID, so even an escape lands as a nobody. 4. Resource limits Without limits, one runaway or compromised container can starve the host (memory leak, fork bomb, crypto-miner). docker run --memory=512m --memory-swap=512m --cpus=1.5 --pids-limit=200 \ --ulimit nofile=4096:4096 myapp:1.4.2 Exceeding the memory limit gets the process OOM-killed (exit code 137): size limits from measured usage plus headroom, and make runtimes aware of the limit (modern JVMs and Go respect cgroup limits; Node needs --max-old-space-size tuned below the container limit). 5. Secrets Method Verdict Hardcoded in code or Dockerfile ( ENV , ARG , COPY .env ) Never. Lives in layers and docker history / inspect forever. Environment variable at run time Acceptable for low-risk setups. Visible in docker inspect , /proc , crash dumps and child processes. File mounted at run time ( /run/secrets/x , Compose/Swarm secrets, Kubernetes Secret volumes) Better. Not in the image, not in inspect . Many images support *_FILE variables. Secret manager fetched at start (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, SSM, external-secrets operator) Best. Central rotation, audit logs, short-lived credentials. Build-time secrets Use BuildKit --mount=type=secret , never ARG . If a secret ever entered an image or a Git repository, treat it as leaked and rotate it. Deleting the layer or commit does not un-leak it. 6. Image hygiene: minimal, pinned, scanned Minimal base: slim, distroless or scratch. Fewer packages, fewer CVEs, no shell for attackers. Pin versions: FROM node:22.11-slim , ideally with @sha256: digest, and automate bumps with Renovate or Dependabot. Pin OS and language packages too (lockfiles, npm ci , pip --require-hashes ). Use trusted sources: Docker Official Images, verified publishers, your own mirrored base images. A random Hub image is arbitrary code running in your infrastructure. Rebuild regularly: a weekly scheduled build picks up base image patches even when your code does not change. Scanning with Trivy trivy image myapp:1.4.2 # OS + language package CVEs trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 --ignore-unfixed myapp:1.4.2 # CI gate trivy fs . # scan source dependencies trivy config . # lint Dockerfile, Compose, Kubernetes, Terraform trivy image --scanners secret myapp:1.4.2 # hunt for leaked secrets in layers trivy image --format cyclonedx -o sbom.json myapp:1.4.2 # produce an SBOM # GitHub Actions step - uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0 with: image-ref: ghcr.io/acme/api:${{ github.sha }} severity: CRITICAL,HIGH ignore-unfixed: true exit-code: "1" A scan is a snapshot: schedule re-scans of what is already deployed. Not every CVE is exploitable in your context; triage, but do not ignore everything. Complement with hadolint (Dockerfile lint) and Docker Bench for Security / CIS Docker Benchmark checks on hosts. 7. Protect the daemon and the host Keep Docker and the kernel patched; most container escapes are kernel or runtime CVEs. Restrict membership in the docker group (it equals root). Never expose the daemon on TCP ( -H tcp://0.0.0.0:2375 ) without mutual TLS. Open Docker ports on the internet are routinely hijacked for crypto-mining. Block containers from the cloud metadata endpoint (enforce IMDSv2 with hop limit 1 on AWS) so a compromised container cannot steal the instance's IAM role. Run untrusted code in stronger sandboxes (gVisor, Kata Containers, Firecracker microVMs). A hardened run command docker run -d --name api \ --user 10001:10001 \ --read-only --tmpfs /tmp \ --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges:true \ --memory 512m --cpus 1 --pids-limit 200 \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \ -e DATABASE_URL_FILE=/run/secrets/dburl \ -v "$PWD/secrets/dburl":/run/secrets/dburl:ro \ ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:<digest> The same in Compose: services: api: image: ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 user: "10001:10001" read_only: true tmpfs: [/tmp] cap_drop: [ALL] security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"] mem_limit: 512m cpus: 1 pids_limit: 200 The 12 do's and don'ts # Do Don't 1 Run as a non-root numeric user Leave the default root user 2 Use minimal, official, version-pinned base images Use :latest or unknown publishers 3 Use multi-stage builds so compilers and dev tools never ship Ship build toolchains and source in the runtime image 4 Inject secrets at run time from a secret manager or files Bake secrets into ENV, ARG, layers or Git 5 Scan images in CI and continuously in the registry Scan once and assume it stays clean 6 Set memory, CPU and PID limits Leave containers unbounded 7 Drop all capabilities; add back only what is needed Use --privileged 8 Use a read-only root filesystem with tmpfs for scratch Let the app write anywhere 9 Keep one process per container, logs to stdout/stderr Run sshd, cron and the app together in one container 10 Add a .dockerignore and a HEALTHCHECK Copy .git , .env , or credentials into the context 11 Build once, sign it, promote the same digest Rebuild per environment, deploy mutable tags 12 Publish only needed ports, bind internal ones to 127.0.0.1 Mount docker.sock or expose the Docker API Security is a trade-off with convenience Read-only filesystems, distroless images and dropped capabilities make debugging and onboarding harder. Adopt them progressively: non-root and pinned versions first (nearly free), then scanning, then read-only and capabilities. Verify each step with tests so hardening does not break production at 3 a.m. Try it Run docker run --rm alpine id , then docker run --rm --user 10001 alpine id . Then try docker run --rm --read-only alpine touch /x and read the error. Run docker run --rm alpine sh -c 'cat /proc/self/status | grep Cap' with and without --cap-drop ALL and compare. Scan an old image such as node:16 with Trivy and a current node:22-slim . Count criticals. Take a Dockerfile from your own project and apply items 1, 2, 3 and 10 from the list. Rescan and compare size and CVE counts.

title: Debugging Containers
text: Debugging Containers Containers fail in a small number of recurring ways: the process exits, gets killed, cannot reach something, or runs but behaves differently than on your laptop. A systematic routine, check the state, read the logs, inspect the config, get inside, compare environments, resolves most problems in minutes. The debugging routine 1. docker ps -a Is it running? Exited? Restarting? What exit code? │ 2. docker logs What did the process say before it died? │ 3. docker inspect What config did Docker really apply? (env, mounts, ports, health) │ 4. docker exec / run Get inside; test DNS, ports, files, permissions │ 5. docker events / stats Resource pressure? OOM? Daemon-level problems? Step 1: state and exit codes docker ps -a --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}' # NAMES STATUS PORTS # api Restarting (1) 5 seconds ago # db Up 2 hours (healthy) 5432/tcp # job Exited (137) 3 minutes ago docker inspect api --format '{{.State.ExitCode}} oom={{.State.OOMKilled}} err={{.State.Error}}' docker inspect api --format '{{json .State.Health}}' | jq Exit code Meaning Typical cause 0 Clean exit The command finished. Expected for batch jobs; for a server it means the main process returned (e.g. daemonized itself, or CMD is a short script) 1 Application error Uncaught exception, bad config, failed DB connection. Read the logs 2 Shell misuse / bad usage Wrong command-line arguments 125 Docker daemon error Invalid docker run flags, port already allocated 126 Command found but not executable Missing chmod +x on entrypoint script, wrong architecture binary 127 Command not found Typo, binary missing in slim/distroless image, CRLF line endings in script ( #!/bin/sh^M ) 130 SIGINT (128+2) Ctrl+C 137 SIGKILL (128+9) OOM kill, or docker stop timeout then forced kill, or docker kill 139 SIGSEGV (128+11) Segfault: native library crash, musl/glibc mismatch, wrong CPU architecture 143 SIGTERM (128+15) Graceful stop requested; normal when an app terminates on docker stop without custom handling The rule: exit codes above 128 mean "killed by signal (code minus 128)". Step 2: logs docker logs api # everything since start docker logs -f --tail 200 api # follow, last 200 lines docker logs --since 10m --timestamps api docker compose logs -f --tail 50 api db # several services interleaved docker logs api 2>&1 | grep -i error # stderr is a separate stream Empty logs? The app may write to a file instead of stdout/stderr, or output is buffered (set PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 ). Link log files to /dev/stdout (nginx images do) or reconfigure the logger. Logs vanish on docker rm . The default json-file driver stores them per container. In production ship logs elsewhere (Loki, CloudWatch, ELK). Logs eating the disk? Default json-file has no rotation. Set max-size and max-file in daemon.json or Compose logging.options . Step 3: inspect docker inspect api | less docker inspect -f '{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}' api # effective env vars docker inspect -f '{{json .Mounts}}' api | jq # actual mounts docker inspect -f '{{json .NetworkSettings.Networks}}' api | jq # IPs, networks docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.RestartPolicy.Name}}' api docker port api # published ports docker compose config # resolved Compose file Much "it works locally" turns out to be a different environment variable, a missing mount or a wrong network, visible instantly here. Step 4: get inside docker exec -it api sh # shell in a running container (try bash if sh is minimal) docker exec api env # environment docker exec api ls -la /app # are the files there? permissions? docker exec api cat /etc/resolv.conf docker exec -u 0 -it api sh # as root (to install debugging tools temporarily) When it crashes immediately (so you cannot exec) # Override entrypoint to keep it alive and look around docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh myapp:1.4.2 docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh --env-file .env myapp:1.4.2 # same env as the real thing # Then run the real command manually and watch it fail: / # node server.js # Inspect the filesystem of an exited container docker commit api debug-snapshot && docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh debug-snapshot docker cp api:/app/error.log . # works on stopped containers too Shell-less and distroless images There is no sh to exec into. Options: use the :debug tag of distroless (it includes BusyBox), or attach a sidecar that shares the target's namespaces: docker run --rm -it --pid=container:api --network=container:api nicolaka/netshoot # Now you see api's processes and network, and have curl, dig, tcpdump, ss, etc. docker debug api # Docker Desktop/Subscription: injects a toolbox shell kubectl debug -it pod/api --image=busybox --target=api # Kubernetes ephemeral containers Common failures and fixes Exit 137 and OOM docker inspect api --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' # true => out of memory docker stats # live CPU / mem / net / IO per container dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'killed process|out of memory' # kernel's view (on the host) If OOMKilled is true, the process exceeded its cgroup memory limit (or the host ran out). Fix by finding the leak or raising the limit; configure the runtime (e.g. Node --max-old-space-size below the limit, JVM -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 ). If OOMKilled is false, the 137 came from a stop timeout: the app ignored SIGTERM, so check exec-form CMD and signal handlers. Crash loops (Restarting...) With restart: always a failing container flaps forever, and Docker backs off exponentially between tries. Read docker logs for the last attempt, check the exit code, and temporarily disable the restart policy ( docker update --restart=no api ) to make it stay failed for investigation. Typical causes: missing env var, DB not ready, wrong file permissions after switching to a non-root user, a port already in use, or migration failures. Permission denied Non-root user cannot write to a volume or bind mount (owned by root or a host UID). Fix ownership at build ( COPY --chown , chown in the Dockerfile before USER ), run with a matching --user , or use chown in an init step. On SELinux hosts add :z to mounts. Cannot reach something Symptom Check Cannot reach container from host docker port ; was -p given? Does the app bind 0.0.0.0 not 127.0.0.1? Is the host port free ( lsof -i :8080 )? Firewall? Container cannot reach another container Same user-defined network? Using the service name and the internal port, not localhost or the published port? Name resolution fails docker exec api getent hosts db ; default bridge has no DNS; check /etc/resolv.conf ; VPN/corporate DNS interference "Connection refused" Target not listening yet (startup race): add healthcheck + depends_on: condition: service_healthy and client retries Cannot reach internet docker exec api wget -qO- https://example.com ; check DNS, proxy env vars, host IP forwarding, overlapping subnets with VPN Reach host service from container host.docker.internal (add --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway on Linux); the host service must listen on non-loopback docker exec api sh -c 'nc -zv db 5432' # TCP reachability docker exec api wget -qO- http://other:3000/health docker exec api nslookup db # DNS docker network inspect appnet | jq '.[0].Containers' "exec format error" The image architecture does not match the host (arm64 image on amd64 or vice versa), or the entrypoint script has no shebang. Check docker image inspect --format '{{.Architecture}}' img , rebuild for the right platform with --platform . Works on my machine, not in the container File missing: .dockerignore excluded it, or COPY path is wrong. docker run --rm img ls -R /app . Case-sensitive paths: macOS is case-insensitive, Linux containers are not. Different env: compare docker exec api env with your local environment. Dev dependencies omitted ( npm ci --omit=dev ) but code needs them at runtime. Time zone, locale, missing CA certificates (slim/scratch) for outbound HTTPS. Stale image: you changed code but ran an old build. Rebuild, check docker images timestamps, or use --no-cache . Build failures docker build --progress=plain --no-cache . # full unfolded output docker build --target build -t dbg . && docker run --rm -it dbg sh # stop at a stage and poke around docker builder prune # clear a corrupted/huge build cache Disk space docker system df -v # who is using space docker system prune -a # unused images/containers/networks (careful) docker volume ls -f dangling=true Daemon-level tools docker events # live stream: create, start, die, oom, health_status docker stats --no-stream # snapshot of resource use docker top api # processes in the container, from the host sudo journalctl -u docker -f # daemon logs (Linux systemd) docker info # storage driver, cgroup version, warnings Habits that make debugging easy Log to stdout/stderr in structured form, include a version and request ID. Add a /health endpoint and HEALTHCHECK; Docker then reports (healthy) or (unhealthy) in docker ps . Keep a debug build target or tag with a shell and tools; ship the minimal one. Do not "fix" a running container by hand. If you change it by exec, you lose that change on the next deploy. Reproduce, fix the Dockerfile or config, rebuild. Try it Run docker run -d --name oom --memory=20m python:3.13-slim python -c "x=bytearray(200*1024*1024)" . Find the exit code and confirm OOMKilled=true with inspect. Run docker run --name bad alpine nonexistent-cmd and read exit code 127 (or 126 for a non-executable file). Start a container that logs to a file only (e.g. sh -c 'echo hi > /tmp/x.log; sleep 100' ) and observe empty docker logs . Then redirect to stdout. Put two containers on the default bridge, show that name lookup fails, then fix it with a user-defined network. Use nicolaka/netshoot to diagnose. Make a crash-looping Compose service ( command: ["sh","-c","exit 1"] , restart: always ), and practice the routine: ps, logs, inspect, stop the loop.

title: Why Container Orchestration?
text: Why Container Orchestration? Running one container on one server is easy. Running two hundred containers across thirty servers, keeping them healthy, updating them without downtime and scaling them with traffic is a different problem entirely. Orchestration is the software that solves it, and Kubernetes is the one that won. Start with the problem Imagine you have containerised your app (see the Docker lessons). On a single VPS you run docker compose up -d and you are done. Now the business grows. Here is what breaks, in the order it usually hurts. 1. Scheduling: where should this container run? With ten servers and fifty containers, someone has to decide which container goes on which machine. A container needs 2 GB of RAM and half a CPU; server 3 has 1.5 GB free; server 7 has 6 GB free but is in a different availability zone from the database. Doing this in a spreadsheet works for a week. This is a bin-packing problem with constraints, and the component that solves it is called a scheduler . 2. Self-healing: things die, constantly Processes crash, nodes lose power, disks fill, kernels panic. At small scale you get paged and restart things. At large scale, something is always broken somewhere. Without automation, every failure is a 3 a.m. phone call. With orchestration, the system notices that three replicas were requested but two exist, and starts a third on a healthy machine, with no human involved. 3. Scaling: capacity should follow demand Traffic doubles at lunchtime. You can over-provision permanently (expensive) or add and remove instances automatically (needs a system that knows how to start new copies, register them with the load balancer and remove them again). 4. Rollouts: updating without an outage Replacing version 1 with version 2 across twenty instances without dropping requests needs ordering: start a new one, wait until it is healthy, route traffic to it, stop an old one, repeat. If version 2 is broken, stop and go back. Hand-written deploy scripts get this wrong in new and creative ways. 5. Service discovery and load balancing When containers move around and IP addresses change every restart, how does the checkout service find the payments service? You need stable names and a load balancer that automatically tracks which instances are alive. 6. Configuration, secrets and storage The same image should run in dev, staging and production with different settings, and databases need disks that follow them when they move. The key idea: declare desired state Older tools were imperative : "start container X on server 3". Kubernetes is declarative : you write down what you want ("five copies of this image, each with 256 MB of memory, reachable at this name") and controllers continuously work to make reality match. You stop issuing commands and start describing outcomes. You write: Kubernetes continuously does: ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────────┐ │ replicas: 5 │ ───────▶ │ observe: 4 running │ │ image: shop:2.3 │ │ diff: need 1 more │ └──────────────────┘ │ act: schedule a new Pod │ desired state │ repeat forever │ └──────────────────────────────────┘ Why this matters Declarative state turns operations into data. Your whole system is described by files you can review in a pull request, diff, roll back with git and re-apply to a brand new cluster. This is the foundation that makes GitOps (see the IaC section) possible. What Kubernetes gives you Problem Kubernetes feature Where to run it? Scheduler places Pods on nodes using resource requests, affinity, taints It crashed kubelet restarts containers; controllers recreate Pods; nodes are replaced Scale with load HorizontalPodAutoscaler, Cluster Autoscaler Zero-downtime updates Deployments with rolling updates and rollback Finding services Services and cluster DNS Config and secrets ConfigMaps and Secrets Stateful data PersistentVolumes, StatefulSets Extensibility Custom Resource Definitions and operators A brief history Google ran an internal system called Borg for over a decade. In 2014 they open-sourced a redesign as Kubernetes (Greek for "helmsman", abbreviated k8s: k, 8 letters, s) and donated it to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. Competitors such as Docker Swarm and Mesos existed, but Kubernetes' extensible API and vendor-neutral governance won. Every major cloud now offers a managed version, so it is the de facto common API for running containers. When you do NOT need Kubernetes This is the most valuable section for a new engineer. Kubernetes is powerful but carries real cost: a steep learning curve, many moving parts, YAML sprawl, and an operational surface (upgrades, networking, security) that someone must own. One app, a few containers. A single VM with Docker Compose and a systemd unit, behind a reverse proxy, is simpler and often more reliable. A small team with no platform experience. A managed PaaS (Render, Fly.io, Railway, Heroku, Cloud Run, App Runner) gives you 90 percent of the benefits with 5 percent of the complexity. Mostly serverless workloads. If your logic is functions and queues, Lambda or Cloud Run may fit better. Low traffic, no HA requirement. Downtime of a minute during a deploy may be perfectly acceptable. You start to genuinely benefit from Kubernetes when you have many services, multiple teams deploying independently, a need for consistent scaling and rollout behaviour, multi-cloud or on-prem portability requirements, or an ecosystem need (operators, service mesh, GPU scheduling). The resume-driven-development trap Many startups adopt Kubernetes at ten users and spend more engineering time on the cluster than on the product. Choose it because you have the problems above, not because it is fashionable. Learning it is still worth it: the concepts (declarative config, reconciliation, service discovery) show up everywhere. Trade-offs summary Option Strength Weakness VM + Compose Simple, cheap, easy to debug Single point of failure; manual scaling Managed PaaS Zero ops Less control, cost climbs at scale, vendor lock-in Kubernetes Powerful, portable, huge ecosystem Complex; needs expertise Try it List the services your team runs. For each, write down how it is scheduled, restarted on failure, scaled and updated today. Count how many of those answers are "a person does it by hand". Those are the places orchestration would help. Decide honestly: would a managed PaaS solve your actual pain with less effort?

title: Kubernetes Architecture
text: Kubernetes Architecture A Kubernetes cluster is a set of machines split into a control plane that makes decisions and worker nodes that run your containers. Underneath, everything is one idea repeated many times: a controller compares desired state with actual state and closes the gap. The big picture CONTROL PLANE ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ kubectl / CI / UIs ─────▶ ┌────────────────┐ │ │ │ kube-apiserver │◀──────┐ │ │ └───────┬────────┘ │ │ │ │ read/write │ │ │ ┌─────▼─────┐ watch │ │ │ │ etcd │ │ │ │ └───────────┘ │ │ │ ┌────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ kube-scheduler │ │ kube-controller-manager│───┘ │ │ └────────────────┘ └───────────────────────┘ │ └──────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘ │ (all talk only via the API server) ┌───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐ ┌──────▼───────────┐ ┌───────▼──────────┐ ┌────────▼─────────┐ │ NODE 1 │ │ NODE 2 │ │ NODE 3 │ │ kubelet │ │ kubelet │ │ kubelet │ │ kube-proxy │ │ kube-proxy │ │ kube-proxy │ │ containerd │ │ containerd │ │ containerd │ │ [Pod][Pod][Pod] │ │ [Pod][Pod] │ │ [Pod][Pod][Pod] │ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ Control plane components kube-apiserver The front door and the only component that talks to etcd. Every client (kubectl, the scheduler, kubelets, controllers, your CI) uses its REST API. It authenticates the caller, authorises the request (RBAC), runs admission controllers (which can validate or mutate objects, e.g. inject defaults or reject privileged Pods) and persists the result. It is stateless and can be run in multiple replicas behind a load balancer. etcd A distributed, strongly consistent key-value store (Raft consensus) holding the entire cluster state: every Deployment, Secret, Node and Pod. If etcd is lost and you have no backup, the cluster forgets everything it was supposed to run. Run 3 or 5 members for quorum, use fast SSDs, and back it up ( etcdctl snapshot save ). Managed offerings do this for you. kube-scheduler Watches for Pods that have no node assigned and picks one. It runs two phases: filtering (remove nodes that cannot host the Pod: not enough CPU or memory, taints the Pod does not tolerate, wrong node selector) and scoring (rank the survivors: spread across zones, prefer nodes with the image cached, balance load). It then writes the chosen node name into the Pod; it never starts anything itself. kube-controller-manager A single binary that runs many controllers: the Deployment controller, ReplicaSet controller, Node controller (marks nodes NotReady, evicts Pods), Job controller, EndpointSlice controller, ServiceAccount controller and more. Each is a loop of the form described below. cloud-controller-manager On cloud providers, this integrates with the cloud API: creating a load balancer when you make a Service of type LoadBalancer, attaching disks, reporting node lifecycle. Node components kubelet The agent on each node. It watches the API server for Pods assigned to its node, tells the container runtime to start the containers, runs probes, reports status back and mounts volumes. It is the one that actually makes a Pod real. Container runtime Anything implementing the Container Runtime Interface (CRI): containerd (most common) or CRI-O . Docker Engine itself has not been supported directly since 1.24, but images built with Docker run fine, since the image format is a standard (OCI). kube-proxy Programs the node's network rules (iptables or IPVS; nftables in newer versions) so that traffic sent to a Service's virtual IP gets load-balanced to the Pods behind it. Some CNI plugins like Cilium replace it with eBPF. Covered in the networking lesson. CNI plugin Not part of core, but required: a Container Network Interface plugin (Calico, Cilium, Flannel, the cloud provider's VPC CNI) gives each Pod an IP and makes Pod-to-Pod traffic work across nodes. The reconciliation loop This is the single most important concept in Kubernetes. ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐ ▼ │ observe actual state ──▶ compare to desired ──▶ act to reduce difference (watch API server) (spec in etcd) (create/delete/update) Every object has a spec (what you want) and a status (what is). Controllers use watches , not polling, to be notified of changes. They are level-triggered : they react to "current state differs from desired" rather than to individual events, so if a controller crashes and restarts it simply re-reads the world and carries on. That makes the system robust. Walkthrough: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml with 3 replicas kubectl sends the Deployment to the API server, which authenticates, authorises, validates, and stores it in etcd. The Deployment controller sees a new Deployment and creates a ReplicaSet. The ReplicaSet controller sees "want 3, have 0" and creates 3 Pod objects (no node assigned yet). The scheduler sees 3 unscheduled Pods, filters and scores nodes, and binds each Pod to a node. The kubelet on each chosen node sees a Pod bound to it, pulls the image, asks containerd to start the containers, then reports status Running. The EndpointSlice controller notices ready Pods and updates Service endpoints; kube-proxy updates rules. No component calls another directly. They coordinate only by reading and writing objects through the API server. That loose coupling is why you can swap in a custom scheduler or add your own controller. Declarative and extensible Because everything is "objects plus controllers", you can add new object types with CustomResourceDefinitions and write your own controller (an operator ) to manage, say, a PostgreSQL cluster. Tools like cert-manager, Argo CD and Crossplane work exactly this way. Self-healing in practice Failure Who reacts What happens Container process exits kubelet Restarts it (with exponential backoff) Pod deleted or evicted ReplicaSet controller Creates replacement Node stops reporting Node controller Marks NotReady, then evicts Pods after a timeout; they reschedule elsewhere Pod fails readiness EndpointSlice controller Removed from Service until healthy Pitfalls and best practices The API server is the bottleneck and the security perimeter. Restrict who can reach it and use RBAC. Do not run workloads on control plane nodes in production; they are tainted by default for this reason. Back up etcd, or use a managed control plane. Keep versions skewed within supported limits (kubelet may lag the API server by a few minor versions); upgrade control plane first. Do not edit objects the controllers manage (e.g. Pods owned by a ReplicaSet): your change will be reverted. Try it On a local cluster (next lesson), run kubectl get pods -n kube-system and identify the control plane components as Pods. Then run kubectl get events -w in one terminal and kubectl create deployment demo --image=nginx --replicas=3 in another; match each event to a step in the walkthrough above.

title: Local Setup and kubectl Essentials
text: Local Setup and kubectl Essentials You do not need a cloud account to learn Kubernetes. A full cluster runs on your laptop in under a minute. This lesson sets one up, teaches the kubectl commands you will use daily, and dissects the shape of every Kubernetes YAML file. Choosing a local cluster Tool How it works Best for kind Runs each "node" as a Docker container; multi-node supported CI pipelines, testing, learning multi-node behaviour minikube VM or container with a single node, many addons ( minikube addons enable ingress ) Beginners, trying addons k3d Runs k3s (lightweight Kubernetes) in Docker Fast, low-memory clusters Docker Desktop / Rancher Desktop Built-in single-node cluster toggle Zero extra install All need a container runtime (Docker, Podman or similar) running first. Install and create a cluster with kind # macOS (Linux: download the binary from the kind releases page) brew install kind kubectl # single-node cluster kind create cluster --name dev # or multi-node, with a port mapped for later ingress experiments cat <<'EOF' > kind-config.yaml kind: Cluster apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4 nodes: - role: control-plane extraPortMappings: - containerPort: 80 hostPort: 8080 - role: worker - role: worker EOF kind create cluster --name dev --config kind-config.yaml kubectl cluster-info --context kind-dev kubectl get nodes Alternatives: minikube start or k3d cluster create dev --agents 2 . Delete with kind delete cluster --name dev . Loading local images A local cluster cannot see images in your Docker daemon automatically. Load them in: kind load docker-image myapp:dev --name dev (minikube: minikube image load myapp:dev ). Use a non- latest tag, since :latest defaults to imagePullPolicy: Always and the cluster will try to pull from a registry. kubectl and contexts kubectl reads ~/.kube/config , which lists clusters , users (credentials) and contexts (a cluster + user + default namespace). The current context determines which cluster every command hits. kubectl config get-contexts # list kubectl config current-context kubectl config use-context kind-dev # switch cluster kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=staging # default namespace Production foot-gun Running kubectl delete against the wrong context is a classic outage. Show the current context in your shell prompt (kube-ps1) and consider tools like kubectx / kubens . Prefer separate kubeconfig files per environment and CI-driven changes to production. Daily commands # Read kubectl get pods # in current namespace kubectl get pods -A # all namespaces kubectl get pods -o wide # node and IP kubectl get deploy,svc,pods -l app=web # multiple kinds, label selector kubectl get pod web-1 -o yaml # full object kubectl describe pod web-1 # human-readable detail + Events kubectl logs web-1 # stdout/stderr kubectl logs -f web-1 -c sidecar --previous # follow, specific container, last crash kubectl api-resources # every kind the cluster knows kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy # built-in schema docs # Write kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml # create or update declaratively kubectl apply -f dir/ -R # a whole folder kubectl delete -f manifest.yaml kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml > web.yaml kubectl diff -f manifest.yaml # preview what apply would change # Interact kubectl exec -it web-1 -- sh kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80 # localhost:8080 -> Service port 80 kubectl scale deploy/web --replicas=5 kubectl top pods # needs metrics-server Set up an alias ( alias k=kubectl ) and shell completion ( source <(kubectl completion zsh) ). Imperative vs declarative kubectl create / run / scale are imperative shortcuts, handy for experiments. kubectl apply -f is declarative and the right way to manage anything real: the YAML file in git is the source of truth. A good trick is generating YAML with --dry-run=client -o yaml and then editing it. Anatomy of a manifest Every Kubernetes object has the same four top-level fields: apiVersion: apps/v1 # API group and version of this kind kind: Deployment # the type of object metadata: # identity name: web # unique within kind + namespace namespace: default labels: # key/values you query and select by app: web annotations: # non-identifying metadata (tools, notes) owner: team-shop spec: # DESIRED state; shape depends on kind replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: app: web template: metadata: labels: app: web spec: containers: - name: web image: nginx:1.27 ports: - containerPort: 80 # status: # ACTUAL state, written by Kubernetes, never by you apiVersion : find it with kubectl api-resources or kubectl explain . Core objects (Pod, Service) use v1 ; Deployments use apps/v1 ; Ingress networking.k8s.io/v1 . Labels and selectors are how objects find each other. A Service picks Pods by label; a Deployment owns Pods that match its selector. A mismatch is the most common beginner bug. Multiple objects can live in one file separated by --- . Learn from the cluster itself kubectl explain pod.spec.containers --recursive prints every legal field with types, offline. Much faster than searching docs. Pitfalls YAML indentation is semantic. Use an editor with a Kubernetes schema plugin and run kubectl apply --dry-run=server to validate against the real API. Unquoted values like yes , on or 1.20 may be parsed as booleans or floats. Quote strings in env values. kubectl edit changes live objects and leaves your files out of date. Edit the file and apply. Try it Create a kind cluster with two workers; run kubectl get nodes -o wide . Run kubectl create deployment hello --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=2 --dry-run=client -o yaml > hello.yaml , apply it, then kubectl port-forward deploy/hello 8080:80 and curl it. Delete one Pod with kubectl delete pod and watch it come back with kubectl get pods -w .

title: Pods and Workload Controllers
text: Pods and Workload Controllers The Pod is Kubernetes' smallest deployable unit, but you almost never create one directly. You create a controller (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job) that manages Pods for you. Choosing the right controller is the core design decision for every workload. Pods A Pod is one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP, they talk over localhost ), can share volumes, and are always scheduled together on the same node. Why not just containers? Because some processes are tightly coupled: a web app plus a log shipper, or a proxy sidecar. The Pod is the unit of co-location. apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: web labels: app: web spec: containers: - name: app image: ghcr.io/example/shop:2.3.1 ports: - containerPort: 8080 env: - name: LOG_LEVEL value: "info" - name: log-shipper # sidecar sharing the Pod image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1 initContainers: # run to completion BEFORE app containers - name: wait-for-db image: busybox:1.36 command: ["sh","-c","until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 2; done"] restartPolicy: Always Pods are ephemeral : when one dies it is not repaired, it is replaced by a new Pod with a new name and IP. Never rely on a Pod's IP or local filesystem surviving. Do not run naked Pods A bare Pod is not rescheduled if its node dies. Always wrap Pods in a controller. The controller family Deployment ──owns──▶ ReplicaSet ──owns──▶ Pod, Pod, Pod (stateless apps) StatefulSet ────────────────────────────▶ Pod-0, Pod-1 (stable identity + disks) DaemonSet ──────────────────────────────▶ one Pod per node (agents) Job ────────────────────────────────────▶ Pods that finish (batch) CronJob ──creates──▶ Job ───────────────▶ on a schedule ReplicaSet Ensures N identical Pods exist, using a label selector. If one dies it makes another. You rarely use it directly because a Deployment manages ReplicaSets for you, which enables rolling updates (a new ReplicaSet per version). Deployment The default choice for stateless apps (web servers, APIs, workers). It gives you replicas, rolling updates, rollbacks and scaling. apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: shop spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: # must match template labels; immutable after creation app: shop strategy: type: RollingUpdate rollingUpdate: maxSurge: 1 maxUnavailable: 0 template: # the Pod template metadata: labels: app: shop spec: containers: - name: shop image: ghcr.io/example/shop:2.3.1 # pin a tag or digest, never :latest ports: - containerPort: 8080 resources: requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi } limits: { memory: 256Mi } readinessProbe: httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 } Changing anything in spec.template (for example the image) triggers a rollout: a new ReplicaSet scales up while the old one scales down. Changing replicas does not. StatefulSet For workloads that need a stable identity : databases, Kafka, ZooKeeper, Elasticsearch. Differences from a Deployment: Pods are named name-0 , name-1 , ... and keep their name across restarts. Each Pod gets its own PersistentVolumeClaim via volumeClaimTemplates , which survives Pod deletion. Created and updated in order (0, then 1, ...) and deleted in reverse. Requires a headless Service ( clusterIP: None ) giving each Pod a DNS name like db-0.db.default.svc . apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: StatefulSet metadata: name: db spec: serviceName: db # headless Service name replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: { app: db } template: metadata: labels: { app: db } spec: containers: - name: postgres image: postgres:17 volumeMounts: - { name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data } volumeClaimTemplates: - metadata: { name: data } spec: accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"] resources: { requests: { storage: 20Gi } } Honest advice A StatefulSet gives you identity and storage, not replication, backups or failover. For production databases, use a managed service (RDS, Cloud SQL) or a mature operator (CloudNativePG, Strimzi) rather than hand-rolling it. DaemonSet Runs exactly one Pod on every node (or a selected subset), including nodes added later. Typical uses: log collectors (Fluent Bit), node metrics exporters, CNI plugins, security agents. apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: DaemonSet metadata: { name: node-exporter } spec: selector: matchLabels: { app: node-exporter } template: metadata: labels: { app: node-exporter } spec: tolerations: - operator: Exists # also run on tainted nodes containers: - name: exporter image: quay.io/prometheus/node-exporter:v1.8.2 ports: [{ containerPort: 9100, hostPort: 9100 }] Job and CronJob A Job runs Pods until a number of them complete successfully: database migrations, report generation. A CronJob creates Jobs on a cron schedule. apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: CronJob metadata: { name: nightly-report } spec: schedule: "0 2 * * *" # 02:00 daily (cluster time, UTC by default) concurrencyPolicy: Forbid # skip if previous still running successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3 jobTemplate: spec: backoffLimit: 3 # retries before marking failed activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600 ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400 template: spec: restartPolicy: OnFailure # Jobs must be OnFailure or Never containers: - name: report image: ghcr.io/example/report:1.4 args: ["--since=24h"] Make jobs idempotent : Kubernetes may run one twice on rare occasions. Choosing Need Use Stateless service, scale and roll out Deployment Stable network identity, per-Pod disk StatefulSet One per node DaemonSet Run once to completion Job On a schedule CronJob Pitfalls Selectors are immutable on Deployments; changing them means recreating. Without resources.requests the scheduler is blind and nodes get overcommitted. Pods are killed with SIGTERM and a 30 s grace period ( terminationGracePeriodSeconds ). Handle SIGTERM and finish in-flight requests. Using :latest makes rollbacks meaningless since you cannot tell what version is running. Try it Apply the Deployment above (use nginx:1.27 if you lack the image). Delete a Pod and watch the ReplicaSet replace it. Run kubectl get rs , change the image tag, apply again, and compare ReplicaSets before and after. Create a Job that runs echo hello and read its logs.

title: Services and Networking
text: Services and Networking Pods come and go and their IPs change constantly. A Service gives a set of Pods one stable name and virtual IP, and load-balances across the healthy ones. This lesson covers the Service types, cluster DNS, what kube-proxy really does, and how NetworkPolicy locks traffic down. The networking model Kubernetes imposes three rules, implemented by the CNI plugin: Every Pod gets its own IP. Any Pod can reach any other Pod by IP without NAT, across nodes. Agents on a node can reach all Pods on that node. This flat network is simple for apps, but Pod IPs are ephemeral. If frontend hard-coded 10.244.1.17 for the API, it would break at the next restart. Hence Services. Service basics A Service selects Pods by label and exposes them on a stable virtual IP (the ClusterIP) and DNS name.
