Only Pods that pass their readiness probe receive traffic. apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: shop spec: type: ClusterIP # default selector: app: shop # matches Pod labels ports: - name: http port: 80 # port on the Service targetPort: 8080 # port on the Pod (number or named port) Behind the scenes the EndpointSlice controller keeps a list of ready Pod IPs for the Service: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=shop . If this list is empty, your selector is wrong or no Pods are ready. This is the number one cause of "my Service doesn't work". Service types Type Reachable from Use ClusterIP Inside the cluster only Internal service-to-service calls (most Services) NodePort Any node IP at port 30000-32767 Dev, or as a building block for external load balancers LoadBalancer Internet or VPC via a cloud load balancer Exposing a service directly; one cloud LB per Service ExternalName Inside the cluster DNS alias (CNAME) to an external hostname Headless ( clusterIP: None ) Inside the cluster DNS returns Pod IPs directly; used with StatefulSets Internet ──▶ Cloud LB ──▶ NodePort (every node) ──▶ ClusterIP ──▶ Pod, Pod, Pod (LoadBalancer) (NodePort) (virtual IP) Each type builds on the previous one. apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: shop-public annotations: service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: "external" # provider specific spec: type: LoadBalancer selector: { app: shop } ports: - port: 443 targetPort: 8080 externalTrafficPolicy: Local # preserve client IP, avoid extra hop Cost trap Each LoadBalancer Service provisions a separate cloud load balancer (typically $15-25/month plus traffic). For many HTTP services, use one Ingress or Gateway in front instead (next lesson). Cluster DNS CoreDNS runs in the cluster and every Pod is configured to use it. Each Service gets: shop.default.svc.cluster.local <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local Within the same namespace just use shop ; across namespaces use shop.other-ns . Pods in a StatefulSet behind a headless Service get db-0.db.default.svc.cluster.local . Environment variables like SHOP_SERVICE_HOST also exist but DNS is the recommended approach. kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup shop kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -s http://shop/healthz How kube-proxy works The ClusterIP is virtual : no interface owns it and nothing listens on it. kube-proxy on each node watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs kernel rules so that packets addressed to the ClusterIP are rewritten (DNAT) to a randomly chosen ready Pod IP. iptables mode (long-time default): chains of rules with probability-based selection. Fine up to a few thousand Services, rule updates get slow beyond that. IPVS mode : kernel load balancer with hash tables and more algorithms; scales better. nftables mode : the modern replacement for iptables, GA in recent releases. eBPF (Cilium) : can replace kube-proxy entirely, with better performance and observability. Load balancing happens at connection level (L4), so a long-lived gRPC or HTTP/2 connection sticks to one Pod. For per-request balancing you need an L7 proxy, a service mesh, or client-side balancing with a headless Service. NetworkPolicy By default all Pods can talk to all Pods . A compromised frontend can reach your database. NetworkPolicy is a firewall at the Pod level. Once any policy selects a Pod, traffic of that direction is denied except what policies allow. It requires a CNI that enforces it (Calico, Cilium; plain Flannel does not). # 1. Default deny all ingress in the namespace apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: default-deny-ingress namespace: shop spec: podSelector: {} # all Pods policyTypes: [Ingress] --- # 2. Allow only the API to reach the database on 5432 apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: db-allow-api namespace: shop spec: podSelector: matchLabels: { app: db } policyTypes: [Ingress] ingress: - from: - podSelector: matchLabels: { app: api } ports: - protocol: TCP port: 5432 If you also deny egress, remember to allow DNS (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns) or everything breaks mysteriously. Pitfalls and best practices Match targetPort to the port your app actually listens on, and make the app listen on 0.0.0.0 , not 127.0.0.1 . Use named ports so changing a number does not require editing every Service. Start with a default-deny policy per namespace, then add allows. Do not use NodePort in production for public traffic; node IPs change. Expose databases only as ClusterIP. Try it Deploy nginx with 3 replicas and a ClusterIP Service. Run kubectl get endpointslices and note the three Pod IPs. From a temporary busybox Pod, wget -qO- shop . Break the selector label and watch the endpoints go empty. On a kind cluster with Calico or Cilium, apply a default-deny policy and confirm the busybox Pod can no longer reach nginx.

title: Ingress and the Gateway API
text: Ingress and the Gateway API Services expose ports; Ingress and Gateway expose HTTP(S) applications. They give you host and path routing, TLS termination and one shared entry point for dozens of services instead of one costly load balancer each. Why Ingress exists Suppose you have shop , blog and api . With LoadBalancer Services you pay for three cloud LBs, get three IPs, and handle TLS three times. What you want is one public entry point that looks at the HTTP Host header and path and routes: shop.example.com to the shop Service, example.com/blog to the blog, and so on. That is a layer 7 reverse proxy (see the Networking section), managed declaratively. Internet ──▶ Cloud LB ──▶ Ingress controller Pods (nginx/Traefik/Envoy) │ routes by host + path ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ Service shop Service blog Service api Two parts: resource and controller An Ingress object is just a set of routing rules. Nothing happens until an Ingress controller is installed to watch those objects and configure a real proxy. Kubernetes does not ship one. Common choices: Controller Notes ingress-nginx Very widespread; the community project is being retired (best-effort maintenance only after March 2026), so check migration plans for new builds Traefik Dynamic config, built-in Let's Encrypt, default in k3s HAProxy, Kong, Contour/Envoy Performance or API-gateway features Cloud-native (AWS Load Balancer Controller, GKE Ingress) Provisions the cloud's own L7 LB per Ingress Pick one with ingressClassName ; a cluster can have several. An Ingress example apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: web annotations: cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod # request a certificate spec: ingressClassName: nginx tls: - hosts: [shop.example.com, api.example.com] secretName: web-tls # cert-manager creates and renews this rules: - host: shop.example.com http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: { name: shop, port: { number: 80 } } - host: api.example.com http: paths: - path: /v1 pathType: Prefix backend: service: { name: api, port: { number: 80 } } Install ingress-nginx on kind or minikube with their documented manifests/addons, then point DNS (or /etc/hosts or a *.localtest.me wildcard) at the controller's address. TLS automation with cert-manager Manually buying and rotating certificates does not scale and expired certs are a classic outage. cert-manager is an operator that obtains certificates from Let's Encrypt (or an internal CA) and renews them automatically about 30 days before expiry. helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io helm install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager \ -n cert-manager --create-namespace --set crds.enabled=true apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1 kind: ClusterIssuer metadata: name: letsencrypt-prod spec: acme: server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory email: ops@example.com privateKeySecretRef: name: letsencrypt-account-key solvers: - http01: ingress: ingressClassName: nginx The flow: the Ingress annotation causes cert-manager to create a Certificate , which creates an ACME Order ; Let's Encrypt validates domain ownership by requesting a token over HTTP (HTTP-01) or via a DNS TXT record (DNS-01, required for wildcard certs); the signed certificate is stored in the Secret named in tls.secretName and the controller picks it up. Use staging first Let's Encrypt production has strict rate limits. Create a second ClusterIssuer pointing at the staging server and test with it before switching. Limitations of Ingress It only models HTTP(S). TCP/UDP, gRPC routing, header matching and traffic splitting need vendor-specific annotations that are not portable. One resource mixes the concerns of infrastructure admins (which load balancer, which certs) and app developers (which paths). Gateway API: the successor The Gateway API ( gateway.networking.k8s.io ) is the official, more expressive replacement, GA for core HTTP features and supported by Envoy Gateway, Istio, Cilium, Traefik, NGINX Gateway Fabric, Contour and cloud providers. It splits roles into separate objects: Object Owned by Purpose GatewayClass Infrastructure provider Which implementation (like StorageClass) Gateway Cluster operator Listeners: ports, protocols, hostnames, TLS HTTPRoute , GRPCRoute , TCPRoute App developers Routing rules attached to a Gateway apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Gateway metadata: name: public namespace: infra spec: gatewayClassName: envoy listeners: - name: https protocol: HTTPS port: 443 hostname: "*.example.com" tls: mode: Terminate certificateRefs: [{ name: wildcard-tls }] allowedRoutes: namespaces: { from: All } --- apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: HTTPRoute metadata: name: shop namespace: shop spec: parentRefs: [{ name: public, namespace: infra }] hostnames: ["shop.example.com"] rules: - matches: - path: { type: PathPrefix, value: / } backendRefs: - { name: shop-v1, port: 80, weight: 90 } # canary: 90/10 split - { name: shop-v2, port: 80, weight: 10 } Native support for weighted traffic splitting, header matching, redirects, rewrites and cross-namespace delegation replaces the pile of annotations. For new clusters, prefer Gateway API; keep Ingress where it already works. Pitfalls Forgetting ingressClassName : no controller claims the Ingress and nothing happens. The backend Service has no ready endpoints: you get 503 from the proxy. Check kubectl get endpointslices . Path rewriting surprises: /api forwarded as-is to an app expecting / . Configure rewrite or make the app base-path aware. HTTP-01 challenges fail if DNS does not point at the controller or a redirect rule blocks /.well-known/acme-challenge . Large uploads hit default proxy body size limits (nginx: 1 MB). Try it On kind (with the extraPortMappings config from lesson 3) install an ingress controller and create an Ingress routing /a and /b to two different echo Services. Read kubectl describe ingress and find the backends and any events. Stretch: install cert-manager with a self-signed ClusterIssuer and get a TLS Secret issued for a local hostname.

title: Configuration and Secrets
text: Configuration and Secrets Build one image, run it everywhere. Anything that differs between environments (URLs, feature flags, passwords) is injected at runtime through ConfigMaps and Secrets. Handling this well, especially secrets, is where many clusters quietly go wrong. Why separate config from images If a database URL is baked into the image you need a different build per environment, so what you tested is not what you ship. The twelve-factor principle: store config in the environment. Kubernetes provides two objects to do that. ConfigMap Key-value pairs of non-sensitive data, either simple values or whole files. apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: shop-config data: LOG_LEVEL: "info" # all values are strings FEATURE_NEW_CART: "true" app.properties: | # a whole file cache.ttl=60 retries=3 Create from the CLI: kubectl create configmap shop-config --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info --from-file=app.properties . Secret Same shape, intended for passwords, tokens and keys. Values are base64-encoded in data , or given as plain text in stringData (converted on write). apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: shop-db type: Opaque stringData: DB_PASSWORD: "s3cr3t-value" DB_URL: "postgres://shop:s3cr3t-value@db:5432/shop" Other types include kubernetes.io/tls (cert + key), kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson (registry login, used as imagePullSecrets ) and kubernetes.io/basic-auth . Base64 is not encryption Anyone who can read the Secret object can decode it with base64 -d . By default Secrets sit unencrypted in etcd. Enable encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration, or KMS provider on managed clusters), restrict get secrets with RBAC, and never commit Secret YAML to git in plain form. Consuming config: env vars vs volumes spec: containers: - name: shop image: ghcr.io/example/shop:2.3.1 envFrom: # every key becomes an env var - configMapRef: { name: shop-config } env: - name: DB_PASSWORD # a single key from a Secret valueFrom: secretKeyRef: { name: shop-db, key: DB_PASSWORD } volumeMounts: - name: cfg mountPath: /etc/shop # app.properties appears as a file readOnly: true - name: creds mountPath: /var/run/secrets/db readOnly: true volumes: - name: cfg configMap: { name: shop-config } - name: creds secret: { secretName: shop-db, defaultMode: 0400 } Environment variables Volume mounts Update behaviour Fixed at container start; need a restart Files update in place after a short delay (not with subPath ) Fit Simple scalar settings Config files, certificates, large values Leak risk Show up in env , crash dumps, child processes Lower; file permissions apply For secrets, volumes (backed by tmpfs, never written to node disk) are the safer choice, though env vars are widely used and acceptable in many setups. Rolling out config changes Changing a ConfigMap does not restart Pods that use it as env vars. Common fixes: put a hash of the config in a Pod template annotation (Helm: checksum/config: {{ include ... | sha256sum }} ), use Kustomize's configMapGenerator (appends a content hash to the name so a change triggers a rollout), or run kubectl rollout restart deploy/shop . For immutability, set immutable: true on the ConfigMap. Managing secrets properly The problem: GitOps wants everything in git, but secrets must not be in git. Three mainstream solutions: Sealed Secrets A controller in the cluster holds a private key. You encrypt a Secret locally with the public key using kubeseal , producing a SealedSecret that is safe to commit. Only that cluster can decrypt it. kubectl create secret generic shop-db --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=x --dry-run=client -o yaml \ | kubeseal --format yaml > shop-db-sealed.yaml git add shop-db-sealed.yaml # safe Simple, no external dependency. Downsides: bound to one cluster's key (back it up!), rotation is manual. External Secrets Operator (ESO) The source of truth lives in a real secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault, 1Password). ESO syncs values into native Kubernetes Secrets. apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1 kind: ExternalSecret metadata: name: shop-db spec: refreshInterval: 1h secretStoreRef: kind: ClusterSecretStore name: aws-secrets target: name: shop-db # the Kubernetes Secret created data: - secretKey: DB_PASSWORD remoteRef: key: prod/shop/db property: password You get central rotation, audit logs and access control, and git only contains references. This is the common choice in production. Others Secrets Store CSI Driver : mounts secrets from a vault straight into Pods as files. SOPS (with age or KMS): encrypts values inside YAML files in git; Flux and Argo CD plugins decrypt on apply. Vault Agent / Vault Secrets Operator : dynamic, short-lived credentials. Best practices Never put secrets in images, ConfigMaps, command-line args or logs. Give each workload its own narrowly scoped Secret and RBAC; prefer workload identity (IAM roles for service accounts) over static cloud keys when possible. Plan for rotation: apps should re-read files or be restarted on change. Enable etcd encryption and audit logging of secret access. ConfigMaps and Secrets are limited to 1 MiB. Try it Create a ConfigMap and mount it as a file in an nginx Pod; kubectl exec and cat it. Edit the ConfigMap and watch the mounted file update (about a minute) while an env var from the same map does not. Create a Secret, read it back with kubectl get secret -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d , and note how little protection base64 gives.

title: Storage: Volumes, PVs and PVCs
text: Storage: Volumes, PVs and PVCs Container filesystems vanish when a container restarts. Anything that must survive, such as a database, uploaded files or a queue, needs a volume whose lifecycle is independent of the Pod. Kubernetes abstracts storage so your YAML does not care whether the disk is an EBS volume, a Google Persistent Disk or an NFS share. The problem A container's writable layer is deleted with the container. Even within a Pod, a restarted container starts clean. And since Pods can be rescheduled to another node, data on a node's local disk may not follow. We need storage that is (a) outside the container, (b) optionally outside the node, and (c) requested by developers without knowing infrastructure details. Ephemeral volumes Type Lifetime Use emptyDir Lives as long as the Pod (survives container restarts) Scratch space, sharing files between containers; medium: Memory for tmpfs configMap / secret Pod Config files hostPath Node's disk Node agents only; a security risk, avoid for apps volumes: - name: cache emptyDir: sizeLimit: 1Gi Persistent storage: three objects Developer Cluster admin / provisioner Cloud / storage ┌────────────┐ binds ┌───────────────┐ backed by ┌───────────────┐ │ PVC │───────▶│ PV │───────────▶│ EBS / PD / NFS │ │ "20Gi, RWO"│ │ real volume │ └───────────────┘ └─────┬──────┘ └───────────────┘ │ created on demand by ┌─────▼──────────┐ │ StorageClass │ "gp3", "premium-ssd": provisioner + parameters └────────────────┘ PersistentVolume (PV) : a piece of storage in the cluster. A cluster-scoped resource, backed by a real disk. PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) : a developer's request: "I need 20 Gi, single-writer". Namespaced. Kubernetes binds it to a matching PV. StorageClass : describes a tier of storage and the provisioner that creates it. With dynamic provisioning , creating a PVC causes the provisioner (a CSI driver) to create the disk and PV automatically. Nobody pre-creates PVs by hand any more. StorageClass apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1 kind: StorageClass metadata: name: fast annotations: storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "false" provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com parameters: type: gp3 encrypted: "true" reclaimPolicy: Delete # or Retain allowVolumeExpansion: true volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer # create the disk in the zone where the Pod lands Check what exists: kubectl get storageclass . kind and minikube include a default one using local disk. PVC and using it in a Pod apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: uploads spec: accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"] storageClassName: fast resources: requests: storage: 20Gi --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: { name: uploader } spec: containers: - name: app image: nginx:1.27 volumeMounts: - { name: data, mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/uploads } volumes: - name: data persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: uploads } Access modes Mode Meaning Typical backing ReadWriteOnce (RWO) One node mounts read-write Block disks (EBS, PD) ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP) Exactly one Pod CSI drivers supporting it ReadOnlyMany (ROX) Many nodes read-only NFS, some file stores ReadWriteMany (RWX) Many nodes read-write EFS, Filestore, CephFS, NFS Block disks are RWO and zone-bound: a Pod using an EBS volume in us-east-1a cannot start in 1b. This is why WaitForFirstConsumer matters, and why Deployments with RWO volumes and several replicas on different nodes fail. Reclaim policy and data safety Delete : deleting the PVC deletes the PV and the cloud disk. Convenient, dangerous for important data. Retain : the PV and disk remain after the PVC is deleted for manual recovery. Use for precious data. PVCs are not backups A volume is one copy of data on one disk. Use VolumeSnapshots (CSI) and tools like Velero for backups, and database-level backups for databases. Test restores. StatefulSet volumes With a Deployment all replicas share one PVC (only works for RWX). A StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates instead creates a PVC per replica ( data-db-0 , data-db-1 ), and when Pod db-1 is rescheduled it reattaches to data-db-1 . Scaling the StatefulSet down does not delete PVCs by default (configurable via persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy ), protecting data but leaving orphaned disks to clean up. Expanding and snapshotting # expand (StorageClass needs allowVolumeExpansion: true); you can only grow kubectl patch pvc uploads -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"50Gi"}}}}' apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1 kind: VolumeSnapshot metadata: { name: uploads-snap } spec: volumeSnapshotClassName: csi-snap source: { persistentVolumeClaimName: uploads } Pitfalls PVC stuck Pending : no default StorageClass, wrong class name, no capacity, or a CSI driver not installed. kubectl describe pvc tells you. Pod stuck ContainerCreating with a "Multi-Attach error": an RWO volume is still attached to another node (old Pod terminating). Running databases on network disks has latency; for high performance consider local SSDs with replication handled by the database. Do not use hostPath for app data: it ties the Pod to one node and is a container-escape risk. Try it On your kind cluster create a PVC and a Pod writing a file into it. Delete the Pod, recreate it, and confirm the file persists. Run kubectl get pv,pvc,storageclass and trace the binding. Create a 2-replica StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates and observe the per-Pod PVCs.

title: Probes, Resources and Autoscaling
text: Probes, Resources and Autoscaling Kubernetes can only keep your app healthy and right-sized if you tell it what healthy means and how much it needs. Probes, resource requests and limits, and autoscalers are the three levers that turn a pile of Pods into a resilient, efficient system. Health probes By default Kubernetes only knows if a container's main process is alive. A deadlocked web server is "alive" but useless. Probes let the kubelet ask the app directly. Probe Question On failure startupProbe Has the app finished booting? Container is killed and restarted; other probes are disabled until it passes readinessProbe Can it serve traffic right now? Removed from Service endpoints; not restarted livenessProbe Is it stuck beyond recovery? Container is restarted containers: - name: shop image: ghcr.io/example/shop:2.3.1 startupProbe: # allows up to 30 x 5 = 150 s to boot httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 } periodSeconds: 5 failureThreshold: 30 readinessProbe: httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 } periodSeconds: 5 timeoutSeconds: 2 failureThreshold: 3 livenessProbe: httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 } periodSeconds: 10 timeoutSeconds: 2 failureThreshold: 3 # other mechanisms: tcpSocket, exec (command), grpc Liveness probes cause outages A common disaster: the liveness probe checks the database. The database blips, every Pod fails liveness, Kubernetes restarts the entire fleet at once and turns a blip into an outage. Keep liveness checks local and cheap (is this process responsive?). Put dependency checks in readiness at most, and be careful there too. If unsure, use no liveness probe rather than a bad one. Readiness is what makes rolling updates safe: a new Pod only receives traffic, and an old one is only removed, once readiness passes. Requests and limits Each container declares resources: resources: requests: # what the scheduler RESERVES; used to place the Pod cpu: 250m # 250 millicores = 0.25 of a core memory: 256Mi limits: # the ceiling enforced at runtime memory: 512Mi # cpu limit often omitted, see below Requests drive scheduling. A Pod requesting 4 Gi only lands on a node with 4 Gi unreserved. Also the guaranteed share under contention. CPU limit : compressible. Exceeding it means throttling (slowness), not death. Many teams set CPU requests but no CPU limits to avoid needless throttling; others keep them for fairness. Both are defensible; know the trade-off. Memory limit : incompressible. Exceeding it means the kernel kills the container: OOMKilled , exit code 137. Without requests, the scheduler thinks Pods are free, overcommits nodes, and everything slows or gets evicted. Without memory limits, one leaky Pod can take down a node's neighbours. QoS classes Derived automatically; determines eviction order when a node runs out of memory. Class Condition Evicted Guaranteed Every container has requests = limits for CPU and memory Last Burstable At least one request or limit set, not Guaranteed Middle BestEffort Nothing set First Right-sizing: watch real usage ( kubectl top pods , Prometheus) and set memory request close to typical peak with a limit with headroom, and CPU request near typical usage. JVM and Node apps need runtime flags aware of the container limit (modern JVMs are; for Node set --max-old-space-size below the limit). Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) Adds or removes replicas based on metrics. It needs metrics-server installed and CPU/memory requests on the Pods (utilisation is computed relative to the request). apiVersion: autoscaling/v2 kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata: { name: shop } spec: scaleTargetRef: apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment name: shop minReplicas: 3 maxReplicas: 20 metrics: - type: Resource resource: name: cpu target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 } behavior: scaleDown: stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300 # avoid flapping scaleUp: policies: - { type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 60 } The formula: desired = ceil(current * currentMetric / targetMetric) . Custom and external metrics (requests per second, queue length) work through a metrics adapter, or use KEDA , which scales on Kafka lag, SQS depth, cron schedules and more, and can scale to zero. HPA works only if your app scales horizontally (stateless or shared-nothing) and starts fast. Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) Adjusts the requests of a workload based on observed usage. Modes: Off (recommendations only, safest start), Initial , and Auto / Recreate (evicts Pods to apply new values; newer versions support in-place resize on recent Kubernetes). Do not let HPA and VPA both react to CPU on the same workload. A common pattern: VPA in recommendation mode to guide manual right-sizing. Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter HPA creates Pods, but if no node has room they sit Pending . The Cluster Autoscaler watches for unschedulable Pods and adds nodes to a node group; it removes nodes that stay underused and whose Pods can move elsewhere. Karpenter (AWS, spreading to others) provisions right-sized individual instances directly without pre-defined node groups, often faster and cheaper, mixing spot and on-demand. traffic ↑ ─▶ HPA adds Pods ─▶ no room? Pods Pending ─▶ Cluster Autoscaler adds a node ─▶ Pods scheduled traffic ↓ ─▶ HPA removes Pods ─▶ nodes underused ─▶ autoscaler drains and removes node Node scale-up takes minutes. For spiky traffic, keep headroom with low-priority "pause" Pods that get preempted, or a higher minReplicas. Pitfalls HPA shows <unknown> targets: metrics-server missing or requests not set. Readiness probe too aggressive, so new Pods never become ready and HPA keeps adding more. Memory limit lower than the real working set: endless OOMKilled restarts. Check kubectl describe pod for "Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled". Slow startup with a short liveness: restart loop. Use a startupProbe. Scale-down kills in-flight requests: handle SIGTERM and use a preStop sleep of a few seconds so endpoints propagate first. Try it Install metrics-server on kind (it needs --kubelet-insecure-tls locally). Run kubectl top nodes . Deploy a CPU-burning app, attach an HPA at 50 percent, and generate load with kubectl run -it load --image=busybox -- sh -c "while true; do wget -q -O- http://shop; done" . Watch kubectl get hpa -w . Set a memory limit of 20Mi on a Pod that allocates more and observe OOMKilled.

title: Rolling Updates and Rollbacks
text: Rolling Updates and Rollbacks Shipping a new version should not mean downtime. Kubernetes Deployments replace Pods gradually, only advancing when the new ones are healthy, and keep history so you can undo a bad release with one command. What happens without it The naive deploy is "stop v1, start v2". Between those two steps users see errors. If v2 crashes on boot, you are down until you manually fix or revert. A rolling update trades speed for safety: at every moment enough healthy Pods exist to serve traffic. How a rolling update works A Deployment owns ReplicaSets, one per Pod template version. On a change to spec.template , the Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts replicas from old to new in steps. replicas: 4, maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 start RS-v1 [■ ■ ■ ■] RS-v2 [ ] step 1 RS-v1 [■ ■ ■ ■] RS-v2 [□] surge: 5 Pods total, new not ready yet step 2 RS-v1 [■ ■ ■ ■] RS-v2 [■] new is Ready step 3 RS-v1 [■ ■ ■ ] RS-v2 [■ □] old terminated, next new started ... end RS-v1 [ ] (kept, 0 replicas, for rollback) RS-v2 [■ ■ ■ ■] Strategy settings spec: replicas: 4 revisionHistoryLimit: 10 # old ReplicaSets kept for rollback progressDeadlineSeconds: 600 # mark rollout "failed" if no progress minReadySeconds: 10 # new Pod must stay Ready this long to count strategy: type: RollingUpdate # the default (alternative: Recreate) rollingUpdate: maxSurge: 25% # extra Pods above desired during update maxUnavailable: 0 # how many may be below desired Setting Effect maxSurge Higher means a faster rollout but needs spare capacity. Number or percentage. maxUnavailable 0 keeps full capacity throughout (needs surge > 0). Default is 25% for both. minReadySeconds Catches Pods that pass readiness then crash a few seconds later. progressDeadlineSeconds Controller sets condition Progressing=False ; CI can fail on it. Recreate kills all old Pods first, then starts new ones. Accept the downtime when two versions can not coexist (for example a schema-incompatible singleton or RWO volume that cannot attach twice). Rolling updates depend on readiness probes Without a readiness probe Kubernetes considers a Pod ready as soon as the process starts, so it may send traffic and tear down old Pods before the new app can answer. A correct readiness probe is what makes a rollout zero-downtime. Also remember that during a rollout v1 and v2 run simultaneously : your APIs and database schemas must be backward compatible (expand and contract migrations). kubectl rollout in practice kubectl set image deploy/shop shop=ghcr.io/example/shop:2.4.0 # or edit YAML and apply kubectl rollout status deploy/shop # blocks until done; exit code != 0 on failure kubectl rollout history deploy/shop # list revisions kubectl rollout history deploy/shop --revision=3 kubectl rollout undo deploy/shop # back to previous revision kubectl rollout undo deploy/shop --to-revision=2 kubectl rollout pause deploy/shop # batch several edits, then... kubectl rollout resume deploy/shop kubectl rollout restart deploy/shop # fresh Pods, same template (pick up new config) Record why a change happened with an annotation ( kubernetes.io/change-cause ) so history is readable. In a CI pipeline, the deploy step usually runs kubectl rollout status --timeout=5m and runs rollout undo if it fails. GitOps rollback If git is the source of truth, rollback means git revert and letting Argo CD or Flux apply it, rather than kubectl rollout undo , which creates drift from git. Graceful shutdown When a Pod is terminated, two things happen concurrently: it is removed from Service endpoints, and SIGTERM is sent. Endpoint removal takes a moment to propagate through kube-proxy and ingress controllers, so requests can still arrive after SIGTERM. Mitigate: spec: terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45 containers: - name: shop lifecycle: preStop: exec: { command: ["sleep", "10"] } # let endpoints drain first And make the app, on SIGTERM, stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests and exit. Many frameworks need explicit shutdown hooks. PodDisruptionBudgets Rolling updates are voluntary disruptions you control . But cluster operations also evict Pods: node drains for upgrades, autoscaler scale-down. A PodDisruptionBudget limits how many Pods of an app may be down at once during such voluntary evictions. apiVersion: policy/v1 kind: PodDisruptionBudget metadata: { name: shop } spec: minAvailable: 2 # or: maxUnavailable: 1 selector: matchLabels: { app: shop } kubectl drain node-1 then evicts Pods one by one while respecting the budget, waiting if necessary. PDBs do not protect against crashes or node failure. Beware minAvailable equal to replicas: nothing can ever be evicted and upgrades hang forever. Beyond built-in rolling updates Strategy How Tool Blue-green Run both versions fully, flip Service selector or route Plain Services; Argo Rollouts Canary Send 5 percent, 25 percent, ... of traffic to v2 while watching metrics, auto-abort on errors Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Gateway API weights Feature flags Deploy dark, enable per user App level Native Deployments shift Pod counts, not traffic percentages; for fine-grained canaries use a progressive delivery controller. Pitfalls A rollout stuck at "Waiting for rollout to finish": new Pods fail readiness, are Pending (no capacity for surge), or image is wrong. Old Pods keep serving, which is the point. Inspect with kubectl describe . :latest image tags: re-applying identical YAML changes nothing, and rollback cannot restore a specific version. revisionHistoryLimit: 0 disables rollback. Database migrations that break the old version during the rollout window. Try it Deploy 4 replicas of nginx:1.26 with a readiness probe. Update to nginx:1.27 while running kubectl get pods -w in another terminal. Update to a nonexistent tag nginx:nope , watch the rollout stall with ImagePullBackOff while old Pods keep serving, then kubectl rollout undo . Add a PDB with minAvailable 3 and run kubectl drain on a worker to see it respected.

title: Helm and Kustomize
text: Helm and Kustomize A real application is a dozen YAML files, and you need several copies of them: dev, staging, production, each slightly different. Copy-pasting YAML does not scale. Helm and Kustomize are the two standard answers: one templates, the other patches. The problem Staging runs 1 replica with a small database; production runs 6 with a big one; the image tag and hostname differ. If you copy the manifests, a fix in one place must be repeated everywhere and the copies drift. We need a single source plus a small, explicit set of differences. Helm Kustomize Approach Go templates + values; packages as versioned charts Plain YAML + declarative patches; no templating Built into kubectl No (separate CLI) Yes: kubectl apply -k Best for Installing third-party software; distributing your app; parametrising Your own app's per-environment variations Extra features Release tracking, hooks, rollback, dependencies Simplicity, valid YAML at every step Many teams use both: Helm for third-party charts (ingress, cert-manager, Prometheus), Kustomize (or Helm) for their own apps. Helm Concepts Chart : a package: templates + default values + metadata. Values : the parameters you override. Release : one installed instance of a chart in a cluster. Helm tracks revisions in a Secret, so you can upgrade and roll back. helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami helm search repo redis helm show values bitnami/redis > redis-values.yaml # see all knobs helm install cache bitnami/redis -n data --create-namespace -f redis-values.yaml helm upgrade cache bitnami/redis -n data -f redis-values.yaml --set replica.replicaCount=3 helm list -A helm history cache -n data helm rollback cache 1 -n data helm uninstall cache -n data helm template cache bitnami/redis -f redis-values.yaml # render YAML locally, no cluster helm lint ./mychart Chart layout shop/ ├── Chart.yaml name, version (chart), appVersion ├── values.yaml defaults ├── values-prod.yaml environment override (optional) ├── templates/ │ ├── _helpers.tpl reusable named templates │ ├── deployment.yaml │ ├── service.yaml │ ├── ingress.yaml │ └── NOTES.txt └── charts/ dependencies Templating # values.yaml replicaCount: 2 image: repository: ghcr.io/example/shop tag: "2.3.1" resources: requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi } ingress: enabled: false host: "" # templates/deployment.yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: {{ include "shop.fullname" . }} labels: app.kubernetes.io/name: shop spec: replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} selector: matchLabels: app.kubernetes.io/name: shop template: metadata: labels: app.kubernetes.io/name: shop annotations: checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }} spec: containers: - name: shop image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}" resources: {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }} # templates/ingress.yaml {{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }} apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress ... {{- end }} Override per environment: helm upgrade --install shop ./shop -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=$GIT_SHA . Precedence: chart defaults, then -f files in order, then --set . Template complexity is Helm's cost Indentation-sensitive text templating generating YAML is error-prone and hard to read. Keep templates simple, always check output with helm template , pin chart versions, and review the rendered diff ( helm diff plugin) before upgrading production. Treat third-party charts as code you depend on: read what they create. Kustomize Kustomize keeps a base of plain, valid YAML and layers overlays that patch it. No placeholders, no template language. shop/ ├── base/ │ ├── kustomization.yaml │ ├── deployment.yaml │ └── service.yaml └── overlays/ ├── staging/ │ └── kustomization.yaml └── production/ ├── kustomization.yaml └── replicas-patch.yaml # base/kustomization.yaml resources: - deployment.yaml - service.yaml labels: - pairs: { app.kubernetes.io/name: shop } includeSelectors: true # overlays/production/kustomization.yaml resources: - ../../base namespace: shop-prod namePrefix: prod- images: - name: ghcr.io/example/shop newTag: 2.3.1 # CI updates this line patches: - path: replicas-patch.yaml configMapGenerator: - name: shop-config literals: - LOG_LEVEL=warn # name gets a content hash; changes roll Pods # overlays/production/replicas-patch.yaml (strategic merge patch) apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: shop spec: replicas: 6 kubectl kustomize overlays/production # render and inspect kubectl diff -k overlays/production kubectl apply -k overlays/production Kustomize can also inline Helm charts ( helmCharts: ) for post-rendering patches, a handy combination. Choosing Installing someone else's software: Helm. Your own app, a handful of environments, want readable diffs: Kustomize. Shipping an app for external users to configure: Helm chart. GitOps: both are first-class in Argo CD and Flux. Pitfalls Helm values with no schema: add values.schema.json to catch typos. Secrets in values.yaml committed to git. Use external secrets instead. Helm CRD handling: CRDs in crds/ are installed once and never upgraded or deleted by Helm. Plan CRD upgrades separately. Kustomize patches silently do nothing if the target name or kind does not match; check the rendered output. Unpinned chart versions: helm upgrade may pull breaking changes. Try it Create a chart with helm create shop , run helm template shop ./shop , then install it on kind and change replicaCount with --set . Build the Kustomize layout above with staging (1 replica) and production (3 replicas) overlays and compare kubectl kustomize output of each. Break a Helm upgrade intentionally (bad image tag) and use helm rollback .

title: Namespaces, RBAC and Pod Security
text: Namespaces, RBAC and Pod Security A cluster is shared by many teams, apps and automation. Without boundaries, one team's mistake deletes another's database. Namespaces partition the cluster, RBAC decides who can do what, quotas stop noisy neighbours, and Pod security keeps containers from escaping. Namespaces A namespace is a named scope for most resources. Names must be unique within a namespace, not across the cluster, so web can exist in both staging and prod . Default ones: default , kube-system (control plane add-ons), kube-public , kube-node-lease . kubectl create namespace shop-prod kubectl get pods -n shop-prod kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop-prod kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false # cluster-scoped kinds: Node, PV, StorageClass, Namespace... Common layouts: one namespace per team, per app, or per environment-per-app. For hard isolation between environments (prod vs dev) use separate clusters; namespaces are a soft boundary (shared nodes, shared kernel, shared control plane). What namespaces do NOT do They do not isolate the network (use NetworkPolicy), do not limit resources (use ResourceQuota), and do not restrict permissions (use RBAC). They are just the scope to which those controls attach. ServiceAccounts: identity for Pods Humans authenticate with certificates or an OIDC identity provider; Pods authenticate as a ServiceAccount . Every namespace has a default one. The token is projected into the Pod at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ and is short-lived and audience-bound in modern clusters. apiVersion: v1 kind: ServiceAccount metadata: name: shop namespace: shop-prod annotations: eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/shop # cloud identity binding automountServiceAccountToken: false # do not mount a token unless the app calls the API Give each workload its own ServiceAccount; never share default . Most apps never talk to the Kubernetes API, so disable the token mount. RBAC Role-Based Access Control answers "may subject S perform verb V on resource R?" It is purely additive: there are no deny rules; absence of a grant means denied. Object Scope Meaning Role One namespace A set of permissions ClusterRole Cluster-wide (or reusable template) Permissions, including non-namespaced resources RoleBinding One namespace Grants a Role or ClusterRole to subjects within that namespace ClusterRoleBinding Cluster-wide Grants across all namespaces apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: pod-reader namespace: shop-prod rules: - apiGroups: [""] # "" = core group resources: ["pods", "pods/log"] verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"] --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: dev-team-read-pods namespace: shop-prod subjects: - kind: Group name: shop-developers # from your identity provider apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io - kind: ServiceAccount name: shop namespace: shop-prod roleRef: kind: Role name: pod-reader apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io Test it without guessing: kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n shop-prod --as=jane kubectl auth can-i list secrets -n shop-prod --as=system:serviceaccount:shop-prod:shop kubectl auth can-i --list -n shop-prod --as=jane Built-in ClusterRoles to reuse: view , edit , admin (namespace-level) and cluster-admin (everything). A typical pattern: bind edit to developers in their own namespaces via RoleBinding, view in prod. RBAC pitfalls Never bind cluster-admin to CI tokens or apps casually; it is root for the cluster. get secrets , create pods , exec and the escalate / bind verbs are powerful: reading secrets reveals credentials, creating a Pod can mount them. Wildcards ( resources: ["*"] ) grow with new CRDs. Be explicit. Audit with tools like kubectl-who-can , rbac-lookup or Kubescape. ResourceQuota and LimitRange Without limits, one namespace can consume the entire cluster. apiVersion: v1 kind: ResourceQuota metadata: { name: team-quota, namespace: shop-dev } spec: hard: requests.cpu: "10" requests.memory: 20Gi limits.memory: 40Gi pods: "50" persistentvolumeclaims: "10" services.loadbalancers: "1" # avoid surprise cloud bills --- apiVersion: v1 kind: LimitRange metadata: { name: defaults, namespace: shop-dev } spec: limits: - type: Container default: { memory: 256Mi } defaultRequest: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi } max: { memory: 2Gi } When a compute quota is set, Pods must declare requests/limits or be rejected; a LimitRange supplies defaults so developers do not hit that wall. Pod security By default a container may run as root, add Linux capabilities or even be privileged , which is nearly host root. The built-in Pod Security Admission enforces three standard profiles per namespace via labels: Profile Allows privileged Anything (system components only) baseline Blocks known escalations: hostNetwork, privileged, hostPath etc. restricted Hardened best practice: non-root, no privilege escalation, seccomp, drop all capabilities kubectl label namespace shop-prod \ pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \ pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted A Pod that passes restricted : spec: securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 10001 seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault } containers: - name: shop image: ghcr.io/example/shop:2.3.1 securityContext: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] } For richer rules (only allow images from your registry, require labels) use a policy engine: Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper, or the built-in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL). Checklist Separate namespaces per team or app; default-deny NetworkPolicy in each. A ServiceAccount per workload, least-privilege Roles, token mounting off by default. Quotas and LimitRanges on shared namespaces. restricted Pod Security on app namespaces. Humans via SSO groups, not shared kubeconfig certificates. Try it Create a namespace, a ServiceAccount, a Role that can only list Pods, and a RoleBinding. Verify with kubectl auth can-i using --as=system:serviceaccount:... . Add a ResourceQuota of 2 Pods and try to scale a Deployment to 5. Read the error events. Label a namespace enforce=restricted and try to run nginx as root; then fix the Pod's securityContext.

title: Debugging Kubernetes
text: Debugging Kubernetes Things will go wrong: Pods that will not start, Services that return nothing, rollouts that hang. Debugging Kubernetes is a learnable skill built on a small toolkit and a consistent flow: read the status, read the events, read the logs, and narrow down. The toolkit kubectl get pods -o wide # status, restarts, node, IP kubectl describe pod NAME # config + EVENTS at the bottom (read this first) kubectl logs NAME [-c container] [--previous] # --previous = logs of the last crashed instance kubectl logs -l app=shop --tail=50 --all-containers kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -n NS # what the cluster has been doing kubectl exec -it NAME -- sh # shell inside kubectl port-forward pod/NAME 8080:8080 # reach it from your laptop kubectl debug -it NAME --image=busybox:1.36 --target=app # ephemeral debug container kubectl debug node/NODE -it --image=ubuntu # host-level debugging kubectl get pod NAME -o yaml # status section: conditions, lastState, exit codes kubectl top pod / kubectl top node # resource usage Events are the cluster talking to you The Events section of kubectl describe says why the scheduler could not place a Pod, why an image failed to pull, why a probe failed. Events expire after about an hour, so check early. Pod lifecycle statuses The STATUS column tells you which stage failed: Pending ─▶ ContainerCreating ─▶ Running ─▶ Succeeded / Failed │ │ │ │ │ └─ CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, Error │ └─ ImagePullBackOff, volume/secret mount errors └─ unschedulable (no node fits) Pending: it was never scheduled Run kubectl describe pod and read the FailedScheduling event: Message Meaning and fix Insufficient cpu / memory No node has enough unreserved resources. Lower requests, add nodes, or check the autoscaler. node(s) had untolerated taint Add a toleration or use different nodes. didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector Label mismatch; check nodeSelector and kubectl get nodes --show-labels . unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims PVC is Pending: no StorageClass, no capacity, wrong zone. exceeded quota (on ReplicaSet events) Namespace ResourceQuota full. ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull The kubelet cannot download the image. In describe events find the real reason: manifest unknown / not found : typo in the image name or tag does not exist. Try docker pull with the exact string. unauthorized / pull access denied : private registry needs imagePullSecrets : kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \ --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=USER --docker-password=TOKEN # then in the Pod spec: imagePullSecrets: [{ name: regcred }] Network or DNS issues from the node, registry rate limits (Docker Hub), architecture mismatch (arm64 image on amd64 nodes shows as exec format error instead). Local clusters: image built locally but not loaded ( kind load docker-image ) and imagePullPolicy forcing a pull. CrashLoopBackOff The container starts, exits, and Kubernetes restarts it with growing delay (10 s, 20 s, up to 5 minutes). The cause is almost always in the app, not Kubernetes. kubectl logs POD --previous : the final output before the crash. Missing env var, cannot reach DB, bad config file, stack trace. kubectl describe pod : look at Last State: Terminated and its Reason and Exit Code . Exit code / reason Likely cause 1 Application error: read logs 0 in a Deployment Process finished immediately (wrong command, daemonizes itself); a long-running container must stay in the foreground 126 / 127 Command not executable / not found (wrong command or entrypoint) 137, OOMKilled Exceeded memory limit (or SIGKILL after grace period). Raise limit or fix the leak. 139 Segmentation fault 143 SIGTERM: terminated normally, often by a failing liveness probe or a rollout Liveness probe failures also look like crash loops: events show Liveness probe failed . Loosen thresholds or add a startupProbe. If the container dies too fast to inspect, override its command to sleep: kubectl debug POD -it --copy-to=debug --container=app -- sh gives you a copy to poke at. Other common states ContainerCreating forever : volume attach/mount failure, missing ConfigMap/Secret ( MountVolume.SetUp failed ), CNI problems ( failed to create pod sandbox ). CreateContainerConfigError : references a ConfigMap/Secret key that does not exist. Terminating forever : stuck finalizer or an unreachable node. Last resort: kubectl delete pod X --force --grace-period=0 (understand the risk for StatefulSets). Evicted : node pressure (disk or memory). kubectl describe node shows conditions. Running but 0/1 READY : readiness probe failing; check the probe path and port. Service and network problems "The Pod is Running but I cannot reach it." Work along the path: client ─▶ Ingress/Gateway ─▶ Service ─▶ EndpointSlice ─▶ Pod:targetPort ─▶ app 1 2 3 4 5 6 Does the app work? kubectl port-forward pod/NAME 8080:8080 and curl localhost:8080. If not, it is an app problem; also confirm it listens on 0.0.0.0 . Does the Service select the Pods? kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=NAME or kubectl get endpoints NAME . Empty means a label selector mismatch or Pods not ready. Do ports match? Service targetPort must equal the container's listening port. Does DNS work? kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup NAME . Check CoreDNS Pods in kube-system . Can a Pod reach the Service? From a debug Pod: curl -v http://NAME.NS:PORT . If it fails but Pod IP works, suspect kube-proxy; if the Pod IP also fails, suspect NetworkPolicy or CNI. Ingress: kubectl describe ingress , check class, host, backend; look at ingress controller logs. A 503 means no endpoints; a 404 means no rule matched; a 502/504 means the backend misbehaved. Rollouts and the control plane Deployment not progressing: kubectl rollout status , then inspect the new ReplicaSet's Pods ( kubectl get rs ), then Pods as above. Pods not being created at all: kubectl describe rs events show quota or admission webhook rejections or PodSecurity violations. Node NotReady : kubectl describe node , then kubelet logs ( journalctl -u kubelet ) via node access or kubectl debug node . kubectl get componentstatuses is deprecated; use kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' . A troubleshooting flow kubectl get pods │ ├─ Pending ───────────▶ describe pod ▶ FailedScheduling? resources / taints / PVC / quota ├─ ImagePullBackOff ──▶ describe pod ▶ name/tag typo? registry auth? network? ├─ ContainerCreating ─▶ describe pod ▶ missing Secret/ConfigMap? volume? CNI? ├─ CrashLoopBackOff ──▶ logs --previous + exit code ▶ app error / OOMKilled / probe ├─ Running 0/1 ───────▶ readiness probe failing ▶ describe, logs, check port/path └─ Running 1/1 but unreachable ▶ port-forward ▶ endpoints ▶ ports ▶ DNS ▶ NetworkPolicy ▶ ingress Habits that save hours Always read the Events before guessing. Change one thing at a time; reproduce with a minimal debug Pod. Ship a debug image or use kubectl debug : distroless images have no shell. Centralised logs and metrics (see the Observability section) make this far faster than live kubectl. Tools: k9s (terminal UI), stern (multi-Pod logs), Lens, kubectl-neat. Try it Break things on purpose, then fix each using only kubectl: Deploy nginx:does-not-exist (ImagePullBackOff). Request cpu: 100 (Pending, Insufficient cpu). Run busybox with command: ["sh","-c","exit 1"] (CrashLoopBackOff). Create a Service whose selector has a typo and diagnose with endpoints. Reference a nonexistent Secret in envFrom (CreateContainerConfigError).

title: Managed Kubernetes and Alternatives
text: Managed Kubernetes and Alternatives Running the Kubernetes control plane yourself (etcd backups, certificate rotation, upgrades) is a job. Almost everyone should let a cloud provider do it. This lesson compares EKS, GKE and AKS, covers lightweight distributions, explains where the money goes, and lists genuine alternatives. Why managed With self-managed Kubernetes (kubeadm, kops, Talos, etc.) you own the control plane: HA etcd, API server certificates, version upgrades every few months (Kubernetes ships roughly three minor versions a year and supports each for about 14 months), security patches. Managed services run and patch the control plane for you, integrate with cloud IAM, load balancers and disks, and offer one-click upgrades. You still own your nodes' configuration, workloads, networking policy, add-ons and cost. The big three EKS (AWS) GKE (Google) AKS (Azure) Control plane cost About $0.10/hour per cluster (about $73/month); extended-support versions cost more Free tier credit covers one zonal or Autopilot cluster; otherwise about $0.10/hour Free tier (no SLA); Standard tier about $0.10/hour with SLA Node options Managed node groups, Fargate, Karpenter, EKS Auto Mode Standard (you manage node pools) or Autopilot (Google manages nodes, billed per Pod) Node pools, virtual nodes, Automatic mode Identity IAM Roles for Service Accounts / Pod Identity Workload Identity Entra Workload Identity Networking VPC CNI (Pods get VPC IPs) VPC-native; Dataplane V2 (Cilium) Azure CNI / overlay, Cilium option Reputation Most flexible, most assembly required Most polished, Kubernetes' birthplace, fast upgrades Good if you live in Azure/Entra Prices change; always check the current pricing pages. The pragmatic choice is usually the cloud your company already uses , because the integration with IAM, networking, databases and billing outweighs small feature differences. Example: create a cluster # EKS with eksctl eksctl create cluster --name demo --region eu-west-1 \ --nodegroup-name std --node-type t3.medium --nodes 3 # GKE gcloud container clusters create-auto demo --region europe-west1 # AKS az aks create -g rg-demo -n demo --node-count 3 --enable-managed-identity # Fetch credentials into kubeconfig aws eks update-kubeconfig --name demo gcloud container clusters get-credentials demo --region europe-west1 az aks get-credentials -g rg-demo -n demo In real projects create clusters with Terraform (see the IaC section) so they are reviewable and reproducible. Where the money goes Monthly bill ├── Worker nodes (compute) usually 60-80 percent. Over-provisioned requests = waste ├── Control plane fee small, fixed per cluster ├── Load balancers one per Service type=LoadBalancer; consolidate with Ingress/Gateway ├── NAT gateways and egress cross-AZ and internet traffic can be a nasty surprise ├── Persistent disks and snapshots └── Observability logs and metrics volume (often large) Cost levers: Right-size requests (VPA recommendations, tools like Kubecost or OpenCost): nodes are billed for what is reserved, not what is used. Spot / preemptible instances for stateless and batch workloads; 60-90 percent cheaper, can be reclaimed with short notice. Use PDBs and multiple instance types. Autoscaling (HPA + Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler) so you do not pay for idle nodes at night. Fewer clusters : each carries a fixed fee and overhead (monitoring, ingress). But too few risks blast radius. Many teams use one per environment or per region, not per app. Reserved capacity / savings plans for the stable baseline. Keep traffic within an availability zone where sensible (topology-aware routing). Managed does not mean hands-off You must still upgrade clusters (providers force it eventually, and unsupported versions cost extra), patch node images, manage add-ons (CNI, CoreDNS, CSI drivers), restrict API server access, and secure workloads. Plan an upgrade routine, for example quarterly, tested on staging first. Lightweight and edge distributions k3s (Rancher/SUSE): a single binary under 100 MB, SQLite or embedded etcd, includes Traefik, a service load balancer and local storage. Runs on a Raspberry Pi or a 1 GB VPS. Excellent for edge, homelabs, CI and small production setups. k0s, MicroK8s, Talos Linux : other minimal options; Talos is an immutable, API-managed OS built only for Kubernetes. OpenShift : Red Hat's enterprise distribution with a built-in developer platform and stricter defaults. Rancher / Cluster API : manage many clusters uniformly. # k3s in one line on a fresh Linux VPS curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh - sudo k3s kubectl get nodes Alternatives to Kubernetes Option What it is Choose it when AWS ECS (+ Fargate) AWS-native container orchestrator; task definitions and services; no control plane to manage You are all-in on AWS and want simplicity. Not portable. Google Cloud Run Serverless containers: give it an image, get an HTTPS URL, scales to zero, pay per request HTTP services and jobs without cluster management. Great default for small teams. AWS App Runner, Azure Container Apps Similar "run my container" platforms (Container Apps is built on Kubernetes + KEDA) Same reasoning HashiCorp Nomad Single-binary scheduler for containers, VMs and binaries; simple to run Mixed workloads, small ops team, already using Consul/Vault. Smaller ecosystem. Docker Swarm Built into Docker Legacy; in maintenance mode, avoid for new projects. PaaS (Fly.io, Render, Railway, Heroku) Push code or image, get a running app Product-focused teams; accept less control and higher unit cost at scale. VM + Compose One or a few servers Still perfectly valid for modest scale. Decision guide Fewer than about five services, small team: Cloud Run / ECS Fargate / PaaS. Many services, multiple teams, need for portability, operators and a vast ecosystem: managed Kubernetes. Edge, on-prem or tight budget: k3s. Strong need to avoid vendor lock-in: Kubernetes (but data gravity and managed databases lock you in anyway). Pick the least complexity that meets the requirement You can always move to Kubernetes later because containers are portable; going the other way is rarer. The skills in this section remain valuable either way: declarative config, health checks, requests and limits, and rolling updates apply to every platform. Try it Install k3s (or k3d) and run the Deployment, Service and Ingress from earlier lessons. Traefik is already there. Deploy the same container to Cloud Run ( gcloud run deploy --image ... --allow-unauthenticated ) or ECS Fargate and compare the effort and what you gave up. Estimate the monthly cost of a 3-node cluster plus one load balancer on your cloud's pricing calculator.

title: Why Infrastructure as Code?
text: Why Infrastructure as Code? Servers, networks, databases and DNS records are infrastructure. If you create them by clicking through a cloud console, nobody can review, repeat or undo what you did. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means describing infrastructure in text files and letting a tool make reality match. The pain of ClickOps "ClickOps" is building infrastructure by hand in a web console or via ad-hoc CLI commands. It feels fast the first time. Then: No memory. Six months later nobody knows why that security group allows port 8443 from an odd IP, or who changed it. Not repeatable. You need a staging environment "just like production". You click for two days and it is subtly different. Not reviewable. A risky change (open a database to the internet) is made with no second pair of eyes. Disaster recovery is a fantasy. If the region fails or an account is compromised, can you rebuild everything in an hour? From memory? Knowledge lives in one head. The person who clicked it leaves. Snowflakes and drift A snowflake server is a machine that was hand-tuned over time and is unique: nobody dares touch it because nobody can recreate it. Configuration drift is the gradual divergence between machines (or between reality and documentation) as people make small manual changes: a hotfix applied to two of three servers, a package upgraded on one. Drift causes the worst class of bug: "works on node A but not node B". Day 0 prod-1 ≡ prod-2 ≡ prod-3 (identical, from the same recipe) Day 90 prod-1 + hotfix, prod-2 + manual tweak, prod-3 unchanged Day 180 nobody knows what differs. Rebuilding any of them is risky. What IaC gives you Benefit How Version control Infrastructure lives in git: history, blame, rollback via revert Code review Pull requests and a visible plan before any change happens Repeatability Same code produces dev, staging and prod; only variables differ Speed Stand up an entire environment with one command, tear it down to save money Documentation The code is an always-accurate description of what exists Disaster recovery Rebuild from code plus data backups Consistency and policy Automated checks: no public buckets, mandatory tags, encrypted disks Testing Validate and even test infrastructure changes before applying Declarative vs imperative This is the central design choice in IaC tools. Imperative (procedural): you write the steps . "Create a VM. Then attach this disk. Then open port 80." A shell script with the AWS CLI is imperative. Running it twice might create two VMs. You must handle "already exists" yourself. Declarative : you write the desired end state . "There is one VM of this size with this disk and port 80 open." The tool compares to what exists, works out the difference and makes only the needed changes. Running it twice does nothing the second time. # Imperative: order and existence checks are YOUR problem aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0abc --instance-type t3.micro aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-123 --protocol tcp --port 80 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0 # Declarative (Terraform): describe the end state; the tool computes the steps resource "aws_instance" "web" { ami = "ami-0abc" instance_type = "t3.micro" } Declarative tools (Terraform/OpenTofu, CloudFormation, Kubernetes manifests, Ansible modules to a degree) are idempotent : applying the same description repeatedly converges to the same result. Imperative code in general-purpose languages (Pulumi, AWS CDK) can still be declarative in effect: your program builds a desired-state graph that the engine reconciles. Idempotency is the superpower An operation is idempotent if doing it once or ten times yields the same state. It makes automation safe to re-run, safe to retry after a partial failure, and safe to run on a schedule to correct drift. Two kinds of IaC tool Category Job Examples Provisioning Create the infrastructure: networks, VMs, databases, DNS, IAM Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, CloudFormation, AWS CDK, Crossplane Configuration management Configure what runs on machines: packages, files, services Ansible, Chef, Puppet, Salt Image building Bake machine images ahead of time Packer, Docker Delivery / reconciliation Keep clusters matching git Argo CD, Flux They compose: Terraform creates the VMs and network, Packer provides the image, Ansible (or cloud-init) configures anything that remains, and GitOps keeps the Kubernetes workloads in sync. The next lessons cover each. Principles to adopt Everything in git. If it is not in code, it does not exist. Change only via the pipeline. Console access becomes read-only for production (break-glass excepted, then back-port the change to code). Small, frequent changes with a reviewed plan. Environments from one codebase , differing only in variables. No secrets in code. Reference a secret manager. Detect drift by scheduled plans that alert on differences. Trade-offs and honest caveats There is a learning curve and up-front investment; for one throwaway VM, a console click is fine. Code can be wrong at scale: a bad destroy is faster than a bad click. Reviews, plans and guard rails matter more, not less. State management (what the tool believes exists) is a new thing to protect, as you will see in the Terraform lessons. Adopting IaC on existing hand-built infrastructure means importing it incrementally; start with new resources. Cloud APIs change; providers and modules need maintenance. Start small You do not need to codify everything on day one. Begin with a new project or one environment, or capture the most error-prone piece (security groups, DNS, IAM) first. Use the console for exploration, but "promote" what you learn into code. Try it List the infrastructure behind one app you run: servers, DNS records, buckets, databases, IAM roles. Mark each as "in code", "documented" or "only in someone's head". Pick the riskiest "only in someone's head" item and think about how long a full rebuild would take. Write the one-sentence declarative description of one thing (for example "a bucket named X, private, versioned") versus the three imperative commands needed.

title: Terraform Fundamentals
text: Terraform Fundamentals Terraform is the most widely used provisioning tool. You describe cloud resources in HCL, run terraform plan to preview exactly what will change, and terraform apply to make it so. This lesson builds a real example: a VM with a security group on AWS. How it works *.tf files (desired) state file (what Terraform believes exists) │ │ └──────────▶ terraform plan ◀─────┘ │ compares, and refreshes against the real cloud API ▼ proposed diff: + create ~ update - destroy │ (you review) ▼ terraform apply ──▶ provider plugin ──▶ AWS / GCP / Azure / ... API Terraform builds a dependency graph from references between resources, so it creates things in the right order and in parallel where possible. Providers are plugins that translate resources into API calls for a specific platform (AWS, Google, Azure, Cloudflare, Kubernetes, GitHub, Datadog and thousands more). Install and workflow brew install terraform # or OpenTofu: brew install opentofu (command: tofu) terraform version terraform init # download providers/modules, set up backend (run first, and after adding providers) terraform fmt # canonical formatting terraform validate # syntax and internal consistency terraform plan # preview; changes nothing terraform apply # make the changes (asks for "yes") terraform destroy # delete everything this configuration manages HCL building blocks Block Purpose terraform Required Terraform and provider versions, backend provider Configure a provider (region, credentials) resource A thing to create and manage data Read-only lookup of something that exists (an AMI, a VPC) variable Input parameter locals Named expressions to avoid repetition output Values to print or share after apply module Reuse a group of resources (next lesson) Resources reference each other with TYPE.NAME.ATTRIBUTE (for example aws_security_group.web.id ), and that reference is what creates the dependency. Complete example: a web server VM and security group Layout: three files in a directory (the names are convention only; Terraform loads every .tf file in the folder). versions.tf terraform { required_version = ">= 1.7" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "~> 5.60" # allow 5.x, at least 5.60 } } } provider "aws" { region = var.region default_tags { tags = { Project = "demo", ManagedBy = "terraform" } # applied to everything } } variables.tf variable "region" { type = string default = "eu-west-1" } variable "instance_type" { type = string description = "EC2 size" default = "t3.micro" } variable "ssh_allowed_cidr" { type = string description = "Your public IP in CIDR form, e.g. 203.0.113.7/32" validation { condition = can(cidrnetmask(var.ssh_allowed_cidr)) error_message = "Must be a valid CIDR block." } } variable "key_name" { type = string description = "Name of an existing EC2 key pair" } main.tf # Look up the latest Ubuntu 24.04 AMI instead of hard-coding an ID data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" { most_recent = true owners = ["099720109477"] # Canonical filter { name = "name" values = ["ubuntu/images/hvm-ssd-gp3/ubuntu-noble-24.04-amd64-server-*"] } } # Use the account's default VPC to keep the example short data "aws_vpc" "default" { default = true } resource "aws_security_group" "web" { name_prefix = "web-" description = "Allow HTTP from anywhere, SSH from my IP" vpc_id = data.aws_vpc.default.id ingress { description = "HTTP" from_port = 80 to_port = 80 protocol = "tcp" cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] } ingress { description = "SSH" from_port = 22 to_port = 22 protocol = "tcp" cidr_blocks = [var.ssh_allowed_cidr] } egress { from_port = 0 to_port = 0 protocol = "-1" cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] } lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } } resource "aws_instance" "web" { ami = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id instance_type = var.instance_type key_name = var.key_name vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.web.id] # implicit dependency user_data = <<-EOT #!/bin/bash apt-get update -y apt-get install -y nginx systemctl enable --now nginx EOT root_block_device { volume_size = 20 encrypted = true } metadata_options { http_tokens = "required" # enforce IMDSv2 } tags = { Name = "web-1" } } outputs.tf output "public_ip" { value = aws_instance.web.public_ip } output "url" { value = "http://${aws_instance.web.public_dns}" } Run it export AWS_PROFILE=dev # credentials come from the environment, never from .tf files terraform init terraform plan -var 'ssh_allowed_cidr=203.0.113.7/32' -var 'key_name=my-key' terraform apply -var 'ssh_allowed_cidr=203.0.113.7/32' -var 'key_name=my-key' # ... # Outputs: # public_ip = "54.12.34.56" curl $(terraform output -raw public_ip) terraform destroy ... # stop paying for it Reading the plan: + create, ~ update in place, -/+ destroy and recreate (some attribute changes force replacement, which for a database means data loss; always read for -/+ and must be replaced ). Variables, locals and loops # terraform.tfvars (auto-loaded) or prod.tfvars (-var-file=prod.tfvars) region = "eu-west-1" ssh_allowed_cidr = "203.0.113.7/32" key_name = "my-key" locals { name = "web-${terraform.workspace}" common_tags = { Owner = "platform" } } # several similar resources with for_each (prefer over count: stable keys) variable "buckets" { default = ["logs", "assets"] } resource "aws_s3_bucket" "b" { for_each = toset(var.buckets) bucket = "acme-${each.key}-prod" } Variable precedence (low to high): defaults, terraform.tfvars , *.auto.tfvars , -var-file , -var , and TF_VAR_name environment variables sit alongside these for CI. Mark secrets sensitive = true to hide them from output (they still end up in state). Best practices Always plan , read it, then apply; in CI save the plan file ( -out=tfplan ) and apply exactly that. Pin provider and Terraform versions; commit .terraform.lock.hcl . Do not commit .terraform/ , *.tfstate or secret tfvars. Add them to .gitignore . Prefer for_each over count for collections; removing the middle item with count shifts indexes and destroys things. Tag everything; use lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } on irreplaceable resources. Never hard-code credentials; use environment, profiles, or OIDC-based roles in CI. Run terraform fmt , validate , and a linter (tflint) and scanner (trivy, checkov) in CI. Pitfalls Editing resources in the console, then running Terraform: it will revert your change (drift). Renaming a resource block in code means "destroy old, create new" unless you use a moved block. Ignoring the state file's importance: the next lesson is about it. Try it Apply the example in a sandbox account (a t3.micro costs pennies, or use the free tier), visit the nginx page, then run terraform destroy . Change instance_type and read the plan: is it an in-place update or a replace? Add an output for the security group ID and re-apply; note that only outputs change. No cloud account? Use the hashicorp/local or hashicorp/docker provider to practice the same workflow.

title: Terraform State, Modules and Environments
text: Terraform State, Modules and Environments State is Terraform's memory: the map between your code and real cloud resources. Understanding it, storing it safely, splitting code into reusable modules and organising environments are what separate a demo from a team-ready setup. What state is and why it exists When you declare aws_instance.web , Terraform must know which actual instance ( i-0abc123 ) that refers to, otherwise it cannot tell "update" from "create a second one". That mapping, plus a cache of attributes, lives in the state file ( terraform.tfstate , JSON). Each plan: read config, read state, query the real world (refresh), diff. State is sensitive and precious It contains resource attributes in plain text, including database passwords and generated keys. Treat it like a secret. If it is lost, Terraform believes nothing exists and will try to create duplicates. Never commit it to git, never edit by hand (use terraform state commands), and never run two applies at once. Remote backends and locking A local state file works for one person. For a team you need shared state with locking (so two applies cannot collide), encryption and versioning. Configure a remote backend: terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = "acme-tf-state" key = "prod/network/terraform.tfstate" region = "eu-west-1" encrypt = true use_lockfile = true # native S3 locking (Terraform 1.10+); older setups used a DynamoDB table } } Create the bucket beforehand (turn on versioning so you can recover prior states, block public access, restrict IAM). Other backends: GCS, Azure Blob, Terraform Cloud / HCP Terraform, GitLab-managed state, Postgres. Run terraform init -migrate-state to move existing state to a new backend. Because state holds secrets, restrict who can read the bucket, and keep state per component (network, database, app) rather than one giant file, which limits blast radius and speeds up plans. Inspecting and fixing state terraform state list terraform state show aws_instance.web terraform state mv aws_instance.web aws_instance.app # rename without recreating terraform state rm aws_instance.legacy # stop managing, don't delete terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID # only if a crashed run left a lock # declarative rename in code (preferred, reviewable) moved { from = aws_instance.web to = aws_instance.app } Importing existing infrastructure For resources created by hand, bring them under management without recreating them. Modern syntax is an import block, which participates in plan: import { to = aws_s3_bucket.assets id = "acme-assets-prod" } resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" { bucket = "acme-assets-prod" } terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf # draft HCL for the imported resource terraform plan # should end with "No changes" once your config matches reality terraform apply Iterate until the plan shows no diff. Tools such as Terraformer or cloud-specific exporters help for large estates. Drift Drift is when real infrastructure differs from state or code because someone changed it outside Terraform. terraform plan -refresh-only # show drift without proposing code changes terraform apply -refresh-only # accept the real values into state terraform plan # normal plan: will propose reverting drift to match code Run a scheduled plan in CI (nightly) and alert if the exit code with -detailed-exitcode is 2. Decide per case: revert (code wins) or back-port the manual change into code. Modules A module is a folder of .tf files with inputs (variables) and outputs. Every Terraform configuration is already a "root module"; you call child modules to avoid copy-paste: a VPC pattern, a "service with load balancer and DNS" pattern. modules/ └── web_server/ ├── main.tf resources ├── variables.tf inputs └── outputs.tf outputs envs/prod/main.tf ──calls──▶ module "web" { source = "../../modules/web_server" ... } # modules/web_server/variables.tf variable "name" { type = string } variable "instance_type" { type = string default = "t3.micro" } variable "vpc_id" { type = string } # modules/web_server/main.tf (uses var.name etc; resources as in the previous lesson) resource "aws_instance" "this" { /* ... */ } # modules/web_server/outputs.tf output "public_ip" { value = aws_instance.this.public_ip } # caller module "web" { source = "../../modules/web_server" name = "shop-prod" instance_type = "t3.large" vpc_id = module.network.vpc_id } output "web_ip" { value = module.web.public_ip } Sources: local paths, git URLs with a version ref ( git::https://github.com/acme/tf-modules.git//web?ref=v1.4.0 ), or the public registry ( source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws" , version = "~> 5.0" ). Always version-pin remote modules. Good module design: small, focused, few required inputs with sensible defaults, outputs for everything callers might need, no provider configuration inside (pass providers in). Avoid wrapping a single resource in a module "just because"; the registry's community modules (VPC, EKS) are well tested and worth reusing. Environments: workspaces vs directories Workspaces terraform workspace new staging terraform workspace select prod terraform workspace list # in code: terraform.workspace gives the name Workspaces keep multiple state files for the same code and backend. They are easy but hide which environment you are in (a classic way to destroy production), and encourage environments that must be identical. Many teams avoid them for dev/staging/prod. Directory per environment (common recommendation) infra/ ├── modules/ reusable building blocks (versioned) │ ├── network/ │ ├── database/ │ └── service/ └── live/ ├── dev/ │ ├── network/ main.tf, backend.tf, terraform.tfvars │ └── app/ ├── staging/ │ ├── network/ │ └── app/ └── prod/ ├── network/ └── app/ Each folder has its own backend key and state, so a mistake in dev/app cannot touch prod/network . Modules carry the logic; environment folders contain only configuration (sizes, counts, names).
