This catches jobs that silently never ran. # Prometheus blackbox_exporter probing an endpoint scrape_configs: - job_name: blackbox-http metrics_path: /probe params: { module: [http_2xx] } static_configs: - targets: [https://www.example.com/, https://api.example.com/healthz] relabel_configs: - source_labels: [__address__] target_label: __param_target - source_labels: [__param_target] target_label: instance - target_label: __address__ replacement: blackbox:9115 # Alerts - alert: SiteDown expr: probe_success{job="blackbox-http"} == 0 for: 2m - alert: CertExpiringSoon expr: probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry - time() < 14*24*3600 for: 1h # Cron heartbeat 0 3 * * * /opt/backup.sh && curl -fsS --retry 3 https://hc-ping.com/your-uuid Probe from at least three locations and require agreement A single prober failing is often its own network. Alert when 2 of 3 locations fail for a couple of minutes to avoid false pages. Also run at least one probe from outside your cloud provider , so a provider-wide issue does not blind your monitor. Status pages When things break, customers want to know: is it me or you? A status page reduces support tickets and builds trust. Host it on separate infrastructure and domain from your main app (otherwise it goes down with it). Options: Atlassian Statuspage, Instatus, Better Stack, Cachet (self-hosted), or a static page. Show components (API, Web app, Payments, Webhooks) with current state: Operational, Degraded performance, Partial outage, Major outage. Post incident updates with timestamps; keep a history and show uptime percentages (matching your SLOs). Offer subscriptions (email, RSS, Slack, webhook). Automate updates from monitors for obvious outages, but have a human write the message for complex ones. Be honest. Hiding problems damages trust more than the problem itself. Putting it together users ─▶ DNS ─▶ CDN ─▶ Load balancer ─(readiness)─▶ instances ─(liveness)─▶ restart if stuck ▲ │ │ external synthetic probes ─ alerts ─▶ on-call │ (uptime, TLS, login flow) │ status page ◀── incident updates ───────────────────────┘ Pitfalls Liveness probes that check dependencies , causing restart storms. One endpoint for everything ( /health returning 200 always, or deep-checking everything). Slow start with an aggressive liveness probe : the app is killed before it finishes booting. Use startup probes. Ignoring graceful shutdown : instance removed from rotation but killed mid-request; deploys drop connections. Handle SIGTERM and drain. Health check endpoints hit by logs/metrics : they flood logs and skew latency statistics; filter them. Green status while users suffer : health checks say 200 but the login flow is broken. Add synthetic journeys and SLI-based alerts. Status page on the same infrastructure as the product. Expired certificates and domains : boring, common, and preventable with a simple probe. Try it Add /livez and /readyz to a service. Make readiness fail for the first 20 seconds after boot and observe a Kubernetes or Docker rollout wait for it. Kill the database and watch readiness fail while liveness stays green. Explain why that is the desired behaviour. Set up a free uptime monitor (UptimeRobot, Better Stack or Healthchecks.io) for a public URL, plus a heartbeat for a cron job. Let the job fail once on purpose and confirm the alert. Run openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates and compute days until your cert expires.

title: Chaos Engineering and Resilience Patterns
text: Chaos Engineering and Resilience Patterns In distributed systems, partial failure is the normal state. Networks drop packets, dependencies slow down, instances disappear. Resilient software expects this and degrades gracefully. Chaos engineering goes further: it breaks things on purpose, in a controlled way, to prove the resilience is real. Failure is normal If your request touches ten services each at 99.9% availability, the combined availability is about 99.0%: roughly 7 hours of downtime a month from "healthy" parts. You cannot make dependencies perfect, so your code must handle their failures. The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing start with: "the network is reliable", and "latency is zero". Neither holds. The most dangerous failure is not a clean crash (easy to detect and retry), but slowness : a dependency that responds in 30 seconds instead of 30 ms ties up your threads and connections until you fall over too. That is why timeouts come first. Timeouts Every network call must have a timeout. No exceptions. Default timeouts in many libraries are infinite or minutes long. Set connect and read/total timeouts separately. Base them on the dependency's normal latency (e.g. p99 x 2-3), not on hope. Use deadline propagation : if the user request has a 2-second budget and you already spent 1.2 s, the downstream call gets at most 0.8 s (gRPC deadlines, Go context deadlines). Timeouts down the chain must be shorter than upstream ones, or the caller gives up while the callee keeps working for nobody. // Go ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 800*time.Millisecond) defer cancel() resp, err := client.Do(req.WithContext(ctx)) # Python requests: (connect, read) requests.get(url, timeout=(0.5, 2.0)) // Node fetch const res = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) }); Retries with exponential backoff and jitter Many failures are transient (a dropped connection, a brief overload, a failover in progress). Retrying often succeeds. But naive retries are dangerous: if 1,000 clients all retry immediately and repeatedly, they hammer a struggling service and keep it down: a retry storm (a self-inflicted DDoS). Naive: t=0 fail ─▶ t=0 retry ─▶ t=0 retry ... (instant hammering) Backoff: wait 100ms, 200ms, 400ms, 800ms ... (exponential: reduces pressure) + Jitter: wait random(0..delay) so clients do not retry in sync (thundering herd) import random, time def call_with_retries(fn, attempts=4, base=0.1, cap=2.0): for i in range(attempts): try: return fn() except TransientError: if i == attempts - 1: raise delay = min(cap, base * (2 ** i)) time.sleep(random.uniform(0, delay)) # "full jitter" Rules of retrying: Retry only transient, safe errors : timeouts, 503, connection resets, 429 (respecting Retry-After ). Never retry 400/401/404 or validation errors. Only retry idempotent operations , or make them idempotent with an idempotency key (e.g. payments: send Idempotency-Key: <uuid> so a retry does not charge twice). Cap attempts and total time , and use a retry budget (e.g. retries may add at most 10% extra load). Retries multiply across layers: three layers each retrying 3 times means 27 calls per failure. Retry at one layer only, usually the closest to the failure or the edge. Circuit breakers When a dependency is clearly failing, continuing to call it wastes resources and slows everyone. A circuit breaker watches failure rates and "trips", failing fast without calling the dependency, then probes occasionally to see if it recovered. failures exceed threshold ┌────────┐ ───────────────────────▶ ┌────────┐ │ CLOSED │ │ OPEN │ all calls fail fast (no network) │ normal │ ◀─────────────────────── └───┬────┘ └────────┘ probe calls succeed │ after cool-down (e.g. 30 s) ▲ ▼ │ ┌─────────────┐ └───────────────────────────│ HALF-OPEN │ allow a few trial calls success └─────────────┘ (failure sends it back to OPEN) // Resilience4j (Java) CircuitBreakerConfig cfg = CircuitBreakerConfig.custom() .failureRateThreshold(50) // open at 50% failures .slidingWindowSize(20) .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(3) .build(); // Node: opossum; Python: pybreaker; Go: sony/gobreaker; .NET: Polly // Service meshes (Istio/Envoy) can do outlier detection without code changes While open, return a fallback : cached data, a default, a degraded feature (hide recommendations), or a clear error. Failing fast keeps your own latency and thread pools healthy. Other patterns Pattern Idea Bulkheads Isolate resources (thread/connection pools) per dependency so one slow dependency cannot exhaust everything, like watertight compartments in a ship. Load shedding / rate limiting When overloaded, reject excess work early (429/503) to keep serving the rest rather than collapsing. Prioritise critical traffic. Graceful degradation Return partial results or a simpler experience when parts fail. Queues / backpressure Decouple producers and consumers with a queue; bounded queues push back instead of growing without limit. Idempotency Make repeated operations safe, so retries and duplicates are harmless. Redundancy & failover Multiple instances/AZs/regions, automatic replacement. Caching stale data Serve stale-on-error ( stale-if-error ) when the origin is down. Feature flags / kill switches Turn off a misbehaving feature instantly without redeploying. How they compose A well-behaved call: timeout bounds each attempt; a few retries with backoff and jitter absorb transient errors; a circuit breaker stops calling a dead dependency; a bulkhead contains the blast radius; a fallback keeps the user experience acceptable; and metrics on all of them show when they are triggering. Chaos engineering Resilience features are code that rarely runs, so they are rarely tested, and untested failure handling usually fails when needed. Chaos engineering , pioneered by Netflix (Chaos Monkey), is the discipline of experimenting on a system to build confidence in its ability to withstand turbulent conditions in production. The scientific method Define steady state : a measurable indicator of normal behaviour, ideally an SLI (orders per minute, p99 latency, error ratio). Hypothesise : "If one app instance dies, the steady state is unchanged." "If the cache is unavailable, checkout latency rises under 2x but stays successful." Inject a realistic fault , with the smallest blast radius that teaches you something. Observe versus the steady state. Did the system behave as hypothesised? Fix the weaknesses found, then rerun and automate. Preconditions: you need decent observability and a working abort button. Do not run chaos on a system you cannot observe, or one already unreliable. Start in staging, then move to production in small, announced experiments (a small percentage of traffic, one instance, off-peak) with automatic halting when the SLI degrades. Fault types to try Category Experiment Instances Kill a pod/instance/process; terminate a random node Zone/region Drain an AZ; simulate region failure for a non-critical service Network Add 300 ms latency; drop 5% packets; partition services; block DNS Dependencies Make a downstream return 500s or hang; revoke a credential Resources CPU hog, memory pressure, full disk, exhausted file descriptors Time/state Clock skew; certificate expiry; failover the primary database Scale Sudden 5x traffic; cold-cache restart Tools Chaos Mesh and LitmusChaos (Kubernetes-native, CNCF projects). Gremlin (commercial platform), Steadybit . AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) , Azure Chaos Studio . Toxiproxy (inject latency/failure on TCP connections in tests), tc netem , stress-ng . # Chaos Mesh: add 200ms latency to checkout pods for 5 minutes apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1 kind: NetworkChaos metadata: { name: checkout-latency, namespace: shop } spec: action: delay mode: one selector: namespaces: [shop] labelSelectors: { app: checkout } delay: { latency: "200ms", jitter: "50ms" } duration: "5m" # Simple: kill a random pod and watch recovery kubectl delete pod -n shop $(kubectl get pods -n shop -l app=checkout -o name | shuf -n1) Game days A game day is a scheduled, collaborative exercise where the team deliberately simulates a failure and practises the response, testing systems, tooling, runbooks and people . Plan : choose a scenario ("primary DB fails over", "payment provider is down", "AZ lost"). Write the hypothesis and expected behaviour. Define abort criteria and a rollback. Brief : assign roles (facilitator, IC, observers/scribe). Tell stakeholders and support when it will run. Run : inject the fault; the responders work from alerts and runbooks, as in a real incident (or the facilitator reveals the scenario). Observers note what was confusing, missing or slow. Debrief : blameless review: did alerts fire? did dashboards help? were runbooks right? how long to detect and mitigate? What surprised us? Follow up : track action items like postmortem items; repeat with harder scenarios. Variations: "Wheel of misfortune" tabletop (talk through an incident with no real fault), disaster recovery drills (restore from backup, fail over to another region), and security red-team exercises. Pitfalls No timeouts : the single most common cause of cascading failure. Retries without backoff, jitter or limits , creating retry storms; retries at multiple layers. Retrying non-idempotent operations (double charges, duplicate emails). Circuit breakers never tuned or monitored : add metrics and alerts for state changes. Fallbacks that were never exercised and themselves crash. Test them. Chaos without a hypothesis or observability : random destruction teaches nothing. Too large a blast radius too early, or experimenting during an existing incident or a peak event. Finding issues and not fixing them : chaos creates a backlog; the value is in the follow-up. Treating it as a one-off : systems change; run experiments continuously or on a schedule, ideally in CI/CD. Try it Audit one service's outbound calls: list each with its timeout, retry policy and fallback. How many have none? Run two containers (your app and a dependency) behind Toxiproxy. Add 3 seconds of latency to the dependency and watch your app. Add a timeout and a fallback, and repeat. Implement retry with exponential backoff and full jitter for a flaky HTTP call, then write a test that proves it retries on 503 but not on 400. Plan a 1-hour game day: pick the scenario "kill one of three app instances during peak-like load", state the hypothesis and steady-state metric, and run it in staging with Chaos Mesh or kubectl delete pod .

title: The Twelve-Factor App
text: The Twelve-Factor App The twelve-factor methodology (written by Heroku engineers around 2011) is still the best short checklist for building applications that are easy to deploy, scale and operate. Almost every modern platform, from Docker to Kubernetes, assumes your app follows it. Why it matters An app that is painful to deploy is usually painful for a reason: config baked into the build, state stored on local disk, logs written to files nobody reads, or a startup procedure that only one person understands. The twelve factors are a set of constraints that remove those reasons. If you follow them, the same artifact runs on your laptop, in CI, in staging and in production, and you can run 1 or 50 copies of it. one codebase ──▶ build once ──▶ release = build + config ──▶ run N stateless processes ▲ │ env vars (per environment) ├──▶ backing services (DB, cache, queue) via URL └──▶ logs to stdout ──▶ platform collects them The twelve factors I. Codebase: one codebase tracked in version control, many deploys One app = one repo. Staging and production are different deploys of the same commit lineage, not different repos or long-lived forks. If two apps share code, extract a library and depend on it. Anti-pattern: a prod branch that diverges from main with hand edits. II. Dependencies: explicitly declare and isolate Never rely on a system-wide package happening to be installed. Declare everything in a manifest and lock exact versions. # Node: package.json + package-lock.json, install reproducibly npm ci # Python: pin hashes pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt # Container: the image itself is the isolation boundary FROM node:22-alpine COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev Commit the lockfile. npm install may change versions; npm ci will not. III. Config: store config in the environment Config is anything that varies between deploys: database URLs, API keys, feature flags, hostnames. It must not live in the code. The litmus test: could you open-source the repo right now without leaking credentials? // config.js - read once, validate, fail fast const required = ['DATABASE_URL', 'SESSION_SECRET']; for (const k of required) { if (!process.env[k]) throw new Error(`Missing env var ${k}`); } export const config = { port: Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000), databaseUrl: process.env.DATABASE_URL, logLevel: process.env.LOG_LEVEL ?? 'info', }; Avoid "config files per environment" Files like config.production.json checked into git grow combinatorially and tempt people to commit secrets. Env vars are language-agnostic and easy to change per deploy without a rebuild. IV. Backing services: treat them as attached resources Postgres, Redis, S3, an SMTP provider: all are reached through a URL and credentials in config. Swapping a local Postgres for a managed RDS instance should require changing DATABASE_URL and nothing else. Code that hardcodes localhost:5432 violates this factor. V. Build, release, run: strictly separate stages Stage What happens Output Build Compile code, fetch dependencies Immutable artifact (image tagged with commit SHA) Release Combine build with environment config Numbered release you can roll back to Run Start processes from a release Running app Never edit code on a running server. Rollback becomes "run the previous release", not "hope you remember what you changed". VI. Processes: execute the app as one or more stateless processes Any data that must outlive a request goes in a backing service, never in process memory or local disk. "Sticky sessions" (the load balancer pins a user to one server because the session lives in RAM) are a smell; store sessions in Redis or use signed tokens. A stateless process can be killed, restarted or duplicated freely, and that property underpins autoscaling and rolling deploys. In-memory caches are fine as an optimisation, as long as losing them is harmless. VII. Port binding: export services via port binding The app is self-contained: it embeds an HTTP server and listens on $PORT . It does not depend on being injected into Apache or Tomcat at runtime. A reverse proxy or load balancer then routes to that port. VIII. Concurrency: scale out via the process model Scale by running more processes, and by running different process types for different workloads: web , worker , scheduler . Horizontal scaling beats making one process enormous. # Procfile style - same image, different command web: node dist/server.js worker: node dist/worker.js cron: node dist/scheduler.js IX. Disposability: fast startup and graceful shutdown Processes get killed constantly (deploys, autoscaling, node failures). Start in seconds, and on SIGTERM stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests, then exit. process.on('SIGTERM', () => { console.log('SIGTERM received, draining'); server.close(async () => { // stops new connections, waits for in-flight await db.end(); process.exit(0); }); setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 25_000).unref(); // hard stop before the platform's SIGKILL }); Workers must make jobs idempotent or re-queueable, because a killed worker means a job is retried. X. Dev/prod parity: keep environments as similar as possible Historically there were three gaps: time (code took weeks to ship), people (devs write, ops deploy) and tools (SQLite locally, Postgres in prod). Close them: deploy often, own what you ship, and run the same Postgres major version locally via Docker Compose. XI. Logs: treat logs as event streams The app writes unbuffered events to stdout , one per line, ideally as JSON. It does not manage log files, rotation or shipping. The platform (Docker, systemd, Kubernetes) captures the stream and forwards it to Loki, CloudWatch or Elasticsearch. {"ts":"2026-10-05T10:21:07Z","level":"error","msg":"payment failed","order_id":9123,"trace_id":"a1b2c3"} XII. Admin processes: run one-off tasks as one-off processes Migrations, data fixes and REPL sessions run from the same codebase, release and config as the app, in a throwaway process: docker compose run --rm app node dist/migrate.js or a Kubernetes Job. Do not SSH in and run ad-hoc scripts against production from your laptop copy of the code. Beyond the original twelve Modern authors (see Kevin Hoffman's "Beyond the Twelve-Factor App") add three more, which matter in 2026: API first : define contracts (OpenAPI) before implementation. Telemetry : expose metrics, traces and health endpoints ( /healthz , /metrics ), not only logs. Authentication and authorization : build security in from the start, not as an afterthought. Quick audit table Smell Violates Fix if (NODE_ENV==='prod') sprinkled through code III, X Drive behaviour by explicit config values Uploads saved to ./uploads VI Object storage (S3) App writes /var/log/app.log and rotates it XI Log to stdout Deploy = SSH + git pull V Build an image in CI Cron inside the web process VIII, VI Separate scheduler process or Kubernetes CronJob Takes 90s to boot IX Lazy init, smaller image, defer warmups Trade-offs and honesty Not every factor is absolute. Some apps legitimately hold state (databases, game servers, WebSocket hubs). The point is to be deliberate: isolate the stateful part, and keep everything else disposable. Env vars also have limits: they are visible to child processes and sometimes leak through crash dumps, so for high-value secrets prefer mounted files or a secret manager (next lesson). Try it Pick one of your own apps and score it 0 or 1 against each factor. Which three failures would hurt most in production? Remove every hardcoded URL or key from it and read them from env vars with fail-fast validation. Add a SIGTERM handler, run it in Docker and confirm docker stop returns in under a second instead of waiting 10 seconds for SIGKILL.

title: Secrets Management
text: Secrets Management Passwords, API keys, tokens, private keys and certificates are the keys to your kingdom. Most real-world breaches involve a leaked credential rather than a clever exploit. This lesson covers where secrets should live, how to hand them to applications, how to rotate them and what to do the minute one leaks. Why it is hard A secret has to be readable by the running application, yet unreadable by almost everyone and everything else. It must travel from a human or a generator to a process, through CI, containers and logs, without being copied somewhere it should not be. Every extra copy is another place it can leak. Where secrets leak most often Committed to git (including in history after being "deleted"). Baked into a Docker image layer ( ENV API_KEY=... or COPY .env ). Anyone who can pull the image can read it with docker history or by extracting layers. Printed in CI logs, crash dumps, error pages or debug endpoints. Shared in Slack, tickets and wikis. Over-broad long-lived keys on developer laptops. Deleting a commit does not delete the secret Once pushed, assume it is compromised: bots scrape public GitHub in seconds. Rewriting history is cleanup, not remediation. The remediation is always to revoke and rotate. The maturity ladder Level Approach Notes 0 Secrets in code Never 1 .env file, gitignored, on the server OK for a hobby VPS; manual, no audit 2 CI/CD secret store (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab variables) Good for pipeline credentials 3 Encrypted secrets in git (SOPS, Sealed Secrets) Reviewable, GitOps friendly 4 Central secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault) Access policy, audit log, rotation 5 Dynamic short-lived credentials and workload identity No static secret to steal Level 1: .env done properly # .gitignore .env .env.* !.env.example # .env.example (committed - names only, no values) DATABASE_URL= SESSION_SECRET= # on the server chmod 600 /opt/app/.env chown deploy:deploy /opt/app/.env In Docker Compose pass it with env_file: .env . Prefer Docker/Compose secrets (mounted as files under /run/secrets/ ) for sensitive values, since environment variables show up in docker inspect and /proc/<pid>/environ . Level 3: SOPS, encrypted secrets in git Mozilla SOPS encrypts the values in YAML/JSON/dotenv files while leaving keys readable, so diffs and code review still work. It encrypts with age, AWS KMS, GCP KMS or Azure Key Vault keys. # one-time: generate an age key (keep the private key out of git!) age-keygen -o ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt # prints: Public key: age1ql3z7hjy54pw3hyww5ayyfg7zqgvc7w3j2elw8zmrj2kg5sfn9aqmcac8p # .sops.yaml - which files get which keys creation_rules: - path_regex: secrets/.*\.yaml$ age: age1ql3z7hjy54pw3hyww5ayyfg7zqgvc7w3j2elw8zmrj2kg5sfn9aqmcac8p sops secrets/prod.yaml # opens editor, saves encrypted sops -d secrets/prod.yaml # decrypt to stdout sops exec-env secrets/prod.env ./start.sh # run a command with decrypted env The encrypted file is safe to commit. Only holders of the private key (or KMS permission) can decrypt. Combine with Flux or Argo CD plugins for Kubernetes, or Bitnami Sealed Secrets / External Secrets Operator as alternatives. Level 4: central secret managers AWS Secrets Manager aws secretsmanager create-secret --name prod/app/db \ --secret-string '{"username":"app","password":"s3cr3t"}' aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/app/db \ --query SecretString --output text Access is controlled by IAM: attach a policy allowing secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on that one ARN to the role of your EC2 instance, ECS task or EKS service account. No static AWS key is needed; the SDK picks up role credentials automatically. Secrets Manager supports automatic rotation via Lambda (native for RDS). Cheaper alternative for plain config: SSM Parameter Store (SecureString). HashiCorp Vault (and its open-source fork OpenBao) Vault is a self-hosted (or HCP-managed) secrets engine with identity-based access, full audit logging and, importantly, dynamic secrets : it creates a fresh database user on demand with a TTL and deletes it afterwards. vault kv put secret/app/stripe api_key=sk_live_xxx vault kv get -field=api_key secret/app/stripe # Dynamic Postgres credentials, valid 1 hour vault read database/creds/app-role # Key Value # lease_duration 1h # username v-approle-app-x8Zk # password A1a-...random... Apps authenticate to Vault with a platform identity (Kubernetes service account, AWS IAM, AppRole, OIDC) and receive a token, never a long-lived password. Costs: you must run, unseal, back up and upgrade Vault (or pay for HCP). Choosing Option Best for Trade-off Cloud-native manager Single-cloud teams Per-secret pricing, vendor lock-in Vault/OpenBao Multi-cloud, dynamic creds, strict audit Operational burden SOPS Small teams, GitOps No dynamic secrets, no built-in audit CI secrets only Pipeline tokens Not for runtime app secrets Secrets in CI/CD Prefer OIDC federation over stored cloud keys: GitHub Actions requests a short-lived token and assumes an AWS role. Nothing long-lived sits in repo settings. Scope secrets to environments ( production environment with required reviewers). Do not echo them; masking only works for exact matches and can be bypassed by transformations such as base64. Never expose secrets to workflows triggered by forks' pull requests. permissions: id-token: write # needed for OIDC contents: read steps: - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with: role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gha-deploy aws-region: eu-west-1 Rotation Rotation limits the damage window and proves you can replace a secret without an outage, which is exactly what you need during an incident. A safe pattern for a database password is two-user alternation : two valid users, rotate the idle one, switch the app over, then rotate the other. The cruder pattern (change password, restart app) causes downtime between the two steps. Make the app reload secrets without a restart, or perform rolling restarts. Automate rotation on a schedule (90 days is common; shorter for high-value keys). Rotate on personnel changes and after any suspected exposure. Leak response runbook Revoke first. Disable the key at the provider (GitHub token settings, AWS IAM, Stripe dashboard). Speed matters more than tidiness. Issue a replacement and deploy it. Audit usage : CloudTrail, provider logs. Look for access between the leak and revocation time. Remove from history ( git filter-repo , BFG) and from image layers; force-push and tell collaborators to re-clone. Find the cause : add a pre-commit scanner so it cannot recur, and write a blameless postmortem. # Prevent: scan before commit and in CI gitleaks detect --source . --verbose trufflehog git file://. --only-verified # GitHub also offers push protection and secret scanning on repos Principles to remember Least privilege (each app gets only its own secrets), short lifetimes, no human ever needs to see a production secret in routine work, and everything auditable. The best secret is one that does not exist because the workload uses identity (IAM roles, workload identity) instead. Try it Install gitleaks and run it against your oldest personal repo. Revoke anything it finds. Create an age key, write a small secrets.yaml , encrypt it with SOPS and commit it. Decrypt it on another machine using only the key. Run docker history --no-trunc on one of your images and check no secret appears in a layer.

title: Server and Application Hardening
text: Server and Application Hardening A public server is probed within minutes of getting an IP address. Hardening is the unglamorous work of shrinking what an attacker can reach and limiting what they can do if they get in. Most of it is a one-time checklist plus automation. The mindset: defense in depth Internet ─▶ [ Firewall / security group ] ─▶ [ Reverse proxy: TLS, headers, rate limit ] ─▶ [ App: validation, authn/z ] ─▶ [ DB: least-privilege user, private network ] each layer assumes the previous one has failed No single control is enough. Assume any layer can be bypassed and make sure the next one still limits the damage ("blast radius"). 1. Patching the operating system Unpatched known vulnerabilities are the most common entry point. Automate security updates and reboot when kernels change. # Debian/Ubuntu: unattended security upgrades sudo apt install unattended-upgrades sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades # check status / pending reboot cat /var/run/reboot-required sudo needrestart For containers, patching means rebuilding images regularly on updated base images (a weekly scheduled CI build) and redeploying. Live-patching a container is an anti-pattern. 2. SSH hardening Put these in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf : PermitRootLogin no PasswordAuthentication no KbdInteractiveAuthentication no PubkeyAuthentication yes AllowUsers deploy alice MaxAuthTries 3 LoginGraceTime 20 X11Forwarding no sudo sshd -t # validate config BEFORE reloading sudo systemctl reload ssh # keep your current session open and test a second one Do not lock yourself out Always keep an existing session open while testing a new SSH config in a second terminal. Know your provider's recovery console before you need it. Use ed25519 keys ( ssh-keygen -t ed25519 ) with a passphrase or hardware key. Optionally move SSH off port 22 (reduces log noise, not real security) or, better, reach servers only through a VPN/bastion or a tool like Tailscale or AWS SSM Session Manager so port 22 is not public at all. 3. Firewall Default deny inbound, open only what you serve. sudo ufw default deny incoming sudo ufw default allow outgoing sudo ufw allow 22/tcp # or restrict: ufw allow from 203.0.113.7 to any port 22 sudo ufw allow 80,443/tcp sudo ufw enable sudo ufw status verbose Docker bypasses ufw Published container ports ( -p 5432:5432 ) are added to iptables ahead of ufw rules and are exposed to the world. Bind to localhost ( 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 ) or do not publish at all and use internal networks. Also use your cloud security group as the primary firewall. 4. fail2ban Bans IPs that repeatedly fail authentication by parsing logs and adding firewall rules. sudo apt install fail2ban # /etc/fail2ban/jail.local [sshd] enabled = true maxretry = 5 findtime = 10m bantime = 1h sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban sudo fail2ban-client status sshd With key-only SSH it mostly reduces noise, but it is also useful on nginx login endpoints ( nginx-limit-req jail). 5. Least privilege Run apps as a dedicated unprivileged user, never root. In containers add USER node (or a numeric UID) and prefer --read-only filesystems. Give the DB user used by the app only SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on its schema, with a separate migration user for DDL. Use sudo with specific commands rather than full access; log it. systemd sandboxing makes a cheap extra layer: [Service] User=app NoNewPrivileges=true ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=true PrivateTmp=true ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/app CapabilityBoundingSet= RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX Check how you are doing with systemd-analyze security app.service . 6. Reduce attack surface Remove unused packages and services ( ss -tlnp shows what is listening). Databases and caches listen on private interfaces only. A public Redis with no password is mining malware's favourite target. Use minimal images ( distroless , alpine , -slim ). Enable audit logs and send them off the box so an intruder cannot erase them. 7. OWASP Top 10: the application basics The OWASP Top 10 lists the most common web risks. A practical translation: Risk What goes wrong Defence Broken access control User A fetches /orders/123 belonging to B (IDOR) Check ownership server-side on every request Cryptographic failures Plain HTTP, weak hashing, secrets in URLs TLS everywhere, argon2/bcrypt for passwords Injection SQL/command/template injection Parameterised queries, never string-concat input Insecure design No rate limits, no abuse thinking Threat model early Security misconfiguration Debug on, default creds, open buckets IaC + config scanning Vulnerable components Old libraries with CVEs Dependency scanning (next lesson) Authentication failures Credential stuffing, weak sessions MFA, lockout/rate limits, secure cookies Integrity failures Unsigned updates, tampered pipelines Signing, pinned dependencies Logging and monitoring failures Breach unnoticed for months Log auth events, alert on anomalies SSRF Server tricked into fetching internal URLs (cloud metadata!) Allow-list outbound targets, IMDSv2 // SQL injection: wrong vs right db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"); // WRONG db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1", [email]); // right 8. Security headers (set at nginx or in the app) add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always; add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always; add_header X-Frame-Options "DENY" always; add_header Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin" always; add_header Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; frame-ancestors 'none'" always; add_header Permissions-Policy "geolocation=(), camera=()" always; server_tokens off; Test with curl -I https://example.com or securityheaders.com. Roll out CSP in Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only mode first so you do not break the site. Set cookies with Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax . 9. Rate limiting and abuse control http { limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=login:10m rate=5r/m; limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=10r/s; server { location /login { limit_req zone=login burst=5 nodelay; proxy_pass http://app; } location /api/ { limit_req zone=api burst=20; proxy_pass http://app; } } } Limit at the edge (CDN/WAF), at nginx and, for per-user logic, in the app (token bucket in Redis). Return 429 with Retry-After . Behind a proxy make sure you key on the real client IP ( X-Forwarded-For from a trusted proxy only), otherwise everyone shares one bucket or attackers spoof it. 10. Verify, continuously lynis audit system gives a hardening report for Linux hosts; CIS Benchmarks are the detailed standard. nmap -sV yourserver from outside: does the list of open ports match your intent? Run OWASP ZAP baseline scan against staging in CI. Enable cloud-native detection (GuardDuty, Security Hub) if on AWS. Trade-offs Every control costs convenience. Strict CSP breaks inline scripts; read-only filesystems break apps that write temp files; aggressive rate limits block users behind shared NAT. Roll out in report-only or monitor mode, measure, then enforce. Try it On a throwaway VPS apply the SSH config, ufw rules and fail2ban above. From another machine confirm password login is refused. Run sudo lynis audit system and fix the top three suggestions. Add the headers to nginx and grade the site; then add a login rate limit and prove it with a loop of curl requests that start returning 429.

title: DevSecOps and Supply Chain Security
text: DevSecOps and Supply Chain Security Your application is perhaps 10% code you wrote and 90% code you imported, plus a base image, a build system and a pipeline. Attackers know it: compromising one popular package or one CI token reaches thousands of victims. DevSecOps means building security checks into the pipeline so they run on every change, not once a year. Why "shift left" A vulnerability found in a pull request costs minutes to fix. The same flaw found in production costs an incident. Automated checks in CI give fast feedback to the developer who just wrote the code, while it is still in their head. commit ─▶ secret scan ─▶ SAST ─▶ dependency scan ─▶ build ─▶ image scan ─▶ sign + SBOM ─▶ deploy │ │ │ │ │ │ │ pre-commit gitleaks Semgrep/ Dependabot/ Trivy/Grype cosign admission CodeQL npm audit/OSV policy verifies The scanning toolbox Type Finds Tools Secret scanning Keys in code/history gitleaks, trufflehog, GitHub push protection SAST (static analysis) Insecure code patterns Semgrep, CodeQL, SonarQube SCA (dependency scanning) Known CVEs in libraries Dependabot, Renovate, OSV-Scanner, npm audit , Snyk Container scanning CVEs in OS packages and libs Trivy, Grype, Docker Scout IaC scanning Open buckets, wide security groups Trivy config, Checkov, tfsec DAST Runtime web flaws OWASP ZAP, Nuclei Dependency scanning in practice Enable Dependabot or Renovate so you receive automated update PRs. A minimal .github/dependabot.yml : version: 2 updates: - package-ecosystem: npm directory: / schedule: { interval: weekly } groups: minor-and-patch: update-types: [minor, patch] - package-ecosystem: docker directory: / schedule: { interval: weekly } - package-ecosystem: github-actions directory: / schedule: { interval: weekly } And a CI gate that fails on serious findings: - name: Scan image uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0 with: image-ref: ghcr.io/acme/api:${{ github.sha }} severity: CRITICAL,HIGH ignore-unfixed: true exit-code: 1 Triage, do not drown Scanners produce noise. Prioritise: is it reachable by your code, is a fix available, is it exploitable in your context? Use ignore-unfixed , VEX statements or documented ignore files with expiry dates. A gate nobody trusts gets disabled. Pinning: make builds reproducible and tamper-evident Lockfiles : commit them, install with npm ci / pip --require-hashes / go.sum verification. Base images by digest : tags are mutable, digests are not. GitHub Actions by commit SHA : a tag like @v4 can be moved by a compromised maintainer (this happened in the 2025 tj-actions/changed-files incident, which leaked secrets from thousands of repos). FROM node:22-alpine@sha256:3a4c...e91f # digest pin; Renovate can bump it - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2 Trade-off: pinning stops silent changes but also stops silent security fixes , so pair it with automated update PRs. SBOM: a bill of materials A Software Bill of Materials lists every component in an artifact. When the next Log4Shell lands, you query SBOMs instead of grepping repos. Common formats: SPDX and CycloneDX. syft ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.0 -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json grype sbom:sbom.spdx.json --fail-on high # Attach it to the image in the registry cosign attest --yes --predicate sbom.spdx.json --type spdxjson ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:... Regulation is pushing this: US executive order 14028 and the EU Cyber Resilience Act both expect SBOMs for many products. Signing images with cosign (Sigstore) Scanning tells you what is inside. Signing tells you who built it and that it was not altered . Sigstore's keyless signing ties a signature to an OIDC identity (for example "the GitHub workflow in repo acme/api on main") and records it in a public transparency log, so you manage no long-lived signing keys. # in CI (needs permissions: id-token: write, packages: write) cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/acme/api@${DIGEST} # verify anywhere cosign verify ghcr.io/acme/api@${DIGEST} \ --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/acme/api/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main$' \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com Enforce verification at deploy time with a Kubernetes admission controller (Kyverno verifyImages , Sigstore policy-controller, or Ratify). Sign the digest , never the tag. SLSA: a maturity framework for build integrity SLSA ("salsa", Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) defines increasing guarantees about how an artifact was built. Build level Meaning How to get it L1 Build is scripted and provenance exists Any CI that emits provenance L2 Hosted build platform signs provenance GitHub Actions + actions/attest-build-provenance L3 Hardened, isolated builds; provenance cannot be forged by the build's own steps slsa-github-generator reusable workflows Provenance is a signed statement: "this digest was built from commit X of repo Y by workflow Z". A consumer can verify it with gh attestation verify or slsa-verifier . Hardening the pipeline itself Set the workflow permissions: to read-only by default; grant write per job. Protect main : required reviews, required status checks, no force pushes, signed commits if you need them. Never use pull_request_target with checkout of untrusted PR code; never interpolate untrusted input ( ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} ) into shell commands. Use ephemeral runners for untrusted builds; self-hosted runners that persist between jobs can be poisoned. Use OIDC to cloud instead of stored keys; require approvals on the production environment. Dependency hygiene Beware typosquatting and dependency confusion (an attacker publishes a public package with your internal package's name). Use scoped names and registry config that pins internal scopes. Be wary of install scripts: npm ci --ignore-scripts where feasible. Prefer fewer, well-maintained dependencies. Every one is trust you extend. Delay adopting brand new releases a few days (Renovate minimumReleaseAge ); most malicious versions are yanked quickly. A sensible starting pipeline Day 1: Dependabot + secret scanning + push protection (free on GitHub). Week 1: Trivy on image and IaC in CI, failing on critical. Month 1: SBOM and provenance generated on release. Quarter 1: cosign signing and cluster-side verification; SHA-pinned actions. Security is a process, not a gate The goal is not zero findings; it is a pipeline that makes the secure path the easy path, keeps fix time short, and lets you answer "are we affected?" within an hour of a new CVE. Try it Run trivy image node:22 and compare with trivy image node:22-alpine and a distroless image. Note the difference in findings. Generate an SBOM with syft for one of your images and query it for a package: grype sbom:./sbom.json . Sign a test image in GHCR using keyless cosign from a GitHub Action, then verify it from your laptop.

title: Databases in Production
text: Databases in Production Your stateless app servers are cattle; the database is the one pet you cannot lose. It is usually the first bottleneck, the hardest thing to scale and the source of the worst outages. This lesson covers connection management, replicas, indexes, safe migrations, the managed-vs-self-hosted decision and caching, with Postgres as the running example. 1. Connections are expensive: pooling A Postgres connection is a whole OS process using several MB of RAM. The default max_connections is 100. If you run 20 app replicas each with a pool of 10, you are already at 200 and the database falls over. Scaling the app can take down the DB. app pod ─┐ ┌─ pg conn 1 app pod ─┤ 200 client conns ─▶ [ PgBouncer ] ─┼─ pg conn 2 (e.g. 20 real server connections) app pod ─┘ └─ pg conn ... In-app pool (node-postgres Pool , HikariCP, SQLAlchemy): size it small. A common formula is connections = (cores * 2) + disks on the DB, shared across all app instances. External pooler (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy, Supavisor): multiplexes many clients onto few server connections. Use pool_mode = transaction ; note it breaks session features such as SET , advisory locks and (older) prepared statements. # pgbouncer.ini [databases] app = host=10.0.0.5 port=5432 dbname=app [pgbouncer] pool_mode = transaction max_client_conn = 1000 default_pool_size = 20 auth_type = scram-sha-256 Symptom: "remaining connection slots are reserved" Usually a leak (connections not released) or too many replicas times pool size. Check SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1; . Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and statement_timeout so a stuck client cannot hold resources forever. 2. Replication and read replicas A primary handles writes and streams its write-ahead log (WAL) to replicas. Replicas provide two different things, which people confuse: Purpose Mechanism Notes High availability Standby that can be promoted (synchronous or async) Failover automation: Patroni, RDS Multi-AZ, Cloud SQL HA Read scaling Async replicas serving read-only queries Reads may be stale (replication lag) The classic bug: a user submits a form (write to primary), the next page reads from a replica that has not caught up, and the data "disappears". Mitigate by reading from the primary right after writes ("read your writes"), or routing only reports and search to replicas. Monitor lag: SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp(); on the replica. 3. Indexes An index trades write speed and disk for read speed. Without one, Postgres scans the whole table. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20; -- "Seq Scan on orders" on a big table = missing index CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC); CONCURRENTLY is mandatory in production. A plain CREATE INDEX takes a lock that blocks writes for the entire build. The concurrent variant takes longer, cannot run inside a transaction and can leave an INVALID index if it fails (drop and retry). Column order matters in composite indexes: equality columns first, then range/sort columns. Index foreign keys; Postgres does not do it for you. Find unused indexes with pg_stat_user_indexes ( idx_scan = 0 ) and slow queries with the pg_stat_statements extension. 4. Safe schema migrations Use a migration tool (Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, Prisma Migrate, golang-migrate, Rails/Django migrations): versioned, in git, applied in CI/CD, never by hand. The danger is that during a rolling deploy old and new code run against the same schema simultaneously , and some DDL takes long locks. The expand / contract pattern Never make a breaking change in one step. Rename a column in phases: Expand : add the new column (nullable). Deploy code that writes to both. Backfill old rows in small batches (not one giant UPDATE). Deploy code that reads from the new column. Contract : stop writing the old column, then drop it in a later release. Dangerous operations and their safe forms Risky Why Safer CREATE INDEX Blocks writes CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT x (PG < 11) Rewrote whole table PG 11+ is instant for constant defaults; otherwise add nullable, backfill ALTER COLUMN TYPE Table rewrite under lock New column + backfill + swap ADD CONSTRAINT FOREIGN KEY / CHECK Full scan under lock Add NOT VALID , then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT SET NOT NULL Full scan Add valid CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) first, then SET NOT NULL Dropping a column still read by old code Errors during rollout Stop using it first, drop later -- always protect yourself from queueing behind a long transaction SET lock_timeout = '3s'; SET statement_timeout = '60s'; ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN currency text; Why lock_timeout : an ALTER waits for a lock, and while it waits every other query queues behind it , so a quick DDL stuck behind a long-running transaction can stall the whole application. Fail fast and retry. Also: test migrations against a copy of production-sized data, take a backup first, and keep migrations backward compatible so you can roll back the app without rolling back the schema. Run them as a separate pipeline step (a one-off job) rather than at app startup when you have many replicas. 5. Managed vs self-hosted Managed (RDS, Cloud SQL, Neon, Supabase, Aiven) Self-hosted (VM or Kubernetes operator) Backups, PITR Built-in You build and test (pgBackRest, WAL-G) Failover Click to enable Patroni/CloudNativePG, you operate Patching Scheduled windows You Cost Higher per unit Cheaper compute, expensive in human time Control Limited extensions/config, no OS access Full Lock-in Moderate (standard Postgres protocol eases exit) None Default advice: use managed unless you have a specific reason and a person who knows how to run databases. The price premium is almost always smaller than one bad weekend. Whichever you pick, a database on the same VPS as the app is acceptable only for small projects, with off-box backups. 6. Caching with Redis Caching removes load from the database for data that is read often and changes rarely. The standard pattern is cache-aside : async function getProduct(id) { const key = `product:${id}`; const hit = await redis.get(key); if (hit) return JSON.parse(hit); const row = await db.query('SELECT * FROM products WHERE id=$1', [id]); // TTL with jitter avoids many keys expiring in the same second await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(row), 'EX', 300 + Math.floor(Math.random()*60)); return row; } // on update: DEL product:{id} (invalidate) Always set a TTL , so stale data and memory growth are bounded. Configure maxmemory and maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru for caches. Cache stampede : a hot key expires and 1000 requests hit the DB simultaneously. Use jittered TTLs, request coalescing or a short lock. Invalidation is the hard part: prefer short TTLs plus explicit deletes on writes over elaborate schemes. Do not treat a cache as the source of truth unless you configure persistence deliberately (AOF/RDB) and accept the trade-offs. Never expose Redis publicly; require auth and TLS. Redis also serves as a session store, rate-limit counter and job queue backend. 7. Operational basics Monitor: connections, replication lag, disk space (a full disk is the classic outage), cache hit ratio, slow queries, locks, autovacuum and transaction ID age. Private network only; TLS to the database; per-service credentials with least privilege. Alert on disk at 70-80%, not 95%. Run EXPLAIN on new queries in code review; add an ORM N+1 detector. Rule of thumb Scale the database in this order: fix queries and indexes, add pooling, cache, add read replicas, scale up the instance, and only then consider sharding. Each step is cheaper than the next. Try it Run Postgres in Docker, create a 5-million-row table with generate_series , run a filtered query with EXPLAIN ANALYZE , add an index with CONCURRENTLY and compare timings. Put PgBouncer in front and use pgbench -c 200 to watch connection counts in pg_stat_activity with and without it. Plan the expand/contract steps (on paper) to rename users.fullname to users.display_name with zero downtime.

title: Backups and Disaster Recovery
text: Backups and Disaster Recovery Nobody wants a backup; everybody wants a restore. A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup. This lesson covers what to protect, how often, how to store it safely, and how to choose a disaster recovery strategy that matches your budget and tolerance for downtime. What can go wrong Human error : DROP TABLE on the wrong terminal, a bad migration, terraform destroy in the wrong workspace. The most common cause. Software bugs corrupting data silently over days. Hardware/provider failure : disk, host, availability zone or entire region. Malicious : ransomware, or an attacker with your credentials deleting data and backups. Note that replication is not a backup. A replica faithfully copies your accidental DELETE within milliseconds. RPO and RTO last good backup DISASTER service restored │◀────── RPO ──────▶│◀──────── RTO ────────▶│ data you can lose time you can be down Term Question it answers Drives RPO (Recovery Point Objective) How much data loss is tolerable, measured in time? Backup frequency, replication, WAL archiving RTO (Recovery Time Objective) How long can we be down? DR architecture, automation, rehearsals Ask the business, not engineering, for the numbers, and show the price of each. "Zero data loss, zero downtime" costs an order of magnitude more than "up to 1 hour of data loss, 4 hours down". The 3-2-1 rule (and the modern 3-2-1-1-0) 3 copies of your data (production plus two backups), 2 different storage media/systems, 1 copy off-site (another region or provider), 1 copy immutable or offline (object lock / WORM, so ransomware or a compromised admin cannot delete it), 0 errors after verification (restore tests). Separate the blast radius Backups in the same account, with credentials the production system can use to delete them, are one compromise away from gone. Use a separate account/project, write-only credentials for the backup job and S3 Object Lock in compliance mode. What to back up Asset Method Databases Logical dumps and/or physical base backups plus WAL archive for point-in-time recovery Uploaded files Object storage versioning + cross-region replication Config, IaC, code Git (it is your backup if everything is in it) Secrets and keys Secret manager export procedure; encryption keys especially, since encrypted backups are useless without them Server state Do not back up servers; rebuild them from IaC. Back up data only. Postgres backup examples # Logical dump: simple, portable, fine for small DBs. Restores are slow for big ones. pg_dump --format=custom --file=app-$(date +%F).dump "$DATABASE_URL" pg_restore --clean --if-exists --no-owner -d restore_test app-2026-10-05.dump # Encrypt and ship off-site pg_dump -Fc "$DATABASE_URL" \ | age -r age1ql3z...cmac8p \ | aws s3 cp - s3://acme-backups-eu/app/$(date +%F).dump.age # cron: nightly at 02:30 30 2 * * * /opt/scripts/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1 For larger or stricter systems use physical backups with WAL archiving (pgBackRest, WAL-G, Barman). Base backup plus continuous WAL shipping gives point-in-time recovery (PITR) : restore to 14:31:59, one second before the bad deploy. Managed databases (RDS, Cloud SQL) provide this with a retention setting; check that it is on and long enough. Schedules and retention A typical grandfather-father-son policy: daily for 14 days, weekly for 8 weeks, monthly for 12 months. Retention should cover how long it might take you to notice corruption. Delete on schedule too: old backups are also a data-protection liability (GDPR erasure requests). Restore testing: the part everyone skips Automate a restore into a scratch environment weekly or monthly. Run sanity queries (row counts, latest timestamps, checksums) and fail loudly if they do not match expectations. Record how long it took. That number is your real RTO, and it usually surprises people. Do a full game day at least twice a year: pretend the database is gone, follow the runbook, with someone who did not write it. Alert on backup absence , not only failure (a dead cron job sends no errors). Use a dead-man's-switch such as a healthchecks.io ping at the end of the job. #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail ./backup.sh curl -fsS -m 10 --retry 3 https://hc-ping.com/YOUR-UUID # only reached on success Disaster recovery strategies AWS's classification is a handy spectrum: pay more to recover faster. Cost / complexity ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ Backup & restore Pilot light Warm standby Multi-site active-active RTO: hours-days RTO: tens of min RTO: minutes RTO: ~zero RPO: hours RPO: minutes RPO: seconds RPO: ~zero Strategy What runs in the DR region Recovery Use when Backup and restore Nothing; only backups copied there Provision infra from IaC, restore data Internal tools, tolerant business, tight budget Pilot light Core data layer replicating (DB replica); app servers defined but off Scale up compute, promote DB, switch DNS Moderate RTO needs Warm standby Full but scaled-down copy, always running and tested Scale up, switch traffic Revenue-critical services Active-active Full capacity in 2+ regions serving users Traffic shifts automatically Highest availability; accept data-consistency complexity and 2x cost Active-active is hard because of the database: you need multi-writer conflict handling (DynamoDB global tables, Spanner, CockroachDB) or careful regional partitioning. Many teams find that a well-rehearsed warm standby is the sweet spot. Availability zones versus regions Multi-AZ inside a region protects against a data centre failure and is cheap and mostly automatic: do this first. Multi-region protects against regional outages and is a bigger investment. Match to need; most outages are caused by bad deploys and config, which neither fixes. Disaster recovery runbook essentials Who declares a disaster, and how are people reached if Slack is down? Step-by-step restore commands, tested, stored somewhere that survives the disaster (printed or in a different provider). DNS TTLs low enough (60-300s) for failover to be quick. Dependencies: third-party APIs, email, auth provider. Does DR work if they do too? Credentials to reach DR resources that do not depend on the failed system (break-glass accounts). Failback plan: moving back is its own migration. Remember The unit of success is a timed, successful restore performed by someone other than the author . Everything else (cron jobs, green dashboards, S3 buckets full of files) is a proxy. Try it Write a script that dumps a local Postgres DB, encrypts it with age and restores it into a fresh container, then asserts a row count. Time it. Write down RPO and RTO targets for a service you run. Does your current setup meet them? What is the cheapest change that would? Enable S3 versioning plus Object Lock on a test bucket and try (and fail) to delete a locked object.

title: Scaling Patterns
text: Scaling Patterns Scaling means keeping latency and error rates acceptable as load grows. There is no single trick; there is a toolbox, and a rule: measure first, then apply the cheapest pattern that removes the actual bottleneck. This lesson walks through the toolbox from cheap to expensive. Vertical vs horizontal Vertical (scale up) Horizontal (scale out) How Bigger machine More machines behind a load balancer Pros No code changes, simplest No hard ceiling, resilient to node failure Cons Ceiling, downtime to resize, single point of failure Requires stateless design (12-factor), more moving parts Scale up first while it is cheap (a bigger instance is far less work than a distributed system), but design the app stateless so scaling out stays possible. The request path and where to relieve it User ─▶ CDN ─▶ Load balancer ─▶ App (stateless) ─▶ Cache (Redis) ─▶ DB primary ▲ │ │ └▶ DB read replicas │ edge │ static + cacheable └▶ Queue ─▶ Workers (async, slow work) └ cache hit returns here; the closer to the user, the cheaper 1. Caching layers The fastest request is one you never serve. Layer caches from the edge inward: Layer Example Notes Browser Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable on hashed assets Free; use content-hashed filenames CDN Cloudflare, CloudFront, Fastly Static files and cacheable API/HTML responses Reverse proxy nginx proxy_cache , Varnish Micro-caching (1-5s) can absorb spikes Application Redis/Memcached cache-aside Query results, rendered fragments Database Buffer cache, materialized views Precompute expensive aggregates Every cache adds an invalidation problem. Use TTLs, version keys ( product:v3:42 ) and stale-while-revalidate ( Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300 ) to make staleness a conscious, bounded choice. 2. CDN A CDN caches content at edge locations near users, cutting latency and shielding your origin. Beyond static assets it provides TLS termination, DDoS absorption and a WAF. Tips: Cache by URL; avoid putting per-user data in cacheable responses ( Vary and Set-Cookie can accidentally disable or poison the cache). Purge by tag or version the URL instead of purging everything. Lock the origin so it only accepts traffic from the CDN, otherwise attackers bypass it. 3. Queues and workers: async processing Do only what the user must wait for inside the request. Everything else (sending email, resizing images, generating PDFs, webhooks, syncing to third parties) goes on a queue and is handled by workers. POST /orders ─▶ API: validate, write order, enqueue "send_receipt" ─▶ 202/201 in 40 ms │ [ queue: SQS / RabbitMQ / Redis (BullMQ) / Kafka ] │ worker pool (scale independently) ─▶ email provider // producer await queue.add('send_receipt', { orderId }, { attempts: 5, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 2000 } }); // consumer new Worker('default', async job => sendReceipt(job.data.orderId), { concurrency: 10 }); Rules for reliable async work: At-least-once delivery is the norm , so jobs must be idempotent (processing twice has the same effect as once). Use an idempotency key or a "processed" record. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter; after N attempts send to a dead-letter queue and alert. Write the DB row and enqueue atomically, using the transactional outbox pattern, or you lose jobs when one succeeds and the other fails. Autoscale workers on queue depth / age of oldest message , not CPU (KEDA does this on Kubernetes). 4. Read replicas Most apps are read-heavy. Route reports, search and list pages to async replicas (see the databases lesson), mindful of replication lag. Replicas scale reads only; writes still go to one primary. 5. Sharding: the last resort When a single primary cannot handle write volume or dataset size, you split data across multiple databases by a shard key (for example tenant_id or hash of user_id ). Strategy How Trade-off Range Users A-M on shard 1 Hot spots if data is skewed Hash hash(id) % N or consistent hashing Even spread; range queries and resharding are harder Directory / tenant Lookup table maps tenant to shard Flexible; extra lookup Costs: cross-shard joins and transactions become hard or impossible, resharding is painful, operations multiply. Before sharding try: better indexes, partitioning ( PARTITION BY , single node), archiving old data, bigger hardware, or a distributed SQL database (CockroachDB, Citus, Vitess, Aurora Limitless) that does it for you. 6. Rate limiting and load shedding Capacity is finite. Decide who gets served when demand exceeds it, rather than letting everyone fail equally. Rate limiting caps requests per client/key/IP. Algorithms: fixed window (simple, bursty at edges), sliding window, token bucket (allows bursts, most popular), leaky bucket. Return 429 Too Many Requests and Retry-After ; expose limits in headers. Use a shared store (Redis) so limits hold across replicas. -- Redis fixed-window counter (atomic via Lua or INCR+EXPIRE) INCR rl:user:42:2026-10-05T10:21 EXPIRE rl:user:42:2026-10-05T10:21 60 -- if value > 100 -> 429 7. Backpressure Backpressure is a downstream system telling upstream "slow down" instead of silently buffering until it dies. Without it, a slow database causes app threads to pile up, memory balloons, timeouts trigger retries, retries add load, and you get a retry storm (metastable failure). Bounded queues : reject or drop when full instead of growing without limit. Timeouts everywhere : every outbound call has a deadline shorter than the caller's. Retries with budgets : exponential backoff, jitter, cap on total retries. Circuit breakers : stop calling a failing dependency for a cool-off period and fail fast. Load shedding : return 503 early when overloaded and protect the critical paths (checkout over recommendations). Autoscaling lag : new instances take minutes; queue and shed in the meantime. Choosing a pattern Symptom Likely first move High TTFB for static assets worldwide CDN, compression, HTTP/2/3 DB CPU high on repeated identical queries Cache-aside, fix N+1 Requests slow because of email/PDF/API calls Queue + workers DB CPU high, mostly SELECTs of varied queries Indexes, read replicas Primary write-saturated Batch writes, partitioning, bigger instance, then sharding Traffic spikes/abuse Rate limits, autoscaling, shedding Premature scaling is its own failure A single well-indexed Postgres on a decent instance with a CDN in front serves a startling amount of traffic. Add complexity when metrics demand it, and keep the system simple enough that you can explain it in five minutes. Try it Add proxy_cache with a 5-second TTL to an nginx in front of a slow endpoint and compare p95 latency under load. Build a tiny queue worker (BullMQ or Celery) where a job randomly fails; confirm retries, backoff and a dead-letter path work and that the job is idempotent. Implement a token-bucket limiter in Redis and demonstrate 429 responses with hey or k6 .

title: Performance and Load Testing
text: Performance and Load Testing You do not know how your system behaves under load until you load it. Load testing finds the breaking point before your customers do, and gives you the numbers needed for capacity planning. This lesson shows how to test with k6, how to read the results and how to hunt the bottleneck. Types of performance tests Type Shape Question Smoke 1-2 users, 1 minute Does the script and system work at all? Load Expected peak, sustained 10-30 min Do we meet our SLOs at normal peak? Stress Ramp beyond peak until failure Where does it break and how (gracefully or catastrophically)? Spike Sudden jump 10x then back Do autoscaling, queues and caches cope? Soak Moderate load for hours Memory leaks, connection leaks, disk growth? Metrics that matter Throughput : requests per second. Latency percentiles : p50, p95, p99. Averages hide pain; if p99 is 8 seconds, one in a hundred users is suffering, and with many requests per page view that is most of your users. Error rate : non-2xx and timeouts. Saturation : CPU, memory, connections, queue depth, disk IO. (This is the Google SRE "four golden signals": latency, traffic, errors, saturation.) Latency rises non-linearly Latency stays flat as load increases, then curves up sharply as a resource saturates (the "knee"). Operating near 100% utilisation of anything means queueing delay explodes. Plan to run steady-state at 50-70% of the knee. k6 in practice k6 (Grafana Labs) scripts tests in JavaScript, runs as a single fast binary, and supports thresholds that make CI fail when performance regresses. // load-test.js import http from 'k6/http'; import { check, sleep } from 'k6'; export const options = { stages: [ { duration: '2m', target: 50 }, // ramp up to 50 virtual users { duration: '10m', target: 50 }, // hold { duration: '1m', target: 0 }, // ramp down ], thresholds: { http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'], // under 1% errors http_req_duration: ['p(95)<300', 'p(99)<800'], // latency SLO in ms }, }; export default function () { const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/products`); check(res, { 'status is 200': (r) => r.status === 200, 'body not empty': (r) => r.body.length > 0, }); sleep(1); // think time: real users pause } k6 run -e BASE_URL=https://staging.example.com load-test.js # stream results to Prometheus/Grafana for correlation with server metrics k6 run --out experimental-prometheus-rw load-test.js Sample output includes http_req_duration ... avg=120ms p(90)=210ms p(95)=290ms and a threshold pass/fail. For realistic modelling prefer the open model (arrival-rate executors such as constant-arrival-rate ) over fixed virtual users: real traffic does not slow down just because your server did, whereas closed-model tests politely back off and hide overload ("coordinated omission"). scenarios: { steady: { executor: 'constant-arrival-rate', rate: 200, timeUnit: '1s', duration: '10m', preAllocatedVUs: 100, maxVUs: 500 }, } Rules for valid tests Test a production-like environment: same instance sizes, same data volume (a 100-row test DB lies), same config. Never casually load-test production or third-party services you do not own. Run the generator on a separate machine, close to the target; check it is not itself the bottleneck (CPU). Use realistic traffic mixes and varied data (cache-busting parameters, many users), or you test your cache and not your system. Warm up first; JIT, caches and connection pools matter. Change one thing at a time and keep results in version control. Put a quick test in CI with strict thresholds to catch regressions (a smoke-level performance gate). Bottleneck hunting While the test runs, watch the system side. The methodology of Brendan Gregg's USE method is the shortcut: for every resource check U tilisation, S aturation, E rrors. Symptom during test Probable bottleneck Tools App CPU at 100%, latency up CPU-bound code, JSON/serialisation, regex, logging volume top , flame graphs ( perf , pprof, clinic.js , py-spy) App CPU low, latency high Waiting: DB, downstream API, locks, pool exhaustion Tracing (OpenTelemetry), pool metrics DB CPU high Missing index, N+1 queries, heavy aggregates pg_stat_statements , EXPLAIN ANALYZE DB connections maxed Pool too large/small, leaks pg_stat_activity , PgBouncer stats Memory climbing Leak, unbounded cache, GC pressure Heap snapshots, free -m , GC logs Disk await high IO-bound DB or logging iostat -x 1 Errors with low resource use Limits: file descriptors, net.core.somaxconn , worker threads, rate limiter ulimit -n , ss -s , nginx error log Latency spikes at regular intervals GC pauses, cron jobs, checkpointing, DNS Correlate timestamps # a quick host-level look while the test runs vmstat 1 # r (run queue) > cores = CPU saturation; si/so = swapping iostat -x 1 # %util and await for disks ss -s # socket counts; TIME_WAIT piles pidstat -u -r 1 # per-process CPU / memory Method: find the first saturated resource, fix or relieve it, rerun, and expect the bottleneck to move somewhere else. Stop when you meet the target with headroom. The slowest code is rarely where you guess, so profile instead of speculating. Capacity planning Define targets : peak requests per second, latency SLO, growth forecast (for example 3x in a year), and event peaks (marketing launch, Black Friday). Measure unit capacity : with a load test, find the throughput a single instance sustains while meeting the SLO (say 220 rps per app instance). Compute : instances = peak rps / (unit capacity * target utilisation) plus redundancy. peak = 1500 rps; unit = 220 rps; target utilisation = 65% instances = 1500 / (220 * 0.65) = 10.5 -> 11 + N+1 (survive losing one) -> 12 instances Find the next constraint : 12 app instances times pool of 10 means 120 DB connections. Does the DB cope? Do the same maths for DB, cache, bandwidth, third-party API quotas and your cloud account limits. Revisit regularly : re-test after significant releases and track trends from monitoring to see when you will hit limits (disk fill date, connection trend). Use autoscaling to absorb variance, but keep minimums high enough for a sudden spike while new capacity boots, and set maximums so a bug or attack cannot create an enormous bill. Pitfalls Testing from your laptop over Wi-Fi, testing with one URL, ignoring think time, testing an empty database, trusting averages, and treating one passing run as proof. Also: a load test hitting a CDN-cached page measures the CDN. Try it Run the capstone API locally (or any service) and write a k6 script with thresholds. Run it at 10, 50 and 100 VUs and plot where p95 starts to climb. While running, watch docker stats and pg_stat_activity . Identify the first resource to saturate. Fix it (an index, a pool size, caching) and rerun. Record the improvement and compute how many instances you would need for 1000 rps.

title: Production Readiness Checklist
text: Production Readiness Checklist "Are we ready to go live?" is answered best with a checklist, not a feeling. Airline pilots use them because memory fails under pressure; so do mature engineering teams. Use this as a launch review: every row should be a tick, a conscious "not needed, because...", or a tracked ticket with an owner. How to use this page Run it as a review meeting 1-2 weeks before launch, not the night before. Be honest about "partial". The goal is visible risk, not a perfect score. Adapt by criticality: an internal tool needs a lighter pass than a payment service. Re-run it after major architectural changes. Keep it in the repo and evolve it after each incident ("what would have caught this?"). 1. Architecture and design Check Why it matters Done when Application is stateless (12-factor) Enables scaling and safe restarts No local-disk state, sessions in a shared store Single points of failure identified One failure should not be an outage Diagram reviewed; accepted SPOFs documented Timeouts, retries with backoff and circuit breakers on all outbound calls Prevents cascading failure Reviewed in code and tested with a failing dependency Graceful shutdown (SIGTERM) and fast startup Deploys without dropped requests Verified by a rolling restart under load Health endpoints: liveness and readiness Orchestrators route only to healthy instances Readiness checks dependencies; liveness does not Capacity estimated and load tested Know your limits Test at 2x expected peak passes SLO 2. Deployment and release Check Why Done when CI builds, tests and scans every commit Fast feedback Required status check on main Immutable, versioned artifact (image tag = commit SHA) Reproducibility and rollback No latest in production manifests Automated deploy, no manual SSH edits Repeatable and auditable Pipeline is the only path to prod Zero-downtime strategy (rolling, blue-green or canary) Users do not notice releases Tested under load Rollback is documented and rehearsed Mean time to recovery Someone rolled back in staging within 5 minutes Database migrations are backward compatible Old and new code overlap during deploys Expand/contract used; no long locks Feature flags for risky features Decouple deploy from release Kill switch exists Staging mirrors production Realistic verification Same config shape, similar data scale 3. Infrastructure Check Why Done when All infrastructure defined as code Rebuildable, reviewable Can recreate environment from repo Multi-AZ / redundancy for critical tiers Survive a host or zone failure Killed an instance; service kept serving Autoscaling (or planned headroom) with sane min/max Absorb spikes, cap cost Tested with a spike run DNS TTLs and domain/cert expiry owned and monitored Expired certs are embarrassing outages Auto-renewal + expiry alert at 14 days Resource limits set (CPU/memory/file descriptors) Noisy neighbours, OOM chaos Limits defined; OOM behaviour known Cloud quotas and service limits checked Hitting a quota during launch Headroom confirmed Cost alerts and budgets Surprise bills Budget alarm configured 4. Security Check Why Done when TLS everywhere, HSTS, modern ciphers Confidentiality and integrity SSL Labs grade A Secrets in a manager, none in git or images Credential leaks Secret scan clean; rotation tested Least privilege IAM, DB users, service accounts Limit blast radius No wildcard admin roles for workloads Only necessary ports open; DB and cache private Reduce attack surface External port scan matches intent SSH key-only, no root login, MFA on cloud and Git accounts Account takeover is the top threat Enforced org-wide Dependency and image scanning in CI Known CVEs Critical findings block merge Security headers and rate limiting on public endpoints Abuse and common web attacks Verified with header scan and test loop Auth/authorization tests for access control Broken access control is #1 risk Automated tests for cross-tenant access Audit logging enabled (cloud + app) Investigations Logs retained off-box Patch process defined Unpatched hosts Unattended upgrades or scheduled image rebuilds 5. Observability Check Why Done when Structured logs to a central place Debug without SSH Can search by request/trace ID Metrics: latency, traffic, errors, saturation See health at a glance Dashboard per service Distributed tracing (where multiple services) Find slow hops Trace propagates through all services External uptime check from outside your network Catches "everything green but site down" Probe on user-facing URL SLOs defined for key user journeys Objective definition of "healthy" Error budget tracked Alerts are actionable, symptom-based and routed to on-call Avoid alert fatigue and silence Every alert has a runbook link; tested page delivery Error tracking (Sentry or similar) Application exceptions with context Releases tagged; source maps uploaded 6. Data and recovery Check Why Done when Automated backups, off-site, immutable copy 3-2-1 rule Backup job monitored with dead-man's switch Restore tested and timed Backups are unproven until restored Restore drill documented with real RTO RPO/RTO agreed with the business Sets expectations and budget Written targets, architecture matches Point-in-time recovery enabled for DB Recover from bad deploys PITR retention covers detection time Connection pooling and limits configured Avoid connection exhaustion Total pool size less than DB max Disk-space alerts on DB and logs Full disk = outage Alert at 70-80% Data retention and privacy compliance (GDPR etc.) Legal exposure Deletion process and data map exist 7. Operations and people Check Why Done when On-call rota and escalation path Someone answers at 3 a.m. Schedule published; paging tested Runbooks for top failure modes Faster, calmer incident response Linked from alerts, reviewed by a newcomer Incident process and comms template Roles and status updates Incident commander role defined; status page ready Blameless postmortem practice Learn instead of blame Template and review cadence agreed Architecture diagram and service ownership documented Know who to call Catalog entry with owner and repo Launch plan: timing, staged rollout, comms, rollback owner Controlled go-live Avoid Friday-evening launches; war-room scheduled Dependencies' SLAs and support contacts known Third parties fail too Fallback behaviour defined 8. Final go-live gate Dry run of the full deploy in staging, including rollback. Load test passed on production-like environment. Restore drill completed this quarter. No open critical security findings; no known data-loss bugs. Dashboards and alerts live before traffic, not after. Rollback owner and decision criteria named ("if error rate > 2% for 5 min we roll back"). Staged traffic: internal users, then 1%, 10%, 50%, 100%, watching metrics at each step. After launch Hypercare for the first days: watch dashboards, hold a short daily review, and capture surprises as checklist improvements. Production readiness is not a one-time gate but a habit. Scale the checklist to the stakes A hobby project may take only the bold basics: HTTPS, backups with a restore test, an uptime check, secrets out of git, and a rollback path.
