Add rows as the consequences of failure grow. Try it Copy this checklist into a spreadsheet and score a real service you run: 0 = absent, 1 = partial, 2 = done. Sort by lowest score times business impact. Pick the top three gaps and write tickets with owners and dates. Run a 30-minute game day: kill one instance and break one dependency in staging. Did alerts fire? Did the runbook work?

title: Capstone Overview: Ship a Real Service End to End
text: Capstone Overview: Ship a Real Service End to End Reading about DevOps does not make you a DevOps engineer; shipping does. In this capstone you will take a small API plus a Postgres database through every stage of the handbook: containerize it, build a CI pipeline, deploy to a real server with HTTPS, define the server with Terraform and watch it with Prometheus and Grafana. The project We will build Notely , a tiny notes API. The language does not matter; the examples use Node.js (Express) because it is compact, but a Python (FastAPI), Go or Java service works identically as long as it has three things: it reads config from environment variables, talks to Postgres and exposes /healthz and /metrics . Endpoint Purpose GET /healthz Returns 200 when the app and database are reachable GET /notes List notes POST /notes Create a note: {"title":"...","body":"..."} GET /metrics Prometheus metrics (request counts, latency) Target architecture ┌─────────────────────────── GitHub ───────────────────────────┐ you ─ git push ──▶ │ repo ─▶ Actions: test ─▶ build image ─▶ push to GHCR │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────┘ │ ssh + docker compose pull Internet ─▶ DNS (notely.example.com) ─▶ VPS (provisioned by Terraform) ◀───────────┘ ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐ │ nginx :443 (TLS via Let's Encrypt) │ │ │ │ │ ▼ │ │ api container ──▶ postgres container │ │ │ /metrics (volume + backup)│ │ prometheus ─▶ grafana │ └───────────────────────────────────────┘ external uptime check (UptimeRobot / Uptime Kuma elsewhere) ─▶ alerts you The stages # Stage Lesson You will practise 0 Write the app this page 12-factor config, health endpoint, graceful shutdown 1 Containerize Capstone: Containerize Multi-stage Dockerfile, Compose, local dev with hot reload 2 CI pipeline Capstone: CI Pipeline GitHub Actions, tests against Postgres, image to GHCR 3 Deploy Capstone: Deploy to a VPS SSH deploy, compose in prod, nginx, TLS, zero-downtime-ish update, rollback 4 IaC and monitoring Capstone: IaC and Monitoring Terraform the server and DNS, Prometheus, Grafana, uptime check, backups Prerequisites Git and a GitHub account. Docker Desktop (or Docker Engine + Compose v2) locally. Node.js 22 LTS if you want to run the app outside Docker. A cheap VPS (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Vultr or AWS Lightsail; roughly 4-6 USD/month) and a domain name (or a free subdomain from DuckDNS / a spare domain). Comfort with the Linux, Docker and CI/CD lessons earlier in the handbook. Stage 0: write the app Create the repo layout: notely/ ├── src/ │ ├── server.js │ └── db.js ├── test/notes.test.js ├── migrations/001_init.sql ├── package.json ├── Dockerfile ├── compose.yaml ├── .github/workflows/ci.yml ├── deploy/ (prod compose, nginx conf) └── infra/ (Terraform) // src/db.js import pg from 'pg'; export const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL, // factor III: config from env max: 10, }); // src/server.js import express from 'express'; import client from 'prom-client'; import { pool } from './db.js'; const app = express(); app.use(express.json()); client.collectDefaultMetrics(); const httpDuration = new client.Histogram({ name: 'http_request_duration_seconds', help: 'request latency', labelNames: ['method', 'route', 'status'], }); app.use((req, res, next) => { const end = httpDuration.startTimer(); res.on('finish', () => end({ method: req.method, route: req.route?.path ?? req.path, status: res.statusCode })); next(); }); app.get('/healthz', async (_req, res) => { try { await pool.query('SELECT 1'); res.json({ status: 'ok' }); } catch { res.status(503).json({ status: 'db unavailable' }); } }); app.get('/notes', async (_req, res) => { const { rows } = await pool.query('SELECT id, title, body, created_at FROM notes ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 100'); res.json(rows); }); app.post('/notes', async (req, res) => { const { title, body = '' } = req.body ?? {}; if (!title) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'title required' }); const { rows } = await pool.query( 'INSERT INTO notes (title, body) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING *', [title, body]); res.status(201).json(rows[0]); }); app.get('/metrics', async (_req, res) => { res.set('Content-Type', client.register.contentType); res.end(await client.register.metrics()); }); const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000); const server = app.listen(port, () => console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: 'info', msg: 'listening', port }))); process.on('SIGTERM', () => server.close(() => pool.end().then(() => process.exit(0)))); export default app; -- migrations/001_init.sql CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, body TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '', created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now() ); Install dependencies with npm init -y && npm i express pg prom-client , set "type": "module" and "start": "node src/server.js" in package.json , and commit to a new GitHub repo. Add a .gitignore containing node_modules and .env . Use your own app if you have one Any small service you already have works better than Notely because you care about it. Just make sure it meets the 12-factor checklist: config in env, logs to stdout, stateless, health endpoint. Definition of done git push to main runs tests, builds an image, publishes it and deploys it without manual steps. https://notely.yourdomain.com/healthz returns 200 with a valid certificate. The server can be destroyed and recreated from Terraform plus one bootstrap script. Grafana shows request rate and latency; an external check alerts you when the site is down. A nightly database backup exists off the server, and you have restored it once. A README documents how to run, deploy, roll back and restore. How to get the most out of it Commit after every step with clear messages; your git history becomes your portfolio story. Break things on purpose (kill the container, fill the disk, push a failing test) and watch what the system does. Write the README as if a stranger had to operate it at 3 a.m. Stretch goals: swap compose for k3s/Kubernetes, add a staging environment, add blue-green deploys, add Trivy and cosign, add a managed database. Try it Create the repo and the app above, start a local Postgres with docker run -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw -p 5432:5432 postgres:17 , apply the migration with psql and run the API with DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:pw@localhost:5432/postgres npm start . Verify with curl -X POST localhost:3000/notes -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"title":"hello"}' then curl localhost:3000/notes . Reserve your VPS and domain now, since DNS and account verification can take time.

title: Capstone: Containerize the App
text: Capstone: Containerize the App Stage 1: package Notely and its database so that docker compose up gives any teammate (or any server) an identical environment in one command. This is the "build once, run anywhere" step everything else depends on. Goals A small, secure, fast-building production image. A Compose file for local development with Postgres, migrations and live reload. Configuration through environment variables only. The Dockerfile (multi-stage) A multi-stage build separates build-time tooling from the runtime image, shrinking size and attack surface. Order instructions from least to most frequently changing so layer caching works. # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 ARG NODE_VERSION=22 # ---- deps: install production dependencies only ---- FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}-alpine AS deps WORKDIR /app COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev # ---- runtime ---- FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}-alpine AS runtime ENV NODE_ENV=production WORKDIR /app # non-root user (the node image ships with one called "node") COPY --from=deps --chown=node:node /app/node_modules ./node_modules COPY --chown=node:node package.json ./ COPY --chown=node:node src ./src COPY --chown=node:node migrations ./migrations USER node EXPOSE 3000 HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s \ CMD wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:3000/healthz || exit 1 CMD ["node", "src/server.js"] Key decisions explained: Copy package*.json before the source : dependency installation is cached until the lockfile changes, so a code edit rebuilds in seconds. npm ci gives reproducible installs from the lockfile. Exec-form CMD ["node", ...] makes node PID 1 so it receives SIGTERM and shuts down gracefully (shell form would wrap it in sh -c and swallow the signal). Add --init or tini if your app spawns children. Non-root user : a compromised app does not own the container. Pin by digest in real production ( node:22-alpine@sha256:... ) and let Renovate bump it. .dockerignore Keeps the build context small and prevents secrets leaking into the image. node_modules .git .env .env.* Dockerfile compose*.yaml npm-debug.log test infra *.md Build and inspect docker build -t notely:dev . docker images notely # check size (aim for well under 200 MB) docker history notely:dev # confirm no secrets in layers docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 -e DATABASE_URL=... notely:dev Compose for local development # compose.yaml services: db: image: postgres:17-alpine environment: POSTGRES_USER: notely POSTGRES_PASSWORD: devpassword # dev only! POSTGRES_DB: notely volumes: - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data - ./migrations:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro # runs *.sql on FIRST init only ports: - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432" # bound to localhost only healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U notely -d notely"] interval: 5s timeout: 3s retries: 10 api: build: . environment: DATABASE_URL: postgres://notely:devpassword@db:5432/notely PORT: 3000 ports: - "3000:3000" depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy # wait until Postgres accepts connections restart: unless-stopped volumes: pgdata: docker compose up --build -d docker compose ps docker compose logs -f api curl -s localhost:3000/healthz docker compose down # keeps the volume (data survives) docker compose down -v # also deletes the volume (fresh start) Pitfalls you will probably hit 1) depends_on without condition: service_healthy only waits for the container to start , not for Postgres to be ready. 2) Inside Compose, the hostname is the service name ( db ), not localhost . 3) Scripts in docker-entrypoint-initdb.d run only when the data directory is empty; later schema changes need a real migration tool. 4) Without a named volume the database vanishes with the container. Development override with live reload Compose automatically merges compose.override.yaml on top of compose.yaml , so developers get a hot-reload workflow while production uses the plain file. # compose.override.yaml services: api: build: target: deps # dev stage with all deps; add a "dev" stage if you need devDependencies command: node --watch src/server.js volumes: - ./src:/app/src # bind mount: edit on host, see changes in container environment: LOG_LEVEL: debug Compose 2.22+ also offers docker compose watch with a develop.watch section that syncs files or rebuilds on change without bind-mount quirks. Proper migrations The initdb trick is fine on day one; replace it soon with a migration runner executed as a one-off container so schema changes are versioned and repeatable (twelve-factor XII): migrate: build: . command: ["node", "src/migrate.js"] # or use flyway/dbmate/golang-migrate images environment: DATABASE_URL: postgres://notely:devpassword@db:5432/notely depends_on: db: { condition: service_healthy } profiles: ["tools"] # run on demand docker compose run --rm migrate Image hygiene checklist Check Command or technique Small image Alpine/slim/distroless base; multi-stage No secrets baked in docker history --no-trunc ; use runtime env or secrets Runs as non-root docker run --rm notely:dev id Vulnerability scan trivy image notely:dev Graceful stop time docker stop should be under 2 seconds Reproducible Lockfile + pinned base Lint the Dockerfile hadolint Dockerfile Trade-offs Alpine uses musl libc, which occasionally breaks native Node modules or changes DNS behaviour; -slim (Debian) is the safer default if you hit odd issues. Distroless images are tiny and have no shell, which is excellent for security and slightly annoying for debugging (use kubectl debug or an ephemeral debug container). Try it Write the Dockerfile, .dockerignore and compose.yaml , then run docker compose up --build and create a note with curl. Run docker compose down then up again and confirm the note persists. Then use down -v and confirm it is gone. Change one line of source and rebuild: observe cached layers in the output. Then change package.json and watch the install layer re-run. Scan with trivy image notely:dev and reduce the highest-severity finding by updating the base image.

title: Capstone: Build the CI Pipeline
text: Capstone: Build the CI Pipeline Stage 2: every push to GitHub should automatically run the tests, build the Docker image and publish it to the GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) with an immutable tag. After this, "what is running in production" is answered by a commit SHA. Pipeline design pull request ─▶ [ test job ] ─▶ (optionally build image, do not push) push to main ─▶ [ test job ] ─▶ [ build-and-push job ] ─▶ ghcr.io/OWNER/notely:sha-abc1234, :main tag v1.2.0 ─▶ same, plus :1.2.0 Principles: fail fast (cheap checks first), build the artifact once and promote it (never rebuild per environment), tag with the commit SHA, use the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN instead of a personal access token, and give each job the least permissions it needs. The workflow Save as .github/workflows/ci.yml : name: ci on: pull_request: push: branches: [main] tags: ['v*'] # cancel superseded runs on the same branch concurrency: group: ci-${{ github.ref }} cancel-in-progress: true permissions: contents: read # default for every job; widen per job below jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 services: postgres: image: postgres:17-alpine env: POSTGRES_USER: notely POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpw POSTGRES_DB: notely_test ports: ['5432:5432'] options: >- --health-cmd "pg_isready -U notely" --health-interval 5s --health-timeout 3s --health-retries 10 env: DATABASE_URL: postgres://notely:testpw@localhost:5432/notely_test steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 cache: npm - run: npm ci - run: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -f migrations/001_init.sql - run: npm test # optional extras: npm run lint, npx audit-ci, gitleaks image: needs: test if: github.event_name == 'push' runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 permissions: contents: read packages: write # push to GHCR id-token: write # keyless signing / provenance steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3 - uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - id: meta uses: docker/metadata-action@v5 with: images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }} tags: | type=sha,format=short type=ref,event=branch type=semver,pattern={{version}} - id: build uses: docker/build-push-action@v6 with: context: . push: true tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }} labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }} cache-from: type=gha cache-to: type=gha,mode=max provenance: true sbom: true - name: Scan image uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0 with: image-ref: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }} severity: CRITICAL ignore-unfixed: true exit-code: 1 Pin third-party actions to commit SHAs once you are comfortable (see the supply-chain lesson); version tags are used here for readability. Walkthrough Triggers and concurrency Pull requests get tests only; pushes to main additionally publish. concurrency cancels an older run when a newer commit lands, saving minutes and money. Service containers The services: block starts Postgres next to your job and waits for the health check. Because the job runs directly on the runner, the database is reachable at localhost:5432 (if the job itself ran in a container you would use the service name as host). Caching setup-node with cache: npm caches the npm download cache keyed on the lockfile. Docker layers are cached in the GitHub Actions cache via cache-from/cache-to type=gha , which can cut image builds from minutes to seconds. Tagging docker/metadata-action generates tags: sha-1a2b3c4 (what you deploy), main (convenience, mutable) and semantic versions on v* tags. Deploy by SHA or digest, never by latest . Permissions GITHUB_TOKEN is created per run and expires with it. packages: write lets it push to GHCR. After the first push, go to the package settings and link it to the repo (or set visibility) so your server can pull it; for a private package, create a read-only token for the VPS (next lesson). A minimal test to make the pipeline meaningful // test/notes.test.js (Node's built-in test runner; "test": "node --test") import { test, after } from 'node:test'; import assert from 'node:assert/strict'; import app from '../src/server.js'; import { pool } from '../src/db.js'; const server = app.listen(0); const base = () => `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}`; after(async () => { server.close(); await pool.end(); }); test('create and list notes', async () => { const created = await fetch(`${base()}/notes`, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'ci note' }), }); assert.equal(created.status, 201); const list = await (await fetch(`${base()}/notes`)).json(); assert.ok(list.some(n => n.title === 'ci note')); }); test('rejects missing title', async () => { const r = await fetch(`${base()}/notes`, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body: '{}' }); assert.equal(r.status, 400); }); Tip: make server.js skip app.listen when imported by tests (or split app.js and server.js ) to avoid binding two ports. Protect main In repository settings add a branch protection rule (or ruleset) for main : require pull requests, require the test status check, block force pushes. Now broken code cannot be merged, and the pipeline is the gatekeeper rather than a suggestion. Common failures and fixes Symptom Cause and fix denied: permission_denied: write_package Missing packages: write permission, or the package was created by another user/repo and is not linked to this repo Tests fail with ECONNREFUSED 5432 Service not healthy yet (add health options) or wrong host Repository name has uppercase, push fails Image names must be lowercase; metadata-action handles it, hand-written tags may not Build always slow Layer order wrong (source copied before dependencies) or cache not configured Workflow cannot access secrets on forked PRs By design for security; do not work around with pull_request_target Where this leads The next stage adds a deploy job that runs after the image job. Later improvements: a staging environment with auto-deploy and a production environment with manual approval, cosign signing, a nightly scheduled build to pick up base-image patches, and Dependabot for actions and npm. Try it Add the workflow and a test, push a branch and open a pull request: confirm only the test job runs. Merge it. Find the package under your profile's "Packages" and pull it: docker pull ghcr.io/OWNER/notely:main . Break a test on purpose and confirm the image job is skipped. Fix and re-run. Enable branch protection requiring the check, then try to push directly to main .

title: Capstone: Deploy to a VPS
text: Capstone: Deploy to a VPS Stage 3: put Notely on a real server behind nginx with a Let's Encrypt certificate, and make the pipeline update it automatically with minimal downtime. This is the same flow as a "real" deployment, just without the orchestrator. Target layout on the server /opt/notely/ ├── compose.yaml # production compose (pulls images, no build) ├── .env # secrets + IMAGE_TAG (chmod 600, not in git) └── nginx/notely.conf # (or nginx runs on the host; see below) Internet :443 ─▶ nginx (host) ─▶ 127.0.0.1:3000 ─▶ api container ─▶ db container (internal network only) Design choice: nginx on the host (installed by apt) handles TLS with certbot, while the app and database run in Compose. It keeps certificates simple and lets nginx survive app redeploys. The alternative is to run nginx or Caddy as another container; Caddy gives automatic HTTPS with almost zero config. 1. Prepare the server # as root on a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 VPS adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" deploy mkdir -p /home/deploy/.ssh # paste YOUR public key and a separate CI deploy key's public key: cat >> /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys chown -R deploy:deploy /home/deploy/.ssh && chmod 700 /home/deploy/.ssh && chmod 600 /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys # harden SSH: no root, no passwords (see hardening lesson), then: systemctl reload ssh # firewall ufw default deny incoming; ufw allow OpenSSH; ufw allow 80,443/tcp; ufw enable # install docker (official convenience script or apt repo) and give deploy access curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh usermod -aG docker deploy # note: docker group is root-equivalent apt install -y nginx certbot python3-certbot-nginx mkdir -p /opt/notely && chown deploy:deploy /opt/notely Docker group = root Anyone who can run docker can mount the host filesystem. That is acceptable for a dedicated deploy user whose key lives only in CI, but restrict that key ( command= and restrict options in authorized_keys ) if you want to go further. 2. Production compose file # /opt/notely/compose.yaml services: db: image: postgres:17-alpine restart: unless-stopped env_file: .env # POSTGRES_USER / POSTGRES_PASSWORD / POSTGRES_DB volumes: - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data networks: [internal] # no published ports at all healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER} -d $${POSTGRES_DB}"] interval: 10s retries: 6 api: image: ghcr.io/OWNER/notely:${IMAGE_TAG} restart: unless-stopped env_file: .env environment: DATABASE_URL: postgres://${POSTGRES_USER}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB} ports: - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000" # only nginx on the host can reach it depends_on: db: { condition: service_healthy } networks: [internal] networks: internal: volumes: pgdata: # /opt/notely/.env (chmod 600) POSTGRES_USER=notely POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<long random value from: openssl rand -base64 32> POSTGRES_DB=notely IMAGE_TAG=sha-1a2b3c4 If the GHCR package is private, log in once on the server with a read-only classic token ( read:packages ): echo $TOKEN | docker login ghcr.io -u USERNAME --password-stdin . Making the package public avoids this for a demo. 3. nginx and TLS Point DNS first: an A record for notely.example.com to the VPS IP (check with dig +short notely.example.com ). Then: # /etc/nginx/sites-available/notely server { listen 80; server_name notely.example.com; location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_read_timeout 30s; } } ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/notely /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/ nginx -t && systemctl reload nginx certbot --nginx -d notely.example.com --agree-tos -m you@example.com --redirect systemctl list-timers | grep certbot # auto-renewal is installed as a timer certbot renew --dry-run curl -I https://notely.example.com/healthz Certbot edits the config to add the 443 listener and the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect. Block /metrics from the public internet ( location = /metrics { deny all; } ) and let Prometheus scrape it internally. 4. First deploy by hand cd /opt/notely docker compose pull docker compose up -d docker compose run --rm api node src/migrate.js # or apply migrations/001_init.sql via psql docker compose ps curl -s localhost:3000/healthz Doing it manually once teaches you what the pipeline must automate. 5. Automate: a deploy job in GitHub Actions Create a dedicated key pair ( ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f deploy_key -N "" ), put the public half in the server's authorized_keys , and store the private half as a repo secret DEPLOY_SSH_KEY , plus DEPLOY_HOST . Capture the host key fingerprint ( ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 host ) as DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS so you verify the server rather than trust blindly. deploy: needs: image if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 environment: production # add required reviewers for manual approval steps: - name: Configure SSH run: | install -m 700 -d ~/.ssh echo "${{ secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY }}" > ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 echo "${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS }}" > ~/.ssh/known_hosts - name: Deploy env: TAG: sha-${{ github.sha }} run: | SHORT=$(echo "${GITHUB_SHA}" | cut -c1-7) ssh deploy@${{ secrets.DEPLOY_HOST }} "SHORT=sha-${SHORT} bash -s" << 'EOF' set -euo pipefail cd /opt/notely sed -i "s/^IMAGE_TAG=.*/IMAGE_TAG=${SHORT}/" .env docker compose pull api docker compose run --rm api node src/migrate.js docker compose up -d --no-deps api for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -fsS localhost:3000/healthz && exit 0 sleep 2 done echo "health check failed" >&2; exit 1 EOF - name: Smoke test run: curl -fsS https://notely.example.com/healthz The docker/metadata type=sha,format=short tag is the first 7 characters of the commit SHA prefixed with sha- , which is what the script reconstructs. Zero-downtime-ish updates docker compose up -d --no-deps api stops the old container and starts the new one, which causes a few seconds of 502 errors. Options, from simple to robust: Approach How Downtime Plain recreate compose up -d A few seconds nginx retry proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502; plus a short retry window masks the blip Near zero for GETs Blue-green with two compose projects Run api-blue on :3001 and api-green on :3002; start the new one, health check, switch the nginx upstream port, nginx -s reload , stop the old one Zero; instant rollback Rolling via Swarm / Kubernetes docker service update with --update-order start-first Zero Tools like Kamal Healthcheck-gated container swap behind kamal-proxy Zero # blue-green sketch (run on the server) CURRENT=$(cat /opt/notely/active_port) # 3001 or 3002 NEXT=$([ "$CURRENT" = 3001 ] && echo 3002 || echo 3001) APP_PORT=$NEXT docker compose -p notely-$NEXT up -d api until curl -fs localhost:$NEXT/healthz; do sleep 1; done sed -i "s/127.0.0.1:$CURRENT/127.0.0.1:$NEXT/" /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/notely nginx -t && nginx -s reload # reload is graceful: no dropped connections docker compose -p notely-$CURRENT stop api echo $NEXT > /opt/notely/active_port Remember migrations must be backward compatible so both versions can run against one database during the switch. Rollback ssh deploy@host cd /opt/notely sed -i 's/^IMAGE_TAG=.*/IMAGE_TAG=sha-PREVIOUS/' .env docker compose up -d --no-deps api Because every image is immutable and tagged by SHA, rollback is a one-line change. Keep the last N tags ( docker image prune carefully) and record each deployed tag in a log file or a GitHub deployment record. Verify like an operator docker compose logs --tail 50 api and journalctl -u nginx for errors. ss -tlnp : only 22, 80, 443 should listen on public interfaces. Verify 5432 is not exposed: nmap -p 5432 your.ip from your laptop. docker stats --no-stream for resource use; add swap or a bigger plan if memory is tight. Reboot the VPS and confirm everything comes back ( restart: unless-stopped plus docker enabled at boot). Back up from day one Add a cron job: docker compose exec -T db pg_dump -U notely -Fc notely | age -r YOUR_PUBKEY | rclone rcat remote:notely-backups/$(date +%F).dump.age , then restore it into a scratch container once to prove it works. Try it Provision the VPS, perform the hardening steps, point DNS and get a valid certificate. Check it with curl -vI . Deploy manually once, then add the deploy job and push a trivial change; watch it roll out and verify the SHA in the running container: docker compose images api . Push a commit that fails the health check (for example, a bad DATABASE_URL ). Does the pipeline fail and leave the old version serving? If not, improve the script. Practise a rollback and time it.

title: Capstone: Infrastructure as Code and Monitoring
text: Capstone: Infrastructure as Code and Monitoring Stage 4: stop clicking in a provider dashboard. Describe the server, firewall and DNS record in Terraform so the whole environment can be rebuilt from git, then add Prometheus, Grafana and an external uptime check so you find out about problems before your users do. Part A: Terraform the VPS We use Hetzner Cloud for the example (cheap and a clean provider), but the pattern is identical for DigitalOcean, AWS Lightsail/EC2 or any other provider: a server resource, an SSH key, a firewall and a DNS record. Cloudflare manages DNS here. Layout infra/ ├── versions.tf # provider + version constraints, backend ├── variables.tf ├── main.tf # ssh key, firewall, server, dns ├── cloud-init.yaml # bootstrap: user, docker, ufw, nginx ├── outputs.tf └── terraform.tfvars # NOT committed if it holds secrets; use TF_VAR_* env vars # versions.tf terraform { required_version = ">= 1.9" required_providers { hcloud = { source = "hetznercloud/hcloud", version = "~> 1.49" } cloudflare = { source = "cloudflare/cloudflare", version = "~> 5.0" } } # Remote state with locking: S3-compatible bucket (Hetzner/R2/AWS). Never commit state - it contains secrets. backend "s3" { bucket = "acme-tfstate" key = "notely/prod.tfstate" region = "eu-west-1" use_lockfile = true } } provider "hcloud" { token = var.hcloud_token } provider "cloudflare" { api_token = var.cloudflare_token } # variables.tf variable "hcloud_token" { type = string, sensitive = true } variable "cloudflare_token" { type = string, sensitive = true } variable "zone_id" { type = string } variable "domain" { type = string, default = "notely.example.com" } variable "ssh_public_keys" { type = list(string) } variable "admin_cidrs" { type = list(string), default = ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"] } # tighten to your IP # main.tf resource "hcloud_ssh_key" "admin" { for_each = toset(var.ssh_public_keys) name = "admin-${substr(sha1(each.value), 0, 8)}" public_key = each.value } resource "hcloud_firewall" "web" { name = "notely-web" rule { direction = "in", protocol = "tcp", port = "22", source_ips = var.admin_cidrs } rule { direction = "in", protocol = "tcp", port = "80", source_ips = ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"] } rule { direction = "in", protocol = "tcp", port = "443", source_ips = ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"] } } resource "hcloud_server" "app" { name = "notely-prod" server_type = "cx22" image = "ubuntu-24.04" location = "fsn1" ssh_keys = [for k in hcloud_ssh_key.admin : k.id] firewall_ids = [hcloud_firewall.web.id] user_data = file("${path.module}/cloud-init.yaml") backups = true # provider-level snapshots: a convenience, NOT a substitute for DB backups lifecycle { ignore_changes = [user_data] } # avoid destroying the server when bootstrap script changes } resource "cloudflare_dns_record" "app" { zone_id = var.zone_id name = var.domain type = "A" content = hcloud_server.app.ipv4_address ttl = 300 proxied = false } # outputs.tf output "ip" { value = hcloud_server.app.ipv4_address } # cloud-init.yaml - runs once at first boot #cloud-config users: - name: deploy groups: [docker] shell: /bin/bash sudo: false ssh_authorized_keys: - ssh-ed25519 AAAA...your-key - ssh-ed25519 AAAA...ci-deploy-key package_update: true package_upgrade: true packages: [nginx, certbot, python3-certbot-nginx, ufw, fail2ban, unattended-upgrades] runcmd: - curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh - usermod -aG docker deploy - sed -i 's/^#\?PermitRootLogin.*/PermitRootLogin no/; s/^#\?PasswordAuthentication.*/PasswordAuthentication no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config - systemctl reload ssh - mkdir -p /opt/notely && chown deploy:deploy /opt/notely - ufw allow OpenSSH && ufw allow 80,443/tcp && ufw --force enable The Terraform workflow export TF_VAR_hcloud_token=... TF_VAR_cloudflare_token=... # secrets from env or a secret manager terraform init terraform fmt -recursive && terraform validate terraform plan -out tfplan # READ the plan: what will be created, changed, destroyed? terraform apply tfplan terraform output ip Terraform pitfalls State holds secrets and is the source of truth: use a remote encrypted backend with locking and never commit it. Treat -/+ destroy and create in a plan as a red flag for stateful resources (set prevent_destroy = true on volumes or databases). Never edit resources by hand in the console; drift makes the next apply surprising. Run terraform plan in CI on pull requests and apply only from main after review. Prove the value: run terraform destroy on a test copy, then apply again and time how long a clean environment takes (a few minutes). Then redeploy the app with your pipeline. That is disaster recovery in miniature. For ongoing configuration of the OS (rather than first boot), Ansible is the next step. Part B: Metrics with Prometheus and Grafana Add a monitoring stack to a second compose file on the server, /opt/notely/monitoring/compose.yaml . Prometheus scrapes /metrics from the API and from exporters for the host (node_exporter) and database (postgres_exporter); Grafana visualises. services: prometheus: image: prom/prometheus:v3.1.0 restart: unless-stopped volumes: - ./prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro - ./alerts.yml:/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml:ro - promdata:/prometheus command: ["--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml", "--storage.tsdb.retention.time=30d"] ports: ["127.0.0.1:9090:9090"] extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"] node-exporter: image: prom/node-exporter:v1.8.2 restart: unless-stopped pid: host network_mode: host # sees real host network stats; listens on :9100 volumes: ["/:/host:ro,rslave"] command: ["--path.rootfs=/host"] grafana: image: grafana/grafana:11.4.0 restart: unless-stopped environment: GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD__FILE: /run/secrets/grafana_admin GF_SERVER_ROOT_URL: https://grafana.example.com secrets: [grafana_admin] volumes: [grafdata:/var/lib/grafana] ports: ["127.0.0.1:3001:3000"] secrets: grafana_admin: { file: ./grafana_admin.txt } volumes: { promdata: {}, grafdata: {} } # prometheus.yml global: { scrape_interval: 15s, evaluation_interval: 15s } rule_files: [alerts.yml] scrape_configs: - job_name: notely-api static_configs: [{ targets: ["host.docker.internal:3000"] }] - job_name: node static_configs: [{ targets: ["host.docker.internal:9100"] }] Note /metrics is blocked in public nginx but reachable on localhost for Prometheus. Expose Grafana through nginx on its own hostname with TLS and a strong password (or only via an SSH tunnel: ssh -L 3001:localhost:3001 deploy@host ). Never publish Prometheus without authentication. In Grafana add Prometheus as a data source ( http://prometheus:9090 , since they share a compose network when in the same file) and build panels with PromQL: # request rate by status sum by (status) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])) # error ratio sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])) # p95 latency histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) # disk free percent 100 * node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"} / node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/"} Import community dashboard "Node Exporter Full" (ID 1860) for instant host graphs. Alert rules # alerts.yml groups: - name: notely rules: - alert: HighErrorRate expr: sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])) > 0.05 for: 5m labels: { severity: page } annotations: { summary: "5xx ratio above 5% for 5 minutes" } - alert: DiskAlmostFull expr: node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"} / node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/"} < 0.15 for: 10m labels: { severity: ticket } - alert: TargetDown expr: up == 0 for: 2m labels: { severity: page } To deliver alerts add Alertmanager (route to email, Slack or ntfy) or use Grafana's built-in alerting with a contact point. Alert on symptoms users feel (errors, latency, availability) more than causes (CPU 80%). Part C: The external uptime check Everything above runs on the same box. If the VPS dies, your monitoring dies with it and nobody is told. You need a probe from outside : A hosted service: UptimeRobot, Better Stack, Uptime Kuma on a second cheap host, or Grafana Cloud synthetic monitoring. Check https://notely.example.com/healthz every minute, expect HTTP 200 and a keyword, alert via email/Slack/phone. Also monitor certificate expiry (alert at 14 days) and the domain's renewal date. Use a dead-man's switch (healthchecks.io) for your backup job: it alerts when the ping stops arriving. Part D: Logs At minimum docker compose logs works but rotates away. Configure Docker's log driver limits so logs cannot fill the disk, and consider shipping them to Loki with Grafana Alloy: # /etc/docker/daemon.json { "log-driver": "local", "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "5" } } # then: systemctl restart docker (containers must be recreated to pick it up) Final acceptance tests Test Expected terraform destroy && terraform apply , then run the deploy pipeline Site back up with HTTPS in under about 20 minutes, with no manual console clicks docker stop the API container TargetDown/uptime alert reaches you within a few minutes; container restarts if policy applies Generate load with k6 or hey Grafana shows request rate and latency change Restore last night's backup into a scratch container Notes present; time recorded Walk the production readiness checklist Gaps listed as issues in your repo You have now done DevOps Code goes in at one end; a monitored, TLS-protected, reproducible service comes out at the other, with rollback, backups and alerts. Every extra tool you learn later (Kubernetes, Argo CD, Vault) is a refinement of one of these steps. Try it Write the Terraform, run plan , and read every line of it before apply . Bring up Prometheus and Grafana, graph request rate while you hit the API with a loop, and create the error-rate alert. Trigger it by making the API return 500s. Set up an external uptime check and verify you receive the alert when you docker compose stop api . Stretch: move Terraform into CI (plan on PR, apply on merge) and add a second environment using a workspace or separate tfvars.

title: The Six-Month DevOps Learning Roadmap
text: The Six-Month DevOps Learning Roadmap DevOps is wide, and the most common mistake is learning tools in random order. This roadmap sequences topics so each month builds on the last, pairs every month with a concrete project and names the milestone that tells you you are done. It assumes roughly 8-10 hours a week and a working knowledge of programming. Principles Fundamentals before tools. Linux, networking and HTTP outlast every tool fashion. Kubernetes without them is cargo cult. Build, do not just watch. For every hour of video, spend two hands-on. Break things deliberately. One project that grows (the capstone) beats ten toy tutorials. Depth over breadth early. Get good at one cloud (AWS is the most common), one CI system, one IaC tool. Write it down. A blog or README per project is both learning and portfolio. Overview M1 Linux+Git+Net ─▶ M2 Docker+CI/CD ─▶ M3 Cloud (AWS)+IaC ─▶ M4 Kubernetes ─▶ M5 Observability+Security ─▶ M6 Capstone polish+Cert+Jobs Month 1: Foundations (Linux, Git, networking, scripting) Learn: shell navigation, permissions, processes, systemd, journalctl, SSH keys, package managers, cron; bash scripting basics ( set -euo pipefail , functions, loops); Git branching/rebasing/PR workflow; IPs, subnets, DNS, HTTP, TLS, ports, firewalls. Project: rent a small VPS, harden it, deploy a simple app by hand with systemd and nginx, add HTTPS with Let's Encrypt. Milestone: you can explain what happens from typing a URL to seeing a page, and you can diagnose "site is down" with ss , curl -v , dig , journalctl . Resources: "The Linux Command Line" (William Shotts, free), OverTheWire Bandit wargame, Pro Git book (free), "Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach" chapters 1-2, Julia Evans' zines. Month 2: Containers and CI/CD Learn: images, layers, Dockerfile best practices, volumes, networks, Compose; a registry; GitHub Actions (workflows, secrets, caching, matrix, environments); basic testing strategy; semantic versioning and trunk-based development. Project: capstone stages 1-3: containerize an API + Postgres, CI pipeline that tests and pushes to GHCR, auto-deploy over SSH. Milestone: a push to main reaches production automatically in under 10 minutes, with a one-command rollback. Resources: Docker official docs "Get started", "Docker Deep Dive" (Nigel Poulton), GitHub Actions docs, Kelsey Hightower's talks, "Accelerate" by Forsgren/Humble/Kim (DORA metrics). Month 3: Cloud (AWS) and Infrastructure as Code Learn: IAM (users, roles, policies, least privilege), VPC (subnets, route tables, NAT, security groups), EC2, S3, RDS, ALB, Route 53, CloudWatch, Auto Scaling; Terraform (providers, state, modules, workspaces, remote backends); intro to Ansible for configuration. Project: rebuild your capstone on AWS with Terraform: VPC, ALB, EC2/ECS Fargate, RDS in private subnets, DNS and TLS via ACM. Set a billing alarm first and destroy when finished. Milestone: terraform apply creates the whole environment from scratch; you can draw its network diagram from memory. Certification target: AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) , or AWS Cloud Practitioner first if you want an easier warm-up. Resources: AWS Skill Builder (free tier of courses), Adrian Cantrill's or Stephane Maarek's SAA courses, Tutorials Dojo practice exams, "Terraform: Up and Running" (Yevgeniy Brikman), HashiCorp tutorials. Month 4: Kubernetes Learn: architecture (control plane, kubelet, etcd), Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress/Gateway API, ConfigMaps, Secrets, probes, resource requests/limits, HPA, PersistentVolumes, RBAC, namespaces, Helm, Kustomize, debugging ( describe , logs , events , exec ); GitOps with Argo CD or Flux. Project: run the capstone on a local cluster (kind/minikube/k3d), then on k3s on a VPS or managed EKS/GKE with Helm and Argo CD; practise rolling updates, rollbacks and autoscaling. Milestone: you can debug a CrashLoopBackOff, a Pending pod and a 503 from the ingress without guessing; you can explain why you would or would not use Kubernetes for a given workload. Certification target: CKA (Certified Kubernetes Administrator) , a hands-on, terminal-based exam: practise with killer.sh (included with the exam purchase) and Mumshad's KodeKloud labs. CKAD is the developer-focused alternative. Resources: kubernetes.io tasks, "Kubernetes Up & Running", KodeKloud, "Kubernetes the Hard Way" (once). Month 5: Observability, reliability and security Learn: Prometheus + Grafana + Alertmanager, structured logging with Loki/ELK, OpenTelemetry tracing, SLIs/SLOs/error budgets, on-call, incident response and blameless postmortems; secrets management (Vault/SOPS), image scanning, SBOMs, signing, OWASP basics, backups and restore drills, load testing with k6. Project: capstone stage 5 plus: dashboards and symptom-based alerts, an SLO for the API, a game day where a friend breaks something, a documented restore, Trivy and cosign in the pipeline. Milestone: you have a written postmortem and a restore you timed. Resources: Google SRE Book and SRE Workbook (free online), "Observability Engineering" (Majors et al.), Prometheus docs, Grafana University, OWASP Top 10. Month 6: Polish, certify, get hired Learn/practice: fill gaps found along the way; cost optimisation (FinOps basics); a second cloud's vocabulary; platform engineering ideas; Python or Go for tooling. Project: publish the capstone repo with an excellent README, architecture diagram, runbook and a short write-up of what went wrong and what you learned. Optionally contribute to an open-source infra project. Certification target: HashiCorp Terraform Associate (003) (inexpensive, achievable in 2-3 weeks after Month 3 work), plus the CKA or SAA if not already done. Milestone: you can walk an interviewer through your project end to end, and answer the questions in the interview lesson. Certifications at a glance Certification Format Best for Difficulty When AWS Cloud Practitioner MCQ Absolute cloud beginners Easy Optional warm-up AWS Solutions Architect Associate MCQ, 130 min Broad AWS credibility; most recognised Medium End of month 3 HashiCorp Terraform Associate MCQ, 60 min IaC proof Easy-medium Month 3 or 6 CKA Hands-on, 2 h Real Kubernetes ability Hard (practical) End of month 4-5 CKAD Hands-on App-developer Kubernetes Medium Alternative to CKA CKS Hands-on Kubernetes security (requires CKA) Hard Later AWS DevOps Engineer Professional MCQ Deep AWS CI/CD and operations Hard Year 2 Azure AZ-400 / Google Professional Cloud DevOps Engineer MCQ If your employer uses those clouds Medium-hard As needed Certs are not the goal They are a structured syllabus and a way past resume filters. Employers value demonstrable projects and clear reasoning more. Pick one or two that match the jobs you want; do not collect them. Study habits that work Time-box: one weekday evening of theory, one of hands-on lab, one long weekend session on the project. Keep a "things I broke" log; it is gold for interviews. Use free tiers and budget alarms; always destroy cloud labs. A forgotten NAT gateway or load balancer costs real money. Join a community (r/devops, CNCF and Kubernetes Slack, local meetups); explaining answers cements knowledge. Read postmortems (the "post-mortems" GitHub list by danluu, Cloudflare and GitHub blogs): the best education in how systems fail. Beyond month six Direction Learn next Platform engineering Backstage, Crossplane, internal developer platforms, golden paths SRE Capacity planning, chaos engineering, distributed systems, advanced observability DevSecOps Policy as code (OPA/Kyverno), runtime security (Falco), threat modelling, CKS Cloud architecture Multi-account design, networking at scale, cost engineering, Pro-level certs Data/ML platforms Workflow orchestration, GPU scheduling, feature stores, model serving Try it Write your own version of this roadmap with real calendar dates and the 3 hours you can protect each week. Choose your first certification and book the exam date now; a deadline changes behaviour. Create a public repo called devops-journal and commit a short note each week on what you built and what broke.
