title: DevOps Interview Questions and Strong Answers
text: DevOps Interview Questions and Strong Answers Forty realistic questions grouped by topic, each with a concise answer of the kind that impresses an interviewer. Do not memorise the wording: understand the reasoning, add an example from your own projects, and be ready for the follow-up "why?" and "what are the trade-offs?". How to answer Structure: one-sentence definition, why it exists, a concrete example, a trade-off or failure mode. Saying "it depends, and here is on what" is a strong answer when followed by actual criteria. For troubleshooting questions, narrate a method (observe, hypothesise, test), not a guess. Fundamentals and culture 1. What is DevOps, in your own words? A culture and set of practices that unifies building and running software so teams ship small changes frequently, safely and with fast feedback. Automation (CI/CD, IaC), shared ownership and measurement (DORA metrics) are the pillars; tools are secondary. 2. What are the DORA metrics? Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service (recent versions also stress reliability). The first two measure speed, the last two stability; high performers are good at both, which disproves the idea that speed trades off against safety. 3. Explain SRE versus DevOps. DevOps is a philosophy; SRE is a concrete implementation of it from Google: treat operations as a software problem, define SLOs, use error budgets to balance feature velocity against reliability, cap toil at around 50% and write blameless postmortems. 4. What is an SLI, SLO, SLA and error budget? SLI is a measured indicator (percentage of requests under 300 ms and non-5xx). SLO is the internal target for it (99.9% over 30 days). SLA is the contractual promise with penalties, usually looser. The error budget is 100% minus the SLO (about 43 minutes a month at 99.9%); when it is spent, you slow feature releases and prioritise reliability. 5. What is a blameless postmortem and why? A written review of an incident that focuses on systemic causes, timeline, impact, what worked and concrete follow-ups with owners, without blaming individuals. People hide mistakes when blamed; hidden mistakes cannot be fixed. Human error is a symptom of a system that allowed it. Linux and networking 6. A server is slow. How do you investigate? Use a method, such as the USE approach, for each resource. uptime / top for load and CPU, free -h and vmstat for memory and swapping, iostat -x for disk, ss -s and sar -n DEV for network, then identify the process with pidstat or top . Check logs and dmesg for OOM kills, and recent deploys or config changes. Narrow before acting. 7. Explain Linux file permissions: what does 754 mean? Octal for owner, group, others: 7 = rwx, 5 = r-x, 4 = r--. Owner full control, group read and execute, others read only. On directories, x means permission to traverse. Special bits: setuid, setgid, sticky. 8. What happens when you type https://example.com in a browser? DNS resolution (cache, resolver, root, TLD, authoritative) gives an IP; TCP handshake (or QUIC for HTTP/3); TLS handshake validates the certificate and negotiates keys; HTTP request goes through CDN/load balancer/reverse proxy to an app server, which may query a cache or database; the response returns and the browser renders, fetching further assets. 9. Difference between a process, a thread and a container? A process has its own memory space; threads share a process's memory. A container is just a process (or group) isolated with namespaces (pid, net, mount, user) and limited with cgroups (CPU, memory), sharing the host kernel, unlike a VM which runs its own kernel on virtualised hardware. 10. "Connection refused" versus "connection timed out"? Refused means the packet reached the host and nothing is listening on that port (or a firewall actively rejects): check the service and bind address. Timeout means packets are being dropped silently or not routed: firewall/security group, wrong IP, routing. Tools: ss -tlnp on the server, nc -zv and traceroute from the client. 11. What is DNS TTL and why does it matter for migrations? The time resolvers may cache a record. Before cutting over an IP, lower the TTL (for example to 60 s) a full old-TTL period in advance, switch, then raise it again. Otherwise some users keep hitting the old server for hours. 12. Reverse proxy versus load balancer versus API gateway? A reverse proxy sits in front of servers handling TLS, caching and routing (nginx). A load balancer distributes traffic across instances using health checks and algorithms (L4 or L7). An API gateway adds API-specific features: auth, rate limiting, request transformation, versioning. Products often combine all three roles. Git and CI/CD 13. What is the difference between CI, continuous delivery and continuous deployment? CI: merge frequently and automatically build and test every change. Continuous delivery: every passing change is releasable and deployable with one approval. Continuous deployment: every passing change goes to production automatically. 14. Merge versus rebase? Merge preserves history with a merge commit; safe on shared branches. Rebase replays your commits on a new base for linear history; never rebase commits others have based work on. Common practice: rebase or squash your own feature branch, then merge via PR. 15. Design a CI/CD pipeline for a web app. On PR: lint, unit tests, dependency and secret scans, build. On merge to main: build an immutable image tagged by commit SHA, scan and sign it, push to a registry, deploy to staging automatically, run integration/smoke tests, then promote the same image to production (with approval if needed) using a rolling or canary strategy, post-deploy health checks and automatic rollback on failure. Add notifications and deployment metrics. 16. How do you keep pipelines fast? Cache dependencies and Docker layers, run jobs in parallel, run only affected tests, fail fast with cheap checks first, use smaller images and better runners, split slow end-to-end suites into a later stage and cancel superseded runs. 17. How do you handle secrets in CI? Use the platform's encrypted secrets scoped per environment, prefer OIDC federation to cloud roles over long-lived keys, never print them, restrict them from fork PRs, rotate regularly, and pull runtime secrets from a manager at deploy time rather than baking them into artifacts. 18. A flaky test fails 1 in 20 runs. What do you do? Do not just re-run. Quarantine it quickly so it stops blocking people, track it as a bug, find the cause (shared state, time, ordering, network, race conditions), fix or delete it. Flaky tests erode trust in the pipeline, which is worse than missing tests. Containers and Kubernetes 19. Explain image layers and why Dockerfile order matters. Each instruction creates a cached layer. A change invalidates that layer and all later ones, so put rarely changing steps (OS packages, dependency install from the lockfile) first and frequently changing source last. Multi-stage builds keep build tools out of the final image. 20. A container keeps restarting. How do you debug it? docker ps -a and exit code (137 = SIGKILL often OOM, 1 = app error), docker logs , docker inspect for OOMKilled and restart policy, run it interactively with the entrypoint overridden, check env vars, mounted files and dependencies, and health checks that may be killing it. 21. What is the difference between a Deployment, StatefulSet and DaemonSet? Deployment: interchangeable stateless replicas with rolling updates. StatefulSet: stable identities and per-pod persistent storage, ordered rollout, for databases/clusters. DaemonSet: one pod per node, for agents like log shippers and node exporters. 22. A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk me through it. kubectl describe pod for events and last state/exit code, kubectl logs --previous for the crashed run, check config and secrets referenced, failing probes, resource limits (OOMKilled), image and command, and dependencies like the database being unreachable. Fix, then watch the rollout. 23. Liveness versus readiness versus startup probes? Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic; failing removes it from Service endpoints. Liveness decides whether to restart the container; use it only for unrecoverable hangs and keep it independent of dependencies, otherwise a database blip restarts everything. Startup probe delays the others for slow-starting apps. 24. How do requests and limits work? Requests are what the scheduler reserves and what QoS is based on; limits are caps enforced at runtime. CPU over limit is throttled; memory over limit gets OOMKilled. Setting requests too low causes noisy neighbours; limits too low cause throttling and kills. Many teams set memory request = limit and avoid tight CPU limits. 25. How does a Service reach pods, and how does Ingress fit? A Service selects pods by label and gets a stable virtual IP and DNS name; kube-proxy (or eBPF dataplane) load balances to ready endpoints. Ingress or Gateway API exposes HTTP(S) routes from outside via a controller such as nginx or Envoy, routing by host and path to Services. 26. When would you not use Kubernetes? Small teams with a handful of services, simple workloads or tight budgets: a PaaS, managed containers (Cloud Run, ECS Fargate) or plain VMs with Compose are cheaper to operate. Kubernetes pays off with many services, multi-team platforms, need for portability or advanced scheduling, and the skills to run it. Infrastructure as Code and cloud 27. Why IaC, and what is Terraform state? IaC makes infrastructure reviewable, versioned, repeatable and testable. Terraform state maps your configuration to real resources so it can compute diffs. Store it remotely with locking and encryption, since it may contain secrets, and never edit it by hand except via terraform state commands. 28. What is drift and how do you handle it? Drift is reality diverging from code, usually from manual console changes. Detect with scheduled terraform plan ; fix by either reverting the change or codifying it; prevent by restricting console write access so IaC is the only path. 29. Terraform versus Ansible? Terraform is declarative provisioning of infrastructure (networks, instances, managed services) with state. Ansible is agentless configuration management over SSH (packages, files, services), procedural by default though idempotent modules help. They combine well: Terraform creates servers, Ansible or cloud-init configures them. Immutable images (Packer) or containers reduce the need for config management. 30. Explain a VPC with public and private subnets. A VPC is an isolated virtual network. Public subnets route to an internet gateway and host load balancers and NAT. Private subnets have no direct inbound internet; their outbound traffic goes via NAT. Put app servers and databases in private subnets; control access with security groups (stateful, per-resource) and NACLs (stateless, per-subnet). 31. IAM best practices? Least privilege, roles with temporary credentials instead of long-lived keys, MFA on humans, no shared accounts, no root usage, separate accounts per environment, policy review with access analyzer, and OIDC for CI. Prefer resource-scoped policies over wildcards. 32. How would you design for high availability on AWS? Multiple AZs: instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB with health checks, RDS Multi-AZ, state in managed services (S3, DynamoDB, ElastiCache), infrastructure in IaC, health-checked DNS failover if multi-region is required. Eliminate single points of failure and test by killing instances. Deployment strategies and reliability 33. Blue-green versus canary versus rolling? Rolling replaces instances gradually using the same capacity; simple, but versions coexist. Blue-green keeps two full environments and switches traffic at once, giving instant rollback at double the cost. Canary sends a small percentage to the new version and expands as metrics stay healthy, limiting blast radius and ideally automated via metric analysis (Argo Rollouts, Flagger). 34. How do you do zero-downtime database migrations? Expand and contract: make additive, backward-compatible changes first (new nullable column, concurrent index), deploy code that handles both, backfill in batches, switch reads, then remove the old structure in a later release. Use lock and statement timeouts, and never combine a breaking schema change with the code deploy. 35. You deployed and error rates spiked. What now? Stabilise first: roll back (or flip the feature flag) rather than debug live, confirm recovery in metrics, communicate status. Then investigate with logs, traces and the diff, write a postmortem, and add a test or guardrail so it cannot recur. Mitigation before root cause. 36. What is the difference between monitoring and observability? Monitoring checks known failure modes (dashboards and alerts on predefined metrics). Observability is the ability to ask new questions about system behaviour from its telemetry (logs, metrics, traces with high-cardinality context), which is needed to debug unknown unknowns in distributed systems. 37. How do you design good alerts? Alert on symptoms that affect users (error rate, latency, availability against SLOs), not every cause. Each alert must be actionable, have a runbook and a clear severity, and page only for urgent issues; route the rest to tickets. Use burn-rate alerts on SLOs, and review noisy alerts regularly to fight fatigue. Security and operations 38. How do you secure the software supply chain? Pin and lock dependencies, scan them and images in CI, generate SBOMs, build in hardened CI with provenance (SLSA), sign artifacts (cosign) and verify signatures at deploy, pin GitHub Actions to SHAs, use OIDC rather than stored credentials, protect branches and require reviews, and keep base images patched. 39. A secret was committed to a public repo. What do you do? Revoke and rotate it immediately (removal from git history is secondary), check provider audit logs for misuse in the exposure window, then clean history if appropriate, find how it slipped through, and add pre-commit and CI secret scanning plus push protection. Document it in a blameless review. 40. How do you decide on backup strategy and prove it works? Start from the business RPO and RTO. Use 3-2-1 with an immutable, separate-account copy, point-in-time recovery for databases, and encryption with keys backed up separately. Prove it by automated, timed restore tests and periodic game days; alert when backups stop arriving. An untested backup is not a backup. Scenario bonus: system design prompts Prompt Points to cover Take a startup's monolith from a single VPS to something resilient Containerise, CI/CD, managed DB with backups, load balancer + 2 instances, CDN, monitoring, IaC, then iterate; avoid premature Kubernetes Site goes down at 3 a.m. and you are on call Acknowledge, assess impact, check recent changes, roll back, communicate, mitigate, then postmortem Cut cloud costs by 30% Measure first (tags, cost explorer), rightsize, remove idle resources, savings plans/spot for stateless, storage tiering, schedule non-prod off-hours, watch egress and NAT costs Onboard 20 developers to deploy themselves Golden-path templates, self-service pipelines, guardrails via policy as code, docs, paved-road defaults and clear ownership Questions to ask them What does the deployment process look like, and how long from merge to production? How is on-call organised, and what was your last major incident and what changed afterwards? How do you handle toil and technical debt in infrastructure? What is the split between feature work and platform work for this role? Try it Pick ten questions at random, answer each aloud in 90 seconds and record yourself. Listen for rambling and missing trade-offs. For five of the answers, attach a real example from your capstone project ("when I did the VPS deploy, I hit..."). Pair with a friend: have them break something in your staging environment and narrate your debugging process aloud.

title: Why Go, and Setting Up
text: Why Go, and Setting Up Go (often "Golang") is a compiled, statically typed language created at Google in 2009 by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson. It was designed to make building fast, reliable network software boring in the best way: small language, fast compiles, one obvious way to do most things. What Go is good at Backend services and APIs : a great standard library for HTTP, JSON, crypto and more. Cloud and DevOps tooling : Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Prometheus and Caddy are all written in Go. CLIs : compiles to a single static binary you can copy anywhere, with no runtime to install. Concurrent programs : goroutines and channels are built into the language. What makes it different Trait What it means for you Compiled to native code Fast startup, low memory, no VM or interpreter on the server Static typing with inference Errors caught at compile time, but you rarely write types twice Garbage collected No manual free ; short GC pauses suit servers Small spec You can learn the whole language in a few weeks Fast compilation Edit, build, run feels almost like a scripting language Cross compilation GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build from your laptop Install Download the installer from go.dev/dl , or use a package manager: brew install go # macOS sudo apt install golang # Debian/Ubuntu (may be an older version) go version # verify, e.g. go version go1.24 darwin/arm64 Your first module mkdir hello && cd hello go mod init example.com/hello # creates go.mod Create main.go : package main import "fmt" func main() { fmt.Println("Hello, Go!") } go run . # compile and run in one step go build # produce a binary named after the module ./hello The toolchain you get for free Command Purpose go run Compile and run go build Produce a binary go test ./... Run all tests go fmt ./... Format code. There is one official style, so no formatting debates go vet ./... Static checks for suspicious code go mod tidy Add missing and remove unused dependencies Editor setup Use VS Code with the official Go extension (or GoLand). It installs gopls , the language server, and runs gofmt on save. Try it Install Go and run the hello program. Change the message, then break it on purpose (delete a quote) and read the compiler error. Run go build and check the binary size with ls -lh . Note that it is self-contained.

title: Variables, Constants and Basic Types
text:
Variables, Constants and Basic Types Go is statically typed, but the compiler infers most types for you. This lesson covers how to declare values, the built-in types, and Go's "zero value" rule that removes a whole class of uninitialized-variable bugs. Declaring variables var name string = "Ada" // explicit var age = 36 // type inferred (int) var count int // zero value: 0 city := "Lisbon" // short declaration, only inside functions x, y := 1, 2 // multiple at once := declares and assigns; = only assigns to something that already exists. Unused local variables and unused imports are compile errors . That keeps code tidy. Basic types Kind Types Booleans bool Integers int , int8/16/32/64 , uint , uint8…64 , uintptr Floats float32 , float64 Complex complex64 , complex128 Text string (immutable UTF-8 bytes), byte (= uint8 ), rune (= int32 , a Unicode code point) Use int and float64 unless you have a reason not to. Zero values Every variable is initialized. Without an explicit value it gets its type's zero value: var i int // 0 var f float64 // 0 var b bool // false var s string // "" (empty string) var p *int // nil var sl []int // nil slice Design for useful zero values Idiomatic Go types work without a constructor when possible. A zero sync.Mutex or bytes.Buffer is ready to use. No implicit conversions var a int = 10 var b float64 = float64(a) * 1.5 // explicit conversion required // var c float64 = a // compile error Constants and iota const Pi = 3.14159 const ( Small = iota // 0 Medium // 1 Large // 2 ) type Weekday int const ( Sunday Weekday = iota Monday Tuesday ) iota is a counter that resets in each const block. It is Go's idiom for enums. Strings and runes s := "héllo" fmt.Println(len(s)) // 6 (bytes, not characters!) for i, r := range s { // range iterates runes fmt.Println(i, string(r)) } multi := `raw string with "quotes" and 
 kept literally` Printing fmt.Println("a", 1) // a 1 fmt.Printf("%s is %d
", "Ada", 36) fmt.Printf("%v %+v %T
", p, p, p) // value, with field names, type s := fmt.Sprintf("%.2f", 3.14159) // format into a string Try it Print the length of "日本語" with len and with utf8.RuneCountInString . Why do they differ? Define a Color enum with iota and give it a String() method (we cover methods soon).

title: Control Flow
text: Control Flow Go keeps control flow minimal: one loop keyword ( for ), if , switch , and defer . No parentheses around conditions, braces always required. if if x > 10 { fmt.Println("big") } else if x > 5 { fmt.Println("medium") } else { fmt.Println("small") } // init statement: variable scoped to the if/else chain if n, err := strconv.Atoi(input); err != nil { fmt.Println("bad number:", err) } else { fmt.Println("parsed", n) } for: the only loop for i := 0; i < 5; i++ { } // classic for x < 100 { x *= 2 } // like while for { /* forever */ break } // infinite, exit with break nums := []int{10, 20, 30} for i, v := range nums { fmt.Println(i, v) } for i := range 3 { fmt.Println(i) } // 0 1 2 (Go 1.22+) for k, v := range map[string]int{"a": 1} { fmt.Println(k, v) } break and continue work as expected; labels let you break out of nested loops: outer: for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { for j := 0; j < 3; j++ { if j == 2 { continue outer } if i == 2 { break outer } } } switch No fallthrough by default, so no break needed: switch day { case "sat", "sun": fmt.Println("weekend") case "fri": fmt.Println("almost") default: fmt.Println("weekday") } // expressionless switch replaces if/else chains switch { case score >= 90: grade = "A" case score >= 80: grade = "B" default: grade = "C" } // type switch (more in the interfaces lesson) switch v := val.(type) { case int: fmt.Println("int", v) case string: fmt.Println("string", v) } Use the fallthrough keyword only when you truly want the next case to run. defer defer schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns, in last-in-first-out order. It is the idiom for cleanup: f, err := os.Open("data.txt") if err != nil { return err } defer f.Close() // runs no matter how we leave the function // ... use f ... Arguments are evaluated immediately defer fmt.Println(i) captures the value of i at the time of the defer statement, not when it runs. Try it Write FizzBuzz for 1..100 using an expressionless switch . Print a 3x3 multiplication table, stopping early with a labeled break when the product exceeds 6.

title: Functions
text: Functions Functions are first-class values in Go. They can return multiple values, be passed around, and close over variables. Multiple returns are the foundation of Go's error handling. Basics func add(a, b int) int { return a + b } func greet(name string) { fmt.Println("Hello,", name) } Multiple return values func divide(a, b float64) (float64, error) { if b == 0 { return 0, errors.New("division by zero") } return a / b, nil } result, err := divide(10, 2) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } _, err = divide(1, 0) // _ discards a value you don't need Named returns func minMax(xs []int) (min, max int) { min, max = xs[0], xs[0] for _, x := range xs { if x < min { min = x } if x > max { max = x } } return // "naked" return: returns min, max } Use sparingly Named returns are great for documentation on short functions. Naked returns in long functions hurt readability. Variadic functions func sum(nums ...int) int { total := 0 for _, n := range nums { total += n } return total } sum(1, 2, 3) xs := []int{4, 5} sum(xs...) // spread a slice Functions as values and closures func counter() func() int { n := 0 return func() int { // closes over n n++ return n } } next := counter() fmt.Println(next(), next(), next()) // 1 2 3 apply := func(f func(int) int, v int) int { return f(v) } fmt.Println(apply(func(x int) int { return x * x }, 5)) // 25 init and main func main() is the program entry point of package main . Each file may also have func init() , which runs automatically before main . Use it sparingly. Pass by value Everything in Go is passed by value: the callee gets a copy. Slices, maps and channels are small headers that point at shared data, so modifications through them are visible to the caller. For other types, pass a pointer (next section) if the function needs to change the original. Try it Write func stats(xs ...float64) (mean, stddev float64) . Write a memoize function that takes func(int) int and returns a caching version, using a map in a closure.

title: Arrays and Slices
text: Arrays and Slices Arrays have a fixed size and are rarely used directly. Slices are the workhorse: a flexible, dynamically sized view over an underlying array. Understanding how slices really work prevents the most common Go bugs. Arrays var a [3]int // [0 0 0] b := [3]string{"x", "y", "z"} c := [...]int{1, 2, 3, 4} // compiler counts: [4]int The length is part of the type: [3]int and [4]int are different types. Arrays are copied on assignment. Slices s := []int{1, 2, 3} // slice literal s = append(s, 4, 5) // grows as needed fmt.Println(len(s), cap(s)) t := make([]int, 3) // len 3, cap 3, zeros u := make([]int, 0, 100) // len 0, cap 100: preallocate sub := s[1:3] // elements 1 and 2 (end exclusive) first2 := s[:2] rest := s[2:] copy(dst, src) // copy elements between slices What a slice really is slice header (3 words) underlying array ┌─────────┬─────┬─────┐ ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐ │ pointer │ len │ cap │ ─────────▶ │ 1 │ 2 │ 3 │ 4 │ 5 │ └─────────┴─────┴─────┘ └───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘ A slice is a small struct: pointer to an array, a length and a capacity. Slicing creates a new header over the same array : a := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5} b := a[1:3] b[0] = 99 fmt.Println(a) // [1 99 3 4 5] — shared memory! append and capacity append reuses the array if capacity allows; otherwise it allocates a bigger one and copies. Always assign the result: s = append(s, x) // correct append(s, x) // compile error: result unused // gotcha: two slices may or may not share memory after append a := make([]int, 3, 10) b := append(a, 1) c := append(a, 2) // overwrites b's last element! fmt.Println(b[3], c[3]) // 2 2 Aliasing gotcha If you need an independent copy, make one: clone := slices.Clone(s) (package slices , Go 1.21+) or append([]int(nil), s...) . nil vs empty var s []int // nil, len 0 t := []int{} // empty, non-nil, len 0 fmt.Println(s == nil, t == nil) // true false // both work fine with len, range and append Useful helpers: the slices package import "slices" slices.Sort(xs) slices.Contains(xs, 3) i, found := slices.BinarySearch(xs, 3) slices.Reverse(xs) slices.Max(xs) xs = slices.Delete(xs, 1, 3) // remove xs[1:3] Try it Predict the output, then run it: create a := []int{1,2,3,4} , b := a[:2] , b = append(b, 100) , print a . Implement filter(xs []int, keep func(int) bool) []int .

title: Maps
text: Maps A map is Go's built-in hash table: an unordered collection of key/value pairs with O(1) average lookup. Creating and using maps ages := map[string]int{ "ada": 36, "linus": 54, } ages["grace"] = 85 // insert/update fmt.Println(ages["ada"]) // 36 delete(ages, "linus") fmt.Println(len(ages)) m := make(map[string][]string) // empty, ready to use The "comma ok" idiom Reading a missing key returns the zero value, so you can't tell "missing" from "present with zero value" without the second return: age, ok := ages["bob"] if !ok { fmt.Println("bob not found") } if v, ok := ages["ada"]; ok { fmt.Println("found", v) } Iterating for k, v := range ages { fmt.Println(k, v) } // order is intentionally randomized! keys := slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(ages)) // sorted keys (Go 1.23+) for _, k := range keys { fmt.Println(k, ages[k]) } Rules and gotchas Keys must be comparable : strings, numbers, bools, pointers, arrays, structs of comparable fields. Not slices, maps or functions. A nil map can be read but not written . Writing panics. Always initialize with a literal or make . Maps are not safe for concurrent writes. Protect with a sync.Mutex or use sync.Map . Maps are reference-like: assigning one to another variable shares the same data. Common patterns // counting counts := map[string]int{} for _, w := range words { counts[w]++ } // grouping groups := map[string][]string{} for _, p := range people { groups[p.City] = append(groups[p.City], p.Name) } // set seen := map[string]struct{}{} seen["a"] = struct{}{} if _, ok := seen["a"]; ok { /* present */ } struct{} takes zero bytes, so map[T]struct{} is the idiomatic set. Try it Count word frequencies in a paragraph and print the top 3. Write func invert(m map[string]int) map[int][]string .

title: Structs and Methods
text: Structs and Methods Go has no classes. Instead you define structs (data) and attach methods (behavior) to any named type. Composition replaces inheritance. Structs type User struct { Name string Email string Age int } u := User{Name: "Ada", Email: "ada@example.com", Age: 36} var z User // zero value: all fields zero fmt.Println(u.Name) u.Age++ p := &u // pointer to struct p.Name = "Ada L." // auto-dereferenced Methods A method is a function with a receiver : func (u User) Greeting() string { // value receiver: works on a copy return "Hi, I'm " + u.Name } func (u *User) Birthday() { // pointer receiver: can modify u.Age++ } u.Birthday() fmt.Println(u.Greeting()) Value or pointer receiver? Use a pointer receiver when… Use a value receiver when… The method modifies the receiver The type is small and immutable (e.g. a point, a time) The struct is large (avoid copying) It is a basic type or map/slice/func wrapper The struct contains a mutex or similar Rule of thumb: if any method needs a pointer receiver, use pointers for all methods of that type. Constructors Go has no constructors, only a convention: a NewX function. func NewUser(name, email string) (*User, error) { if !strings.Contains(email, "@") { return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid email %q", email) } return &User{Name: name, Email: email}, nil } Embedding: composition over inheritance type Animal struct{ Name string } func (a Animal) Speak() string { return a.Name + " makes a sound" } type Dog struct { Animal // embedded: Dog gets Animal's fields and methods Breed string } d := Dog{Animal: Animal{Name: "Rex"}, Breed: "Lab"} fmt.Println(d.Name, d.Speak()) // promoted from Animal // override by defining the method on Dog func (d Dog) Speak() string { return d.Name + " barks" } Struct tags type Product struct { ID int `json:"id"` Name string `json:"name"` Price float64 `json:"price,omitempty"` } Tags are metadata read via reflection. The encoding/json package uses them (see the JSON lesson). Exported vs unexported Capitalized names ( User , Name ) are visible outside the package. Lowercase names are private to the package. That is Go's only access control. Custom types and methods on any type type Celsius float64 func (c Celsius) Fahrenheit() float64 { return float64(c)*9/5 + 32 } type Color int const (Red Color = iota; Green; Blue) func (c Color) String() string { return [...]string{"Red", "Green", "Blue"}[c] } fmt.Println(Green) // prints "Green" because it satisfies fmt.Stringer Try it Model a BankAccount with Deposit and Withdraw (returning an error when funds are insufficient). Embed a Logger struct in a Server struct and call its methods through the server.

title: Pointers
text: Pointers A pointer holds the memory address of a value. Go has pointers but no pointer arithmetic, so you get the performance benefits without most of C's danger. Basics x := 42 p := &x // p is *int, the address of x fmt.Println(*p) // 42: dereference *p = 100 // modify x through the pointer fmt.Println(x) // 100 var np *int // nil pointer // fmt.Println(*np) // panic: nil pointer dereference Why pointers matter: pass by value func incrementBad(n int) { n++ } // changes a copy func increment(n *int) { *n++ } // changes the original v := 1 incrementBad(v); fmt.Println(v) // 1 increment(&v); fmt.Println(v) // 2 new and composite literals p := new(int) // *int pointing to 0 u := &User{Name: "Ada"} // pointer to a new struct (most common) Pointers to structs Field access through a pointer needs no * : u.Name works the same for a value or pointer. Returning a pointer to a local variable is fine. Go's escape analysis moves it to the heap automatically: func newCounter() *int { n := 0 return &n // safe! } When to use pointers You need a function or method to mutate its argument. The value is large and copying would be wasteful. You need to signal absence ( nil ) of an optional value. The type contains a lock or must not be copied. Don't over-use them For small values (ints, strings, small structs) copying is cheap and often faster than pointer chasing. Slices, maps and channels are already reference-like, so you rarely need a pointer to them. The classic loop-variable trap var ptrs []*int for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { ptrs = append(ptrs, &i) } // Go 1.22+: each iteration has its own i → prints 0 1 2 // Go ≤1.21: all point to the same i → prints 3 3 3 Go 1.22 changed loop variables to be per-iteration, fixing this long-standing bug. Make sure your go.mod says go 1.22 or later. Try it Write swap(a, b *int) . Create a linked list node type with a Next *Node and write a function to append to it and print it.

title: Interfaces
text: Interfaces Interfaces are Go's mechanism for abstraction and polymorphism. They are satisfied implicitly : a type implements an interface simply by having the right methods. No implements keyword. Defining and using type Shape interface { Area() float64 Perimeter() float64 } type Rect struct{ W, H float64 } type Circle struct{ R float64 } func (r Rect) Area() float64 { return r.W * r.H } func (r Rect) Perimeter() float64 { return 2 * (r.W + r.H) } func (c Circle) Area() float64 { return math.Pi * c.R * c.R } func (c Circle) Perimeter() float64 { return 2 * math.Pi * c.R } func describe(s Shape) { fmt.Printf("area=%.2f perimeter=%.2f\n", s.Area(), s.Perimeter()) } describe(Rect{3, 4}) describe(Circle{5}) // both satisfy Shape without declaring it Small interfaces are best The standard library's most powerful interfaces have one method: type Reader interface { Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) } type Writer interface { Write(p []byte) (n int, err error) } type Stringer interface { String() string } type error interface { Error() string } Because io.Reader is so small, files, network connections, HTTP bodies, gzip streams and in-memory buffers are all interchangeable. func countBytes(r io.Reader) (int64, error) { return io.Copy(io.Discard, r) } countBytes(strings.NewReader("hello")) countBytes(os.Stdin) "Accept interfaces, return structs" Define small interfaces where they are consumed , not where the type is defined. Functions accept the narrowest interface they need and return concrete types. The empty interface and any var x any = 42 // any == interface{}: holds a value of any type x = "hello" Type assertions and type switches var v any = "hi" s, ok := v.(string) // safe: ok is false on mismatch n := v.(int) // panics if v is not an int! switch t := v.(type) { case string: fmt.Println("string of length", len(t)) case int: fmt.Println("int", t) case nil: fmt.Println("nil") default: fmt.Printf("other: %T\n", t) } Composing interfaces type ReadWriter interface { Reader Writer } The nil interface gotcha func find() error { var e *MyError = nil return e // non-nil interface holding a nil pointer! } fmt.Println(find() == nil) // false An interface value is a (type, value) pair. It is nil only if both are nil. Return a literal nil for "no error". Try it Write a Logger interface with Log(string) and two implementations: console and in-memory slice. Write a function that accepts a Logger . Implement io.Writer on a type that uppercases everything written, and use it with fmt.Fprintln .

title: Error Handling
text: Error Handling Go has no exceptions. Errors are ordinary values returned from functions. It is verbose by design: every failure path is visible in the code, which makes programs easier to reason about. The basic pattern f, err := os.Open("config.json") if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("open config: %w", err) } defer f.Close() The built-in error interface has a single method: Error() string . A nil error means success. Creating errors errors.New("something broke") fmt.Errorf("user %d not found", id) // sentinel error: a package-level value callers can compare against var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found") Wrapping with %w Add context as the error travels up the stack, while preserving the original: func loadUser(id int) (*User, error) { u, err := db.Find(id) if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("loadUser(%d): %w", id, err) } return u, nil } // message: "loadUser(7): sql: no rows in result set" Inspecting errors: errors.Is and errors.As if errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) { // matches anywhere in the wrap chain http.Error(w, "not found", 404) } var pe *fs.PathError if errors.As(err, &pe) { // extract a specific error type fmt.Println("failed path:", pe.Path) } Custom error types type ValidationError struct { Field, Reason string } func (e *ValidationError) Error() string { return fmt.Sprintf("invalid %s: %s", e.Field, e.Reason) } func validate(u User) error { if u.Email == "" { return &ValidationError{"email", "required"} } return nil } Joining errors err := errors.Join(err1, err2) // Go 1.20+: reports all failures Guidelines Handle an error once. Either log it or return it, not both. Add context where you have it ("what was I doing?"), with lowercase messages and no trailing punctuation. Don't ignore errors. If you truly must, write _ = f.Close() to make it explicit. Use sentinel errors or custom types for conditions the caller needs to branch on. Otherwise plain wrapped errors are fine. Early return, avoid else Handle the error and return, keeping the happy path un-indented. This "line of sight" style is idiomatic. Try it Write readConfig(path) that wraps errors at each step. In main , use errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist) to print a friendly message. Create a ValidationError and extract it with errors.As from a wrapped error.

title: defer, panic and recover
text: defer, panic and recover defer guarantees cleanup. panic is for unrecoverable bugs, not ordinary errors. recover lets you stop a panic at a boundary, such as an HTTP handler. defer in depth func process(path string) error { f, err := os.Open(path) if err != nil { return err } defer f.Close() // runs when process returns mu.Lock() defer mu.Unlock() // pair lock/unlock together // ... return nil } Multiple defers run in LIFO order: for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { defer fmt.Println(i) } // prints 2, 1, 0 Defer in loops Defers run at function exit, not loop-iteration exit. Opening thousands of files in a loop with defer f.Close() leaks until the function returns. Extract the loop body into its own function. Modifying named results func readAll(path string) (data []byte, err error) { f, err := os.Open(path) if err != nil { return nil, err } defer func() { if cerr := f.Close(); err == nil { err = cerr } // surface close error }() return io.ReadAll(f) } panic A panic stops normal execution, runs deferred functions while unwinding the stack, then crashes the program with a stack trace. var m map[string]int m["a"] = 1 // panic: assignment to entry in nil map s := []int{1, 2, 3} _ = s[5] // panic: index out of range panic("this should never happen") Use panic only for programmer errors (impossible states, failed invariants) or during startup (e.g. regexp.MustCompile of a bad constant pattern). Expected failures should be error s. recover recover works only inside a deferred function and returns the panic value: func safe(fn func()) (err error) { defer func() { if r := recover(); r != nil { err = fmt.Errorf("recovered: %v", r) } }() fn() return nil } err := safe(func() { var m map[string]int; m["x"] = 1 }) fmt.Println(err) // recovered: assignment to entry in nil map Real-world use: middleware func recoverMiddleware(next http.Handler) http.Handler { return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { defer func() { if rec := recover(); rec != nil { log.Printf("panic: %v\n%s", rec, debug.Stack()) http.Error(w, "internal error", 500) } }() next.ServeHTTP(w, r) }) } (The net/http server already recovers per-request panics, but custom middleware lets you log and respond your way.) Try it Write a function that opens three files with defer and prints when each closes. Confirm the LIFO order. Write safeDivide(a, b int) (int, error) that converts a divide-by-zero panic into an error using recover .

title: Packages and Modules
text: Packages and Modules A package is a directory of .go files that share a namespace. A module is a collection of packages versioned together, defined by a go.mod file. Together they form Go's code organization and dependency system. Packages // mathutil/mathutil.go package mathutil // Exported (capital letter): visible to other packages func Double(n int) int { return n * 2 } // unexported: private to this package func helper() {} // main.go package main import ( "fmt" "example.com/hello/mathutil" ) func main() { fmt.Println(mathutil.Double(21)) } All files in a directory must declare the same package name. Package main with func main() builds an executable; any other name is a library. Import cycles are forbidden by the compiler. Modules and go.mod go mod init github.com/you/myapp module github.com/you/myapp go 1.24 require ( github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0 github.com/spf13/cobra v1.8.1 ) Dependencies go get github.com/google/uuid@latest # add or upgrade go get github.com/google/uuid@v1.6.0 # pin a version go mod tidy # sync go.mod/go.sum with your imports go list -m all # list all dependencies go mod vendor # optional: copy deps into ./vendor go.sum holds cryptographic checksums of dependencies for reproducible, tamper-evident builds. Commit both go.mod and go.sum . Recommended layout myapp/ ├── go.mod ├── go.sum ├── cmd/ │ └── myapp/ │ └── main.go # thin entry point(s) ├── internal/ # private: cannot be imported by other modules │ ├── server/ │ └── store/ ├── pkg/ # optional: public reusable libraries └── README.md internal/ is enforced Code under internal/ can only be imported by code rooted at the parent of internal . It lets you keep implementation details private without worrying about outside users. Import tricks import ( str "strings" // alias _ "embed" // import only for side effects . "fmt" // dot import (avoid) ) Naming conventions Package names are short, lowercase, single words: http , store . Avoid util and common . Avoid stutter: http.Server , not http.HTTPServer . Try it Create a module with an internal/greeter package and call it from cmd/app/main.go . Add github.com/google/uuid , print a UUID, then run go mod tidy and inspect the go.mod diff.

title: Testing
text: Testing Testing is built into the language and toolchain: no framework required. Test files end in _test.go , test functions start with Test , and go test runs them. Your first test // calc.go package calc func Add(a, b int) int { return a + b } // calc_test.go package calc import "testing" func TestAdd(t *testing.T) { got := Add(2, 3) want := 5 if got != want { t.Errorf("Add(2,3) = %d; want %d", got, want) } } go test ./... # all packages go test -v # verbose go test -run TestAdd # filter by regex go test -cover # coverage summary go test -race ./... # data race detector (use it in CI!) t.Errorf marks failure and continues; t.Fatalf stops the test immediately. Table-driven tests (the Go idiom) func TestDivide(t *testing.T) { tests := []struct { name string a, b float64 want float64 wantErr bool }{ {"normal", 10, 2, 5, false}, {"negative", -9, 3, -3, false}, {"by zero", 1, 0, 0, true}, } for _, tc := range tests { t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) { got, err := Divide(tc.a, tc.b) if (err != nil) != tc.wantErr { t.Fatalf("err = %v, wantErr %v", err, tc.wantErr) } if got != tc.want { t.Errorf("got %v, want %v", got, tc.want) } }) } } Each row becomes a named subtest, so failures point to the exact case, and adding a case is one line. Helpers and setup func newTestServer(t *testing.T) *Server { t.Helper() // report failures at the caller's line dir := t.TempDir() // auto-cleaned temp directory t.Cleanup(func() { /* teardown */ }) return NewServer(dir) } Testing HTTP handlers func TestHealth(t *testing.T) { req := httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/health", nil) rec := httptest.NewRecorder() healthHandler(rec, req) if rec.Code != http.StatusOK { t.Fatalf("status = %d", rec.Code) } } Benchmarks and fuzzing func BenchmarkAdd(b *testing.B) { for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { Add(1, 2) } } // go test -bench=. -benchmem func FuzzParse(f *testing.F) { f.Add("42") f.Fuzz(func(t *testing.T, s string) { Parse(s) }) // must not panic } // go test -fuzz=FuzzParse Testing with interfaces (fakes) type Store interface { Get(id int) (*User, error) } type fakeStore struct{ users map[int]*User } func (f fakeStore) Get(id int) (*User, error) { if u, ok := f.users[id]; ok { return u, nil } return nil, ErrNotFound } // the service depends on the interface, so tests inject the fake svc := NewService(fakeStore{users: map[int]*User{1: {Name: "Ada"}}}) Keep it simple The standard testing package is enough for most projects. Optional helpers like testify or go-cmp are popular but never required. Try it Write a table-driven test for a function IsPalindrome(string) bool , including empty strings and mixed case. Run with -cover and open the HTML report: go test -coverprofile=c.out && go tool cover -html=c.out .

title: Goroutines
text: Goroutines A goroutine is a lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime. You start one with the go keyword. They cost a few KB of stack each, so programs routinely run hundreds of thousands of them. Concurrency is not parallelism Concurrency : structuring a program as independently executing tasks. Parallelism : running tasks at the same instant on multiple cores. Go's scheduler multiplexes many goroutines onto a few OS threads (by default one per CPU core, controlled by GOMAXPROCS ), giving you both. Starting a goroutine func say(msg string) { for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { fmt.Println(msg, i) time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond) } } func main() { go say("goroutine") // runs concurrently say("main") } main exiting kills everything When main returns, the program ends, even if goroutines are still running. You need a way to wait. Waiting with sync.WaitGroup var wg sync.WaitGroup for i := 1; i <= 5; i++ { wg.Add(1) go func() { defer wg.Done() fmt.Println("worker", i) }() } wg.Wait() // blocks until the counter hits zero Call wg.Add before starting the goroutine. Since Go 1.25 you can also write wg.Go(func() { ... }) . Data races counter := 0 var wg sync.WaitGroup for i := 0; i < 1000; i++ { wg.Add(1) go func() { defer wg.Done(); counter++ }() // RACE } wg.Wait() fmt.Println(counter) // not reliably 1000 counter++ is read-modify-write, not atomic. Detect such bugs with go run -race . or go test -race . Fix with a mutex, an atomic, or by communicating over channels (next lessons). Goroutine leaks A goroutine blocked forever on a channel nobody will use is never freed. Always make sure every goroutine has a way to finish: closing a channel, cancelling a context, or reaching the end of its work. Go proverb "Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating." Try it Fetch five URLs concurrently with goroutines and a WaitGroup , printing each status code. Run the racy counter with -race and read the report.

title: Channels
text: Channels A channel is a typed conduit through which goroutines send and receive values. It both transfers data and synchronizes the two sides. Basics ch := make(chan int) // unbuffered channel of ints go func() { ch <- 42 // send (blocks until someone receives) }() v := <-ch // receive (blocks until someone sends) fmt.Println(v) Unbuffered vs buffered unbuf := make(chan int) // send and receive rendezvous buf := make(chan int, 3) // holds up to 3 values buf <- 1; buf <- 2; buf <- 3 // fine, no receiver needed // buf <- 4 // would block: buffer full fmt.Println(len(buf), cap(buf)) // 3 3 Unbuffered Buffered Send blocks when… no receiver is ready buffer is full Receive blocks when… no sender is ready buffer is empty Good for Handoff and synchronization Smoothing bursts, bounded queues Closing and ranging func produce(n int) <-chan int { out := make(chan int) go func() { defer close(out) // sender closes, signalling "no more" for i := 0; i < n; i++ { out <- i } }() return out } for v := range produce(5) { // loops until closed fmt.Println(v) } v, ok := <-ch // ok == false when closed and drained Only the sender should close a channel, and only once. Sending on a closed channel panics. Receiving from one returns the zero value immediately. You do not have to close channels for garbage collection. Close only to signal completion. Directional channels func producer(out chan<- int) { out <- 1 } // send-only func consumer(in <-chan int) { <-in } // receive-only Directions make APIs self-documenting and let the compiler catch misuse. Worker pool func worker(id int, jobs <-chan int, results chan<- int) { for j := range jobs { results <- j * j } } func main() { jobs := make(chan int, 100) results := make(chan int, 100) var wg sync.WaitGroup for w := 1; w <= 4; w++ { wg.Add(1) go func() { defer wg.Done(); worker(w, jobs, results) }() } for i := 1; i <= 20; i++ { jobs <- i } close(jobs) go func() { wg.Wait(); close(results) }() for r := range results { fmt.Println(r) } } Deadlocks ch := make(chan int) ch <- 1 // fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock! If every goroutine is blocked, the runtime detects it and crashes. A nil channel blocks forever on both send and receive. That is occasionally useful inside select . Try it Build a pipeline: generator → square → print, each stage a goroutine connected by channels. Change the worker pool to 1 worker and 10 workers and time it with simulated time.Sleep work.

title: select and Timeouts
text: select and Timeouts select is like switch for channels: it waits on multiple channel operations and runs whichever is ready first. Basic select select { case msg := <-ch1: fmt.Println("from ch1:", msg) case ch2 <- 10: fmt.Println("sent to ch2") case <-time.After(1 * time.Second): fmt.Println("timeout") } If several cases are ready, one is chosen at random. If none is ready, select blocks. Non-blocking operations select { case v := <-ch: fmt.Println("got", v) default: fmt.Println("nothing ready") // runs immediately if no case is ready } Timeouts func fetchWithTimeout(url string) (string, error) { result := make(chan string, 1) // buffered so the goroutine can't leak go func() { result <- slowFetch(url) }() select { case r := <-result: return r, nil case <-time.After(2 * time.Second): return "", errors.New("timeout") } } Tickers ticker := time.NewTicker(500 * time.Millisecond) defer ticker.Stop() done := time.After(2 * time.Second) for { select { case t := <-ticker.C: fmt.Println("tick at", t.Format("15:04:05")) case <-done: return } } The done-channel pattern func worker(done <-chan struct{}, out chan<- int) { for i := 0; ; i++ { select { case out <- i: case <-done: return // stop cleanly when asked } } } done := make(chan struct{}) go worker(done, out) // ... later close(done) // broadcasts to every listener Closing a channel wakes all receivers, so it works as a broadcast signal. This pattern is formalized by context (next lesson). Try it Merge two channels into one with a select loop (fan-in). Write a function that returns the first result from three simulated slow servers and ignores the rest.

title: The sync Package
text: The sync Package Channels are great for passing ownership of data, but sometimes you simply need to protect shared state. The sync and sync/atomic packages give you the classic tools. Mutex type SafeCounter struct { mu sync.Mutex n map[string]int } func (c *SafeCounter) Inc(key string) { c.mu.Lock() defer c.mu.Unlock() c.n[key]++ } func (c *SafeCounter) Get(key string) int { c.mu.Lock() defer c.mu.Unlock() return c.n[key] } Keep critical sections short, and always defer Unlock() . Never copy a struct containing a mutex (use pointer receivers). go vet warns about it. RWMutex Allows many concurrent readers or one writer: var mu sync.RWMutex mu.RLock(); v := cache[k]; mu.RUnlock() // readers mu.Lock(); cache[k] = v; mu.Unlock() // writer Once var ( once sync.Once cfg *Config ) func GetConfig() *Config { once.Do(func() { cfg = loadConfig() }) // runs exactly once, even if concurrent return cfg } Newer alternatives: sync.OnceValue and sync.OnceFunc . atomic var hits atomic.Int64 hits.Add(1) fmt.Println(hits.Load()) Lock-free operations on single values. Great for counters and flags. sync.Pool and sync.Map sync.Pool : reuse temporary objects (e.g. buffers) to reduce GC pressure. sync.Map : a concurrent map optimized for keys written once and read many times, or disjoint key sets. For most cases a plain map plus a mutex is simpler and faster. errgroup From golang.org/x/sync/errgroup . It runs goroutines, waits, and returns the first error: g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx) for _, url := range urls { g.Go(func() error { return fetch(ctx, url) }) } if err := g.Wait(); err != nil { return err } Mutex or channel? Use a channel to… Use a mutex to… Transfer ownership of data Protect a shared cache or counter Distribute work, pipelines Guard internal struct state Signal events and completion Keep a critical section tiny and obvious Try it Fix the racy counter from the goroutines lesson with a mutex, then with atomic.Int64 . Benchmark both. Build a concurrency-safe in-memory cache with RWMutex and a TTL per key.

title: Context
text: Context context.Context carries cancellation signals, deadlines and request-scoped values across API boundaries and goroutines. It is how Go programs stop work that is no longer needed. Creating contexts ctx := context.Background() // root, never cancelled ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(ctx) // cancel manually defer cancel() ctx, cancel = context.WithTimeout(ctx, 3*time.Second) // auto-cancel after 3s defer cancel() ctx, cancel = context.WithDeadline(ctx, time.Now().Add(time.Minute)) defer cancel() Always call cancel (usually with defer ) to release resources. Respecting cancellation func work(ctx context.Context) error { for i := 0; i < 10; i++ { select { case <-ctx.Done(): return ctx.Err() // context.Canceled or context.DeadlineExceeded case <-time.After(500 * time.Millisecond): fmt.Println("step", i) } } return nil } ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Second) defer cancel() err := work(ctx) fmt.Println(err) // context deadline exceeded Conventions Pass ctx as the first parameter , named ctx : func Fetch(ctx context.Context, url string) . Don't store contexts in structs. Pass them through calls. Derived contexts are cancelled when their parent is, forming a tree. Pass context.TODO() when you haven't decided yet. Contexts in the standard library // HTTP client request with timeout req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", url, nil) resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req) // database rows, err := db.QueryContext(ctx, "SELECT ...") // HTTP server: each request has its own context, cancelled if the client disconnects func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { ctx := r.Context() // pass ctx to everything you call } Values type ctxKey string const requestIDKey ctxKey = "requestID" ctx = context.WithValue(ctx, requestIDKey, "abc-123") id, _ := ctx.Value(requestIDKey).(string) Use values sparingly Only for request-scoped metadata like trace IDs and auth identity. Never for optional function parameters. Use a private key type to avoid collisions. Graceful shutdown ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM) defer stop() go func() { srv.ListenAndServe() }() <-ctx.Done() // wait for Ctrl+C or SIGTERM shutdownCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second) defer cancel() srv.Shutdown(shutdownCtx) // finish in-flight requests, then exit This is exactly what Kubernetes expects when it sends SIGTERM during a rolling deploy. Try it Make an HTTP GET with a 1-second timeout against a slow endpoint (e.g. httpbin.org/delay/5 ) and print the error. Run 5 workers that all stop when you press Ctrl+C, using signal.NotifyContext .

title: Generics
text: Generics Since Go 1.18 you can write functions and types that work with many types while staying type-safe. Use them to remove duplication, not to build elaborate abstractions. Generic functions func Map[T, U any](xs []T, f func(T) U) []U { out := make([]U, 0, len(xs)) for _, x := range xs { out = append(out, f(x)) } return out } lengths := Map([]string{"a", "bb", "ccc"}, func(s string) int { return len(s) }) // [1 2 3]. Type arguments are inferred. [T, U any] declares type parameters. any is the constraint, meaning "any type". Constraints import "cmp" func Max[T cmp.Ordered](a, b T) T { if a > b { return a } return b } Max(3, 7) // 7 Max("a", "b") // "b" // custom constraint: a union of types type Number interface { ~int | ~int64 | ~float64 } func Sum[T Number](xs []T) T { var total T for _, x := range xs { total += x } return total } The ~int means "int or any type whose underlying type is int" (such as type Age int ). comparable is a built-in constraint for types usable with == and as map keys. Generic types type Stack[T any] struct { items []T } func (s *Stack[T]) Push(v T) { s.items = append(s.items, v) } func (s *Stack[T]) Pop() (T, bool) { var zero T if len(s.items) == 0 { return zero, false } v := s.items[len(s.items)-1] s.items = s.items[:len(s.items)-1] return v, true } var s Stack[string] s.Push("a") v, _ := s.Pop() A generic set type Set[T comparable] map[T]struct{} func (s Set[T]) Add(v T) { s[v] = struct{}{} } func (s Set[T]) Has(v T) bool { _, ok := s[v]; return ok } When to use generics Good fit Poor fit Containers: stacks, queues, sets, caches When an interface with methods already works Slice/map helpers ( Map , Filter , Keys ) Only one concrete type is ever used Same algorithm over numeric types Clever "type-level" programming Look before you write The standard library already provides generic helpers: packages slices , maps and cmp . Try it Write Filter[T any](xs []T, keep func(T) bool) []T and Reduce . Implement a generic Cache[K comparable, V any] with Get / Set , guarded by a mutex.

title: JSON, Files and I/O
text: JSON, Files and I/O Most real programs read configuration, write files and speak JSON. The standard library handles all of it with encoding/json , os , io and bufio . Encoding JSON type Product struct { ID int `json:"id"` Name string `json:"name"` Price float64 `json:"price"` Tags []string `json:"tags,omitempty"` // omitted when empty internal string // unexported: ignored } p := Product{ID: 1, Name: "Mug", Price: 9.5} data, err := json.Marshal(p) fmt.Println(string(data)) // {"id":1,"name":"Mug","price":9.5} pretty, _ := json.MarshalIndent(p, "", " ") Decoding JSON var p Product err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(`{"id":2,"name":"Pen","price":1.2}`), &p) // unknown shape? decode into a map var m map[string]any json.Unmarshal(data, &m) fmt.Println(m["name"]) // numbers decode as float64! Fields must be exported (capitalized) to be encoded or decoded. Streaming with Encoder/Decoder json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(p) dec := json.NewDecoder(r.Body) dec.DisallowUnknownFields() // strict: reject unexpected keys if err := dec.Decode(&p); err != nil { /* 400 Bad Request */ } Custom marshaling type Status int const (Active Status = iota; Disabled) func (s Status) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) { return json.Marshal([...]string{"active", "disabled"}[s]) } Files // small files: read or write in one call data, err := os.ReadFile("config.json") err = os.WriteFile("out.txt", []byte("hello\n"), 0o644) // line by line (large files) f, err := os.Open("big.log") if err != nil { return err } defer f.Close() sc := bufio.NewScanner(f) for sc.Scan() { line := sc.Text() fmt.Println(line) } if err := sc.Err(); err != nil { return err } // create or append out, err := os.OpenFile("app.log", os.O_APPEND|os.O_CREATE|os.O_WRONLY, 0o644) Paths and directories path := filepath.Join("data", "users", "ada.json") // OS-correct separators os.MkdirAll("data/users", 0o755) entries, _ := os.ReadDir(".") filepath.WalkDir(".", func(p string, d fs.DirEntry, err error) error { return err }) Environment, arguments and flags port := os.Getenv("PORT") if port == "" { port = "8080" } name := flag.String("name", "world", "who to greet") verbose := flag.Bool("v", false, "verbose output") flag.Parse() fmt.Println("hello", *name) Embedding files in the binary import "embed" //go:embed templates/*.html var templates embed.FS Ship static assets inside your single binary, which is handy for Docker and for CLIs. Try it Read a todos.json file into []Todo , add an item, and write it back with indentation. Write a CLI using flag that counts lines/words in a file (a tiny wc ).

title: Building an HTTP API
text: Building an HTTP API Go's standard library is production-grade for web services. Since Go 1.22 the built-in router supports methods and path parameters, so you can build a clean REST API with zero dependencies. Hello, server package main import ( "fmt" "log" "net/http" ) func main() { mux := http.NewServeMux() mux.HandleFunc("GET /health", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { fmt.Fprintln(w, "ok") }) log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux)) } A small todo API type Todo struct { ID int `json:"id"` Title string `json:"title"` Done bool `json:"done"` } type Server struct { mu sync.Mutex todos map[int]Todo nextID int } func writeJSON(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, v any) { w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json") w.WriteHeader(status) json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v) } func (s *Server) list(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { s.mu.Lock(); defer s.mu.Unlock() out := make([]Todo, 0, len(s.todos)) for _, t := range s.todos { out = append(out, t) } writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, out) } func (s *Server) create(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { var in struct{ Title string `json:"title"` } if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&in); err != nil || in.Title == "" { writeJSON(w, http.StatusBadRequest, map[string]string{"error": "title required"}) return } s.mu.Lock(); defer s.mu.Unlock() s.nextID++ t := Todo{ID: s.nextID, Title: in.Title} s.todos[t.ID] = t writeJSON(w, http.StatusCreated, t) } func (s *Server) get(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { id, err := strconv.Atoi(r.PathValue("id")) // path parameter if err != nil { writeJSON(w, 400, map[string]string{"error": "bad id"}); return } s.mu.Lock(); defer s.mu.Unlock() t, ok := s.todos[id] if !ok { writeJSON(w, 404, map[string]string{"error": "not found"}); return } writeJSON(w, 200, t) } func main() { s := &Server{todos: map[int]Todo{}} mux := http.NewServeMux() mux.HandleFunc("GET /todos", s.list) mux.HandleFunc("POST /todos", s.create) mux.HandleFunc("GET /todos/{id}", s.get) log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux)) } curl -X POST localhost:8080/todos -d '{"title":"learn go"}' curl localhost:8080/todos curl localhost:8080/todos/1 Middleware Middleware is just a function that wraps an http.Handler : func logging(next http.Handler) http.Handler { return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { start := time.Now() next.ServeHTTP(w, r) log.Printf("%s %s %v", r.Method, r.URL.Path, time.Since(start)) }) } http.ListenAndServe(":8080", logging(mux)) Production-ready server settings srv := &http.Server{ Addr: ":8080", Handler: logging(mux), ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second, ReadTimeout: 10 * time.Second, WriteTimeout: 15 * time.Second, IdleTimeout: 60 * time.Second, } Never use bare ListenAndServe in production The defaults have no timeouts, so slow or malicious clients can hold connections open forever. Use an explicit http.Server with timeouts, and pair it with graceful shutdown (see the context lesson). Databases and frameworks Database : database/sql with a driver like pgx , or sqlc to generate type-safe code from SQL. Routers/frameworks (optional): chi, Gin, Echo, Fiber. The stdlib mux is often enough now. Structured logging : the standard log/slog package. Try it Add PUT /todos/{id} and DELETE /todos/{id} . Write handler tests with httptest . Persist todos to a JSON file or SQLite instead of memory.

title: Shipping Go: Build and Docker
text: Shipping Go: Build and Docker Go compiles to one static binary, which makes deployment unusually simple. This lesson ties Go back to the DevOps topic: cross-compiling, tiny container images and CI. Building a release binary CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o bin/server ./cmd/server Flag Effect CGO_ENABLED=0 Pure Go, fully static binary with no libc dependency -trimpath Remove local file paths (reproducible builds) -ldflags="-s -w" Strip debug info: smaller binary Cross-compilation GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -o server-linux-amd64 . GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build -o server-linux-arm64 . GOOS=darwin GOARCH=arm64 go build -o server-mac . GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build -o server.exe . Build for your Linux servers straight from a Mac, with no extra toolchain. Multi-stage Dockerfile # ---- build stage ---- FROM golang:1.24 AS build WORKDIR /src COPY go.mod go.sum ./ RUN go mod download # cached layer unless dependencies change COPY . . RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/server ./cmd/server # ---- runtime stage ---- FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot COPY --from=build /out/server /server EXPOSE 8080 USER nonroot ENTRYPOINT ["/server"] The final image contains only your binary: typically 10-25 MB instead of 800 MB+, with a minimal attack surface (no shell, no package manager). For even smaller images use FROM scratch , but you'll need to copy in CA certificates yourself if you make HTTPS calls. Configuration the 12-factor way cfg := struct { Addr string DSN string }{ Addr: getenv("ADDR", ":8080"), DSN: os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"), } func getenv(k, def string) string { if v := os.Getenv(k); v != "" { return v } return def } Health checks and shutdown Expose GET /healthz for liveness and /readyz for readiness (Kubernetes probes). Handle SIGTERM with graceful shutdown so rolling deploys drop no requests. Log to stdout as JSON with slog.New(slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stdout, nil)) . CI with GitHub Actions name: ci on: [push, pull_request] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-go@v5 with: { go-version-file: go.mod } - run: go vet ./... - run: go test -race -cover ./... - run: go build ./... Add golangci-lint for deeper static analysis. See the Git & CI/CD section of the DevOps topic for pipelines in depth. Where to go next Read Effective Go and the Go Code Review Comments on go.dev. Work through the Tour of Go ( go.dev/tour ) and Go by Example . Build something real: a URL shortener, a CLI tool, a chat server with WebSockets, or a Kubernetes operator. Read the standard library source. It is some of the best Go code around. Capstone Take the todo API, persist data to SQLite or Postgres, and add structured logging and graceful shutdown. Write a multi-stage Dockerfile and confirm the image is under 25 MB. Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs tests with -race and builds the image. Deploy it to a VPS or a Kubernetes cluster using what you learned in the DevOps topic.
